### [1] [ELECTRIC: Evidential Learning-Enhanced CT Reconstruction via Iterative Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00060)
*Ge Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ELECTRIC is a physics-guided Bayesian framework for low-dose CT reconstruction that combines an evidential neural network (producing both an image proposal and epistemic-uncertainty surrogate) with a Poisson-weighted MAP update in an iterative closed loop, achieving ~70% reconstruction error reduction over filtered back-projection and robust adaptive-precision reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CT reconstruction from low-dose acquisitions suffers from noise and ill-posedness. Existing methods do not jointly exploit learned priors with physics-based iterative reconstruction in a principled, uncertainty-aware manner. The authors aim to unify deep learning-based prior knowledge with measurement-consistent MAP reconstruction by treating prior confidence as a learned, adaptive state variable.

Method: ELECTRIC combines (1) an evidential neural network providing an image proposal and an error-predictive epistemic-uncertainty surrogate; (2) conversion of the uncertainty surrogate into an adaptive precision field; (3) a Poisson-weighted MAP update incorporating this precision field; and (4) a closed image-evidence-precision-reconstruction loop where prior confidence is treated as a learned state variable. Validation uses two simulation studies: a mechanism-validation pilot with transparent surrogate estimators and a feasibility study with a trained Normal-Inverse-Gamma evidential network driving the full loop.

Result: On held-out AAPM Mayo Clinic Low-Dose CT patients, the learned prior mean reduces reconstruction error by ~70% vs. filtered back-projection. The learned epistemic uncertainty is error-predictive and supports selective trust. The physics-guided update restores measurement consistency, and adaptive-precision reconstruction matches or exceeds a validation-tuned fixed prior while being markedly more robust to prior-strength misspecification.

Conclusion: The complete ELECTRIC closed-loop pipeline is demonstrated end-to-end. Formal uncertainty calibration and joint training of the evidential network with the reconstruction update are identified as the principal directions for future work.

Abstract: Here we introduce ELECTRIC (Evidential Learning-Enhanced CT Reconstruction via Iterative Correction), a physics-guided Bayesian formulation. An evidential neural network provides an image proposal and an error-predictive epistemic-uncertainty surrogate. The latter is converted into an adaptive precision field and inserted into a Poisson-weighted MAP update. The resulting image-evidence-precision-reconstruction loop treats prior confidence as a learned state variable of iterative reconstruction. In addition to the formulation and theoretical analysis, we report two simulation studies on image slices from the AAPM Mayo Clinic Low-Dose CT dataset: a mechanism-validation pilot using transparent surrogate estimators, and a feasibility study in which a trained Normal-Inverse-Gamma evidential network drives the full closed loop. On held-out patients, the learned prior mean reduces reconstruction error by roughly 70 percent relative to filtered back-projection, the learned epistemic uncertainty is error-predictive and supports selective trust, and the physics-guided update restores measurement consistency while the adaptive-precision reconstruction matches or exceeds a validation-tuned fixed prior and remains markedly more robust to prior-strength misspecification. Together these results demonstrate the complete ELECTRIC closed-loop pipeline, while identifying formal uncertainty calibration and joint training as the principal directions for future work.

</details>


### [2] [Noise-Robust Conditional Flow Matching: Generating Clean Samples from Noisy Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00064)
*Adrian Urbański,Gabriel della Maggiora,Artur Yakimovich*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: NR-CFM is an unconditional generative model based on conditional flow matching that learns clean image distributions directly from one corrupted observation per image, providing a closed-form correction for white Gaussian noise and a data-driven correction for general Gaussian corruptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific imaging often produces noisy measurements while clean references are costly or unattainable; training generative models directly on corrupted data reproduces the noise, so methods are needed to learn clean distributions from noisy observations alone.

Method: The paper introduces Noise-Robust Conditional Flow Matching (NR-CFM), an unconditional generator built on conditional flow matching. It provides a closed-form clean endpoint correction for additive white Gaussian noise and a learned data-driven correction for general Gaussian corruptions with complex covariance structures.

Result: NR-CFM outperforms NR-GAN in most tested corruption settings and remains competitive with Ambient Diffusion in the high-noise regime. It also generates plausible particle images from severely corrupted measurements at signal-to-noise ratios as low as 0.001.

Conclusion: Conditional flow matching with noise-robust endpoint corrections is an effective framework for learning clean generative models from corrupted scientific imaging data, achieving competitive or superior performance compared to existing noise-robust generative approaches.

Abstract: Generative models learn the statistical properties of their training data, so high-quality generation depends on clean and representative datasets. In scientific imaging, acquisition often yields noisy measurements, while collecting clean references can be costly, impractical or even unattainable. Training directly on these measurements results in a model that reproduces the corrupted data. This can be circumvented by learning the clean population distribution directly from the noisy data. Conditional flow matching (CFM) combines a simple regression objective with stable training, efficient sampling, and strong image-generation performance, making it a natural framework for this setting. We introduce Noise-Robust Conditional Flow Matching (NR-CFM), an unconditional generator that learns from one corrupted observation per image. NR-CFM provides a closed-form clean endpoint correction for additive white Gaussian noise and learns a data-driven correction for general Gaussian corruptions with more complex covariance structure. Across the evaluated corruption settings, NR-CFM outperforms NR-GAN in most cases and remains competitive with Ambient Diffusion in the high-noise regime. We further evaluate NR-CFM on scientific data at signal-to-noise ratios as low as $0.001$, where it generates plausible particle images from severely corrupted measurements.

</details>


### [3] [PhysAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Reliable Remote Heart Rate Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00066)
*Yehui Yang,Bo Zhao,Junzhe Cao,Hui Ma,Yue Sun,Wenjin Wang,Zitong Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhysAgent is an inference-time multi-agent candidate-verification framework for remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) that treats outputs from multiple base heart-rate estimators as hypotheses, uses a lightweight 4B MLLM (Qwen3-VL-4B) to drive multi-agent reasoning over video conditions and candidate disagreement, and applies a deterministic physiological verifier with reproducible numerical fusion to produce the final heart rate, improving fusion stability and reliability across public rPPG benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing rPPG methods rely on a single model to directly predict heart rate or recover pulse waveforms, but different strong estimators can produce conflicting yet individually plausible candidates for the same video due to weak physiological signals corrupted by motion, illumination, occlusion, skin-appearance variation, and device noise. This motivates resolving inter-estimator conflicts rather than relying on a single prediction.

Method: PhysAgent neither trains a new base rPPG model nor asks MLLMs to output heart rate directly. Instead, it treats outputs from multiple base estimators as physiological hypotheses, uses a lightweight 4B MLLM (Qwen3-VL-4B) to drive multi-agent reasoning over video conditions, signal reliability, and candidate disagreement, then a deterministic physiological verifier checks the fusion proposal, and a reproducible numerical fusion process produces the final heart rate.

Result: On multiple public rPPG benchmarks, PhysAgent improves fusion stability and reliability across different datasets and source-domain settings, while avoiding the irreproducibility and physiological inconsistency of direct MLLM prediction or unconstrained ensemble fusion.

Conclusion: PhysAgent demonstrates that an inference-time multi-agent candidate-verification paradigm—combining MLLM-driven reasoning with deterministic physiological verification and reproducible numerical fusion—provides a stable and reliable alternative to direct prediction approaches for rPPG heart-rate estimation. Code will be released.

Abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables non-contact heart-rate estimation from facial videos, but its weak physiological signal is easily corrupted by motion, illumination changes, occlusion, skin-appearance variation, and device noise. Existing rPPG methods typically rely on a single model to directly predict heart rate or recover pulse waveforms, while different strong estimators may produce conflicting yet individually plausible candidates for the same video. To resolve these conflicts, we propose PhysAgent, an inference-time multi-agent candidate-verification framework. Unlike direct prediction approaches, PhysAgent neither trains a new base rPPG model nor asks Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to output heart rate directly. In contrast, it treats outputs from multiple base estimators as physiological hypotheses to be verified and uses a lightweight 4B MLLM, Qwen3-VL-4B, to drive multi-agent reasoning over video conditions, signal reliability, and candidate disagreement. A deterministic physiological verifier checks the fusion proposal, and a reproducible numerical fusion process produces the final heart rate. Experimental results on multiple public rPPG benchmarks show that PhysAgent improves fusion stability and reliability across different datasets and source-domain settings, while avoiding the irreproducibility and physiological inconsistency of direct MLLM prediction or unconstrained ensemble fusion. The code will be released soon.

</details>


### [4] [SafeBuild-Bench: A Temporal-Robust Construction Safety Benchmark with Graph-Enhanced Data Mining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00068)
*Yi Cui,Zilin Wang,Yijie Xu,Qianyi Cai,Huizai Yao,Shuai Jiang,Bingzhuo Zhong,Hui Xiong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces SafeBuild-Bench, a metadata-driven benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on construction safety under realistic temporal and site variation. It is mined from 100K+ industrial image-text records and contains 3,314 task instances from over 3,000 expert-verified images. The authors also develop GEMS, a graph-enhanced multimodal selection pipeline that combines proxy-model confusion signals with graph-based diversity for scalable expert verification. Current MLLMs achieve only ~60 on the benchmark, indicating they remain far from reliable construction-safety understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Construction-safety models must handle concrete deployment risks (e.g., worker near a scaffold edge without guardrails) rather than recognizing common objects in curated images. However, real inspection archives are redundant, long-tailed, and collected across changing sites and months, posing challenges for evaluation.

Method: SafeBuild-Bench is constructed from 100K+ industrial image-text records via metadata-driven mining, producing 3,314 task instances from 3,000+ expert-verified images covering multiple-choice hazard identification and free-form hazard description. To scale expert verification, GEMS combines a proxy-model confusion signal with graph-based diversity to select informative candidates from redundant streams.

Result: GEMS-selected subsets preserve robustness-oriented performance under small data budgets on public instruction-tuning data. On SafeBuild-Bench, the best MLLM achieves a score near 60, showing current models remain unreliable for construction-safety understanding.

Conclusion: The benchmark, evaluation scripts, and GEMS codebase are publicly released. The results highlight a significant gap between current MLLM capabilities and the reliability required for real-world construction-safety deployment.

Abstract: Construction-safety models must handle concrete deployment risks, such as a worker standing near a scaffold edge without guardrails, rather than only recognize common objects in curated images. Yet real inspection archives are redundant, long-tailed, and collected across changing sites and months. We introduce SafeBuild-Bench, a metadata-driven benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models on construction safety under realistic temporal and site variation. It is mined from 100K+ industrial image-text records and contains 3,314 task instances from over 3,000 expert-verified images, covering multiple-choice hazard identification and free-form hazard description. To make expert verification scalable, we develop GEMS, a graph-enhanced multimodal selection pipeline that combines a proxy-model confusion signal with graph-based diversity to identify informative candidates from redundant streams. On public instruction-tuning data, GEMS-selected subsets preserve robustness-oriented performance under small data budgets. On SafeBuild-Bench, current MLLMs remain far from reliable construction-safety understanding, with the best overall score near 60. We release the benchmark, evaluation scripts, and GEMS codebase at https://github.com/safebuild/gems.

</details>


### [5] [Empirical investigation of 3D CT Foundation Models and Unsupervised Adaptation for Head and Neck Cancer Recurrence Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00071)
*Bilel Guetarni,Feryal Windal,David Pasquier,Halim Benhabiles*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks 3D CT foundation models for predicting recurrence-free survival in head and neck cancer across two public datasets (3,644 patients), evaluating adaptation strategies and modality fusion. Results show persistent difficulty in cross-distribution generalization with significant external validation performance drops, and find that integrating imaging features with clinical data remains the most accurate approach, though universal generalization remains a substantial challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As 3D CT foundation models become increasingly available, there is a critical need to evaluate how well their learned representations generalize across diverse clinical settings and whether task-specific adaptation is necessary to fully exploit their potential—especially given that traditional radiomics suffers from reproducibility and acquisition protocol sensitivity issues.

Method: Benchmarked several 3D CT foundation models for recurrence-free survival prediction in head and neck cancer across two public datasets totaling 3,644 patients, evaluating various adaptation strategies and modality fusion mechanisms (imaging features combined with clinical data).

Result: Significant performance drops were observed on external validation cohorts, indicating persistent difficulty in identifying features that generalize consistently across different imaging distributions. Imaging feature integration with clinical data proved to be the most accurate approach for prognostic prediction.

Conclusion: While CT foundation models offer promise for predictive modeling, achieving universal generalization across varied clinical contexts remains a substantial challenge for the current generation of models. Combining imaging features with clinical data yields the most accurate prognostic predictions.

Abstract: The rapid emergence of 3D CT foundation models has opened new avenues for predictive modeling from CT imaging, offering a compelling alternative to traditional radiomics which is known to suffer from reproducibility issues and sensitivity to acquisition protocol variations. Yet, as these models grow in availability, a critical need arises to evaluate how well their learned representations generalize across diverse clinical settings and whether adaptation to specific downstream tasks is necessary to unlock their full potential. To address these questions, we benchmarked several 3D CT foundation models for predicting recurrence-free survival in head and neck cancer across two public datasets totaling 3,644 patients, evaluating various adaptation strategies and modality fusion mechanisms. Our findings reveal persistent difficulty in identifying features that generalize consistently across different imaging distributions, as evidenced by significant performance drops on external validation cohorts. Ultimately, the integration of imaging features with clinical data remains the most accurate approach for prognostic prediction, though achieving universal generalization across varied clinical contexts continues to represent a substantial challenge for the current generation of models.

</details>


### [6] [PlantRig - From Bones to Branches: Adaptation of Autoregressive Rigging Models for Plant Skeletal Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01072)
*Nathan Hu,Yang Yang,Fumio Okura*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper evaluates autoregressive rigging models (UniRig, SkinTokens) for plant skeletal reconstruction, diagnoses their failures on non-canonical branching topologies, and demonstrates that multi-round fine-tuning on procedurally generated synthetic datasets enables the models to generalize to diverse plant forms including foliage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive rigging models excel on articulated characters but their generalization to plant structures is unexplored. Plant topologies have highly variable, non-canonical branching patterns that challenge learned skeletal priors, so it is important to assess whether these models can be adapted for automated plant rigging.

Method: The authors evaluate UniRig and SkinTokens on synthetic L-system-generated trees and real scanned data covering monopodial, sympodial, whorled, and vine-like archetypes. They diagnose failures via token-level analysis and mesh-encoder sensitivity checks, then apply multi-round fine-tuning over multiple procedurally generated synthetic datasets, progressively adding foliage to test harder cases.

Result: UniRig collapsed complex branching into near-linear chains while SkinTokens preserved topology but over-segmented and produced unstable outputs. Diagnosis revealed a geometric bottleneck in the frozen mesh-encoder tokenization pipeline rather than purely learned bias. Multi-round fine-tuning progressively recovered accurate branching topology and generalized to foliage-bearing plants without leaf-specific architectural changes.

Conclusion: Targeted fine-tuning can substantially close the domain gap between character-rigging priors and plant skeletal structure, pointing toward a viable path for automated plant rigging across branch topology and foliage types, including those not covered in this study.

Abstract: Autoregressive rigging models such as UniRig and SkinTokens perform well on articulated characters, but their ability to generalize to plant structures remains largely unexplored, since plant topologies exhibit highly variable, non-canonical branching patterns that challenge learned skeletal priors. We evaluate these models for plant skeletal reconstruction using synthetic L-system-generated trees and real scanned data spanning monopodial, sympodial, whorled, and vine-like archetypes. Preliminary testing showed UniRig collapsing complex branching into near-linear chains, while SkinTokens preserved topology better but over-segmented branches and produced an unstable output space, so we focused on UniRig for its greater stability. Diagnosis traced the collapse to sampling-level suppression of branch tokens, and further analysis showed the frozen mesh encoder had limited sensitivity to structural variation, pointing to a geometric bottleneck in the tokenization pipeline rather than a purely learned bias. Building on these findings, we applied multi-round fine-tuning over multiple procedurally generated synthetic datasets. Across rounds, the model progressively recovered accurate branching topology and generalized beyond branch-only structures to plants with foliage, a harder case given the zero-thickness, mesh-normal-dependent geometry of leaves. The resulting model generalized well across diverse plant forms without leaf-specific architectural changes, indicating that targeted fine-tuning can substantially close the domain gap between character-rigging priors and plant skeletal structure. As such, our work points toward a viable path for automated plant rigging across both branch topology and foliage type, even those not considered in our findings.

</details>


### [7] [Scene2Sound: Auditory-Grounded Soundscape Generation for 3D Gaussian Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00463)
*Masaki Yoshida,Ren Togo,Takahiro Ogawa,Miki Haseyama*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Scene2Sound is a training-free framework that generates spatially consistent soundscapes for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) worlds by identifying sound-emitting objects via vision-language models, anchoring them to persistent 3D positions through Gaussian set matching, and spatializing per-object audio in real time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3DGS creates photorealistic 3D worlds that users can freely explore, but these worlds remain silent. Existing audio generation methods condition on a single image or viewpoint, so their sound is tied to that observation and breaks consistency as the listener moves through the 3D scene.

Method: Scene2Sound uses a training-free pipeline that: (1) selects viewpoints jointly covering the scene, (2) identifies sound-emitting objects with a vision-language model, (3) associates multi-view detections into 3D instances via Gaussian set matching (measuring overlap between Gaussian sets rendering each detection), and (4) generates audio per source that a standard object-based audio engine spatializes in real time at arbitrary listener poses.

Result: Scene2Sound preserves the audio quality of strong per-viewpoint baselines while remaining spatially consistent where per-viewpoint and single-panorama pipelines fail. Two new spatial-consistency metrics are proposed to evaluate listener-motion responsiveness and held-out source support. A user study confirms the perceptual benefit.

Conclusion: Scene2Sound demonstrates that spatial audio consistency in explorable 3D worlds can be achieved without training, using auditory grounding to give persistent 3D positions to sound sources, validated on both generated and real-world 360-degree capture 3DGS scenes.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) turns captured or generated imagery into photorealistic 3D world simulations that users can freely explore, yet these worlds remain silent. Because existing audio generation methods condition on a single image or viewpoint, their sound is tied to that observation and cannot stay consistent while a listener moves. We introduce the task of generating a spatially consistent soundscape for a given 3DGS world through auditory grounding, identifying which objects in the world should emit sound and anchoring each to a persistent 3D position, and present Scene2Sound, a training-free framework built on this grounding. From the input world alone, our pipeline selects viewpoints that jointly cover the scene, identifies sound-emitting objects with a vision-language model, and associates the multi-view detections into 3D instances through Gaussian set matching, which measures the overlap between the Gaussian sets that render each detection. Each source then receives generated audio that a standard object-based audio engine spatializes in real time at arbitrary listener poses. We further propose two spatial-consistency metrics, one testing whether rendered audio responds consistently to listener motion and one testing whether the claimed sources are supported by views held out from their placement. On a curated set of generated 3DGS worlds and on 3DGS scenes generated from real-world 360-degree captures, Scene2Sound preserves the audio quality of strong per-viewpoint baselines while remaining spatially consistent where per-viewpoint and single-panorama pipelines do not, and a user study confirms the perceptual benefit. Project page: https://masaki-lmd.github.io/scene2sound/.

</details>


### [8] [Volcanic Clouds Detection through QCNN and Geostationary Satellite Multispectral Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00072)
*Federica Torrisi,Claudia Corradino,Alessandro Grilli,Tommaso Catuogno,Mattia Verducci,Elisabetta Paladino,Luigi Giannelli,Alessandro Sebastianelli*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates the potential of hybrid quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) for classifying satellite images containing volcanic clouds from SEVIRI data, comparing 2-qubit and 4-qubit QCNN variants against classical architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate detection of volcanic clouds from satellite imagery remains challenging due to their similarity to meteorological clouds, variability of eruption signatures, and coarse spectral sampling of geostationary sensors. Quantum machine learning, leveraging superposition and entanglement, may offer novel approaches to address these long-standing challenges in remote sensing.

Method: Two hybrid QCNN architectures (with 2 and 4 qubits) were designed by integrating quantum computational layers into a classical convolutional framework. These models were trained and evaluated on a dataset of SEVIRI satellite images containing volcanic clouds (ash, SO2, or mixed components) and non-volcanic backgrounds, and their performance was compared with purely classical convolutional architectures.

Result: The paper reports on the classification performance of the 2-qubit and 4-qubit QCNN variants on the volcanic cloud dataset, along with a comparative analysis against purely classical architectures (specific numerical results are presented in the full paper).

Conclusion: The findings assess whether quantum-enhanced hybrid QCNN models can effectively classify volcanic clouds in geostationary satellite imagery, contributing insights into the viability of QML approaches for Earth Observation data analysis.

Abstract: Recent advances in quantum computing are opening new possibilities for Earth Observation (EO) data analysis. Quantum machine learning (QML) approaches offer novel ways to process information by exploiting quantum phenomena such as superposition and entanglement. These capabilities have motivated the exploration of whether quantum-enhanced models can address long-standing challenges in satellite remote sensing, where complex spectral and spatial signals often require sophisticated feature extraction. Among various fields of application, EO data allow the global monitoring of volcanic clouds and are crucial for aviation safety, hazard assessment, real-time eruption response, and evaluation of volcanic impacts on climate. Yet accurate detection of volcanic clouds remains difficult due to their similarity with meteorological clouds, the variability of eruption signatures, and the coarse spectral sampling of geostationary sensors. In this work, the potential of hybrid quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) for the classification of satellite images containing volcanic clouds was investigated. These architectures integrate quantum computational layers into a classical convolutional framework. Two QCNN variants (with 2 and 4 qubits) have been considered to evaluate their ability to classify a dataset of SEVIRI images, including scenes with volcanic clouds (composed of ash, $SO_2$, or mixed components) as well as non-volcanic backgrounds. Finally, the performance of the hybrid QCNN models was compared with that of purely classical architectures.

</details>


### [9] [StreamTalk: Streaming Co-Speech Gesture Generation with Key-Pose Anchoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01643)
*Xiangyue Zhang,Jianfang Li,Jiaxu Zhang,Kaixing Yang,Steven Hoi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: StreamTalk is a closed-loop real-time co-speech gesture generation framework that addresses long-horizon drift in streaming generation by periodically generating, retrieving, and refining motion clips using plausible tail-pose anchors. It achieves state-of-the-art FGD on BEAT2, reduces drift versus open-loop baselines, and runs at 76 FPS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing streaming co-speech gesture generation methods are open-loop: each generated clip depends only on past context and cannot be corrected, causing small errors to accumulate and drift over long sequences. The authors observe that this failure mainly stems from lacking a forward constraint rather than poor short-clip quality, motivating a closed-loop approach with destination anchors.

Method: StreamTalk uses a periodic generate-retrieve-refine cycle. Streaming Pose-Guided Generation first predicts a coarse clip, then retrieves a plausible tail pose from a speaker-specific motion database as a destination anchor, and refines the clip conditioned on this pose before advancing the window. Training employs Stochastic Anchor Masking to randomly mask pose and translation frames so the model learns to recover complete motion from sparse boundary conditions. A part-aware DiT separates hand, body, and translation streams to reduce interference between global displacement and local articulation.

Result: On BEAT2, StreamTalk achieves state-of-the-art FGD, reduces long-horizon drift relative to open-loop baselines, and runs in real time at 76 FPS.

Conclusion: Providing forward constraints (destination tail poses) in a closed-loop framework effectively limits drift in streaming co-speech gesture generation, enabling real-time, high-quality long-horizon motion synthesis.

Abstract: Real-time co-speech gesture generation must produce 3D motion clip by clip as speech arrives. Existing streaming methods are open-loop: each clip depends on past context, but the model cannot check or correct its trajectory. Small errors therefore accumulate and cause drift over long sequences. We observe that this failure is mainly caused by the lack of a forward constraint rather than poor short-clip quality. A plausible key pose at the end of each clip provides a destination anchor that limits drift. Based on this observation, we propose StreamTalk, a closed-loop framework with a periodic generate-retrieve-refine cycle. Streaming Pose-Guided Generation first predicts a coarse clip, retrieves a plausible tail pose from a speaker-specific motion database, and refines the clip using this pose before continuing to the next window. During training, Stochastic Anchor Masking randomly masks pose and translation frames, teaching the model to recover complete motion from sparse boundary conditions. A part-aware DiT separates hand, body, and translation streams to reduce interference between global displacement and local articulation. On BEAT2, StreamTalk achieves state-of-the-art FGD, reduces long-horizon drift relative to open-loop baselines, and runs in real time at 76 FPS. Project page: https://xiangyue-zhang.github.io/StreamTalk/.

</details>


### [10] [CultureVidBench: Benchmarking Cultural Understanding in Text-to-Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01942)
*Xianjing Han,Yuhan Su,Yang Deng,Dong Ma,Wee Peng Tay,Bin Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CultureVidBench is a new benchmark with 1,000 curated prompts across 12 countries, 6 continents, 8 cultural regions, and 14 cultural aspects to evaluate cultural understanding in text-to-video generation. Evaluation of seven T2V models reveals they achieve strong semantic adherence and perceptual quality but fail to faithfully capture fine-grained cultural details, especially for underrepresented regions, rituals, and multimodal cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing T2V benchmarks focus on perceptual quality, physical plausibility, and text-video alignment but do not assess whether generated videos capture culturally specific objects, actions, rituals, visible text, or audio cues. Cultural context representation in T2V models remains underexplored.

Method: The authors construct CultureVidBench with 1,000 curated prompts spanning 12 countries, 6 continents, 8 cultural regions, and 14 cultural aspects organized into three categories: material culture, social practice & performance, and ritual & ceremony. The benchmark emphasizes dynamic and multimodal cultural representation including social interactions, ritual procedures, and culturally appropriate visible text and audio. Seven representative T2V models are evaluated via human user studies and MLLM-based automatic assessment across cultural faithfulness, multimodal cultural rendering, semantic adherence, and perceptual quality.

Result: Current models achieve strong semantic adherence and visual quality but often fail to faithfully capture fine-grained cultural details, particularly for underrepresented regions, rituals, and multimodal cultural cues.

Conclusion: There remains a significant gap in T2V models' ability to faithfully represent cultural details, motivating further work on culturally-aware video generation, particularly for underrepresented cultures and multimodal cultural elements.

Abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models have advanced rapidly, yet their ability to represent diverse cultural contexts remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks mainly focus on perceptual quality, physical plausibility, and text-video alignment, but do not directly assess whether generated videos capture culturally specific objects, actions, rituals, visible text, or audio cues. We introduce CultureVidBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating cultural understanding in T2V generation. CultureVidBench contains 1,000 curated prompts covering 12 countries, 6 continents, 8 cultural regions, and 14 cultural aspects organized into three categories: material culture, social practice & performance, and ritual & ceremony. Designed specifically for video generation, CultureVidBench emphasizes dynamic and multimodal cultural representation, including social interactions, ritual procedure, and culturally appropriate visible text and audio. We evaluate seven representative T2V models through human user studies and MLLM-based automatic assessment across cultural faithfulness, multimodal cultural rendering, semantic adherence, and perceptual quality. Results show that although current models achieve strong semantic adherence and visual quality, they often fail to faithfully capture fine-grained cultural details, particularly for underrepresented regions, rituals, and multimodal cultural cues.

</details>


### [11] [Beyond Random Partitioning: Unsupervised Spatio-Temporal Stratification for Cohort Balancing in Longitudinal Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00073)
*Qinghui Liu,Jon André Ottesen,Atle Bjørnerud,Kyrre Eeg Emblem*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A Tripartite Dataset Analytics Framework systematically characterizes spatial, intensity, and temporal properties of longitudinal medical imaging cohorts, then applies an unsupervised spatio-temporal cohort-balancing SOP combining elbow-optimized K-means clustering with intra-cluster stratified sampling. On a longitudinal brain MRI cohort (N=149), this reduces maximum cross-subset intensity bias from 34.1% (random shuffling) to under 2.1% while aligning follow-up intervals, with robust performance verified via Monte Carlo stress testing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Naive random shuffling of small clinical cohorts in longitudinal medical imaging introduces covariate shifts and temporal sampling imbalances across train/validation/test partitions, exposing downstream models to out-of-distribution evaluation. Rigorous dataset partitioning is foundational yet often overlooked, motivating a reproducible, auditable protocol for cohort engineering.

Method: The paper proposes a Tripartite Dataset Analytics Framework characterizing three dimensions: spatial grid integrity, multi-parametric intensity fingerprints, and longitudinal temporal trajectories. It quantifies heavy-tailed feature dispersion and irregular episodic sampling. A spatio-temporal cohort-balancing SOP is then formalized: elbow-optimized K-means clustering over a standardized six-dimensional joint intensity-temporal feature space, combined with intra-cluster proportionate stratified sampling. Validation uses Monte Carlo stress testing across ten random seeds and three split configurations.

Result: On a longitudinal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI cohort (N=149), the protocol reduces maximum cross-subset intensity bias from 34.1% under random shuffling to under 2.1%, while aligning longitudinal follow-up intervals closely around the population mean. Monte Carlo stress testing confirms this alignment remains tightly bounded across seeds and split configurations, in contrast to the substantial variability of random partitioning.

Conclusion: The resulting protocol offers a reproducible, generalizable procedure for cohort engineering in variable-length longitudinal clinical imaging workflows, mitigating out-of-distribution evaluation risks inherent in small clinical cohorts.

Abstract: Rigorous dataset partitioning is a foundational, yet frequently overlooked, prerequisite for reliable deep learning in longitudinal medical imaging. Naively shuffling small clinical cohorts routinely introduces covariate shifts and temporal sampling imbalances across training, validation, and test subsets, exposing downstream models to out-of-distribution evaluation. We address this vulnerability with an auditable Tripartite Dataset Analytics Framework that systematically characterizes spatial grid integrity, multi-parametric intensity fingerprints, and longitudinal temporal trajectories, quantifying the heavy-tailed feature dispersion and irregular, episodic sampling intervals typical of real-world clinical cohorts. Building on this characterization, we formalize an unsupervised spatio-temporal cohort-balancing standard operating procedure (SOP) that combines elbow-optimized K-means clustering over a standardized, six-dimensional joint intensity-temporal feature space with intra-cluster proportionate stratified sampling. On a longitudinal, contrast-enhanced $T1$-weighted brain MRI cohort (N=149), the protocol reduces the maximum cross-subset intensity bias from 34.1% under conventional random shuffling to under 2.1%, while aligning longitudinal follow-up intervals closely around the population mean. Monte Carlo stress testing across ten random seeds and three split configurations confirms that this alignment remains tightly bounded, in clear contrast to the substantial variability of random partitioning. The resulting protocol offers a reproducible, generalizable procedure for cohort engineering in variable-length longitudinal clinical imaging workflows.

</details>


### [12] [Déjà Cue: Localizing States in Object Histories via Vocabulary-Relative Coordinates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02044)
*Haofan Cao,Zhichao You,Yunkai Yang,Liang Guo,Jie Wang,Chongshou Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Déjà Cue is a training-free framework for identity-conditioned state-moment retrieval that uses alternative state descriptions as a vocabulary-relative coordinate system, subtracting their state-balanced centroid from each description to calibrate frame scores in a frozen encoder. It nearly doubles R@1 at tIoU 0.5 (10.3% to 20.5%) and raises Top-1 tIoU (16.0% to 21.5%) on 78 VOST histories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While object tracking can link observations of the same object through visual change, it cannot determine when the object's state (e.g., empty/filled, intact/cut) changes. Absolute image-text similarity scores fail because every visible frame depicts the same target, so shared object compatibility masks the state-specific evidence needed to identify the target interval. The key insight is that alternative state descriptions provide the missing reference: evidence for one state should be measured against the others.

Method: Déjà Cue introduces a training-free framework that treats alternative state descriptions as a vocabulary-relative coordinate system. It subtracts a state-balanced centroid from each description, calibrates per-frame scores, and scans multiple temporal durations within contiguous visible runs using a frozen encoder. The approach requires no training and only changes the query reference at test time.

Result: On 78 VOST histories, holding the temporal scan fixed and changing only the query reference nearly doubles R@1 at tIoU 0.5 from 10.3% to 20.5% and raises Top-1 tIoU from 16.0% to 21.5%. Candidate-rank analyses show vocabulary-relative queries rank useful intervals higher within the same candidate set.

Conclusion: Related state descriptions can serve as an object-specific, query-time coordinate system for reading frozen visual representations, enabling effective state-moment retrieval without any model training or fine-tuning.

Abstract: Tracking links observations of the same object through visual change, yet cannot by itself determine when the object is empty or filled, intact or cut. We formulate identity-conditioned state-moment retrieval: given a tracked-object history and alternative state descriptions, localize an interval in which each described state holds. Absolute image-text similarity scores descriptions independently; because every visible frame depicts the same target, shared object compatibility can obscure the state evidence needed to identify the target interval. The alternatives provide the missing reference: evidence for one state should be measured against the others. We introduce Déjà Cue, a training-free framework that turns these alternatives into a vocabulary-relative coordinate system. It subtracts their state-balanced centroid from each description, calibrates frame scores, and scans multiple durations within contiguous visible runs using a frozen encoder. On 78 VOST histories, holding the temporal scan fixed and changing only the query reference nearly doubles R@1 at tIoU 0.5 from 10.3\% to 20.5\% and raises Top-1 tIoU from 16.0\% to 21.5\%. Candidate-rank analyses show that vocabulary-relative queries rank useful intervals higher within the same candidate set. Related state descriptions can therefore serve as an object-specific, query-time coordinate system for reading frozen visual representations.

</details>


### [13] [Explainable Multimodal AI for Adaptive Calibration of Archaeological Sensing Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00074)
*Nevio Dubbini,Daniel P. van Helden,Claudia Sciuto,Martina Naso,Arthur Leck,Clement Joubert,Heeli C. Schechter,Remy Chapoulie,Gabriele Gattiglia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a multimodal machine-learning framework for calibration monitoring, quality assessment, and adaptive acquisition support in archaeological digitisation, combining deterministic quality indicators, statistical features, ML classification, anomaly detection, and XAI across photogrammetric 3D reconstruction, hyperspectral imaging, XRF, and Raman spectroscopy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the need for an algorithmic layer that evaluates whether multi-sensor archaeological acquisitions are statistically consistent, physically plausible, and suitable for downstream multimodal integration, rather than relying solely on instrument-level calibration.

Method: A unified pipeline combining deterministic quality indicators, statistical feature representations, supervised/unsupervised ML classification, anomaly detection, and XAI. Each modality is encoded into structured feature spaces capturing geometric, spectral, spatial, and statistical properties to detect degradation patterns. Adaptive feedback links feature-space deviations to acquisition-level corrective actions.

Result: Experiments on multimodal archaeological datasets show the methodology captures meaningful acquisition variability and enables robust quality assessment across heterogeneous sensing modalities.

Conclusion: The framework provides an effective, explainable quality-assessment layer for multimodal archaeological digitisation workflows, supporting automatic discrimination between acceptable and problematic acquisitions along with interpretable causes of degradation and resource-aware acquisition strategies.

Abstract: This paper presents a multimodal machine-learning framework for calibration monitoring, quality assessment, and adaptive acquisition support in archaeological digitisation workflows. The proposed approach operates across photogrammetric 3D reconstruction, hyperspectral imaging, X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy, and Raman spectroscopy through a unified pipeline combining deterministic quality indicators, statistical feature representations, machine-learning classification, anomaly detection, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Rather than replacing instrument-level calibration, the framework introduces an additional algorithmic layer that evaluates whether acquisitions are statistically consistent, physically plausible, and suitable for downstream multimodal integration. For each sensing modality, acquisitions are represented through structured feature spaces encoding geometric, spectral, spatial, and statistical properties. These representations are used to identify degradation patterns such as reconstruction artefacts, illumination inconsistencies, spectral distortions, detector instability, baseline fluctuations, and low signal-to-noise conditions. Supervised and unsupervised learning methods are combined with XAI techniques to support both automatic discrimination between acceptable and problematic acquisitions and interpretation of the underlying causes of degradation. The framework additionally supports adaptive feedback and resource-aware acquisition strategies by linking feature-space deviations to acquisition-level corrective actions. Experimental results obtained on multimodal archaeological datasets demonstrate that the proposed methodology captures meaningful acquisition variability and enables robust quality assessment across heterogeneous sensing modalities.

</details>


### [14] [PartMat: Material-Aware 3D Part Decomposition with a Single Global Latent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01825)
*Guangming Fu,Jin Song,Yiyun Fei,Guoqiu Li,Ruigao Yang,Jianan Jiang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PartMat is a material-aware 3D part decomposition pipeline that represents multi-part geometry with a single global latent, using a PartVAE to decode all material parts in one forward pass, a diffusion model refined via reinforcement learning for part generation, and a sparse-voxel flow-matching model for geometric detail recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing part-level 3D generation methods decompose objects by functional semantics rather than editable material boundaries (e.g., fabric, wood, metal) needed in practical applications like interior design. Additionally, current methods generate parts independently, causing computational costs to scale linearly with part count.

Method: PartMat consists of three components: (1) PartVAE that learns a unified single-global-latent representation and decodes all material parts in a single forward pass, decoupling inference cost from part count; (2) a diffusion model trained for part generation and refined via reinforcement learning for accurate material assignment and overlap suppression; (3) a sparse-voxel flow-matching model with part attention for geometry post-processing to recover fine-grained geometric details.

Result: PartMat significantly outperforms existing baselines in material-aware decomposition accuracy and achieves comparable geometric quality while maintaining efficient inference.

Conclusion: PartMat demonstrates that material-boundary-based part decomposition with a shared global latent representation enables both accurate decomposition and efficient inference, suitable for practical 3D applications.

Abstract: Part-level 3D generation has recently attracted increasing attention for producing structured and editable 3D assets. However, existing methods typically decompose objects according to functional semantics rather than the editable material boundaries (e.g., fabric, wood, metal) required in practical 3D applications such as interior design. Additionally, current methods often generate parts independently, causing computational costs to scale linearly with the part count. To address these limitations, we present PartMat, an efficient material-aware 3D part decomposition pipeline that represents multi-part geometry with a single global latent. Given a reference image and a single whole-object geometry, PartMat decomposes the object into parts that follow material boundaries. First, we propose PartVAE to learn such a unified representation and decode all material parts in a single forward pass, thereby decoupling inference cost from the number of parts. Second, with this representation, a diffusion model is trained for part generation and refined via reinforcement learning for accurate material assignment and overlap suppression. Finally, to recover fine-grained geometric details, we introduce a sparse-voxel flow-matching model with part attention for geometry post-processing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PartMat significantly outperforms existing baselines in material-aware decomposition accuracy and achieves comparable geometric quality, while maintaining efficient inference.

</details>


### [15] [MIEScore: Human-Aligned Evaluation for Multi-Source Image Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02059)
*Zitong Xu,Huiyu Duan,Xinyun Zhang,Weifei Xiong,Tianyi Zheng,Xiongkuo Min,Qiang Hu,Zhengxue Cheng,Bo Li,Guangtao Zhai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces MIE-Bench, the first large-scale multiple image editing benchmark with fine-grained human preference annotations, comprising 3,000 editing instances across 16 tasks, 36K edited images from 12 models, and over 108K MOS scores. It also proposes MIEScore, an MLLM-based evaluation model enhanced with skill optimization and multi-dimensional supervised fine-tuning, which achieves state-of-the-art alignment with human preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks and image editing assessment methods focus primarily on single-image editing tasks and overlook the more challenging multi-source image editing (MIE) setting, despite recent unified multimodal models demonstrating emerging capabilities in tasks such as object synthesis, person-background composition, and cross-image style fusion. This creates an urgent need for a comprehensive, human-aligned benchmark for MIE.

Method: The authors construct MIE-Bench with 3,000 editing instances spanning 16 tasks, each involving more than two source images and an editing prompt. They generate 36K edited images using 12 state-of-the-art editing models and collect over 108K mean opinion scores covering visual quality, instruction following, and attribute preservation. They then develop MIEScore, a multimodal large language model-based evaluation model enhanced with skill optimization and multi-dimensional supervised fine-tuning.

Result: MIEScore achieves state-of-the-art performance in aligning with human preferences and generalizes well across other image editing assessment datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed MIE-Bench benchmark and MIEScore evaluation model address the gap in multi-source image editing assessment, providing a comprehensive human-aligned evaluation framework. Both the dataset and model are publicly released.

Abstract: Recent advances in unified multimodal models have significantly improved text-guided image editing abilities. In particular, models such as Nano-Banana-Pro and GPT-Image-2 demonstrate emerging capabilities in multi-source image editing (MIE), including tasks such as object synthesis, person-background composition, and cross-image style fusion. However, existing benchmarks and image editing assessment (IEQA) methods remain primarily focused on single-image editing tasks and largely overlook the more challenging setting of MIE. This highlights the urgent need for a comprehensive and human-aligned benchmark for MIE. To this end, we introduce MIE-Bench, the first large-scale multiple image editing benchmark with fine-grained human preference annotations. Specifically, MIE-Bench includes 3,000 editing instances across 16 tasks, each involving more than two source images and an editing prompt, together with 36K edited images produced by 12 state-of-the-art editing models and over 108K mean opinion scores (MOSs) covering visual quality, instruction following, and attribute preservation. Based on MIE-Bench, we propose MIEScore, a multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based evaluation model enhanced with skill optimization and multi-dimensional supervised fine-tuning, to provide human-aligned feedback for MIE. Extensive experiments show that MIEScore achieves state-of-the-art performance in aligning with human preferences and generalizes well across other IEQA datasets. Both the dataset and the model are available at https://github.com/IntMeGroup/MIEScore.

</details>


### [16] [K-space Gaussian Representation for Parallel MRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00075)
*Yu Guan,Mingyu Hu,Jiale Hu,Zhuoxu Cui,Dong Liang,Qiegen Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes K-space Gaussian Representation (KGR), the first explicit continuous representation directly formulated in the native k-space domain for accelerated MRI reconstruction. Instead of estimating discrete frequency coefficients, KGR parameterizes the continuous signal using Gabor-Gaussian primitives with shared spatial geometry, preserves inter-coil correlations, and enforces low-rank manifold constraints to satisfy multi-coil structural properties. A frequency-adaptive fitting strategy handles heterogeneous k-space characteristics. Comprehensive experiments show consistent improvements over existing baselines in quantitative metrics and visual quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing k-space reconstruction methods estimate missing samples on discrete sampling grids using interpolation operators or structure priors, which exploit local interpolation relationships and global k-space redundancy but do not explicitly model the underlying continuous signal, limiting reconstruction fidelity.

Method: KGR parameterizes the continuous k-space signal using Gabor-Gaussian primitives with shared spatial geometry, preserving inter-coil correlations. The estimated representation is projected onto a low-rank manifold to enforce algebraic constraints from smoothly varying phase and coil redundancy, and a frequency-adaptive fitting strategy accommodates heterogeneous k-space region characteristics.

Result: Comprehensive validation across multiple datasets and sampling schemes demonstrates consistent improvements over representative reconstruction baselines in both quantitative metrics and visual quality.

Conclusion: Explicit continuous parameterization of native k-space provides a principled framework for integrating continuous signal modeling with structured low-rank reconstruction, showing that modeling the underlying continuous signal directly in k-space is both feasible and beneficial.

Abstract: Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) aims to recover the k-space signal from acquired measurements, where accurate estimation of missing samples is essential for high-fidelity reconstruction. Existing k-space reconstruction methods estimate missing samples through interpolation operators or structure priors defined on discrete sampling grids. Although these formulations effectively exploit local interpolation relationships and global k-space redundancy, they reconstruct only discrete frequency coefficients and therefore do not explicitly model the underlying continuous signal. To overcome this limitation, we propose K-space Gaussian Representation (KGR), the first explicit continuous representation formulated directly in the native k-space domain. Rather than estimating unknown samples on discrete grids, KGR parameterizes the continuous signal using Gabor-Gaussian primitives with shared spatial geometry, yielding a compact representation that naturally preserves inter-coil correlations. Because unconstrained continuous fitting does not necessarily satisfy the intrinsic structural properties of multi-coil signal, the estimated representation is projected onto a low-rank manifold to enforce the algebraic constraints arising from smoothly varying phase and coil redundancy. A frequency-adaptive fitting strategy accommodates the heterogeneous characteristics of different k-space regions. Comprehensive validation across multiple datasets and sampling schemes shows consistent improvements over representative reconstruction baselines in both quantitative metrics and visual quality. These results suggest that explicit continuous parameterization of native k-space provides a principled framework for integrating continuous signal modeling with structured low-rank reconstruction.

</details>


### [17] [Deep Multimodal Fusion Detection through Spatial Mask and Channel Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02092)
*Guandi Wang,Ming Li,Yunsen Xing,Junle Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes an Attention-Driven Complementarity Resampling (ADCR) framework for cross-modality object detection that addresses the overfitting/over-specialization issue in existing feature-level fusion methods. It introduces semantic mask exchange to mix modality boundaries during training and a learnable channel competition mechanism for channel-wise feature sampling and aggregation, achieving competitive results on multiple datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing feature-level fusion methods for multimodal object detection simply weigh between two modalities and unify them in a shared representation space, which can lead to overfitting or over-specialization on single-modality statistical properties within dual-backbone architectures. A more robust fusion approach is needed.

Method: The framework consists of two key components: (1) a shared channel spatial attention mechanism, followed by semantic mask exchange that actively mixes modality boundaries during training to force the backbone to learn generalized features without relying on fixed modal labels; and (2) a learnable channel competition module that samples and aggregates features in a channel-wise, learnable manner.

Result: Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed ADCR method is effective and achieves competitive results among existing state-of-the-art approaches for cross-modality object detection.

Conclusion: The proposed Attention-Driven Complementarity Resampling framework successfully mitigates the overfitting/over-specialization problem in multimodal object detection fusion by introducing semantic mask exchange and learnable channel competition, providing a robust improvement over existing feature-level fusion methods.

Abstract: Deep multimodal fusion for object detection has demonstrated good performance through mining modal characteristics. However, existing feature-level fusion methods mainly weigh between two modalities and unify them in a unified representation space. This can lead to overfitting or over-specialization of the statistical properties of a single modality within a dual-backbone architecture. This paper proposes an Attention-Driven Complementarity Resampling framework for robust improvement of cross-modality object detection. Based on a shared channel spatial attention mechanism, we first introduce the semantic mask exchange to actively mix the boundaries of the modalities during the training phase, forcing the backbone network to learn generalized features without relying on fixed modal labels. Then we propose a learnable channel competition to sample and aggregate features in a channel-wise and learnable way. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed method is effective and yields competitive results among existing state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is provided in the supplementary material.

</details>


### [18] [Which Modality Decides? Counterfactual Modality Attribution for Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00076)
*Vahidin Hasic,Chao Wang,Luis C. Garcia-Peraza-Herrera,David Watson,Senka Krivic*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces Counterfactual Modality Attribution (CMA), the first framework for quantifying modality-level contributions in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), using coupled diffusion priors to generate image-only, text-only, and joint counterfactuals, and a Shapley-value-based cooperative game-theoretic formulation to produce modality attribution scores. CMA correctly identifies the decision-driving modality in 98% of controlled cases and outperforms baselines on both synthetic benchmarks and a real-world multimodal clinical dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing explainability methods for MLLMs identify influential image regions or text tokens but cannot answer the fundamental question of which modality drives a prediction. This leaves a critical blind spot: a model may produce correct outputs while relying on the wrong source of evidence, masking shortcut learning and unsafe reasoning in high-stakes applications.

Method: CMA generates image-only, text-only, and joint multimodal counterfactuals using coupled diffusion priors, then converts these counterfactuals into principled modality attribution scores via a cooperative game-theoretic formulation based on Shapley values.

Result: CMA correctly identifies the decision-driving modality in 98% of controlled synthetic cases and consistently outperforms baselines, revealing failures of cross-modal reasoning that remain invisible to predictive accuracy alone. Validation was performed on both controlled synthetic benchmarks with known ground-truth modality reliance and a real-world multimodal clinical dataset.

Conclusion: Modality attribution constitutes a complementary dimension of explainability beyond feature attribution, and CMA provides a principled framework for auditing multimodal foundation models in safety-critical applications by surfacing cross-modal reasoning failures that accuracy metrics alone cannot detect.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly support high-stakes decision making by combining complementary information from images and text. While existing explainability methods identify influential image regions or text tokens, they cannot answer a fundamental question: which modality drives a prediction? Consequently, a model may produce the correct output while relying on the wrong source of evidence, masking shortcut learning and unsafe reasoning. We formulate modality attribution as a complementary explainability objective for multimodal foundation models and propose Counterfactual Modality Attribution (CMA), the first framework for quantifying modality-level contributions in MLLMs. CMA generates image-only, text-only, and joint multimodal counterfactuals using coupled diffusion priors and converts them into principled modality attribution scores through a cooperative game-theoretic formulation based on Shapley values. We evaluate CMA on controlled synthetic benchmarks with known ground-truth modality reliance and on a real-world multimodal clinical dataset. CMA correctly identifies the decision-driving modality in 98% of controlled cases and consistently outperforms baselines, revealing failures of cross-modal reasoning that remain invisible to predictive accuracy alone. Our results establish modality attribution as a complementary dimension of explainability beyond feature attribution, providing a principled framework for auditing multimodal foundation models in safety-critical applications.

</details>


### [19] [Beyond Accuracy: Auditing Spatial Provenance in Visual Token Pruning for OCR-Critical MLLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00077)
*Feixiang Liu,Qiang Qiu,Hao Zhang,Xinyue Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces an evidence-risk audit for visual-token pruning in multimodal LLMs, coupling answer behavior with geometric token-origin provenance, interventions, and realized cost. It shows that accuracy alone masks critical failures where answers remain correct despite no retained token being locally traceable to supporting OCR regions, and demonstrates that pruning methods yield sharply different positive-support coverage at the same retention budget. The work reports model-specific quality-risk-traceability frontiers across three MLLMs, up to 4.32x batch-prefill speedup, 76.4% lower incremental peak memory, and cautions that favorable target-verification points do not imply task-general compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional visual-token pruning evaluation only judges answer quality at a fixed retention budget, which misses a distinct failure mode: answers can remain correct even when no retained token is locally traceable to the small OCR region that supports the answer. The authors aim to turn this blind spot into a comprehensive audit that reveals what accuracy alone cannot expose.

Method: The audit couples answer behavior with three additional dimensions: geometric token-origin provenance (spatial traceability of retained tokens), interventions (matched controlled experiments), and realized cost (latency and memory). Transparent training-free selectors (Target, Random, Grid) isolate controlled operating points. Experiments lock image-disjoint confirmation and cover Qwen3-VL-8B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and InternVL3.5-8B, with full-validation on TextVQA and DocVQA, including external method comparisons and detector tests.

Result: At 30% retention, Qwen Target achieves observed accuracy 0.786 vs. 0.783 for Full (paired difference +0.003, 95% CI [-0.014, +0.020]), yet Target, Random, and Grid retain sharply different positive-support coverage: 0.620, 0.270, and 0.318 respectively. Across models, matched controls reveal model-specific quality-risk-traceability frontiers. Materialized prefixes yield up to 4.32x batch-prefill speedup and 76.4% lower incremental peak memory, while full-validation shows favorable target-verification points do not imply task-general compression.

Conclusion: Visual-token pruning should report surviving spatial provenance and realized cost alongside quality and compression. Accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize pruning safety, and the proposed evidence-risk audit provides a more complete evaluation framework that exposes model-specific trade-offs invisible to conventional protocols.

Abstract: Visual-token pruning is usually judged by answer quality at a fixed retention budget. For text-rich multimodal large language models (MLLMs), this protocol can miss a distinct failure: an answer remains correct even when no retained token is locally traceable to the small OCR region that supports it. We turn this blind spot into an evidence-risk audit that couples answer behavior with geometric token-origin provenance, interventions, and realized cost; transparent training-free selectors isolate controlled operating points. On locked image-disjoint confirmation, Qwen Target at 30% retention has observed accuracy 0.786 versus 0.783 for Full (paired image-cluster difference +0.003, 95% CI [-0.014, +0.020]), yet same-budget Target, Random, and Grid retain sharply different positive-support coverage: 0.620, 0.270, and 0.318. Across Qwen3-VL-8B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and InternVL3.5-8B, matched controls, interventions, detector tests, and external methods reveal model-specific quality-risk-traceability frontiers that accuracy alone does not expose. Materialized prefixes yield up to 4.32x batch-prefill speedup and 76.4% lower incremental peak memory; full-validation TextVQA and DocVQA further show that favorable target-verification points do not imply task-general compression. Visual-token pruning should therefore report surviving spatial provenance and realized cost alongside quality and compression.

</details>


### [20] [Device-First Feedback: Toward Mobile-Native LLM-Driven Neural Architecture Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00078)
*Saif U Din,Muhammad Ahsan Hussain,Radu Timofte,Dmitry Ignatov*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an automated mobile deployment pipeline that closes the loop from QLoRA fine-tuning of an LLM architecture generator through GPU evaluation, INT8 TFLite export, and physical-device benchmarking, feeding gated results back into the training corpus. Evaluated on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with a Samsung SM-P613 tablet, the pipeline shows that iterative GPU fine-tuning does not guarantee monotonic mobile deployment improvements, especially on harder tasks, with only CIFAR-10 cycle 1 passing the mobile gate (25.6x score improvement).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying LLM-generated CNN architectures on real mobile hardware requires more than GPU validation accuracy. INT8 TensorFlow Lite export, delegate selection, and on-device latency are jointly critical to usability, yet existing approaches rarely close the loop between architecture generation and physical-device evaluation. This paper addresses the gap by building a fully automated, resume-capable pipeline that measures and feeds back on-device performance into the model-generation process.

Method: The pipeline consists of: (1) QLoRA fine-tuning of an architecture-generating LLM; (2) GPU evaluation of generated architectures; (3) INT8 TensorFlow Lite export with delegate selection; (4) physical-device benchmarking on a Samsung SM-P613 tablet; and (5) gated augmentation of the training corpus. The entire cycle is scripted end-to-end without manual intervention, with resume support. The protocol is frozen and run on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (seed 42, 20 models/cycle, cycles 0-6).

Result: On CIFAR-10, cycle 1 is gate-accepted and improves the mobile deployment score ~25.6x over baseline with a mean quantized accuracy of 46.9%; later cycles improve GPU accuracy but fail the non-decreasing mobile deployment gate. On CIFAR-100, the pre-QLoRA baseline retains the best mobile score; iterative rounds improve GPU accuracy (up to 26.2%) but cannot surpass cycle 0 on-device, and the training pool stalls at 19 examples after the first accepted round. These results demonstrate that closed-loop GPU fine-tuning does not guarantee monotonic mobile gains.

Conclusion: Closed-loop GPU fine-tuning alone is insufficient to ensure monotonic improvements in mobile deployment metrics. On-device measurement is essential and must be multi-dataset to robustly stress-test deployment objectives, as harder classification tasks such as CIFAR-100 show that GPU accuracy gains do not translate to better mobile performance. The paper releases per-cycle metrics with 95% confidence intervals, figures, and complete reproduction commands for transparency.

Abstract: Deploying convolutional neural networks generated by large language models (LLMs) on real mobile hardware requires more than GPU validation accuracy: INT8 TensorFlow Lite export, delegate selection, and on-device latency jointly determine whether a model is usable. We present an automated mobile deployment pipeline that closes the loop from QLoRA fine-tuning of an architecture-generating LLM through GPU evaluation, INT8 export, and physical-device benchmarking to gated augmentation of the training corpus. The pipeline is fully scripted and runs cycle-by-cycle without manual intervention, with resume support after interruptions. We evaluate the same frozen protocol on two benchmarks, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, on a Samsung SM-P613 tablet (seed 42, 20 models per cycle, cycles 0-6). On CIFAR-10, cycle 1 is gate-accepted and improves the mobile deployment score approximately 25.6x over the baseline with a mean quantized accuracy of 46.9%; later cycles raise GPU accuracy but fail the non-decreasing mobile gate. On CIFAR-100, the pre-QLoRA baseline retains the best mobile score; iterative rounds improve GPU accuracy (up to 26.2%) yet cannot surpass cycle 0 on-device, and the training pool stalls at 19 examples after the first accepted round. Together, the two studies show that closed-loop GPU fine-tuning does not guarantee monotonic mobile gains, especially on harder classification tasks, and that multi-dataset, on-device measurement is needed to stress-test deployment objectives. We release per-cycle metrics with 95% confidence intervals, all figures, and complete reproduction commands.

</details>


### [21] [LeapTalk: Breaking the Latency-Quality Trade-off in Talking Head Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00079)
*Rongxiang Zhang,Songhua Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LeapTalk is a single-step, real-time talking-head generation framework that uses Brownian-bridge-based data-to-data distillation from a diffusion teacher, achieving stable long-video generation at up to 200 FPS with fine lip synchronization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form and real-time talking-head generation faces a latency-quality trade-off: multi-step diffusion models are too slow for streaming, while real-time autoregressive methods accumulate errors and suffer from identity drift over time.

Method: LeapTalk proposes a single-step bridge distillation scheme. It replaces the conventional noise-to-data paradigm with a data-to-data transport formulation based on a Brownian bridge, anchored by a persistent reference to mitigate identity drift and enhance temporal stability. It also introduces a heterogeneous distillation framework using an SNR-aligned time transformation Φ(τ) to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained diffusion teacher to the student bridge model. Additionally, an audio-driven classifier-free guidance mechanism maintains fine-grained lip synchronization under extreme step reduction.

Result: The method achieves high-fidelity, temporally consistent talking-head video generation with only 1 step at up to 200 FPS, significantly outperforming existing approaches in both efficiency and stability.

Conclusion: By combining single-step bridge distillation with a persistent reference anchor and SNR-aligned knowledge transfer, LeapTalk resolves the latency-quality trade-off in talking-head generation, enabling stable real-time generation scalable to arbitrarily long videos.

Abstract: Long-form and real-time talking-head generation remains challenging due to a latency-quality trade-off: inefficient multi-step diffusion prohibits streaming generation, whereas real-time autoregressive approaches suffer from error accumulation and identity drift. To address this drawback, we propose LeapTalk, a novel framework that achieves stable and real-time talking-head generation with a single forward step, scaling to arbitrarily long videos. At the heart of our approach lies a single-step bridge distillation scheme. On the one hand, departing from the conventional noise-to-data paradigm, we introduce a data-to-data transport formulation based on a Brownian bridge. Anchored by a persistent reference, this strategy effectively mitigates identity drift and enhances long-term temporal stability. On the other hand, to enable smooth knowledge transfer from a pre-trained diffusion teacher to the student bridge model, we explore a heterogeneous distillation framework with an SNR-aligned time transformation $Φ(τ)$, which bridges the functional discrepancy between the two models. Moreover, we propose an audio-driven classifier-free guidance mechanism to maintain fine-grained lip synchronization under extreme step reduction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves high-fidelity and temporally consistent video generation with only 1 step at up to 200 FPS, significantly outperforming existing approaches in both efficiency and stability. Project Page: https://zhangrongxiang.github.io/leaptalk-page/

</details>


### [22] [Beyond Edge Maps: Wavelet-Domain Conditioning for Multi-Adapter Map-to-Satellite Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00083)
*Arisha Prasain*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A ControlNet-based diffusion framework synthesizes satellite imagery from cartographic data (OSM raster maps and their stationary wavelet transform subbands) without requiring the target satellite image. Two adapters are fused via MultiControlNet, and combined conditioning achieves superior per-image fidelity metrics across two datasets compared to map-only or wavelet-only baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial mapping partnerships are often unavailable in low-resource regions, leaving satellite basemaps stale. Existing methods condition on structural signals extracted from the target image itself, assuming imagery already exists, which limits their use precisely where synthesis is most needed. Map-conditioned alternatives omit frequency-domain structure.

Method: Proposes a ControlNet-based diffusion framework conditioned only on independently obtainable cartographic sources: OSM raster maps and their stationary wavelet transform (SWT) subbands. Two ControlNet adapters, trained separately on map and wavelet representations atop a frozen Stable Diffusion backbone, are fused via MultiControlNet to jointly leverage spatial structure and frequency detail without retraining a multi-input model.

Result: Combined conditioning wins six of eight metric-dataset comparisons: SSIM and PSNR on both datasets, plus LPIPS (Alex and VGG backbones) on the Nepal dataset, ties map-only on both Pix2Pix LPIPS backbones, and edges past wavelet-only there. Wavelet-only achieves the lowest FID on both datasets, reflecting a tradeoff between per-image fidelity and distributional realism.

Conclusion: The combined map+wavelet conditioning provides the best per-image fidelity, while wavelet-only offers superior distributional realism. The FID gap is treated cautiously due to small test-set sizes and FID's known small-sample bias.

Abstract: Commercial mapping partnerships are often unavailable in low-resource regions, leaving satellite basemaps stale and motivating synthesis of satellite imagery from independently maintained cartographic data. Existing ControlNet-based diffusion methods typically condition on structural signals like edges or segmentation extracted from the target image itself, assuming the imagery already exists and limiting their use exactly where synthesis matters most.
