Map-conditioned alternatives add cues like edge detection but omit frequency-domain structure. We propose a ControlNet-based diffusion framework conditioned only on cartographic sources obtainable independently of the target imagery: OpenStreetMap (OSM) raster maps and their stationary wavelet transform (SWT) subbands, a conditioning signal previously unexplored for map-to-satellite diffusion. Two ControlNet adapters, trained separately on the map and wavelet representations atop a frozen Stable Diffusion backbone, are fused via MultiControlNet, jointly drawing on spatial structure and frequency detail without retraining a multi-input model. We evaluate on a new paired map-satellite dataset curated for Nepal, a data-scarce, topographically diverse region, alongside the Pix2Pix maps-satellite benchmark. Combined conditioning wins six of eight metric-dataset comparisons -- SSIM and PSNR on both datasets, plus LPIPS (both Alex and VGG backbones) on ours and ties map-only on both Pix2Pix LPIPS backbones while still edging past wavelet-only there. Wavelet-only takes the lowest FID on both datasets, matching the tradeoff between per-image fidelity and distributional realism. We treat this gap cautiously given our modest test-set sizes and FID's known small-sample bias.

</details>


### [23] [From Pixels to PCells: A Neurosymbolic Approach to Photonic Component Creation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00084)
*Aadarsh Agarwal,Kenaish Al Qubaisi,Dirk Englund*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PixCell is a neurosymbolic system where multimodal agents convert visually presented photonic components into parametric programs using a DSL of geometric primitives. With a deterministic verifier for asymmetric-cheap evaluation, PixCell's agents achieve >0.9 mean IoU (up to 0.974) across eight component targets, outperform multi-seed sampling baselines (0.416), enable cross-stack retargeting to SOI/SiN/TFLN, and use the verifier as a training reward to improve a fine-tuned Qwen model via GRPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish a controlled framework for measuring, retargeting, and improving visual-to-parametric photonic component design, where deterministic verification makes evaluation cheaper than generation attempts.

Method: PixCell combines multimodal agents with a DSL of geometric primitives, an interface for iterative interaction, and a deterministic visual verifier; it also uses the verifier as a reward signal for GRPO/LoRA training of a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model without supervised demonstrations.

Result: Multimodal agents achieve mean IoU >0.9 (peaks 0.974 and 0.955) across eight photonic component targets, far exceeding the 0.416 baseline. Cross-stack reconstructions satisfy an 8.0 nm FSR target on SOI, SiN, and TFLN; a paper-derived splitter is validated via full-wave SOI simulation with symmetric outputs; the fine-tuned model improves mean champion IoU from 0.422 to 0.491 after three verifier-guided revision rounds on held-out figures.

Conclusion: PixCell demonstrates that frontier multimodal agents can reliably understand and render executable parametric representations from visual photonic targets, providing a scalable, verifier-driven framework for photonic component design and model improvement.

Abstract: We present PixCell, a neurosymbolic system in which multimodal agents convert a visually presented photonic component into a parametric program over a small domain-specific language (DSL) of geometric primitives. A system enabling deterministic visual verification renders evaluation asymmetrically cheaper than the generation attempt. While models using multi-seed sampling and iterative revision reach a mean best-turn IoU of only 0.416, multimodal agents through PixCell's interface and verifier consistently exceed 0.9 mean IoU, with scores reaching 0.974 and 0.955 across eight component targets while also satisfying source contracts. These results demonstrate that frontier multimodal agents can reliably understand and render executable parametric representations from visual targets. Using these live parameters, cross-stack studies on an interferometer reconstruct primitive programs that satisfy an 8.0 nm free spectral range target and the original footprint constraint on modeled 220-nm SOI, 400-nm SiN, and 400-nm TFLN stacks. PixCell further carries a paper-derived splitter from visual reconstruction through SOI full-wave simulation, producing symmetric propagation and balanced outputs. Finally, the same executable verifier supplies a training reward and dataset used to train a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model with LoRA and GRPO without supervised demonstrations. On eight training-excluded paper figures, its mean champion IoU rises from 0.422 after eight initial attempts to 0.491 after three verifier-guided revision rounds. These results therefore establish a controlled framework for measuring, retargeting, and improving visual-to-parametric photonic component design.

</details>


### [24] [DS@GT ARC at MEDIQA-CORE-Task-1 2026: Trimodal Model Fusion with Task-Specific Gates for Brain Tumor Subtype Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00086)
*Hoang Thanh Thanh Truong,Charles R. Clark*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The DS@GT ARC team presents a trimodal fusion system for brain tumor subtype classification (ImageCLEFmed MEDIQA-CORE 2026 Task 1), combining MRI embeddings (NeuroVFM), histopathology embeddings (Prov-GigaPath), and free-text radiology reports via two encoders (RadBERT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), achieving a mean macro-F1 of 0.801 under the Fully Multimodal condition—second place among verified teams—though performance degrades when histopathology is unavailable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Brain tumor diagnosis is time-sensitive; patients may wait weeks for finalized pathology reports. The authors seek automated systems to classify tumor subtypes from multimodal inputs to accelerate this process.

Method: The team combines pre-extracted MRI embeddings (NeuroVFM) and histopathology embeddings (Prov-GigaPath) with free-text radiology reports using two trimodal fusion architectures, two report encoders (RadBERT and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and a biologically motivated post-processing stage. Three glioma classification tasks are addressed: Level-1 Molecular Type, LGG vs HGG, and WHO Grade.

Result: The system achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.801 under the Fully Multimodal condition, exceeding the organizers' baseline (0.796) and ranking second among code-verified teams. However, modality-dropping evaluation shows the advantage depends heavily on histopathology availability; the system falls behind the baseline when modalities are missing.

Conclusion: Trimodal fusion with MRI, histopathology, and radiology report embeddings can outperform baselines for brain tumor subtype classification, but robustness across missing-modality conditions remains a limitation that needs further attention.

Abstract: Brain tumor diagnosis is a time-sensitive process in which patients may wait weeks for a finalized pathology report. This problem motivates automated systems that classify tumor subtype from multimodal inputs. This paper details the DS@GT ARC team's work for ImageCLEFmed MEDIQA-CORE 2026 Task~1, Brain Tumor Subtype Classification. The task evaluates three glioma classification problems: Level-1 Molecular Type, LGG vs HGG, and WHO Grade. We combine pre-extracted MRI (NeuroVFM) and histopathology (Prov-GigaPath) embeddings with free-text radiology reports. Our team explored two trimodal fusion architectures, two report encoders (RadBERT and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and a biologically motivated post-processing stage. We achieve a mean macro-F1 of 0.801 under the Fully Multimodal condition, exceeding the organizers' baseline of 0.796 and ranking second among the teams whose code passed verification. Additional evaluation across modality-dropping conditions shows that this advantage depends heavily on the availability of the histopathology modality, and that our system falls behind the baseline when modalities are missing. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/dsgt-arc/imageclef-mediqacore-2026.

</details>


### [25] [DODA: A Database of Datasets for Aesthetics Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00089)
*Lisa Koßmann,Ralf Bartho,Christoph Redies,Johan Wagemans*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The authors present DODA (Database Of Datasets for Aesthetics), a web application that centralizes and organizes large image datasets annotated for aesthetics research, providing metadata (size, resolution, annotation type, annotator count) and precomputed quantitative image properties to facilitate dataset discovery and selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid growth in empirical and computational aesthetics has produced many large image datasets with varied standards and annotations. The lack of a centralized open-science search system makes it tedious and time-consuming for researchers to find suitable datasets, often requiring downloading entire datasets to assess image quality and content.

Method: The authors developed DODA, an intuitive web application that allows researchers to browse all important aesthetics datasets. It provides general information about each dataset (size, resolution, type of annotation, number of annotators) and precomputed quantitative image properties for many datasets. They also discuss criteria for dataset selection and illustrate the benefits of reusing datasets.

Result: DODA provides a centralized platform for browsing aesthetics datasets with metadata and precomputed quantitative image properties, eliminating the need for manual searching across papers and platforms like OSF, GitHub, or Dropbox.

Conclusion: DODA facilitates collaboration across empirical and computational aesthetics fields by streamlining dataset discovery and selection, promoting open science and dataset reuse.

Abstract: With rapid growth in the fields of empirical and computational aesthetics we have seen a vast increase in large image datasets annotated for aesthetics. As the image databases differ widely in many respects (e.g., different standards for annotation), it can be tedious to find the dataset that fits one's research needs best. The absence of a centralized open-science search system causes additional problems. Currently, researchers typically share dataset links in papers or on diverse platforms like OSF, GitHub or Dropbox. Manually searching for details like image quality and content often requires downloading all datasets. Therefore, we present the Database Of Datasets for Aesthetics (DODA), an intuitive Web application in which researchers can browse all important datasets for aesthetics research. DODA provides general information about these datasets (size, resolution, type of annotation, number of annotators, etc.) and for many of them also precomputed quantitative image properties. We discuss relevant criteria for selecting a suitable dataset with DODA and illustrate the benefits of reusing datasets. Our approach facilitates collaboration across the fields of empirical and computational aesthetics. Keywords: empirical aesthetics, computational aesthetics, machine learning, image annotation, quantitative image properties, Open Science

</details>


### [26] [Video Models as Native 4D Renderers: World-Grounded Conditioning from Animated Mesh](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00094)
*Junhao Chen,Mingjin Chen,Henghaofan Zhang,Minglin Chen,Liaoyuan Fan,Boran Zhang,Saining Zhang,Mingze Sun,Hao Zhao,Ruqi Huang,Zhihao Li,Yufei Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DAR is a reference-guided renderer that extends video diffusion models to 4D generative rendering by injecting a neural 4D G-buffer (tracking, world position, normal) from animated meshes through a widened control adapter, achieving superior results over depth-based conditioning on the DAR-4D benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the representation question of what image-format condition allows a pretrained video diffusion backbone to simultaneously obey camera motion and scene-internal animation in the 4D generative rendering setting. Depth-based conditioning is shown to be suboptimal because depth is a camera-dependent chart that mixes camera and object motion.

Method: DAR extends Wan2.2 camera control from Plücker rays alone to a joint camera-plus-geometry interface. It projects a neural 4D G-buffer (tracking, world position, and normal) from the animated mesh and injects it through a widened control adapter while preserving the pretrained image-to-video prior. The key design choice is pairing tracking (persistent surface element) with world position (current scene-coordinate state), augmented by normal for local shape.

Result: On the 68-case DAR-4D benchmark, LoRA DAR achieves PSNR 23.22, SSIM 0.895, and LPIPS 0.134, improving over off-the-shelf Wan2.2-Depth by 1.54 dB PSNR. A full fine-tune reaches PSNR 25.36 and SSIM 0.917. Ablations show replacing world position with depth reduces PSNR by 1.26-1.55 dB at every checkpoint.

Conclusion: Tracking + world-position correspondence serves as a practical and superior 4D rendering condition compared to depth, providing a better representation for video diffusion models to render dynamic scenes from animated meshes, camera trajectories, and reference images.

Abstract: Pretrained video diffusion models can act as renderers when the desired scene state is already specified by an animated mesh, a camera trajectory, and a reference image. This 4D generative rendering setting raises a representation question: what image-format condition lets a video backbone obey both camera motion and scene-internal animation? We propose DAR, a reference-guided renderer that extends Wan2.2 camera control from Plücker rays alone to a joint camera-plus-geometry interface. DAR projects a neural 4D G-buffer (tracking, world position, and normal) from the animated mesh and injects it through a widened control adapter while preserving the pretrained image-to-video prior. The central design choice is the pair of tracking and world position. Tracking identifies the persistent surface element that should carry appearance; world position gives its current scene-coordinate state; normal supplies local shape. Depth plus calibrated rays can recover 3D in principle, but depth is a camera-dependent chart in which camera and object motion are mixed. On the 68-case DAR-4D benchmark, LoRA DAR reaches PSNR 23.22, SSIM 0.895, and LPIPS 0.134, improving over off-the-shelf Wan2.2-Depth by 1.54 dB PSNR; a full fine-tune reaches PSNR 25.36 and SSIM 0.917. Matched ablations show that replacing world position by depth reduces PSNR by 1.26--1.55 dB at every checkpoint, supporting tracking+world-position correspondence as a practical 4D rendering condition.

</details>


### [27] [Logographic Character Visual Pretraining via Semantic-based Contrastive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00096)
*Daqian Shi,Wei Cao,Xiaoyu Zheng,Lida Shi,Xiaolei Diao,Cedric M John*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a multi-modal learning method for logographic character recognition (e.g., Chinese) that combines visual semantics with contextual semantics extracted from language models. A novel pre-training strategy enhances deep visual representations to handle imbalanced and rare character datasets, showing state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks and downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning-based character vision studies rely on large and balanced datasets, which are rare for real-world logographic character languages like Chinese due to imbalanced usage frequency and continuously created new characters. This data imbalance limits performance of existing methods on realistic character datasets.

Method: The method introduces a multi-modal learning approach that fuses visual semantics of characters with contextual semantics extracted from corresponding language models. A novel contrastive pre-training strategy is designed to strengthen deep visual representations, particularly for datasets with imbalanced and rare instances.

Result: Experiments across various datasets demonstrate that the proposed character recognition method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and the contrastive pre-training strategy is further validated through several downstream tasks.

Conclusion: Multi-modal learning with contextual semantics from language models effectively addresses the challenge of imbalanced logographic character recognition, improving representation learning and achieving superior performance over existing approaches.

Abstract: Current deep learning-based character vision studies, e.g., text recognition, character image denoising, and historical text completion, are offering new solutions for learning, managing, and utilizing character resources. However, the performance of these studies peaks only with large and balanced datasets, which is a rarity with real-world character datasets, especially for logographic character languages, e.g., Chinese. The imbalance in data distribution of logographic characters is a common issue due to differences in character usage frequency and new characters being continuously created. In this paper, we propose a novel method for logographic character recognition, which introduces a multi-modal learning approach using visual semantics and contextual semantics of characters. A novel pre-training strategy is designed to enhance deep visual representations, especially for datasets suffering from issues of imbalanced and rare instances, by extracting the contextual semantics of each character from the corresponding language models. We conduct experiments across various datasets to evaluate our character recognition method and further validate the contrastive pre-training strategy by several downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method compared to state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [28] [SPARC-Rad: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset and Evaluation Pipeline for Spatial and Anatomical Reasoning in Radiology Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00100)
*Satvik Tripathi,Mustafa Ege Seker,Kristian Quevada,Ebubechukwu D Enwerem,Pratham Khandelwal,Emine Meltem,Bera Koca,Shahriar Faghani,Jacinta Arnold,Dania Daye,Tessa S. Cook*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPARC-Rad is a manually curated multimodal benchmark with 300 image-question pairs and an evaluation pipeline for assessing spatial perception and anatomical reasoning capabilities of vision-language models in clinical radiology, covering CT, MRI, and radiography across five anatomical categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLMs benchmarks for medical imaging focus on disease classification, report generation, or broad VQA, but fail to evaluate the spatial and anatomical reasoning capabilities that are essential for radiology practice.

Method: The authors developed a benchmark containing 300 image-question pairs derived from healthy control TCIA imaging studies spanning CT, MRI, and radiography across abdomen, chest, breast, neuro, and musculoskeletal categories. Questions were manually designed by radiology trainees to evaluate anatomical identification, localization, laterality, regional recognition, device identification, and inter-structure spatial relationships. The evaluation pipeline includes standardized prompting, structured output collection, response normalization, LLM-as-judge grading, human quality review, binary correctness scoring, and subgroup analysis by modality, anatomy, and reasoning type.

Result: The paper introduces the benchmark and evaluation pipeline but does not report specific model performance results in the abstract.

Conclusion: SPARC-Rad provides a reusable framework for evaluating whether VLMs can reason about radiologic anatomy as a spatial system, supporting future model development, failure-mode analysis, and pre-deployment assessment.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for medical imaging, but many available benchmarks emphasize disease classification, report generation, or broad visual question answering rather than the spatial and anatomical reasoning required for radiology. We developed the Spatial Perception and Anatomical Reasoning in Clinical Radiology (SPARC-Rad) Benchmark, a manually curated multimodal benchmark dataset and evaluation pipeline for assessing these capabilities in radiology VLMs. SPARC-Rad includes 300 image-question pairs derived from healthy control imaging studies in The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA), spanning CT, MRI, and radiography across the abdomen, chest, breast, neuro, and musculoskeletal categories. Radiology trainees manually designed and annotated questions to evaluate anatomical identification, localization, laterality, regional recognition, device identification, and inter-structure spatial relationships. The evaluation pipeline supports standardized prompting, structured output collection, response normalization, LLM-as-judge grading, human quality review, binary correctness scoring, and subgroup analysis by modality, anatomy, and reasoning type. SPARC-Rad provides a reusable framework for evaluating whether VLMs can provide reasoning for radiologic anatomy as a spatial system, supporting future model development, failure-mode analysis, and pre-deployment assessment.

</details>


### [29] [What Carries the Signal in Pathology Foundation-Model Atlases? A Patient-Level Controlled Benchmark in Breast Cancer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00105)
*Chimdi Walter Ndubuisi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Rebuilding pathology foundation model molecular-programme prediction with the patient as the unit of evidence, the authors show ridge regression on mean-pooled embeddings predicts held-out programme scores (rho=0.25–0.56, Holm-adjusted p=0.0044 across 11 backbones, 4 programmes, 285 TCGA-BRCA patients). Embedded signal is real but variant across programmes; the geometric (Riemannian) machinery contributes nothing measurable because its geodesic graph is Euclidean by construction, and a driver-count metric is near-uninformative.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evidence that pathology foundation models encode molecular programmes in morphology is based on cohort-wide ranked gene lists rather than patient-level held-out predictions. The authors rebuild the analysis with the patient as the unit of evidence and isolate which pipeline component actually carries predictive signal, to gauge whether the claimed morphological-molecular link is genuine and largely attributable to the embedding itself or to downstream geometric/metric machinery.

Method: Using 11 frozen foundation-model backbones, 4 pre-specified gene programmes, and 285 TCGA-BRCA patients with paired slides and RNA-seq (44 cells; GroupKFold by patient, preprocessing fitted inside folds), they fit ridge regression on mean-pooled embeddings to predict held-out programme scores. They compare against competing models (tissue composition, 54 interpretable cell-count features, graph-and-metric decoder) on the same folds, run a matched permutation null (10,000 permutations, Holm adjustment), and dissect the Riemannian vs Euclidean geometric machinery including the geodesic graph construction and a driver-count metric.

Result: Ridge regression on embeddings predicts held-out programme scores at Spearman rho = 0.25–0.56 (UNI2 strongest on all four, immune 0.556); permutation null gives raw p~1e-4 and Holm-adjusted p=0.0044 for every cell. Embeddings beat tissue composition on ER/luminal, proliferation, immune (+0.280/+0.284/+0.479, p<=0.003) but not basal (0.493 vs 0.469, p=0.77); 54 cell-count features come within 0.043–0.085. Geometry adds nothing measurable: Riemannian minus Euclidean = +0.0010 (95% CI [-0.0007,+0.0029]), worse when applied consistently (-0.0117); ridge beats graph-and-metric decoder by +0.097; 91.8% of random six-gene panels recover >=5/6 drivers.

Conclusion: Pathology foundation-model embeddings carry genuine but not uniformly morphological predictive signal for molecular programmes, with the simple mean-pooled linear decoder being the effective component. The elaborate geometric/topological machinery contributes nothing because it is Euclidean by construction under nearest-neighbour reweighting, and common driver-count metrics are near-uninformative in this regime. The findings caution against attributing success to exotic geometric components and emphasize patient-level, fully nested validation.

Abstract: Pathology foundation models are reported to encode molecular programmes in tissue morphology, but the evidence is usually a cohort-wide ranked gene list rather than a prediction for a held-out patient. We rebuild such an analysis with the patient as the unit of evidence and ask which pipeline component carries signal.
  Across 11 frozen backbones, four pre-specified gene programmes and 285 TCGA-BRCA patients with paired slides and RNA-seq (44 cells; GroupKFold by patient, all preprocessing fitted inside the fold), ridge regression on mean-pooled embeddings predicts held-out programme scores at Spearman rho = 0.25-0.56, UNI2 strongest on all four (immune 0.556). A matched permutation null gives raw p ~ 1e-4 at 10,000 permutations for every cell; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0044.
  The signal is real but not uniformly morphological. Against competing models on the same patients and folds, embeddings beat tissue composition for ER/luminal, proliferation and immune (+0.280, +0.284, +0.479; p <= 0.003) but not basal, where compartment fractions alone reach 0.469 against the embedding's 0.493 (p = 0.77). Fifty-four interpretable cell-count features come within 0.043-0.085 on every programme.
  The geometric machinery contributes nothing measurable, and we identify why: the geodesic graph selects neighbours by Euclidean nearest-neighbour search and only reweights edges already chosen, so the topology is Euclidean by construction (Riemannian minus Euclidean = +0.0010, 95% CI [-0.0007, +0.0029]). Applied consistently the geometry is worse (-0.0117). Ridge regression beats the graph-and-metric decoder by +0.097 (CI [+0.069, +0.127]). The driver-count metric common in this literature is near-uninformative here: 91.8% of random six-gene panels recover >=5/6 drivers.

</details>


### [30] [Distill What RGB Can Recover: Privileged 3D Evidence for RGB-Only Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00110)
*Yanbin Hu,Jin Cui,Jun Ye,Jiepeng Zhou,Jiangcheng Song,Boran Zhao,Pengju Ren*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a privileged-evidence distillation framework that converts training-time 3D evidence (e.g., depth, position-aware inputs) into spatial reasoning capabilities that remain effective under RGB-only inference, eliminating the need for additional 3D inputs at deployment time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RGB images alone provide insufficient 3D cues for scene understanding, and existing 3D-VLMs require depth or 3D-position-aware inputs at inference, which introduces extra acquisition, reconstruction, or annotation costs and limits RGB-only deployment.

Method: The framework (1) constructs a distillable teacher using a unified evidence interface and controlled residual injection, (2) transfers knowledge to a deployable RGB-only student via logit and structured representation distillation, and (3) introduces evidence-sensitivity-guided distillation that uses corrupted evidence to identify highly evidence-dependent targets and down-weights their supervision. They also define a recoverability decomposition based on matched baseline, teacher, and student to separate RGB-recoverable improvements from residual teacher advantages.

Result: Across four benchmarks, the teacher achieves the best result on 7 of 11 metrics among compared methods. The RGB-only student outperforms its matched baseline on all 11 metrics, including gains of 10.4 ScanQA CIDEr and 19.1 Scan2Cap CIDEr@0.5, without additional inference-time inputs.

Conclusion: Training-time privileged 3D evidence distillation is effective for both improving teacher performance and enabling deployable RGB-only spatial reasoning; the matched baseline-teacher-student analysis characterizes privileged-gain transfer across evidence types and spatial skills.

Abstract: 3D scene understanding requires reasoning about entity existence, spatial layout, and object relations, yet RGB images alone often provide insufficient 3D cues. Existing 3D-VLMs commonly rely on depth or 3D-position-aware inputs at inference time, introducing additional acquisition, reconstruction, or annotation costs that limit RGB-only deployment. We therefore study how training-time 3D evidence can be converted into spatial reasoning capabilities retained under RGB-only inference. We propose a privileged-evidence distillation framework that constructs a distillable teacher through a unified evidence interface and controlled residual injection, and transfers its knowledge to a deployable student receiving only RGB images and questions through logit and structured representation distillation. To avoid imitating teacher signals unsupported by RGB, we further introduce evidence-sensitivity-guided distillation, which uses corrupted evidence to identify highly evidence-dependent targets and down-weight their supervision. We also define a recoverability decomposition based on the matched baseline, teacher, and student, separating privileged gains into RGB-recoverable improvements and residual teacher advantages. Across four benchmarks, the teacher achieves the best result on 7 of 11 reported metrics among the compared methods. The RGB-only student outperforms its matched baseline on all 11 metrics, including gains of 10.4 ScanQA CIDEr and 19.1 Scan2Cap CIDEr@0.5, without additional inference-time inputs. These results validate the effectiveness of training-time privileged 3D evidence distillation for both teacher performance and deployable RGB-only spatial reasoning. Separately, our matched baseline-teacher-student analysis characterizes privileged-gain transfer across evidence types and spatial skills.

</details>


### [31] [Counting the Cost of War Under Satellite Embargo: Zero-Shot Estimation of Impacted Infrastructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00119)
*Saleh Sakib Ahmed,M. Sohel Rahman*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A zero-shot crisis mapping framework that estimates impacted structures from archival pre-strike maps using LLM-extracted weapon payloads, blast-scaling physics (Hopkinson-Cranz), adaptive field-of-view SAM segmentation, and depth-augmented LVLMs to bypass post-strike satellite data embargoes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-strike satellite data embargoes and imagery blackouts hinder rapid estimation of damaged structures in conflict zones, creating an operational bottleneck for humanitarian response.

Method: The method reframes impacted building mapping as a zero-shot geometric projection on pre-strike archival maps. It uses LLMs to extract weapon payloads (W) from LiveUAMap/ArcGIS incident text, applies Hopkinson-Cranz scaling (R_base = Z * W^(1/3)) to project blast perimeters, and introduces two innovations: Adaptive Field-of-View to remove resolution/zoom bias in 2D SAMGeo segmentation, and 2.5D pseudo-height depth maps combined with masks to help LVLMs resolve dense overlapping rooftops.

Result: On 2026 Middle East conflict data, depth-augmented LVLMs dramatically outperform traditional segmentation in congested urban centers, while ultra-fast 2D segmentation works well in sparse rural zones.

Conclusion: Establishes a hybrid zero-shot crisis mapping paradigm: fast 2D segmentation for rural areas and depth-augmented LVLMs for dense urban environments, circumventing the need for post-strike imagery.

Abstract: Rapid estimation of impacted structures - critical for conflict-zone humanitarian response - is frequently hindered by post-strike satellite data embargoes and imagery blackouts. We bypass this operational bottleneck by reframing impacted building mapping as a zero-shot geometric projection task on archival, pre-strike maps. Using coordinate and incident text from LiveUAMap and ArcGIS, Large Language Models extract weapon payloads (W) to project kinetic blast perimeters via Hopkinson-Cranz scaling (R_base = Z * W^(1/3)). To count exposed structures within these zones without post-strike imagery, we introduce two technical innovations: Adaptive Field-of-View to eliminate resolution (zoom) bias in 2D segmentation (SAMGeo), and 2.5D pseudo-height depth maps combined with segmentation masks to help Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) resolve overlapping, dense rooftops. Evaluated on 2026 Middle East conflict data, depth-augmented LVLMs dramatically outperform traditional segmentation in congested urban centers. This establishes a powerful hybrid paradigm for zero-shot crisis mapping: ultra-fast 2D segmentation for sparse rural zones, and depth-augmented LVLMs for dense urban environments.

</details>


### [32] [RadPRISM: Schema-stratified radiology-report supervision for concept-disentangled image representations and visual grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00147)
*Fabian Drexel,Marlene Fritzsche,Era Stambollxhiu,Miriam Kumpf,Lena Schmitzer,Lea Schumann,Jannik Kahmann,Friedrich Puttkammer,Johannes Moll,Jannik Lübberstedt,Zeineb Ben Chaaben,Anirudh Narayanan,Cosmin I. Bercea,Sebastian Ziegelmayer,Marcus R. Makowski,Daniel Rueckert,Lisa C. Adams,Keno K. Bressem*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RadPRISM is a vision-language pretraining framework for chest radiographs that uses a clinician-defined radiology schema as a designated stratification axis, aligning each clinical concept in its own dedicated visual subspace. Using an on-premise LLM to extract per-concept text spans from reports, RadPRISM improves zero-shot classification from 0.717 to 0.868 macro AUROC over a global-alignment baseline, matches CARZero externally while outperforming it up to 4.3-fold in visual grounding, and demonstrates concept-stratified retrieval capability per a radiologist reader study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional vision-language pretraining models operate in a single shared embedding space, requiring post hoc recovery of concept-level structure and interpretability. This limits model transparency and clinical utility, motivating the need for native concept-stratified representations shaped by clinicians.

Method: RadPRISM uses an on-premise large language model to extract per-concept text spans from free-text radiology reports. Each clinical concept is aligned in its own dedicated visual subspace, turning a clinician-defined radiology schema (19 concepts) into direct top-level alignment supervision on 203,602 chest radiograph examinations.

Result: RadPRISM improved internal dataset zero-shot classification from 0.717 to 0.868 macro AUROC over a matched global-alignment baseline, performed on par with CARZero in external zero-shot classification while outperforming it up to 4.3-fold in pointing-game visual grounding. A radiologist reader study demonstrated 0.78 macro retrieval correctness rate within rank 3 for concept-stratified retrieval.

Conclusion: RadPRISM yields discriminative, spatially faithful, natively concept-stratified representations that are shaped by and transparently inspectable by clinicians, offering a clinically transparent alternative to global-alignment vision-language pretraining.

Abstract: Vision-language pretraining learns rich medical image representations from radiology reports, but previous model variants commonly operate within a single shared embedding space, so concept-level structure and interpretability must be recovered post hoc, limiting model transparency and, hence, clinical utility. We introduce RadPRISM, which makes a clinician-defined radiology schema a designated stratification axis: an on-premise large language model extracts per-concept text spans from free-text reports, and each clinical concept is aligned in its own dedicated visual subspace, turning concept stratification into direct, top-level alignment supervision. Instantiated on chest radiographs with a 19-concept schema over $203{,}602$ examinations from an internal multi-year archive, RadPRISM improved internal dataset zero-shot classification from $0.717$ (95% CI, $0.710-0.723$) to $0.868$ (95% CI, $0.863-0.872$) macro AUROC over a matched global-alignment baseline, performed on par with the purpose-built CARZero reference in external zero-shot classification while substantially outperforming it (up to 4.3-fold) in pointing-game visual grounding. In addition, a radiologist reader study demonstrated concept-stratified retrieval ability ($0.78$ macro retrieval correctness rate within rank 3), surfacing disentangled descriptive findings that report-level retrieval and fixed-label vocabularies cannot express. RadPRISM yields discriminative, spatially faithful, natively concept-stratified representations shaped by and transparently inspectable by clinicians.

</details>


### [33] [SCALP: Semi-Supervised Statistical Shape Modeling from Imperfect 3D Photogrammetry via Landmark-Anchored Spectral Warp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00187)
*Nawazish Khan,Sanjay Bhandari,Sarang Joshi,Alzbeta Novotna,Tiffany Jeong,Loretta Bowman,Michael Hernandez,Tobi Somorin,Viraj Govani,Jesse Glodstein,Shireen Elhabian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SCALP is a two-stage semi-supervised framework for statistical shape modeling that constructs consistent shape models directly from raw, imperfect photogrammetry scans. It combines landmark localization (via a semi-supervised Point Transformer) with Laplace–Beltrami spectral warping to generate dense correspondences and isolate the cranium from clutter, outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised point-cloud methods on infant photogrammetry data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional SSM pipelines require clean, fully registered surfaces, but real-world clinical photogrammetry scans are noisy, partial, and cluttered. This prevents the adoption of radiation-free surface imaging as a safe alternative to CT for infant craniosynostosis analysis.

Method: SCALP operates in two stages: (1) a semi-supervised Point Transformer trained on a small expert-annotated dataset plus a large unlabeled cohort localizes craniofacial landmarks with minimal annotation overhead; (2) these landmarks anchor a Laplace–Beltrami spectral deformation of an anatomical template, producing dense correspondences and automatically isolating the cranium from peripheral clutter without manual preprocessing.

Result: Experiments on infant photogrammetry scans show SCALP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised point-cloud approaches for shape modeling from imperfect surfaces.

Conclusion: SCALP provides a clinically practical pathway toward objective, radiation-free head shape analysis, overcoming the data quality barriers that previously hindered adoption of photogrammetry-based SSM for infant craniosynostosis.

Abstract: Correspondence-based statistical shape modeling (SSM) is vital for population-level morphometric analysis, but conventional pipelines assume clean, fully registered surfaces. Real-world clinical photogrammetry scans are often noisy, partial, and cluttered, hindering the adoption of radiation-free surface imaging as a safe alternative to computed tomography (CT) for infant craniosynostosis. We present SCALP (Semi-supervised Correspondence via lAndmark Localization and sPectral warping), a two-stage framework that constructs consistent shape models directly from raw, imperfect surface scans. First, a semi-supervised Point Transformer leverages a small expert-annotated dataset alongside a large unlabeled cohort to accurately localize craniofacial landmarks with minimal annotation overhead. Second, these landmarks anchor a Laplace--Beltrami spectral deformation of an anatomical template, generating dense correspondences while naturally isolating the cranium from peripheral scanning clutter without manual preprocessing. Experiments on infant photogrammetry scans demonstrate that SCALP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised point-cloud approaches, offering a clinically practical pathway toward objective, radiation-free head shape analysis.

</details>


### [34] [Manifold-GS: Certified Hybrid Assets via Varifold-Conservative Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00214)
*Boyang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Manifold-GS is a certified hybrid asset layer for 3D Gaussian Splatting that separates appearance opacity from geometric quadrature mass, represents surface-like Gaussians as discrete unoriented varifolds, and exports confidence-certified open surface patches while retaining uncertified content as residual splats. It provides refinement-conservative mass transport, local realizability diagnostics, source-preserving patch bindings, and conservative collision candidates, achieving zero patch-defined edit leakage, high texture round-trip PSNR, and lower collision floater area than official 2DGS meshes on DTU scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting produces high-quality novel-view synthesis but its adaptive radiance primitives are not directly usable as structured assets: opacity is not an additive area measure, refinement can change induced geometry, and watertight mesh extraction can hallucinate collision surfaces in unobserved regions. The paper addresses this gap by introducing a certified hybrid asset layer.

Method: The method (1) separates appearance opacity from geometric quadrature mass, (2) represents surface-like Gaussians as a discrete unoriented varifold, (3) exports only confidence-certified open surface patches while retaining uncertified content as residual splats, (4) provides refinement-conservative mass transport, local realizability diagnostics, source-preserving patch bindings, and conservative collision candidates.

Result: On three DTU scenes, a frozen asset benchmark shows zero patch-defined edit leakage, texture round-trip PSNR of 30.1/35.3/33.7 dB, and lower collision floater area than official 2DGS meshes on all scenes with large gaps on two scenes. External-region annotations, phantom-collision probes, and 5k-face simplification support the certified asset interpretation. RGB-only experiments show local realizability is not sufficient for sparse-view surface identifiability.

Conclusion: The result is a precision-coverage tradeoff rather than a universal reconstruction claim. Manifold-GS offers certified, editable, and collision-safe assets from Gaussian scenes, but acknowledges limitations in sparse-view surface identifiability.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) gives high-quality novel-view synthesis, but its adaptive radiance primitives are not directly usable as structured assets: opacity is not an additive area measure, refinement can change the induced geometry, and watertight mesh extraction can hallucinate collision surfaces in unobserved regions. We introduce Manifold-GS, a certified hybrid asset layer for Gaussian scenes. The method separates appearance opacity from geometric quadrature mass, represents surface-like Gaussians as a discrete unoriented varifold, and exports only confidence-certified open surface patches while retaining uncertified content as residual splats. It provides refinement-conservative mass transport, local realizability diagnostics, source-preserving patch bindings, and conservative collision candidates. On three DTU scenes, a frozen asset benchmark shows zero patch-defined edit leakage, texture round-trip PSNR of 30.1/35.3/33.7 dB, and lower collision floater area than official 2DGS meshes on all scenes, with large gaps on two scenes. The result is a precision-coverage tradeoff rather than a universal reconstruction claim. External-region annotations, phantom-collision probes, and 5k-face simplification further support the certified asset interpretation, while RGB-only experiments show that local realizability is not sufficient for sparse-view surface identifiability.

</details>


### [35] [Learning How Much, Not Just What: Cross-Patient Burden Order for CT Vision-Language Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00231)
*Guoliang You,Haifan Gong,Xiaomeng Chu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Spectrum is an anatomy-conditioned framework for volumetric CT vision-language pretraining that learns burden-aware (graded severity) 3D representations by leveraging weak cross-patient ordering cues, without requiring scarce longitudinal data. It uses rule-based scoring to mine pathology-matched lower-to-higher burden pairs across patients and applies Burden-Direction Alignment (BDA) to align image deltas with report deltas per organ scope, achieving strong zero-shot AUROC (85.6 on CT-RATE, 72.7 on RAD-ChestCT).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing volumetric CT vision-language pretraining learns from scan-report pairs using global and anatomy-aware objectives, but these only establish what is present, not how severe. Graded burden language in reports collapses into a present/absent signal because nothing separates mild from extensive cases along a consistent direction. Longitudinal supervision could supply this order but patient-matched CT pairs are scarce at scale, whereas cross-sectional cohorts already encode weak burden cues across different patients.

Method: Spectrum represents each study at whole-study and organ scopes. For each organ-mapped pathology, a rule-based scorer mines confidence-filtered lower-to-higher burden pairs from different patients. Burden-Direction Alignment (BDA) aligns the pathology-conditioned image delta with the report delta at each scope, separating the burden direction from its reverse. Since endpoints are different people, a target-conditioned aligner first makes them comparable so the delta reflects burden rather than patient variation. BDA additionally separates the direction from its reverse, anchors it to the observed higher-burden endpoint, and enforces consistency across ordered triplets. Every pair is drawn within a single pathology, so BDA constrains intra-class structure that image-report contrast alone never touches.

Result: Spectrum achieves 85.6 zero-shot AUROC on CT-RATE and 72.7 on external RAD-ChestCT, with consistent gains in linear probing and retrieval tasks.

Conclusion: Weak cross-patient order is a scalable complement to anatomy-aware correspondence, yielding burden-aware CT representations without requiring longitudinal data.

Abstract: Volumetric CT vision-language pretraining learns 3D representations from scan-report pairs, but global and anatomy-aware objectives supervise only correspondence: they establish what is present and leave how much unconstrained. Nothing separates a mild from an extensive case of the same finding along a consistent direction, so the graded burden language in reports collapses into a present/absent signal. Longitudinal supervision would supply this order, but patient-matched CT pairs are scarce at scale; cross-sectional cohorts already encode weak burden cues across different patients. We introduce Spectrum, an anatomy-conditioned framework that represents each study at whole-study and organ scopes. For each organ-mapped pathology, a rule-based scorer mines confidence-filtered lower-to-higher pairs of different patients, and Burden-Direction Alignment (BDA) aligns the pathology-conditioned image delta with the report delta at each scope, separating that direction from its reverse. Because the endpoints are different people, a target-conditioned aligner first makes them comparable, so the delta reflects burden rather than between-patient variation. BDA further separates the selected direction from its reverse, anchors it to the observed higher-burden endpoint, and enforces consistency across ordered triplets. Since every pair is drawn within a single pathology, BDA is designed to constrain intra-class structure that image-report contrast alone never touches. Spectrum attains 85.6 zero-shot AUROC on CT-RATE and 72.7 on external RAD-ChestCT, with consistent gains in linear probing and retrieval. Weak cross-patient order is thus a scalable complement to anatomy-aware correspondence, yielding burden-aware CT representations without longitudinal data.

</details>


### [36] [Real-Time Visual Obstruction Detection in Surgical Augmented Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00232)
*Shih-Chin Yang,Yanming Xiu,Hanting Ye,Qi Chen,Elias Rotondo,Maria Gorlatova*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper presents a latency-aware visual obstruction detection pipeline for surgical augmented reality that combines vision-language model (VLM)-based surgical-object recognition with segmentation-based obstruction reasoning. Using a cascaded small-to-large VLM architecture with segmentation-guided early exiting and attention-based visual token pruning, the system achieves 87.43% obstruction detection accuracy with an average end-to-end latency of 479 ms, a 62.90% reduction compared to a cloud large-model baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Virtual content in surgical AR can obstruct task-relevant real-world information such as surgical instruments, potentially interfering with users' perception during time-sensitive surgical tasks. Detecting when virtual content obstructs important visual information is therefore critical, yet requires a latency-aware approach suitable for real-time surgical settings.

Method: The system employs a cascaded small-to-large VLM architecture. Small VLM handles easy frames when its key-object prediction is supported by segmentation consistency; difficult frames are forwarded to a large VLM with attention-based visual token pruning for reduced inference overhead. A pseudo-AR surgical obstruction detection benchmark was constructed by overlaying virtual content onto surgical-tool images and labeling occlusion of task-relevant instruments.

Result: The proposed system achieves 87.43% obstruction detection accuracy with an average end-to-end latency of 479 ms, reducing latency by 62.90% compared to a cloud large-model baseline.

Conclusion: Results demonstrate the feasibility of latency-aware obstruction detection for surgical AR, motivating future work on dynamic surgical videos, multi-object scenes, and clinically grounded AR guidance content.

Abstract: Surgical augmented reality (AR) can provide contextual guidance by overlaying virtual annotations, tool cues, and procedural information onto the surgical workspace. However, the virtual content may obstruct task-relevant real-world information, such as surgical instruments, and interfere with users' perception during time-sensitive surgical tasks. In this paper, we investigate visual obstruction detection for surgical AR and present a latency-aware pipeline that combines vision-language model (VLM)-based surgical-object recognition with segmentation-based obstruction reasoning. To reduce inference overhead, the system adopts a cascaded small-to-large VLM architecture with segmentation-guided early exiting and attention-based visual token pruning. The small VLM handles easy frames when its key-object prediction is supported by segmentation consistency, while difficult frames are forwarded to a large VLM with pruned visual tokens. We construct a pseudo-AR surgical obstruction detection benchmark by overlaying virtual content onto surgical-tool images and labeling whether the virtual content obstructs task-relevant instruments. Evaluation results show that the proposed system achieves 87.43% obstruction detection accuracy with an average end-to-end latency of 479 ms, reducing latency by 62.90% compared with a cloud large-model baseline. These results demonstrate the feasibility of latency-aware obstruction detection for surgical AR and motivate future work on dynamic surgical videos, multi-object scenes, and clinically grounded AR guidance content.

</details>


### [37] [Attention-Steered Vision-Language Models for Sign Language Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00235)
*Meibo Hu,Guohao Sun,Annemarie D. Ross,Sheng Li,Zhiqiang Tao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AttnSign is a VLM-based spatial-temporal attention steering framework for sign language translation that addresses poor spatial-temporal visual grounding in existing VLM-based translators by supervising attention on sign-relevant regions (face, hands) and using RL-based motion-cadence steering to focus on sign-level keyframes, outperforming existing methods on How2Sign and OpenASL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLM-based sign language translators suffer from poor spatial-temporal visual grounding. Standard next-token cross-entropy loss does not provide explicit signal for where and when the model should attend, causing models to overlook sign-relevant regions (spatial) and frames (temporal).

Method: AttnSign consists of two key components: (1) spatial attention supervision that guides the model's attention to sign-relevant regions such as face and hands within each frame, and (2) an RL-based motion-cadence steering method that encourages the model to explore and focus on sign-level keyframes for temporal grounding.

Result: Experiments on How2Sign and OpenASL benchmarks demonstrate that AttnSign consistently outperforms existing methods for sign language translation.

Conclusion: AttnSign effectively addresses the spatial-temporal visual grounding failure mode in VLM-based sign language translation by steering attention both spatially (toward sign-relevant body regions) and temporally (toward sign-level keyframes), achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for multimodal video understanding. However, they remain limited in the sign language translation task, where we identify a key failure mode of existing VLMbased translators: poor spatial-temporal visual grounding. In particular, we find that standard next-token cross-entropy does not directly provide signal for where and when the model should attend, causing models to overlook sign-relevant regions and frames. To address this challenge, we propose AttnSign, a VLM-based spatial-temporal attention steering framework for sign language translation. AttnSign first introduces spatial attention supervision for sign-relevant regions, such as face and hands, in each frame; then develops an RL-based motion-cadence steering method that encourages the model to explore and focus on sign-level keyframes. Experimental results on How2Sign and OpenASL benchmarks show that our proposed AttnSign consistently outperforms existing methods.

</details>


### [38] [Latent-Centroid Steering: Single-Pass Classifier-Free Guidance for Command-Aligned Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00237)
*Meibo Hu,Jiamian Wang,Pichao Wang,Zhiqiang Tao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the command-following gap in vision-language models for autonomous driving by framing it as a conditional policy collapse. The authors introduce Latent-Centroid Steering (LCS), a single-pass classifier-free guidance mechanism that uses class-level latent shifts (command-specific centroids) instead of instance-level residuals, reducing inference latency by ~50% while improving command adherence and driving performance on Bench2Drive and nuScenes benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models for autonomous driving exhibit a persistent command-following gap where predicted trajectories show weak sensitivity to navigation instructions, resulting in incorrect behavior at critical decision points. This is identified as a conditional policy collapse caused by regression-based training under multimodal trajectory distributions, which encourages reliance on dominant visual priors while marginalizing language-conditioned signals.

Method: The paper formulates classifier-free guidance (CFG) for regression-based vision-language driving, interpreting it as isolating instruction-induced residuals in action space by contrasting conditional and unconditional predictions. To address the latency and noise issues of standard two-pass CFG, the authors propose Latent-Centroid Steering (LCS), a single-pass guidance mechanism that replaces instance-level residuals with class-level latent shifts by projecting conditional representations toward precomputed command-specific centroids, based on a mean-shift interpretation of CFG.

Result: LCS reduces inference latency by approximately 50% while achieving stronger command adherence and improved driving performance on both closed-loop (Bench2Drive) and open-loop (nuScenes) benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed LCS demonstrates that class-level latent steering based on cluster geometry is both more stable and computationally efficient than instance-level CFG, effectively closing the command-following gap in vision-language driving models while maintaining real-time control feasibility.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving, enabling agents to map multimodal inputs and high-level navigation instructions directly to executable trajectories. However, in practice, these models exhibit a persistent command-following gap: predicted trajectories often show weak sensitivity to navigation commands, resulting in incorrect behavior at critical decision points. We identify this issue as a form of conditional policy collapse, where regression-based training under multimodal trajectory distributions encourages the model to rely on dominant visual priors while marginalizing the language-conditioned signal. To address this issue, we introduce a principled formulation of classifier-free guidance (CFG) for regression-based vision-language driving. We show that CFG can be interpreted as isolating the instruction-induced residual in the action space by contrasting conditional and unconditional predictions, thereby explicitly amplifying the effect of the navigation command at inference time. However, a standard two-pass CFG introduces prohibitive latency for real-time control and produces noisy instance-level guidance directions. Building on a mean-shift interpretation of CFG, we propose Latent-Centroid Steering (LCS), a single-pass guidance mechanism that replaces instance-level residuals with class-level latent shifts. By projecting conditional representations toward precomputed command-specific centroids, LCS performs class-level latent steering based on cluster geometry that is both more stable and computationally efficient. We demonstrate that LCS reduces inference latency by approximately 50% while achieving stronger command adherence and improved driving performance on both closed-loop (Bench2Drive) and open-loop (nuScenes) benchmarks. Code will be released.

</details>


### [39] [Semantically Calibrated Evidence Composition for CT Vision-Language Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00239)
*Guoliang You,Haifan Gong,Xiaomeng Chu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SCOPE is a framework for semantically calibrated evidence composition in CT vision-language learning, which extracts context-aware organ evidence via mask-guided queries and composes it into a unified representation through Local-Global Coupling, calibrated with diagnostic summaries, achieving SOTA performance on CT-RATE (85.0 macro AUC) and RadChestCT (72.2 macro AUC).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CT-report representation learning methods either emphasize global alignment (which leaves localized evidence implicit) or anatomy-level correspondence (which does not specify how independent evidence should interact and acquire study-level meaning). There is a gap in explicitly bridging localized evidence with study-level semantics without reducing the CT representation to a fixed set of organs.

Method: SCOPE uses organ-specific report supervision with mask-guided queries that have fixed anatomical identities to extract context-aware organ evidence from shared, uncropped volumetric features. An unrestricted global query retains whole-volume context and drives Local-Global Coupling to compose organ evidence into a unified representation. The composed evidence is calibrated with the diagnostic summary for study-level semantic supervision, then integrated as a controlled residual into a context-preserving whole-volume representation aligned with the complete report.

Result: On CT-RATE and RadChestCT, SCOPE achieves macro AUCs of 85.0 and 72.2, respectively, outperforming previous SOTA by 7.2 and 4.2 points, with substantial gains in linear probing and cross-modal retrieval.

Conclusion: The progressive pathway connecting localized evidence with study-level semantics is effective, demonstrating that semantically calibrated evidence composition improves CT vision-language representation learning without constraining the representation to a predefined organ set.

Abstract: Learning transferable representations from CT-report pairs requires combining whole-volume context with anatomy-specific evidence. Existing methods typically emphasize either global CT-report alignment or fine-grained anatomy-level correspondence. Global alignment preserves broad study context but leaves the contribution of localized evidence implicit, whereas anatomy-level alignment explicitly grounds local findings but does not specify how independently represented evidence should interact, acquire study-level meaning, and contribute to a global CT representation. To address this gap, we propose SCOPE (Semantic Calibration Of comPosed Evidence), a framework for semantically calibrated evidence composition in CT vision-language learning. Under organ-specific report supervision, mask-guided queries with fixed anatomical identities extract context-aware organ evidence from shared, uncropped volumetric features, while an unrestricted global query retains access to whole-volume context. The global query then drives Local-Global Coupling to compose the organ evidence into a unified evidence representation. The composed evidence is subsequently calibrated using the diagnostic summary, providing study-level semantic supervision beyond local organ descriptions, and is finally integrated as a controlled residual into a context-preserving whole-volume representation aligned with the complete report. This progressive pathway connects localized evidence with study-level semantics without reducing the CT representation to a predefined set of organs. On CT-RATE and RadChestCT, SCOPE achieves macro AUCs of 85.0 and 72.2, respectively, outperforming the previous SOTA by 7.2 and 4.2, while also yielding substantial gains in linear probing and cross-modal retrieval. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of semantically calibrated evidence composition.

</details>


### [40] [MDWD: A Street-Level Dataset for Municipal Solid Waste Detection in Dense Urban Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00257)
*Andrea Filiberto Lucas,Mark Bugeja,Carl James Debono,Dylan Seychell*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Maltese Domestic Waste Dataset (MDWD), a street-level benchmark with 3,697 high-resolution images and 11,461 annotated instances across five domestic waste categories, establishing reproducible baselines with YOLO-family models and transformer-based detectors. RF-DETR-M achieves the best performance with 94.49% mAP50 and 93.56% F1-score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Municipal solid waste detection is under-represented in dedicated benchmark resources. Existing waste datasets only address individual litter detection, aerial imagery, or image-level classification, and none simultaneously provide street-level imagery, instance-level localization, and categorization of domestic waste streams within a structured municipal collection context.

Method: The authors constructed MDWD by collecting and manually annotating 3,697 high-resolution street-level images with 11,461 instances across five domestic waste categories reflecting Malta's municipal collection system. They then conducted a cross-architecture benchmark comparing multiple generations of YOLO detectors against a transformer-based detector (RF-DETR) to establish reproducible baselines.

Result: RF-DETR-M achieved the strongest overall performance with an mAP50 of 94.49% and F1-score of 93.56%. Smaller-capacity variants maintained competitive accuracy with substantially reduced parameter counts, demonstrating that the dataset supports both compact real-time detectors and transformer-based models.

Conclusion: MDWD provides a comprehensive street-level benchmark for vision-based municipal waste monitoring, establishing a foundation for future research in automated urban waste detection with reproducible baselines across diverse detection architectures.

Abstract: Automated visual monitoring of urban environments is a growing Computer Vision research area, but municipal solid waste detection remains under-represented in dedicated benchmark resources. Existing waste-related datasets predominantly address individual litter detection, aerial imagery, or image-level classification, and none simultaneously provide street-level imagery, instance-level localization, and categorization of domestic waste streams within a structured municipal collection context. This paper introduces the Maltese Domestic Waste Dataset (MDWD), a street-level benchmark comprising 3,697 high-resolution images and 11,461 manually annotated instances across five domestic waste categories representative of Malta's municipal collection system. The dataset captures substantial variation in location, illumination, object scale, occlusion, and urban context. To establish reproducible baselines, a cross-architecture benchmark is conducted across multiple generations of the YOLO family and a transformer-based detector. On the test set, RF-DETR-M achieves the strongest overall performance with an mAP50 of 94.49% and an F1-score of 93.56%, whilst smaller-capacity variants maintain competitive accuracy at substantially reduced parameter counts. These results indicate that MDWD supports effective training across both compact real-time detectors and transformer-based models, establishing a benchmark for future research in vision-based municipal waste monitoring.

</details>


### [41] [Interpretability-Guided Soft Pruning of Attention Heads in Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00264)
*Kamil Książek,Piotr Suszyński,Michał Jan Włodarczyk,Jacek Tabor,Przemysław Biecek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces SAPER, an interpretable-guided, end-to-end differentiable pruning framework for Vision Transformers that uses spectral analysis of attention head Laplacian eigenvectors to identify functional redundancies and prune attention heads, achieving favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs on ImageNet-1K.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision foundation models like DINOv2 produce rich representations but rely on massive, opaque architectures with high computational and memory costs. There is a need for interpretable-guided, efficient pruning solutions to reduce these costs.

Method: The approach has three components: (1) spectral analysis and visualization of individual attention heads using Laplacian eigenvectors of their attention maps, (2) semantic clustering of attention heads based on block structure observations to identify functional redundancies, and (3) SAPER, a soft attention pruning framework using the LapSum Soft Top-K approach for end-to-end differentiable pruning.

Result: Experiments on ImageNet-1K show SAPER achieves a highly favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, outperforming the RAPTOR baseline in FLOPs reduction while maintaining strong classification performance.

Conclusion: SAPER demonstrates that interpretable spectral analysis of attention heads can guide effective pruning in Vision Transformers, providing an efficient alternative to opaque pruning methods while preserving performance.

Abstract: Vision foundation models, such as DINOv2, learn highly expressive representations but rely on massive, opaque architectures that demand substantial computational power and memory. To provide an interpretable-guided and efficient solution to this issue, we first propose a spectral analysis and new visualization technique for individual attention heads based on the Laplacian eigenvectors of their attention maps. Building upon recent observations regarding the block structure of Vision Transformers, we perform semantic clustering of attention heads and identify functional redundancies. Leveraging these insights, we introduce SAPER (Soft Attention PrunER), an end-to-end differentiable pruning framework based on the LapSum Soft Top-K approach. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K demonstrate that SAPER achieves a highly favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, outperforming the competitive RAPTOR baseline in FLOPs reduction while preserving strong classification performance.

</details>


### [42] [ORCA: ORgan-Centroid Aggregation for Training-Free 3D CT Visual Token Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00345)
*Renjie Liang,Zijian Xu,Jinqian Pan,Chengkun Sun,Zhengkang Fan,Shawn Li,You Qin,Mei Liu,Jie Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ORCA (ORgan-Centroid Aggregation) is a training-free, plug-and-play token compressor for 3D CT volumes that merges adjacent visual tokens using organ guidance and sinusoidal centroid encoding to preserve spatial layout. It achieves 64x visual context reduction and 50x KV-cache reduction while being 31x faster, consistently outperforming existing compression methods across two datasets and five encoders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D CT scans produce extremely long token sequences (thousands to tens of thousands per volume) when fed into vision-language models, which must be compressed before a language model can process them. Existing compression methods (e.g., grid average pooling) fail to preserve anatomical structure, blending distinct anatomy, lesions, and air into single tokens.

Method: ORCA merges adjacent tokens with organ guidance and adds a sinusoidal encoding of each region's centroid to preserve spatial layout. It is training-free and plug-and-play, producing an adjustable token set without any model change or text query.

Result: Evaluated on two datasets (CT-RATE and Merlin) and five encoders across attribute prediction (size, density, location, texture, disease) and text generation (VQA and report generation). At matched token budgets, ORCA consistently outperforms existing compression methods, achieving 64x visual context reduction, 50x KV-cache reduction, and 31x faster processing per volume.

Conclusion: ORCA demonstrates that organ-guided token aggregation with spatial encoding effectively preserves anatomical information for downstream 3D CT vision-language tasks, providing a practical and efficient compression solution without requiring training or model modifications.

Abstract: A 3D CT scan entering a vision-language model produces a long sequence of visual tokens, often thousands to tens of thousands per volume, and this sequence must be compressed before a language model can consume it. Token compression is well studied in general vision, but little of it targets 3D CT specifically. A common baseline is grid average, which pools regular grid cells and can blend distinct anatomy, lesion, and air into one token. We present \textbf{ORCA} (ORgan-Centroid Aggregation), a token compressor for 3D CT. It merges adjacent tokens with organ guidance and adds a sinusoidal encoding of each region's centroid to preserve spatial layout. This preserves the anatomical information a downstream model needs. ORCA is training-free and plug-and-play, producing an adjustable token set without any model change or text query. We evaluate it across two datasets (CT-RATE and Merlin) and five encoders. The evaluation spans two task types: attribute prediction over five families (size, density, location, texture, and disease) and text generation (visual question answering and report generation). At matched token budgets, ORCA improves consistently over existing compression methods. It shrinks the visual context $64\times$ and its KV-cache $50\times$, and is $31\times$ faster to process each volume. Code released at https://github.com/renjie-liang/ORCA-3DCT.

</details>
