Motivation: While LLMs are increasingly used for coding and can boost developer productivity, they still struggle with complex tasks. Prior research on errors in LLM-generated code has been limited in scope (single language, few problems, or few models), leaving no comprehensive understanding of which errors are common versus model- or language-specific. This gap motivates the need for systematic error characterization to set realistic expectations and design mitigation strategies.

Method: The authors compiled a corpus of 86,726 code samples containing compilation or runtime errors, generated by seven LLMs across four compiled languages. They used an LLM to classify errors by underlying cause, manually validated these classifications, and performed a comparative analysis measuring error prevalence by model, language, and problem difficulty.

Result: Error types vary strongly across languages and models. Even the largest models frequently make simple mistakes. Generated code often omits basic input validation or memory-safety checks, which can lead to overflows, resource exhaustion, or other reliability/security issues.

Conclusion: The labeled dataset and comparative analysis provide a comprehensive characterization of error patterns in LLM-generated code, highlighting common pitfalls across models and languages, and identifying systematic weaknesses (particularly around input validation and memory safety) that should inform mitigation strategies and expectations for LLM code generation quality.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being widely used for coding, with reports indicating that AI now generates an increasing share of production code. Studies show that LLMs can significantly improve developer productivity, yet they still struggle with more complex coding tasks. Just as understanding error modes in human-written code has been central to improving software quality, identifying and characterizing the errors in LLM-generated code is critical for setting realistic expectations and designing mitigation strategies. Prior research has been limited in scope, often focusing on a single language, a small number of problems, or a limited selection of models. As a result, there is still no comprehensive understanding of which errors are common and which are specific to certain models or languages. To address these gaps and develop a deeper understanding of the quality of LLM-generated code, we analyzed a corpus of 86,726 code samples that contained compilation or runtime errors. These samples were generated by seven LLMs across four compiled languages. We classified errors by their underlying causes using an LLM, manually validated these classifications, and performed a comparative analysis. This labeled data is then used to measure error prevalence by model, language, and problem difficulty, to identify common error patterns. Results show that, although error types vary strongly across languages and models, even the largest models frequently make simple mistakes. We also observe that generated code often omits basic input validation or memory-safety checks, which can lead to overflows, resource exhaustion, or other reliability/security issues.

</details>


### [302] [Vul4Py: Benchmarking Automated Vulnerability Repair in Python with Paired Exploit and Functional Oracles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00692)
*Tan Bui,Ting Zhang,Ferdian Thung,Yunpeng Xiong,Penghao Jiang,Xin Zhou,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces Vul4Py, a Python benchmark for Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) with paired oracles—both an exploit oracle and a pytest functional oracle—for 100 real vulnerabilities across 60 projects. Comparing six AVR approaches, software engineering agents dominate (OpenHands repairs 41/100), far outperforming directly prompted LLMs (4) and a specialized tool (2), with the paired oracle rejecting 15 patches that exploit-only oracles would wrongly accept.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Python AVR benchmarks lack rigorous verification: they accept patches based solely on proof-of-concept exploits, or apply functional tests only to a subset of projects that ship them. This misses functional regressions where a patch defeats the exploit but breaks unrelated behavior, making AVR comparisons unreliable.

Method: Vul4Py provides a benchmark where each of 100 real vulnerabilities (from 60 projects, 60 CWEs, 2017-2025) has a paired oracle: an exploit oracle (fail on vulnerable, pass on fixed) and a project-native pytest functional oracle (pass on both). Each instance has a pinned, reproducible environment. Six approaches across three categories (specialized repair tool, directly prompted LLMs, software engineering agents) are compared using this benchmark.

Result: Software engineering agents dominate: OpenHands repairs 41 of 100 vulnerabilities, versus 4 for the strongest directly prompted LLM and 2 for the specialized tool, all sharing the same backbone model. The paired oracle rejected 15 of 119 patches that an exploit-only oracle would accept, and 98 of 104 admitted patches were manually confirmed semantically equivalent to developer fixes.

Conclusion: Vul4Py enables trustworthy AVR evaluation by catching functional regressions that exploit-only benchmarks miss. The results demonstrate that software engineering agents significantly outperform both directly prompted LLMs and specialized repair tools, highlighting the importance of agentic workflows for effective vulnerability repair on Python.

Abstract: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has advanced rapidly across program analysis, machine learning, and Large Language Models (LLMs), but a verifiable, head-to-head comparison of AVR approaches on Python is still missing. Python underpins critical web, data, and machine-learning infrastructure, yet existing Python benchmarks accept a patch on the strength of a proof-of-concept exploit alone, or apply a functional test only on the subset of entries whose upstream project happens to ship one. Both therefore miss functional regressions, in which a patch defeats the exploit but breaks unrelated behavior. We present Vul4Py, a Python AVR benchmark in which every entry carries a paired oracle: an exploit oracle that must fail on the vulnerable revision and pass on the fixed one, together with a project-native pytest functional oracle that must pass on both. Vul4Py comprises 100 real vulnerabilities from 60 open-source projects, spanning 60 distinct CWEs and the years 2017 to 2025, each packaged with a pinned, reproducible per-instance environment. Using Vul4Py, we compare six approaches in three categories: a specialized vulnerability repair tool, directly prompted LLMs, and software engineering agents. The agents dominate: OpenHands repairs 41 of 100 vulnerabilities, against 4 for the strongest directly prompted LLM and 2 for the specialized tool, despite all three sharing the same backbone model. The paired oracle is what makes these counts trustworthy: it rejects 15 of the 119 patches that an exploit-only oracle would accept, and 98 of the 104 patches it admits are manually confirmed to be semantically equivalent to the developer's patches

</details>


### [303] [EduPluginBench: Executable Assurance for AI-Generated Educational Plugins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00739)
*Nizam Kadir*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: EduPluginBench is an executable benchmark and staged admission method for evaluating code-generation models on governed-plugin compliance concerns beyond compilation and functional testing, covering least privilege, telemetry consent, provenance, privileged-write authority, lifecycle constraints, and bounded failure. P0-P4 admission staging increased release-blocking-defect recall by 74.7 percentage points over P0-P2 with near-zero false rejections, but frozen transfer studies on 600 unmodified generations and a Moodle vulnerability dataset showed no conformance passes, preventing the results from being interpreted as independent real-defect effectiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation of code-generation models relies on compilation and functional tests, which fail to establish compliance with critical governance properties such as least privilege, telemetry consent, provenance, privileged-write authority, lifecycle constraints, and bounded failure. There is a need for an executable benchmark and admission method that assesses generated plugins for these governed-ecosystem compliance properties.

Method: The authors introduce EduPluginBench, an executable benchmark comprising 30 specifications and 1,440 activation-checked first-order mutants, with a staged admission method (P0-P4) for generated plugins. They conduct evaluations including a frozen transfer study of 600 unmodified generations from two coding models, an independently labelled Moodle vulnerability study with 16 vulnerable/fixed pairs, and a diagnostic 540-generation experiment testing post-hoc bounded repair.

Result: P0-P4 staged admission increased release-blocking-defect recall by 74.7 percentage points over P0-P2 (specification-clustered 95% CI 73.4-75.8) with no rejection among 120 clean references (95% Wilson upper bound 3.1%). However, in the frozen transfer study, only 300/600 generations parsed and none passed P0 or P0-P4 conformance (95% upper bound 0.64%); downstream assurance estimands were undefined. The Moodle study found no vulnerable revisions detected by the frozen generic PHP detector. The 540-generation diagnostic showed post-hoc bounded repair yielded 112 P0 passes all nonconforming, with recall increasing from 13.4% to 100%.

Conclusion: The benchmark demonstrates that staged admission with execution checks substantially improves recall of release-blocking defects in controlled settings. However, negative transfer and external-validation results mean the method's effectiveness on independent real defects cannot be established from these experiments. The negative results caution against reading controlled contract consistency as evidence of real-world vulnerability detection effectiveness, while the full artifact is released for reproduction.

Abstract: Code-generation models can produce executable components, but compilation and functional tests do not establish compliance with least privilege, telemetry consent, provenance, privileged-write authority, lifecycle constraints, or bounded failure. We introduce EduPluginBench, an executable benchmark and staged admission method for generated plugins in governed software ecosystems. Across 1,440 activation-checked first-order mutants from 30 specifications, P0-P4 increased release-blocking-defect recall by 74.7 percentage points (specification-clustered 95% CI 73.4-75.8) over P0-P2, with no observed rejection among 120 clean references (95% Wilson upper bound 3.1%). A frozen transfer study of 600 unmodified generations from two current coding models found that 300/600 parsed, but none passed P0 or achieved P0-P4 conformance (95% upper bound 0.64%); downstream assurance estimands were undefined. An independently labelled Moodle study retained 16 vulnerable/fixed pairs; the frozen generic PHP detector found no vulnerable revisions. These negative transfer results prevent controlled contract consistency from being read as independent real-defect effectiveness. An earlier 540-generation diagnostic found that post-hoc bounded repair yielded 112 P0 passes, all nonconforming, with recall increasing from 13.4% to 100%. The artifact retains protocols, public-source provenance, raw generations, row-level decisions, audits, analysis code, and reproduction instructions.

</details>


### [304] [Less Is More: Tuning Configurable Systems with Imperfect Fidelity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00759)
*Yulong Ye,Miqing Li,Tao Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MFTune leverages imperfect-fidelity environments (similar but cheaper to measure than the perfect-fidelity target) to partially tune highly configurable systems first, generating high-quality seeds that improve tuning efficiency and budget utilization, outperforming 10 state-of-the-art tuners in 83.33% of cases with up to 19.34% improvement and hours of budget savings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Configuration tuning for highly configurable systems is essential yet challenging due to the large number of options and the high cost of configuration measurement. The authors observe that tuning can be greatly improved by partially tuning under imperfect-fidelity environments, which are similar but cheaper to measure than the concerned perfect-fidelity environment.

Method: The paper codifies a conceptual framework of fidelity for configurable systems and proposes MFTune, a tuner that proactively explores over 10^4 possible imperfect-fidelity settings to approximate a useful one, striking a balance for tuning wideness. This generates high-quality seeds for perfect-fidelity tuning, ensuring tuning depth.

Result: Against 10 state-of-the-art tuners across diverse real-world systems (19 months of 24x7 running), MFTune performs considerably better on 83.33% of cases with up to 19.34% improvement, while achieving hours of budget savings in general.

Conclusion: The "less can be more" phenomenon is validated: partial tuning in imperfect-fidelity environments can significantly improve overall configuration tuning performance and budget utilization compared to directly tuning at perfect fidelity.

Abstract: Configuration tuning is essential for optimizing the performance of highly configurable systems, e.g., throughput or runtime, under a given environment. Yet, this is a challenging process as there can be many options to tune, and configuration measurement is often highly expensive. In this paper, we demonstrate the phenomenon of ``less can be more'': system configuration tuning can be greatly improved with much superior budget utilization by partially tuning under the imperfect-fidelity---an environment that is similar, but cheaper to measure, compared with the concerned perfect-fidelity of environment under which the system should be tuned. We codify a conceptual framework of fidelity for configurable systems, drawing on which allows us to propose MFTune, a tuner that proactively explores in the space of $>10^4$ possible imperfect-fidelity settings to approximate a useful one, which strikes for the wideness of tuning. This creates high-quality seeds for the perfect-fidelity, which in turn ensures the tuning depth. Experiment results against $10$ state-of-the-art tuners, obtained from running diverse real-world systems for $19$ months $24 \times 7$, show that MFTune performs considerably better on $83.33$\% cases with up to $19.34\%$ improvement while achieving hours of budget saving in general.

</details>


### [305] [Turning Interaction History into Execution State: A Runtime Layer for Long-Horizon Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00808)
*Zehao Wang,Yisen Xu,Chenglin Li,Chao Peng,Bram Adams,Ahmed E. Hassan,Tse-Hsun,Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Ledger is a deterministic runtime layer that maintains an explicit execution ledger—tracking what has been observed, modified, and attempted—for long-horizon coding agents. It injects a compact state view before each decision and checks/validates proposed commands before they run, eliminating redundant work and stale-state errors. Across 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, it boosts Pass@1 from 56.2% to 64.2% (GPT-5 mini) and 75.8% to 81.0% (MiniMax M2.5) while cutting cost by ~29–32%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon coding agents accumulate long action-observation trajectories but their raw history contains no explicit record of which observations still reflect the current repository state. The model must implicitly infer execution status before every decision, leading to actions based on stale file contents or redundant re-execution of still-valid work.

Method: Ledger is a deterministic runtime layer that distills completed agent interactions into an explicit execution state (observed, modified, attempted) maintained in an online ledger. It applies at two boundaries per step: (1) an inform path appends a compact runtime state view to the prompt before the model acts, and (2) a govern path checks proposed commands against the ledger before they execute, returning still-valid earlier results instead of re-execution and flagging redundant repetition. It adds no language-model calls and wraps an unmodified agent.

Result: Across 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, Ledger raises Pass@1 from 56.2% to 64.2% with GPT-5 mini and from 75.8% to 81.0% with MiniMax M2.5, cutting total cost by 28.9% and 31.8%. With OpenAI Codex it adds 3.4 percentage points of Pass@1 at 24.4% lower cost. Ablations attribute most resolution gain to govern and most efficiency gain to inform, with the combination performing best.

Conclusion: What long-horizon agents lack is not a shorter view of history but an explicit account of their own execution state. An explicit, maintained execution ledger—provided via prompt augmentation and command validation—substantially improves both task success and cost efficiency without any additional language-model calls.

Abstract: Long-horizon coding agents accumulate hundreds of actions and observations in their trajectories, yet nothing in this record indicates which observations still describe the repository as it currently stands. Before every decision, the model must implicitly infer the execution status from raw history, and when this inference falls short, the agent acts on outdated file contents or re-executes work whose results are still valid. We propose Ledger, a deterministic runtime layer that distills an agent's completed interactions into an explicit execution state: what has been observed, what has been modified, and what has been attempted. Ledger keeps this state in an online execution ledger and applies it at two boundaries of every step. Before the model acts, an inform path appends a compact runtime state view to the prompt; before a proposed command runs, a govern path checks it against the ledger, returning still-valid earlier results in place of re-execution and flagging likely-redundant repetition. The layer adds no language-model calls and wraps an otherwise unmodified agent. Across all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, Ledger raises Pass@1 from 56.2% to 64.2% with GPT-5 mini and from 75.8% to 81.0% with MiniMax M2.5, while cutting total cost by 28.9% and 31.8%. Attached to OpenAI Codex, it adds 3.4 percentage points of Pass@1 at 24.4% lower cost. Ablations attribute most of the resolution gain to govern and most of the efficiency gain to inform, with their combination performing best. What long-horizon agents lack, we conclude, is not a shorter view of their history but an explicit account of their own execution state.

</details>


### [306] [Structure-Aware Semantic Chunking with Title-Chain Prefixes: A 1600-Query Evaluation and the Measurement Trap in Text-Transform Ablations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00824)
*Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A chunk-side-only semantic chunking pipeline (header-split, semantic merge, title-chain prefixing) that costs zero additional LLM calls improves MRR@5 from 0.374 to 0.463 (+23.8%) on a 1600-query production Markdown knowledge base. The central methodological finding is that stripping title-chain context in ablations collapses annotator agreement from kappa 0.45 to 0.04, revealing a measurement trap that invalidates common evaluation practices in chunking research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chunking is the first and most consequential step in RAG since every downstream retrieval decision inherits chunk boundaries. The authors aim to improve retrieval quality through better chunking while avoiding the cost of additional LLM calls, and to uncover measurement pitfalls in chunking evaluation.

Method: The pipeline has three stages: (1) header-split that segments documents by their header hierarchy, (2) semantic merge that combines related chunks, and (3) title-chain prefixing that reuses the document's own header hierarchy as context (rather than generating a summary). The evaluation uses 1600 stratified queries over a production Markdown knowledge base with dual-annotator relevance scoring. The paper also systematically reports failed approaches: three unevaluated design dead ends, one measured failure (prefix weight decay), and a protocol-level failure investigated via a same-pool prefix on/off ablation.

Result: The pipeline improves MRR@5 from 0.374 to 0.463 (+23.8%) on the full set and from 0.828 to 0.925 (+11.7%) on the answerable subset (n=563), with dual-annotator Cohen's kappa 0.45 across 16,000 score pairs. The protocol-level ablation shows that removing title-chain context collapses annotator agreement from kappa 0.45 to 0.04 under identical prompts, demonstrating that common evaluation practice (same-pool prefix on/off ablation) is invalid for chunking research.

Conclusion: The chunk-side-only semantic chunking pipeline with title-chain prefixing is effective and cost-free (no extra LLM calls). More importantly, the authors identify a critical measurement trap: evaluating chunking methods in a same-pool ablation framework strips the disambiguation signal annotators need, destroying agreement and invalidating results. They recommend retrieval-time per-candidate prefix evaluation as the direction forward.

Abstract: Chunking is the first and most consequential step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): every downstream retrieval decision inherits the chunk boundaries. We present a three-stage, chunk-side-only semantic chunking pipeline---header-split, semantic merge, and title-chain prefixing---that costs zero additional LLM calls: the title chain reuses the document's own header hierarchy instead of a generated summary. On a 1600-query stratified evaluation over a production Markdown knowledge base, the pipeline improves MRR@5 from 0.374 to 0.463 (+23.8%) on the full set and from 0.828 to 0.925 (+11.7%) on the answerable subset (n=563), with dual-annotator Cohen's kappa 0.45 (unweighted, 16,000 score pairs). We then report what we tried and what failed: three query-side or architecture-level follow-ups are design dead ends (unevaluated---no comparable run artifacts), one measured failure (prefix weight decay), and one protocol-level failure that is the paper's central methodological finding. In a same-pool prefix on/off ablation, dual-annotator agreement collapsed from kappa 0.45 to 0.04 under identical prompts---stripping the title-chain context strips the disambiguation signal annotators need to agree on relevance. This measurement trap invalidates a common evaluation practice in chunking research and motivates retrieval-time per-candidate prefix evaluation, the direction we recommend from all our evidence.

</details>


### [307] [Documentation vs. Code Patterns: What Drives LLM-Based Exception Oracle Generation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00884)
*Soneya Binta Hossain,Matthew B. Dwyer,Tasfia Tasnim*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper conducts an intervention-based study of three LLM-based test oracle generation (TOG) systems to determine what evidence drives exception oracle predictions. It finds that removing Javadoc @throws clauses causes only marginal accuracy changes (<1 percentage point), and attribution-guided substitution ablations reveal that high accuracy is often driven by shortcut signals (e.g., structural tokens or lexical cues) rather than meaningful exception semantics. The authors call for evaluating TOG systems not just on prediction correctness but also on whether predictions are grounded in genuine exception-triggering evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based TOG methods report high accuracy on exception oracle generation, but the underlying evidence driving these predictions is unclear. The authors aim to determine whether models rely on explicit exceptional-behavior documentation (e.g., Javadoc @throws) or on recurring patterns in tests, code, and documentation, challenging the assumption that high accuracy reflects robust use of exception semantics.

Method: The study employs a large-scale intervention-based methodology across three TOG systems (classifier-based and generative architectures, ~110M to 7B parameters) evaluated on three real-world benchmarks, including two generated-test datasets and a new developer-written test benchmark. Interventions include (1) removing Javadoc @throws clauses to test documentation dependence, and (2) attribution-guided substitution ablations to identify signals driving predictions.

Result: Removing Javadoc @throws clauses yields only marginal accuracy changes (largest drop below 1 percentage point), indicating structured exception documentation is not the primary predictor driver. Attribution-guided substitution ablations show high accuracy can be driven by shortcut signals: some models are highly sensitive to a small number of structural tokens, while others distribute reliance across many lexical cues.

Conclusion: Strong exception-oracle accuracy does not necessarily reflect robust use of exception semantics. Future TOG systems should be evaluated both on whether they predict the correct oracle type and on whether their predictions are grounded in meaningful exception-triggering evidence.

Abstract: LLM-based test oracle generation (TOG) methods report high accuracy on exception oracle generation, but it remains unclear what evidence drives these predictions. In particular, do models use explicit exceptional-behavior documentation such as Javadoc @throws clauses, or do they rely on recurring patterns in tests, code, and documentation?
  We investigate this question through a large-scale intervention-based study of three TOG systems spanning classifier-based and generative architectures and model sizes from roughly 110M to 7B parameters, evaluated on three real-world benchmarks comprising two generated-test datasets and a new benchmark of developer-written tests. We first remove Javadoc @throws clauses and find that accuracy changes only marginally, with the largest drop below one percentage point. This indicates that structured exception documentation is not the primary driver of exception-oracle prediction. We then apply attribution-guided substitution ablations to identify the signals that predictions depend on. The results show that high accuracy can be driven by shortcut signals: some models are highly sensitive to a small number of structural tokens, while others distribute reliance across many lexical cues. These findings challenge the assumption that strong exception-oracle accuracy reflects robust use of exception semantics. Future TOG systems should therefore be evaluated not only by whether they predict the correct oracle type, but also by whether their predictions are grounded in meaningful exception-triggering evidence.

</details>


### [308] [Joint Optimization of Human Headcount and Stochastic AI Resource Capacity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00886)
*Marco Montes de Oca*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper models the optimal allocation of a fixed budget between human headcount and generative-AI token capacity under stochastic token consumption and cognitive auditing costs, deriving closed-form solutions and comparative statics via a chance-constrained stochastic budget frontier with Cornish-Fisher skewness correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations adopting generative AI face unpredictable and often significant token costs that strain fixed budgets. Standard deterministic planning ignores both the heavy-tailed volatility of token consumption and the cognitive cost of auditing AI output, so leadership lacks a rigorous framework for splitting budgets between human headcount and AI token capacity.

Method: The authors model the joint allocation by intersecting a cognitive-friction-adjusted production function with a chance-constrained stochastic budget frontier. Per-engineer token usage is treated as i.i.d., non-negative, and right-skewed, requiring only mean, variance, and skewness (no parametric family). The chance constraint is reduced to a deterministic equivalent using the CLT with a Cornish-Fisher skewness correction. A Lagrangian formulation yields closed-form optimal headcount, a transcendental condition for optimal per-capita token intensity, and a bordered-Hessian second-order condition.

Result: Rising individual token volatility increases optimal per-capita token intensity while contracting headcount—human labor and tokens are production complements but stochastic-budget substitutes at the margin. Individual usage skewness acts as a pure deadweight tax shrinking the budget without altering substitution dynamics. If usage dispersion scales proportionally with the mean instead of being invariant, the substitution effect reverses.

Conclusion: The framework provides closed-form, testable conditions for optimal human-AI budget allocation under stochasticity. The key empirical question is whether usage dispersion is invariant to the planned mean allocation or scales with it, as this determines the direction of substitution between headcount and token capacity.

Abstract: Generative AI tools are rapidly becoming standard for coding and other business operations. However, while these tools can drive productivity, their unpredictable, and often significant, costs are putting severe financial strain on organizations. The leadership of such organizations must split a fixed budget between human headcount and generative-AI token capacity, yet standard deterministic planning ignores both the heavy-tailed volatility of token consumption and the cognitive cost of auditing AI-generated output. We model the joint allocation by intersecting a cognitive-friction-adjusted production function with a chance-constrained stochastic budget frontier. Per-engineer token usage is treated as i.i.d., non-negative, and right-skewed; no parametric family is assumed, as only its mean, variance, and skewness enter the analysis. The chance constraint is reduced to a deterministic equivalent via the Central Limit Theorem with a Cornish--Fisher skewness correction. Solving the resulting Lagrangian yields a closed-form optimal headcount, a transcendental condition for optimal per-capita token intensity, and a bordered-Hessian second-order condition that holds for any reasonable volatility-to-headcount ratio. Comparative statics show that rising individual token volatility raises optimal per-capita token intensity while contracting headcount: although human labor and tokens are complements in production, the stochastic budget makes them substitutes at the margin. Individual usage skewness acts as a pure deadweight tax that shrinks the budget without altering the substitution dynamics. Both conclusions presuppose that usage dispersion is invariant to the planned mean allocation. In the case where dispersion instead scales proportionally with the mean, the substitution reverses, so which regime applies is a sharp, empirically testable question.

</details>


### [309] [RefactorAssist: Agentic Refinement for Reliable Code Refactoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00924)
*Jonathan Cordeiro,Shayan Noei,Ying Zou*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces RefactorAssist, an agentic approach that improves the functional correctness of LLM-generated code refactorings by analyzing root causes of failures and using static checks plus test-guided, context-aware iterative repair, achieving up to a 70.8% repair rate on remaining failures and a 94.2% cumulative pass rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs show promise for automating code refactoring, but their generated refactorings often introduce subtle errors that change functional behavior and cause unit test failures, limiting practical adoption. The authors seek to understand and address these reliability issues.

Method: The authors (1) manually evaluate LLM-generated refactorings against native test suites across 10 open-source Java projects to identify failure root causes; (2) design RefactorAssist, an agentic approach that leverages unit-test logs, error explanations, project context retrieval, and code diffs to guide iterative refactoring; (3) apply a static repair step (dealing with missing imports, unbalanced brackets, compilation errors) before invoking LLMs to reduce cost.

Result: Root causes include context misunderstanding/hallucination (24.3%), incorrect renaming (15.3%), added functionality/variables (13.7%), code incompleteness (11.3%), syntax errors (9.7%), edge cases (9%), type handling (8.7%), and out-of-scope variables (8%). RefactorAssist achieves up to a 70.8% repair rate on remaining failures and a 94.2% cumulative pass rate under the best configuration.

Conclusion: Static checks combined with test-guided, context-aware agentic repair can significantly increase the reliability of LLM-generated refactorings, making them more viable for practical integration into developer workflows.

Abstract: Code refactoring aims to enhance the internal structure of source code without affecting its functional behavior. The recent advancements of Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential for automating software engineering tasks, such as code refactoring. However, the refactorings produced by LLMs often introduce subtle errors, leading to functional behavior changes and failed unit tests, which limit their practical adoption. To address the limitations of LLM-generated refactorings, we analyze the root causes of their failures and develop the RefactorAssist agent to improve the functional correctness of LLM-generated refactorings. To this end, we use 10 open-source Java projects with their native test suites and manually evaluate why LLM-generated refactorings fail unit tests. We then design an agentic approach that leverages unit-test logs, error explanations, project context retrieval, and code diffs to guide the iterative refactoring. Our findings show that the main reasons for failure are context misunderstanding/hallucination (24.3%), incorrect or inconsistent renaming (15.3%), adding new functionality or variables (13.7%), code incompleteness (11.3%), syntax and structural errors (9.7%), edge cases not handled (9%), improper type handling (8.7%), and variables outside scope (8%). To make our approach cost-effective, RefactorAssist first applies a static repair step for missing imports, unbalanced brackets, and compilation errors without LLMs. For remaining failures, RefactorAssist incorporates error logs and code diffs, achieving up to a 70.8% repair rate on the remaining failures and a 94.2% cumulative pass rate under the best-performing configuration. These results indicate that static checks and test-guided, context-aware agentic repair can increase the reliability of LLM-generated refactorings, bringing them closer to practical integration within developer workflows.

</details>


### [310] [Claim Plane: Reliability Gains and the Limits of Selective Concurrency for Parallel Coding Agents: A 30-Pair, Three-Seed Confirmatory Study of Deterministic Pre-Write Admission](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00947)
*Maxim Nikolaev*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Claim Plane is a deterministic pre-write admission mechanism for parallel coding agents that validates versioned change intents before writes. A confirmatory study on 30 CooperBench feature pairs (15 conflict, 15 clean) with 360 executions shows static Claim Plane raises pair pass from 23.3% to 50.0% and integration success from 65.6% to 96.7%, but largely by serializing 96.7% of executions. Dynamic admission serializes less (66.7% conflict, 13.3% clean) but fails closed on 46/90 executions due to region undercoverage, reducing pair pass to 22.2%. The mechanism improves reliability but does not establish wall-clock parallel speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parallel coding agents frequently produce locally valid but globally conflicting changes when combined. The authors aim to address this failure mode through a deterministic pre-write admission control mechanism over versioned change intents, and to empirically assess whether such admission improves reliability (pair pass) and whether it preserves parallel speedup.

Method: Confirmatory study on 30 frozen CooperBench feature pairs (15 conflict, 15 clean), with three coder seeds and four coordination arms, totaling 360 completed executions. DeepSeek V4 Pro generated 60 frozen feature-level planner declarations; DeepSeek V4 Flash performed coding. Static admission checks change intents before writes; dynamic admission selectively applies checks. Pair pass, integration success, serialization rate, and failure modalities are measured via paired task-cluster bootstrap analysis.

Result: Static Claim Plane raised pair pass from 23.3% to 50.0% (+26.7 pp, 95% CI 9.6–60.0) and integration success from 65.6% to 96.7%. On conflict-labeled pairs, pair pass rose from 6.7% to 60.0%. However, static admission serialized 96.7% of executions (93.3% of clean cases). Dynamic admission serialized 66.7% conflict and 13.3% clean cases, but 46/90 executions failed closed on undeclared scope (45 targeting files already in frozen declarations), reducing pair pass to 22.2%.

Conclusion: Pre-write admission is an effective reliability mechanism for parallel coding agents, but static admission recovers reliability primarily by collapsing toward serial execution, and dynamic admission suffers from region undercoverage and insufficient amendment handling. The study does not establish useful wall-clock parallel speedup since provider calls were physically sequential. All artifacts and clustered bootstrap analysis are publicly released for reproduction.

Abstract: Parallel coding agents can produce locally valid changes that fail when combined. Claim Plane addresses this failure mode as deterministic pre-write admission over versioned change intents. This paper reports a confirmatory study on 30 frozen CooperBench feature pairs, balanced between 15 conflict and 15 clean labels, with three coder seeds, four coordination arms, and 360 completed executions. DeepSeek V4 Pro generated 60 feature-level planner declarations once; the declarations were frozen across all arms and coder seeds, while DeepSeek V4 Flash performed the coding work. Static Claim Plane raised pair pass from 23.3% under unconstrained parallel execution to 50.0%, a paired task-cluster difference of +26.7 percentage points (95% bootstrap CI 9.6 to 60.0), and raised integration success from 65.6% to 96.7%. On conflict-labeled pairs, pair pass rose from 6.7% to 60.0%. However, static admission serialized 96.7% of executions, including 93.3% of clean cases, and therefore recovered reliability largely by collapsing toward serial execution. Dynamic admission was more selective, serializing 66.7% of conflict cases and 13.3% of clean cases, but 46 of 90 executions failed closed on undeclared scope, reducing pair pass to 22.2%. Forty-five of those 46 blocks targeted files already present in the frozen declarations, indicating region undercoverage and insufficient amendment handling rather than wholly unknown files. The results support pre-write admission as a reliability mechanism, but they do not establish useful wall-clock parallel speedup: provider calls were physically sequential, and the conservative policy largely serialized the workload. The complete study artifacts, hashes, and clustered bootstrap analysis are publicly released for reproduction.

</details>


### [311] [AgenTag: Attribution of AI Coding Agents from Behavioral Fingerprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00966)
*Taher A. Ghaleb*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgenTag is a multimodal framework for open-world attribution of AI coding agents in pull requests, achieving a weighted F1 of 0.96 on a dataset of 33,580 AI-authored and 6,618 human-authored PRs. Key findings: PR descriptions and commit messages carry nearly all attribution signal while code diffs contribute little, and latent stylistic fingerprints persist even after removing explicit self-disclosed markers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents increasingly author pull requests under developers' accounts, obscuring true authorship. Reliable attribution is critical for repository governance, empirical studies of AI-assisted development, and measuring AI coding agent impact. Existing work only handles closed-set identification of known agents, leaving open-world attribution limits unexplored.

Method: AgenTag represents PRs using three modalities—textual, behavioral, and code-based—and compares conventional classification with supervised contrastive learning for open-set recognition and few-shot enrollment of unseen agents. Evaluation is performed on the AIDev dataset comprising 33,580 PRs from five AI coding agents and 6,618 human-authored PRs.

Result: AgenTag achieves weighted F1 of 0.96 (macro F1 0.84) for agent identification, balanced F1 of 0.89 for distinguishing AI- from human-authored PRs, and AUC of 0.84 for detecting previously unseen agents. Ablation shows PR descriptions and commit messages provide nearly all attribution signal, while code diffs contribute little. Behavioral fingerprints persist after removing explicit self-disclosed markers.

Conclusion: Reliable open-world attribution of AI coding agents is feasible. Attribution relies largely on latent stylistic characteristics in how agents communicate changes rather than the code they generate, and there are clear practical trade-offs between attribution accuracy and the information required to achieve it.

Abstract: AI coding agents increasingly author pull requests (PRs), often under developers' own accounts, obscuring who actually produced a change. Reliable attribution is important for repository governance, empirical studies of AI-assisted software development, and measuring the impact of AI coding agents. Existing work focuses on closed-set identification of known agents, leaving the practical limits of open-world AI coding agent attribution largely unexplored. In this paper, we present AgenTag, a multimodal framework for open-world AI coding agent attribution, evaluated on AIDev, comprising 33,580 PRs from five AI coding agents and 6,618 human-authored PRs. We represent each PR using textual, behavioral, and code-based modalities, and compare conventional classification with supervised contrastive learning for open-set recognition and few-shot enrollment of previously unseen agents. AgenTag identifies authoring agents with a weighted F1 of 0.96 (macro F1 of 0.84), distinguishes AI- from human-authored PRs with a balanced F1 of 0.89, and detects previously unseen agents with an AUC of 0.84. We further show that PR descriptions and commit messages provide nearly all of the attribution signal, whereas code diffs contribute little across multiple representations, indicating that coding agents are distinguished primarily by how they communicate changes rather than by the code they generate. Moreover, these behavioral fingerprints persist after removing explicit self-disclosed markers, demonstrating that attribution relies largely on latent stylistic characteristics. These findings show that reliable attribution of AI coding agents is feasible and clarify the practical trade-offs between attribution accuracy and the information required to achieve it.

</details>


### [312] [Registry Descriptions Go Stale Unevenly: An 89-Day Measurement of Model Context Protocol Drift, and Why Drift-Ranked Re-Auditing Under-Covers It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00997)
*Gautam Bharti*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper audits the official MCP (Model Context Protocol) registry over 88.6 days with 120 observations (19,099 distinct servers, growing from 3,510 to 18,966), finding that description-level security findings cannot be kept current by re-auditing the most-drifted servers due to a sparse description surface and many changes landing on new arrivals. Content-binding (hash-based revalidation) plus a periodic full-catalog sweep is the recommended control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior security studies of the MCP ecosystem audit a registry at a single point in time, but none report how long the registry descriptions those audits judged stay current. This is a necessary condition for any description-level finding to still apply, so the authors measure the shelf-life of audited description text to evaluate whether single-point audits remain valid over time.

Method: The authors reconstruct 120 observations of the official MCP registry over 88.6 days, covering 19,099 distinct servers. They measure description drift versus descriptor drift, evaluate a drift-history-based re-audit ranking at a top-5% budget against held-out windows, and compare content-binding (revalidate when a description hash changes) against periodic full-catalog sweeps.

Result: At a top-5% re-audit budget, ranking by prior drift catches only ~20% of previously-seen description changers (~27% vs descriptor drift overall) and only ~10% of all description changers, though the ranking still buys ~4x lift. Only 8.6% of servers ever rewrite a description (vs 24.8% for descriptors); roughly half of all description changes land on new arrivals. Three-quarters of persistently observed servers never change, the most active 5% generate 61% of change events, and only 11.9% of a cohort's descriptors change within 30 days versus 35.8% predicted by naive compounding (73% at 89 days).

Conclusion: The limit is not unpredictability (ranking still buys 4x lift) but that the description surface is sparse and history rankings cannot reach new arrivals. The fitting control is content-binding (revalidate on hash change) plus a sized periodic full-catalog sweep; drift-history ranking is at best a partial, blind-to-new-arrivals control. This is scanner hygiene for a description-level auditor, not a runtime trust signal.

Abstract: Security studies of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem share a design: each audits a registry at a single point in time. None reports how long the registry descriptions those audits judged stay current - a necessary condition for any description-level finding to still apply, though not a sufficient one: we measure the shelf-life of the audited text, not the validity of a security finding itself (Sec. 7.1). We reconstruct 120 observations of the official MCP registry over 88.6 days, covering 19,099 distinct servers as it grew from 3,510 to 18,966. Our central result is a policy one: you cannot keep description-level findings current by re-auditing the servers that drift most. At a top-5% re-audit budget, ranking by prior drift catches only ~20% of the previously-seen servers whose description changes in a held-out window - versus ~27% for descriptor drift overall - and only ~10% of all description changers. The limit is not unpredictability: the ranking still buys ~4x lift. It is that the description surface is sparse - 8.6% of servers ever rewrite one, against 24.8% for descriptors - and that roughly half of all description changes land on new arrivals a history ranking cannot reach, so the same lift buys far less coverage. The control that fits is content-binding - revalidate the moment a description's hash moves - plus a sized periodic full-catalog sweep; a drift-history ranking is at best a partial, blind-to-new-arrivals control. This is scanner hygiene for a description-level auditor, not a runtime trust signal. Of servers observed across at least ten intervals, three-quarters never change, the most active 5% generate 61% of all change events, and only 11.9% of a cohort's descriptors change within 30 days; naive compounding predicts 35.8% at 30 days (73% at 89), a heavy-tail overestimate we use only as a diagnostic. We release the panel, figure generator, and analysis code.

</details>


### [313] [What Could the Agent See at 19:05? Generating Temporal Enterprise Scenarios from Real Research and Replaying Them to Evaluate Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01042)
*Tezan Sahu,Himani Arora*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a system that evaluates enterprise AI agents against temporally-evolving data worlds rather than static snapshots. It generates realistic, persona-driven enterprise environments from research data, then uses a schema-inferred temporal description with a deterministic-plus-LLM approach to rebuild historical record states. Since queryable moments are finite, all rebuilds are precomputed into a compact difference cache, making evaluation a fast, reproducible lookup with no model in the inference path.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AI agents operate in environments where data changes continuously, making answers correct only relative to the data state and access permissions at query time. Existing offline evaluation uses a single static snapshot (end of episode), which can only evaluate one situation and cannot capture the multi-app, time-ordered nature of real enterprise work. Recreating per-moment snapshots via tenant re-provisioning is prohibitively costly, and single snapshots leak future state from hidden records.

Method: The system generates a realistic, persona-driven, temporally-evolving enterprise world from real research, and replays that world at any chosen moment to evaluate pluggable agents. It uses a schema-inferred temporal description to drive a deterministic-plus-LLM rebuild of each record's past state. Because the number of queryable moments is finite, all rebuilds are precomputed into a compact difference cache, so evaluation is a fast, reproducible lookup with no model in the evaluation path.

Result: The authors describe the system design, an architecture spanning both the world-generation and evaluation flows, and report early experience evaluating enterprise agents.

Conclusion: The approach closes two gaps simultaneously: generating temporally-evolving enterprise worlds and enabling evaluation at any historical moment without prohibitive re-provisioning costs or future-state leakage, by precomputing finite historical states into a compact difference cache.

Abstract: Enterprise AI agents act across many apps whose data changes continuously, so an answer is correct only relative to what data existed and who could see it at the moment it was asked. Offline evaluation today grades against a single static snapshot, effectively the end of the episode. So, it can only evaluate one situation, the final one, even though every earlier moment of the episode is a different situation that invites its own realistic questions with its own correct answers. Recreating each of those moments as a separate snapshot would mean re-provisioning a whole tenant per instant, which is prohibitively costly; and even a single snapshot leaks future state hidden inside records and cannot represent the multi-app, time-ordered way real work happens. Our system closes two gaps at once: it generates a realistic, persona-driven, temporally-evolving enterprise world from real research, and replays that world at any chosen moment to evaluate any pluggable agent. A schema-inferred temporal description drives a deterministic-plus-LLM rebuild of each record's past state; because the queryable moments are finite, all rebuilds are precomputed into a compact difference cache, making evaluation a fast, reproducible lookup with no model in the path. We describe the design, an architecture spanning both flows, and early experience evaluating enterprise agents.

</details>


### [314] [MADE: Belief-Driven Dual-Agent Coordination for Autonomous Model Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01189)
*Yicheng Liu,Bolin Zhang,Weiran Liu,Yakun Zhang,Yangqin Jiang,Zhiying Tu,Dianhui Chu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MADE is a dual-agent coordination system that automates the deployment of open-source AI models into ready-to-call APIs, achieving a 68.85% deployment success rate—outperforming SWE-agent and OpenHands by 13.93 and 44.26 percentage points respectively—and introduces M2ABench, a benchmark with 122 real-world models for evaluating this task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents excel at general tasks but struggle with domain-specific ones, requiring external tools to broaden capabilities. While the open-source community offers numerous AI models, they are typically released as heterogeneous research artifacts that are costly to transform into callable APIs, and automated model deployment—a long-horizon, multi-stage task—remains underexplored.

Method: MADE employs a dual-agent coordination system that, given a model resource, iteratively constructs and validates deployment artifacts, updates its deployment belief based on execution feedback, and revisits invalid upstream artifacts until the model is successfully served as a ready-to-call API. The paper also constructs M2ABench, a benchmark comprising 122 real-world models with standardized test cases.

Result: MADE achieves a deployment success rate of 68.85%, outperforming SWE-agent and OpenHands by 13.93 and 44.26 percentage points, respectively.

Conclusion: The dual-agent iterative deployment system effectively bridges the gap between model resources and tool usability, demonstrating significant improvements over existing agents and providing a public benchmark to facilitate further research in automated model deployment.

Abstract: LLM-based agents now have strong general capabilities. However, they still struggle with domain-specific tasks, motivating the integration of external tools to broaden their capabilities. The open-source community offers a vast array of AI models typically released as heterogeneous research artifacts, whereas transforming them into ready-to-call APIs is costly and labor-intensive. Automated model deployment is therefore essential for bridging the gap between model resources and tool usability, yet it remains a long-horizon, multi-stage task that has not been sufficiently explored. To tackle this challenge, we introduce Model Automated Deployment Engine (MADE), a dual-agent coordination system. Specifically, given a model resource, MADE iteratively constructs and validates the deployment artifacts, updates its deployment belief based on execution feedback, and revisits invalid upstream artifacts until the model is successfully served as a ready-to-call API that can then be used by other agents. We further introduce M2ABench, a benchmark for the task of transforming Models to ready-to-call APIs. M2ABench comprises 122 real-world models with standardized test cases for evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that MADE achieves a deployment success rate of 68.85%, outperforming SWE-agent and OpenHands by 13.93 and 44.26 percentage points, respectively. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/HITDiSC/MADE.

</details>


### [315] [Doc2CI: A Multi-Service Study of CI Configuration Generation Using Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01451)
*Taher A. Ghaleb*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents DOC2CI, a benchmark of 3,363 description-to-YAML pairs from four CI services, and evaluates 16 LLMs (14 open-weight from 7B-34B plus GPT-4o and GPT-4.1) producing over 53,000 CI configurations. Results show exact reference reproduction never exceeds 3.1%, only 71% satisfy service schemas despite 97% parsing as YAML, model differences are driven by output completeness, and a training-free schema-guided repair method improves schema validity to 94% while fine-tuning improves similarity but reduces validity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CI configuration generation from natural language is a promising LLM application, but its effectiveness across CI services and model families is unclear. Given that YAML CI configs are error-prone and hard to maintain, understanding how well LLMs can generate them is essential to guide tooling and evaluation practices.

Method: The authors build DOC2CI, a benchmark of 3,363 description-to-YAML pairs from official documentation of four CI services. They evaluate 14 open-weight models (7B-34B parameters) alongside GPT-4o and GPT-4.1, generating over 53,000 configurations. They assess both reference alignment and schema validity, develop a failure taxonomy from manual analysis of 385 configurations, and investigate causes of disagreement. They also test a training-free schema-guided repair method and fine-tuning approaches.

Result: Exact reference reproduction never exceeds 3.1% across models and services. While 97% of outputs parse as YAML, only 71% satisfy service schemas. Larger models improve structural validity, but code-specialized models show no consistent advantage over general models. Model disagreements stem primarily from output completeness (some generate expected fragments while others produce full workflows). Schema-guided repair raises schema validity to 94%, whereas fine-tuning improves similarity to documentation but reduces standalone validity.

Conclusion: LLM-based CI configuration generation remains far from perfect: reference alignment is very low, and structural validity is a distinct objective from documentation similarity. The authors advocate for schema-aware evaluation and tooling for LLM-based configuration generation, since similarity and validity are not interchangeable goals.

Abstract: Adopting Continuous Integration (CI) often requires writing YAML configurations that are error-prone and challenging to maintain. Despite increasing LLM use in software engineering, their ability to generate CI configurations from natural language across services and model families remains unclear. This paper presents a large empirical study on using LLMs to generate CI configurations. We introduce DOC2CI, a benchmark of 3,363 description-to-YAML pairs collected from the official documentation of four CI services, and evaluate 14 open-weight models from 7B-34B parameters together with GPT-4o and GPT-4.1, producing over 53,000 configurations. We assess both reference alignment and schema validity to determine whether the generated configurations are structurally valid. We further develop a failure taxonomy from a manual analysis of 385 configurations and examine why LLMs disagree. Across models and services, exact reference reproduction never exceeds 3.1%, and while 97% of outputs parse as YAML, only 71% satisfy service schemas. Larger models improve structural validity, but code specialization provides no consistent advantage over comparable general models. Model differences are driven largely by output completeness: for the same request, some models generate the expected fragment while others produce a full workflow. Finally, a training-free schema-guided repair method improves schema validity to 94%, while fine-tuning improves similarity to documentation but reduces standalone validity. This suggests that similarity and validity are distinct objectives for CI generation and motivate schema-aware evaluation and tooling for LLM-based configuration generation.

</details>


### [316] [An Empirical Investigation of Soft Skills and Corresponding Challenges in International Software Engineering Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01469)
*Sajid Ibrahim Hashmi,Jouni Markkula*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents empirical findings from two focus groups on group work in international software engineering education, identifying the soft skills students need for teamwork and the associated challenges in international settings, offering guidance for university teachers and pedagogy experts to plan more effective student group work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Soft skills such as teamwork are essential for professional software development, and SE education should provide students opportunities to practice these skills. Understanding which soft skills are needed and what challenges arise in international group work can help educators design better collaborative learning experiences.

Method: The study employs empirical research through two focus groups conducted on group work, with emphasis on soft skills necessary for teamwork in international software engineering education, specifically student collaboration in higher education.

Result: The paper identifies several soft skills students should learn while practicing teamwork in course-related assignments and exercises, as well as challenges that arise in international educational settings.

Conclusion: The findings provide guidelines for university teachers and pedagogy experts to plan student group work more effectively in international SE education.

Abstract: Joint software development work requires the application of technical skills and professional practices. Soft skills, such as teamwork, remain essential to succeeding in a professional software development environment. The phenomenon is reflected by group work in SE (software engineering) education, where students can learn and practice teamwork-related soft skills. Therefore, SE education requires students to practice those skills so that they can actively embark on their professional careers in the software industry. In this research study, empirical findings from two focus groups we conducted on group work are presented, with emphasis on the soft skills necessary for teamwork in international software engineering education, specifically student collaboration in higher education. There are several soft skills students should learn as they practice teamwork in their course-related assignments and exercises, as well as the challenges that come with it in international settings. The findings serve as a guideline to university teachers and pedagogy experts to plan student group work more effectively.

</details>


### [317] [Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01507)
*Amirkia Rafiei Oskooei,Bora Ilci,Alperen Kayim,Mehmet Egemen Uzun,Berat Can,Kaan Emre Kara,Ozan Orhan,Mehmet S. Aktas*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper compares two approaches used by code agents to locate code in a repository: Semantic Search (vector index retrieval) and Deep Agentic Search (planning agent delegating to a subagent). On the SWE-QA benchmark, semantic search outperformed deep agentic search significantly (65.2% vs 46.2% accuracy) at less than half the cost. A failure-mode taxonomy reveals that deep agentic search introduces a new class of failures at the planner-subagent hand-off, which accounts for 41.8% of its failures and often produces confident but wrong answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep agentic search has been rapidly adopted by recent code agents (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, etc.) under the premise that it prevents context pollution, but there is little evidence on whether it actually produces better answers than the simpler semantic search approach. The paper aims to empirically test this assumption.

Method: The authors compare semantic search and deep agentic search on SWE-QA, a benchmark for repository-level code question answering. They measure accuracy and cost for both approaches, then code every failed run into a taxonomy of failure modes to understand why one approach outperforms the other.

Result: Semantic search answered 65.2% of questions correctly compared to 46.2% for deep agentic search, and produced correct answers at less than half the cost. The failure taxonomy shows deep agentic search did not eliminate failures but introduced a new major class: 41.8% of its failures occurred at the planner-subagent hand-off, usually silently ending in fluent but incorrect answers.

Conclusion: While deep agentic search addresses the real problem of context pollution and is now a preferred design in many code agents, the protection it offers comes at a cost. For read-only questions over an indexable repository, semantic search is both the stronger and cheaper option.

Abstract: Code agents spend much of their effort simply locating the right code inside a repository. Two approaches dominate current practice. In Semantic Search, the agent retrieves code blocks from a vector index built from the repository in advance. In Deep Agentic Search (also known as grep-search by subagent), a planning agent delegates the exploration to a separate subagent that works in an isolated context window and returns only a condensed result. The second design, which is considered good context engineering practice, exists to protect the main agent from context pollution (also known as context rot), the loss of accuracy that occurs as unrelated material accumulates in the context window. Recent code agents (such as Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, etc) have adopted it quickly, but there is little evidence on whether it produces better answers. We compare the two approaches on SWE-QA, a benchmark for repository-level code question answering. Semantic search answered 65.2% of questions correctly against 46.2% for deep agentic search, and it produced each correct answer at less than half the cost. To explain the gap, we then coded every failed run into a taxonomy of failure modes. The taxonomy shows that deep agentic search did not remove failures but introduced a new class of them: the single largest share of its failures, 41.8%, occurred at the hand-off between the planner and its sub-agent, and these were usually silent, ending in a fluent and confident answer that was wrong. Deep agentic search addresses a real problem and is now the preferred design in many code agents. However, our results show that the protection it offers may not be free, and that for read-only questions over a repository that can be indexed, retrieval was the stronger and cheaper option.

</details>


### [318] [Algorithm-driven Development: A Proactive Approach to Improving Software Quality and Reducing Defects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01533)
*Philippe Jawish,Pierre Evrard,Alexandre Lemerle,Adrian Genin,Layal Dergham,Séverin Lanfranchi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces Algorithm-Driven Development (ADD), an industrial methodology that translates requirements into algorithmic flowcharts from which acceptance tests are systematically derived, linking requirement modeling with automated test generation. Evaluated over four years at Dassault Systèmes across two teams, ADD demonstrated sustained code coverage above 95%, low defect density, and stable delivery cadence, with comparative analysis against TDD and test-last practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software engineering faces persistent challenges in ensuring quality while meeting deadlines and adapting to evolving requirements. There is a need for a methodology that bridges the gap between requirements, testing, and implementation to produce reliable, testable, and maintainable software behavior in industrial settings.

Method: ADD translates requirements into algorithmic flowcharts that serve dual purposes as specification artifacts and technical blueprints. These flowcharts enable systematic derivation of acceptance tests, providing coverage of functional scenarios including edge cases from the outset. The methodology was evaluated over four years in an industrial project at Dassault Systèmes involving two teams (22,444 lines of production code for Team 1; 157 APIs for Team 2), using longitudinal quality/delivery indicators and comparative analysis of ADD vs. TDD vs. test-last practices across API functions of varying complexity. Data was collected from internal lifecycle management and CI/CD systems.

Result: ADD supported sustained code coverage above 95%, demonstrated low defect density in both QA and post-release phases, and maintained a stable delivery cadence. Comparative analysis across API functions of different complexity levels showed favorable outcomes for ADD relative to TDD and test-last development practices.

Conclusion: ADD shows evidence of strengthening the connection between requirements, testing, and implementation in industrial software development contexts, offering a practical methodology that improves quality and delivery stability in real-world settings.

Abstract: Ensuring software quality while meeting deadlines and adapting to evolving requirements is a persistent challenge in software engineering practice. This paper introduces Algorithm-Driven Development (ADD), a methodology developed from industrial practice to address recurring challenges in translating requirements into reliable, testable, and maintainable software behavior. ADD translates requirements into algorithmic flowcharts from which acceptance tests are systematically derived. These flowcharts serve both as specification artifacts and as technical blueprints, supporting shared understanding between stakeholders and developers. By linking requirement modeling with automated test generation, ADD provides systematic coverage of functional scenarios, including edge cases, from the outset of development. The approach was evaluated over a four-year period within an industrial project at Dassault Systèmes, involving two development teams, 22,444 lines of production code for Team 1, and 157 APIs analyzed for Team 2. The evaluation combined longitudinal quality and delivery indicators with a comparative analysis of ADD, TDD, and test-last development practices across API functions of different complexity levels. Empirical data collected from internal lifecycle management and CI/CD systems show that ADD supported sustained code coverage above 95%, low defect density in both QA and post-release phases, and a stable delivery cadence. These findings provide evidence of ADD's potential to strengthen the connection between requirements, testing, and implementation in industrial software development contexts.

</details>


### [319] [How Well Do LLMs Generate Taxonomies in the SE Domain? A Multi-perspective Evaluation Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01592)
*Sota Nakashima,Yuta Ishimoto,Masanari Kondo,Tao Xiao,Yasutaka Kamei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents the first comprehensive empirical evaluation of automated taxonomy generation methods (TnT-LLM and CLIMB) applied to software engineering artifacts using five state-of-the-art LLMs. It finds a trade-off: TnT-LLM produces higher-quality taxonomies comparable to human-defined ones but is more expensive and slower, while CLIMB is 15-40x faster and 8-49x cheaper but struggles with technical inference. The authors recommend assessing taxonomy complexity and cost on a data subset before choosing between automated methods and human experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manually constructing taxonomies in SE research is labor-intensive and requires domain expertise. Although LLM-based automated taxonomy generation exists outside SE, its applicability to technically complex SE artifacts was unclear, motivating the need for a systematic evaluation in the SE context.

Method: The authors collected seven SE papers with publicly available artifacts and human-defined taxonomies, then evaluated two automated taxonomy generation methods (TnT-LLM and CLIMB) combined with five state-of-the-art LLMs. A multi-perspective evaluation framework was used covering taxonomy quality, alignment with human-expert-defined taxonomies, reliability under independent annotation, and efficiency.

Result: TnT-LLM generates high-quality taxonomies comparable to human-defined ones but at substantially higher cost and runtime, and tends to produce overly complex taxonomies. CLIMB is 15-40x faster and 8-49x cheaper but scores lower on quality when technical inference beyond surface-level similarity is required.

Conclusion: Both TnT-LLM and CLIMB can be practically used in SE domain, but researchers should first evaluate generated taxonomy complexity and cost on a subset of target data to decide between automated methods and human experts. This work provides a foundational step toward systematic understanding and offers actionable insights for future SE research and practice.

Abstract: Taxonomies provide a shared conceptual framework for organizing heterogeneous observations in software engineering (SE) research. Manually constructing such taxonomies is labor-intensive and requires annotators with expertise in the SE domain. While advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to the emergence of automated taxonomy generation methods outside the SE domain, their applicability to technically complex SE artifacts remains unclear. In this experience paper, we present the first comprehensive empirical evaluation of how state-of-the-art automated methods perform on SE artifacts through a multi-perspective evaluation framework, including taxonomy quality, alignment with taxonomies defined by human experts, reliability under independent annotation, and efficiency. To support this evaluation, we systematically collect seven SE papers with publicly available artifacts and human-defined taxonomies, and conduct experiments using two automated methods (TnT-LLM and CLIMB) with five state-of-the-art LLMs. Our evaluation reveals a clear trade-off: TnT-LLM constructs high-quality taxonomies comparable to human-defined ones but incurs substantially higher cost and runtime and tends to generate overly complex taxonomies, whereas CLIMB is 15--40$\times$ faster and 8--49$\times$ cheaper but tends to score lower on quality when technical inference beyond surface-level similarity is required. These findings suggest that TnT-LLM and CLIMB can be used in practical situations in the SE domain, while researchers should first assess the complexity of the generated taxonomies and their cost using a subset of the target data to decide whether to use automated methods or human experts. Our work represents a first step toward a systematic understanding of automated taxonomy generation in SE, offering actionable insights for future research and practice.

</details>


### [320] [AI-assisted Script Management for Requirements Elicitation Interviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01640)
*Anmol Singhal,Paulo Carvalho,Travis Breaux*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents an AI-assisted requirements elicitation workflow that combines theory-guided script generation with live topic coverage tracking and on-demand follow-up question generation. In a quasi-experimental study comparing AI-assisted (no training) vs. AI-unassisted (training-only) interviews, AI-generated scripts scored higher (92.8 vs. 74.8), AI-assisted interviews covered fewer topics but went deeper (more follow-ups per topic), and produced more refined goal models. Script management was deemed useful by participants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Requirements elicitation interviews demand interviewers balance topic coverage, active listening, and adaptive probing in real time. While prior work explored isolated AI support tasks (script generation, follow-up generation), integrated support's effect on the interview process and resulting artifacts is unknown, and script management—tracking topic coverage and deciding when to probe—remains underexplored.

Method: The authors developed an AI-assisted elicitation workflow combining theory-guided script generation (grounded in business goals), live topic coverage tracking, and on-demand follow-up question generation. They evaluated it via a between-subjects quasi-experimental study comparing a no-training AI-assisted condition with a training AI-unassisted condition. Assessment used a rubric based on elicitation best practices, along with quantitative metrics on topic coverage, scripted question usage, follow-up frequency, and goal model refinement.

Result: AI-generated scripts scored 92.8 vs. 74.8 out of 100 compared to training-only scripts. AI-assisted interviews covered fewer topics (9.6 vs. 14.5), covered more scripted questions (86% vs. 69%), asked more follow-ups per topic (3.43 vs. 1.15), and produced more refined goal models (lowest-level goal fraction 0.653 vs. 0.598). Topic tracking was rated the most useful workflow feature (86% agreement).

Conclusion: AI-assisted elicitation is associated with a different interview trajectory and different requirements outcomes compared to training-only approaches. The results position AI-assisted workflows as effective elicitation scaffolds, warranting further studies on integrated AI support in requirements engineering.

Abstract: Requirements elicitation interviews require interviewers to balance topic coverage, active listening, and adaptive probing while responding to stakeholders in real time. Although prior work has explored AI support for isolated interviewing tasks, such as script generation and follow-up question generation, little is known about how integrated support affects the interview and what requirements artifacts emerge. Furthermore, script management---which helps the interviewer track topic coverage in real time and decide when to probe further---remains underexplored. This paper presents an AI-assisted elicitation workflow that combines theory-guided script generation grounded in business goals with live support for topic coverage tracking and on-demand follow-up question generation. We evaluate the workflow in a between-subjects quasi-experimental study comparing a no-training, AI-assisted condition with a training, AI-unassisted condition. Based on a rubric derived from elicitation best practices, the AI-generated scripts score higher than training-only scripts (92.8 vs. 74.8 out of 100). AI-assisted interviews cover fewer topics (9.6 vs. 14.5), cover more scripted questions (86% vs. 69%), ask more follow-ups per topic (3.43 vs. 1.15), and produce more refined goal models (lowest-level goal fraction 0.653 vs. 0.598). Participants find script management useful, rating topic tracking as the most useful workflow feature (86% agreement). Collectively, these results show that the AI-assisted condition is associated with a different interview trajectory and different elicited requirements than a training-only condition, positioning AI-assisted workflows as elicitation scaffolds for future studies.

</details>


### [321] [Coding Agents as Test-Suite Auditors: Finding What Official Suites Miss While Approaching What They Catch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01715)
*Shuyang Xie,Shuxiao Xie,Feng Zhu,Yanli Ji,Wangmeng Zuo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a practical remedy for the problem of accepted-but-buggy submissions in online-judge datasets. It uses an off-the-shelf coding agent as a test-suite auditor to build adversarial test suites (and supply suites where none exist), combined with a certification chain (multiple accepted solutions agreement, brute-force settling, and per-problem input validation) to verify whether agent-flagged submissions are genuinely buggy without relying on the official judge. The method identifies 906 union-floor accepted-but-buggy submissions across five agents on AtCoder, and outperforms baselines on post-cutoff Codeforces problems with no official suites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior audits of online-judge datasets and benchmarks revealed that official test suites accept buggy submissions, yet these audits only warned about the issue without offering any practical solution.
