The authors aim to provide an actionable remedy that both exposes such bugs and addresses the gap where official suites are unavailable.

Method: The remedy consists of two parts: (1) an off-the-shelf coding agent acts as a test-suite auditor, building adversarial test suites to expose what official suites miss, and supplying test suites where none exist; (2) a certification chain verifies each agent-flagged submission as genuinely buggy without relying on the official judge, using three criteria: multiple independently written accepted solutions agree on expected outputs, brute-force solutions settle disagreements, and a per-problem validator certifies each failing input as legal.

Result: One agent identified 589 verified accepted-but-buggy submissions among 20,375 audited accepted submissions on AtCoder; extending certification to all five agents yields a union floor of 906 such submissions. The five agents stayed within 1.7 percentage points of official-suite coverage on logic bugs those suites catch. On post-cutoff Codeforces problems with no official suites, the test-building method led all five reproduced baselines at every tested input budget.

Conclusion: The proposed approach provides a practical, scalable remedy for auditing and supplementing online-judge test suites. Where official suites exist, the agent audits suite adequacy rather than assuming correctness; where they don't, agent-generated suites catch the most buggy submissions among reproduced and tested methods.

Abstract: Online-judge verdicts and the datasets and benchmarks built on them are treated as ground truth for evaluating and training large language models for code. Yet prior audits have sounded a warning: official suites accept buggy submissions. These audits, however, stop at the warning and offer no practical remedy. Our remedy has two parts: an off-the-shelf coding agent, serving as a test-suite auditor, both builds adversarial test suites to expose what official suites miss and supplies these suites where no official suite exists; a certification chain determines whether each agent-flagged submission is genuinely buggy without relying on the official judge: multiple independently written accepted solutions agree on the expected output for every test, brute-force solutions settle disagreements, and a per-problem validator certifies each failing input legal. One such agent identifies 589 verified accepted-but-buggy submissions among AtCoder's 20,375 audited accepted submissions; extending the same certification to all five agents yields a union floor of 906 such submissions. Five agents, scored separately, each stay within 1.7pp of official-suite coverage on logic bugs those suites catch. On post-cutoff Codeforces problems with no available official suites, the same test-building method leads all five reproduced baselines at every tested input budget. Where an official suite exists, the agent audits suite adequacy instead of assuming it; where none exists, agent suites catch the most buggy submissions among methods we reproduced and tested.

</details>


### [322] [Effective and Efficient Context Retrieval via Partial Dependency Graph for Repository-Level Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01927)
*Zhongxin Liu,Zhonghao Jiang,Zhifan Ye,Haoye Wang,Jiakun Liu,Xiaoxue Ren*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces DyRetriever, an efficient context retrieval method for LLM-based repository-level code generation that uses partial dependency graphs built on-demand. Unlike prior graph-based approaches that rely on manually designed rules and static global graphs, DyRetriever leverages an LLM to select entry-point functions and perform multi-hop reasoning along the code dependency graph with semantic validation. Integrated with similarity-based retrieval as DyCoder, it achieves Pass@1 improvements of 25.63% on CoderEval and 59.73% on DevEval over existing RAG-based methods, while being 7.4x faster than static dependency graph baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG-based approaches for repository-level code generation have two key limitations: similarity-based retrieval often fails to capture code dependencies, and graph-based retrieval relies on manually designed rules and static global dependency graphs that are inflexible and expensive to construct and maintain. The authors are motivated by how human developers implicitly construct partial dependency graphs and iteratively inspect them, inspiring a more adaptive and efficient retrieval approach.

Method: DyRetriever works in two stages: (1) it uses an LLM to select a set of entry-point functions relevant to the target code generation task, and (2) it performs multi-hop reasoning along the code dependency graph, where the LLM's semantic understanding validates whether each function genuinely helps generate the target function. This eliminates the need for manually designed rules and supports flexibility across scenarios. A partial dependency graph is built on-demand and discarded after use, avoiding the cost of maintaining a static global graph. DyRetriever is integrated with a similarity-based code retriever to form the DyCoder system.

Result: On CoderEval and DevEval benchmarks, DyCoder achieves relative Pass@1 improvements of 25.63% and 59.73% respectively compared with existing RAG-based methods. It is also 7.4x faster than baselines based on static dependency graph construction.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that LLM-guided partial dependency graph construction for context retrieval substantially outperforms both similarity-based and static graph-based retrieval methods for repository-level code generation, while being computationally more efficient. This validates that mimicking human developers' iterative, on-demand context discovery behavior is an effective design principle.

Abstract: LLM-based repository-level code generation aims to generate code using the context available in a software repository, requiring LLMs to reason over complex code dependencies. Due to limited context windows and insufficient repository-specific understanding, LLMs typically rely on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to incorporate relevant code. Early RAG approaches primarily employ similarity-based retrieval, which often fails to retrieve code snippets that the target function depends on. Recent work introduces graph-based retrieval to model such dependencies, but typically relies on manually designed rules and static global graphs, leading to limited flexibility and high construction and maintenance costs. In contrast, human developers collect helpful context by implicitly constructing a partial dependency graph and iteratively inspecting along it. Inspired by this behavior, we propose DyRetriever, an efficient context retrieval method via partial dependency graphs. DyRetriever uses an LLM to first select a set of entry-point functions and then perform multi-hop reasoning along the code dependency graph. During multi-hop reasoning, it uses the LLM's semantic understanding to validate whether a function can help generate the target function, eliminating manually designed rules and enabling flexibility across scenarios. Instead of statically constructing a global dependency graph, DyRetriever builds a partial graph on demand and discards it after use, reducing construction and maintenance costs. We integrate DyRetriever with a similarity-based code retriever to build DyCoder and evaluate it on CoderEval and DevEval. Experimental results show that DyCoder achieves relative Pass@1 improvements of 25.63% and 59.73% on CoderEval and DevEval, respectively, compared with existing RAG-based methods, while being 7.4x faster than baselines based on static dependency graph construction.

</details>


### [323] [TELLER: Non-intrusive Cross-Layer Root-Cause Analysis for LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01975)
*Ruilin Xu,Junyi Li,Pengfei Chen,Zongxuan Xie*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TELLER is a non-intrusive framework for root-cause analysis of LLM inference that collects NVTX/CUPTI traces and service logs, reconstructs per-request call-chain trees, encodes them into compact structural token sequences via a Trace Pair Encoding tokenizer, and uses a multimodal model to localize abnormal steps and generate natural-language explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Root-cause analysis for LLM inference is hard because a single request spans multiple layers (inference engine, Python/C++ backend, CUDA APIs, GPU kernels, distributed communication), and existing profilers only expose raw timelines while log-based diagnosis misses cross-layer semantics and request-level structure.

Method: TELLER collects NVTX/CUPTI traces and service logs without modifying model binaries, reconstructs per-request call-chain trees, aligns logs with execution steps, builds dependency-aware causal-context slices (preserving parent-child, temporal, and communication relations), and uses a TPE tokenizer to compress slices into structural token sequences. A multimodal root-cause model jointly predicts abnormal steps, localizes suspicious operators, and generates explanations, aided by numeric candidate localization.

Result: On multi-node GPU inference workloads, a moderate TPE vocabulary reduces per-step trace length by over 80% while achieving the best diagnosis performance on both horizontal (cross-node communication) and vertical (within-node execution stack) views; more aggressive compression degrades quality. Further analyses confirm robustness under low-fault priors, strengthened baselines, modality ablations, and explanation-quality checks.

Conclusion: TELLER provides a practical triage and evidence-localization substrate for LLM inference root-cause analysis, demonstrating a clear compression-accuracy trade-off and offering a scalable, non-intrusive solution for continuously operated LLM services.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has evolved from an offline workload into a continuously operated software service, yet root-cause analysis remains difficult because a single request spans the inference engine, Python/C++ backend, host CUDA APIs, GPU kernels, and distributed communication. Existing profilers expose raw timelines, while log-based diagnosis often misses cross-layer execution semantics and request-level structure. We present TELLER, a non-intrusive Trace- and Log-aware LLM inference Root-cause analysis framework. TELLER first collects NVTX/CUPTI traces and service logs without modifying model binaries, then reconstructs per-request call-chain trees and aligns log lines with the corresponding execution steps. We introduce a dependency-aware causal-context slice that preserves parent-child structure, temporal order, and communication relations, and a Trace Pair Encoding (TPE) tokenizer that compresses such slices into compact structural token sequences with parent, depth, and duration attributes. On top of these representations, TELLER combines numeric candidate localization with a multimodal root-cause model that jointly predicts abnormal steps, localizes suspicious operators, and generates natural-language explanations. Experiments on multi-node GPU inference workloads show a clear compression-accuracy trade-off: a moderate TPE vocabulary reduces per-step trace length by more than 80% while achieving the best overall performance on both horizontal (cross-node communication) and vertical (within-node execution stack) views, whereas more aggressive compression substantially degrades diagnosis quality. Further analyses under low-fault priors, strengthened baselines, modality ablations, explanation-quality checks, and tracing overhead show that TELLER provides a practical triage and evidence-localization substrate for LLM inference RCA.

</details>


### [324] [VulnGym: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Repository-Level Vulnerability Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02001)
*Kexing Ji,Jiachen Liu,Enze Hu,Cuiyun Gao,Keke Lian,Yongheng Liu,Lei Zhang,Tian Dong,Hao Chen,Wang Bin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: VulnGym is a real-world repository-level benchmark for evaluating coding agents in vulnerability detection, containing 184 advisories and 408 vulnerabilities across 23 repositories with line-level trace annotations. It defines an end-to-end detection task and three oracle-based subtasks to jointly evaluate detection and diagnose limitations in code localization and evidence construction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing vulnerability detection benchmarks focus on classification over preselected code snippets, which limits their ability to evaluate coding agents that must autonomously explore entire repositories. Additionally, the lack of fine-grained vulnerability trace annotations makes it difficult to diagnose capability limitations in the detection process.

Method: VulnGym aligns reviewed GitHub advisories with their corresponding vulnerable version repositories, yielding 184 advisories and 408 vulnerability entries across 23 repositories. Each entry is annotated with line-level entry points, critical operations, and vulnerability traces. The benchmark defines an end-to-end detection task alongside three oracle-based subtasks to evaluate detection performance and diagnose limitations in code localization and evidence construction.

Result: Evaluation shows that current coding agents remain limited in both end-to-end repository-level vulnerability detection and the construction of accurate supporting traces.

Conclusion: VulnGym provides a comprehensive benchmark that not only evaluates end-to-end vulnerability detection by coding agents but also enables fine-grained diagnosis of where agents fail, highlighting that existing agents are insufficient for accurate repository-level vulnerability detection and trace construction.

Abstract: Recent advances in LLM-based vulnerability detection have shown promising results, while coding agents further extend this capability from isolated code snippets to complete repositories. This shift requires agents to autonomously explore repositories and locate vulnerability-relevant code, instead of performing detection on preselected functions. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on vulnerability classification over preselected code snippets, limiting their ability to evaluate coding agents in repository-level vulnerability detection. Moreover, without fine-grained vulnerability trace annotations, the capability limitations underlying the detection process remain difficult to explore. To address these limitations, we present \textbf{VulnGym}, a real-world repository-level benchmark for evaluating vulnerability detection by coding agents. VulnGym aligns reviewed GitHub advisories with their corresponding vulnerable version repositories. It contains 184 advisories and 408 vulnerability entries across 23 repositories, with each entry annotated with line-level entry points, critical operations, and vulnerability traces. Using this fine-grained ground truth, VulnGym defines an end-to-end detection task and three oracle-based subtasks to jointly evaluate vulnerability detection and diagnose limitations in code localization and evidence construction. Our evaluation indicates that current coding agents remain limited in both end-to-end repository-level vulnerability detection and the construction of accurate supporting traces.

</details>


### [325] [Pretraining on Call Graphs: When Binary Analysis Tasks Profit From Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02084)
*Samuel Valenzuela,Johannes Kinder*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper dissects the impact of call graph-based refinements on binary function embeddings, showing that improvements on binary code similarity detection (BCSD) do not necessarily generalize to downstream semantic or syntactic tasks, and that optimizing for semantic similarity correlates with worse syntactic performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Binary function embeddings are widely used for reverse engineering tasks, and while graph-based refinements have shown success in improving BCSD, it is unclear whether these improvements transfer to other downstream tasks. The authors aim to systematically dissect the implications of these embedding refinements across different task types.

Method: The authors conduct experiments using multiple graph-based models applied to embeddings generated by two state-of-the-art binary function embedding models. They evaluate improvements across BCSD and downstream tasks of both semantic and syntactic nature, and perform an explanatory analysis on the dataset to understand when call graph-based enhancements help or hurt.

Result: Call graph-based improvements on BCSD do not generalize to downstream tasks. Optimizing for semantic similarity correlates with worse syntactic task performance. Call graph enhancements improve embedding robustness, especially in scenarios where initial models struggle, and are more beneficial for namespace-related functions than for functions focused on individual logic.

Conclusion: Call graph context should be applied selectively rather than universally, as it is most effective in context-dependent scenarios such as namespace-related functions, while potentially degrading performance on syntactic tasks and scenarios where the base model already performs well.

Abstract: Binary function embedding models are trained to encode the semantics of binary code in such a way that they can be generalized to a variety of reverse engineering tasks, such as binary code search, vulnerability detection, or malware classification. While many models only take the function in question as contextual input, there have been successful attempts to improve function embeddings by leveraging information from the call graph. In this study, we dissect the implications of these embedding refinements. We conduct experiments using a range of graph-based models on the embeddings generated by two state-of-the-art binary function embedding models. Integrating inter-procedural context, we show that improvements on binary code similarity detection (BCSD) will not necessarily generalize to downstream tasks, neither of semantic nor of syntactic nature. More generally, we find that optimizing for semantic similarity tasks correlates with worse performance on syntactic tasks. By conducting an explanatory analysis on the dataset, we find that the call graph-based enhancements significantly enhance the robustness of embeddings, particularly in scenarios where the initial models struggle. Furthermore, we observe that the added context is more beneficial for namespace-related functions than for those focused on individual logic, confirming that the call graph can be leveraged most effectively in context-dependent scenarios.

</details>


### [326] [Lossless Tensor Compression as Program Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02162)
*Jieke Shi,Junda He,Wenjia Jiang,Weifeng Sun,Shidong Pan,Zhensu Sun,Chengran Yang,Peixin Zhang,Yifan Jia,Zhou Yang,Thong Hoang,Xiwei Xu,Zhenchang Xing,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Brevis is a lossless tensor compression system that frames compression as program synthesis, using a typed DSL with reversible operators to capture recurring tensor structures. It reduces checkpoint data by 33.93%, outperforming general-purpose and tensor-specific compressors while achieving 3.60 GB/s compression and 6.61 GB/s decompression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model checkpoints are growing in number and size, making archival, transfer, and deployment increasingly costly. General-purpose compressors ignore tensor structure, while existing tensor-specific compressors rely on fixed, format-specific pipelines that lack flexibility.

Method: Brevis formulates lossless tensor compression as program synthesis. It designs a typed domain-specific language (DSL) with reversible operators capturing recurring tensor structures (e.g., repeated regions, floating-point fields). A checkpoint-specific production prior, learned from a small representative sample, guides a bounded A* search to synthesize compact, self-contained DSL programs that reconstruct tensors bit-exactly.

Result: On 10 public checkpoints spanning language, audio, and image generation models, Brevis reduces 2.13 TB of checkpoint data to 1.41 TB (33.93% reduction). It produces archives up to 30.87% smaller than zstd and gzip, and smaller archives than ZipNN and DFloat11, while achieving 3.60 GB/s compression and 6.61 GB/s decompression under practical concurrency.

Conclusion: Brevis demonstrates that program-synthesis-based tensor compression can outperform both general-purpose and existing tensor-specific compressors, providing bit-exact lossless compression at high throughput, making it a practical solution for large-scale model checkpoint management.

Abstract: Model checkpoints are growing in both number and size, which makes archival, transfer, and deployment increasingly costly. General-purpose compressors can reduce storage requirements but ignore tensor structure, whereas existing tensor-specific compressors rely on fixed and format-specific pipelines. We present Brevis, which formulates lossless tensor compression as program synthesis. We design a typed domain-specific language (DSL) that captures recurring tensor structures, such as repeated regions and floating-point fields, through a set of reversible operators. Given a tensor, Brevis synthesizes a self-contained DSL program that reconstructs it bit-exactly. A checkpoint-specific production prior, learned from a small representative sample of tensors, guides a bounded A* search to synthesize compact programs, which can later be executed directly for bit-exact decompression. On 10 public checkpoints spanning language, audio, and image generation models, Brevis reduces 2.13 TB of checkpoint data to 1.41 TB, a 33.93% storage reduction. It produces archives up to 30.87% smaller than those of four general-purpose compressors, including zstd and gzip, and smaller archives than the tensor-specific compressors ZipNN and DFloat11. Under a practical concurrency configuration, Brevis achieves 3.60 GB/s compression and 6.61 GB/s decompression while preserving every source byte.

</details>


### [327] [ECLAIR: A Causally-Grounded AI Framework for Scientific Discovery in Empirical Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02323)
*Alejandro Velasco,Daniel Rodriguez-Cardenas,Dipin Khati,David N. Palacio,Denys Poshyvanyk*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces ECLAIR, a causally grounded AI framework that integrates LLMs as active scientific agents into every stage of the scientific method for software engineering research, demonstrated through a case study on how prompt design affects code generation accuracy in two LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern software systems are increasingly complex, hindering the systematic application of the scientific method in empirical Software Engineering (SE) research. There is a need for a principled methodology that leverages AI while maintaining rigorous, causally sound reasoning.

Method: ECLAIR treats LLMs as active scientific agents operating under principles of causal inference, integrated across the scientific process (hypothesis generation, analysis, interpretation) with a human-in-the-loop design to safeguard against unsound automated reasoning. It is demonstrated via a case study examining how prompt design factors (instruction-style, few-shot length, signature-augmentation) causally affect code generation accuracy.

Result: For both LLMs studied, instruction-style, longer few-shot, and signature-augmented prompts produce small negative causal effects on code generation accuracy, showing how causal reasoning can explain why software phenomena occur.

Conclusion: This work presents the first causally grounded structured methodology for embedding LLMs within the scientific method in SE, designed around the epistemological demands of empirical SE research, establishing a foundation for rigorous AI-assisted research.

Abstract: The scientific method has long guided empirical research in Software Engineering (SE), but the complexity of modern software systems often hinders its systematic application. This paper introduces _ECLAIR_, a causally grounded AI framework that integrates Large Language Models (_LLMs_) into every stage of the scientific process, from hypothesis generation to analysis and interpretation. _ECLAIR_ treats _LLMs_ as active **scientific agents** operating under the principles of causal inference, within a human-in-the-loop design that safeguards against the risks of unsound automated reasoning. We demonstrate the framework through a case study examining how prompt design influences code generation accuracy in two _LLMs_. Results show that, for both models, instruction-style, longer few-shot, and signature-augmented prompts yield small negative causal effects on accuracy, illustrating how causal reasoning provides a principled foundation for explaining _why_ software phenomena occur. This study presents the first causally grounded structured methodology for embedding _LLMs_ within the scientific method in SE, designed around the epistemological demands of empirical SE research, establishing a basis for rigorous AI-assisted research.

</details>


### [328] [On Automated and Explainable Provenance of AI-Generated Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02329)
*Alejandro Velasco,Nathan Wintersgill,Trevor Stalnaker,Oscar Chaparro,Denys Poshyvanyk*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a research vision, grounded in an NSF-funded grant, arguing that next-generation CodeGenAI tools must be built on a foundation of explainable provenance—automated post-hoc traceability linking generated code back to prompt components, training data, global data features, and internal model components. The vision is supported by empirical evidence from developers, model users, and compliance professionals showing provenance is a practical necessity, and outlines a research program combining large-scale studies with causal and interpretability techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI for code generation introduces a critical transparency problem: the origins of AI-generated code are opaque to developers, organizations, and compliance professionals. Existing mitigations only flag problems after the fact without explaining why a model produced them or improving future generation.

Method: The research program combines empirical studies of software developers, model users, and compliance/legal professionals with post-hoc causal and interpretability techniques. The problem is characterized across four traceability dimensions (prompt components, training data instances, global data features, and internal model components).

Result: Empirical evidence from stakeholders shows that provenance information is a practical necessity that current tools do not provide, grounding the vision in demonstrated user needs.

Conclusion: The community must address key open challenges to realize the vision of explainable provenance as the foundation for next-generation CodeGenAI tools.

Abstract: Generative AI for code generation has transformed software development, but it has also introduced a critical transparency problem: the origins of AI-generated code are opaque to the developers who use it, the organizations that deploy it, and the compliance professionals responsible for ensuring its legal and quality standards. Existing mitigations flag problematic outputs after the fact without explaining why a model produced them or how future generation could be improved. We present a research vision, grounded in a U.S. NSF-funded research grant, that argues that the next generation of CodeGenAI tools must be built on a foundation of explainable provenance: automated, post-hoc traceability that links generated code back to the prompt components, training data instances, global data features, and internal model components that caused its generation. We grounded this vision in empirical evidence from studies of software developers, model users, and compliance/legal professionals, which show that provenance information is a practical necessity that current tools do not provide. We characterize the problem across four traceability dimensions, outline a research program combining large-scale empirical studies with post-hoc causal and interpretability techniques, and identify the key open challenges that the community must address to realize this vision.

</details>


### [329] [Profitability of Open-Source Software Product Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02398)
*Shivendu P. Singh,Narayan Ramasubbu,Chris F. Kemerer,M. Zia Hydari*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Analyzing 977 U.S. high-tech firms from 2001-2025, this study finds open-source adoption raises gross margins by 4-5% on average, primarily through higher labor productivity via knowledge integration. The payoff only emerges when outside volunteers contribute ~35% of the work and depends on firm resource configuration, with sustained internal R&D being a core condition for high profitability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether openness in product development—inviting outside developers to contribute on platforms like GitHub—actually pays off financially for technology firms, addressing a gap in understanding the economic returns of open-source strategies.

Method: Analyzed 977 U.S. high-tech firms from 2001 to 2025, measuring the impact of open-source adoption on gross margins, labor productivity, and knowledge integration. Employed configurational analysis to identify pathways to profitability and threshold conditions for payoff.

Result: Open-source adoption raised gross margins by 4-5% on average, driven by higher labor productivity as external contributors' knowledge is integrated into internal workflows. The payoff requires a meaningful external contribution share (~35%) and specific resource configurations; sustained internal R&D paired with open-source development is a core condition across all high-profitability configurations.

Conclusion: Open source should be viewed as a knowledge-integration strategy aligned with firm resources rather than merely a low-cost sourcing approach. For policymakers, the findings highlight the economic value of open-source ecosystems and the need for policies supporting skilled volunteer communities and public-private open-source infrastructure.

Abstract: Many technology firms now build software products in the open, inviting outside developers to contribute alongside their employees on platforms like GitHub. Does this openness in product development pay off? Analyzing 977 U.S. high-tech firms from 2001 to 2025, this study finds that open-source adoption raised firms' gross margins by 4-5% on average. These gains flow largely through higher labor productivity, as firms integrate external contributors' diverse knowledge into internal workflows, broadening the organizational knowledge base without a commensurate rise in labor costs. However, the payoff emerges only when outside volunteers supply a meaningful share of the work (around 35% in this sample), and hinges on the firm's resource configuration. While there are multiple pathways to profitability, pairing open-source product development with sustained internal R&D is a core condition present in all high-profitability configurations. For managers, the lesson is to treat open source as a knowledge-integration strategy matched to the firm's resources, not merely a means of sourcing external effort at lower cost. For policymakers, the findings underscore the broad economic value of open-source ecosystems and the need for policies that foster skilled volunteer communities and public-private open-source infrastructure.

</details>


### [330] [SWE-Touch: Benchmarking Coding Agents When Users Touch the Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02499)
*Yuqiao Tan,Jinxiang Meng,Fangyu Lei,Minzheng Wang,Shizhu He,Jun Zhao,Kang Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SWE-Touch is a framework that stress-tests coding agents in shared workspaces where users may modify code mid-task. It injects validated Counter-Edits (plausible but task-conflicting code changes) into repository-level coding tasks, showing they degrade average resolve rates by 7.7 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified and persist on longer-horizon benchmarks, revealing that strong autonomous performance doesn't yet ensure the state awareness needed for shared-workspace collaboration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world coding agents operate in shared workspaces where users can inspect and modify code during ongoing tasks, yet existing repository-level benchmarks typically evaluate agents working alone or restrict user participation to messages. This gap motivates the question of how coding agents understand and respond to code changes in such dynamic environments.

Method: SWE-Touch mines task-critical regions from multiple repair trajectories, uses a separate User Patch Generator to construct Counter-Edits (validated plausible edits that conflict with task completion), and injects them with contextual user messages when agents reach relevant code. It is evaluated on nine coding models across SWE-bench Verified, SWE-Bench Pro, and DeepSWE.

Result: Counter-Edits lower average resolve rates by 7.7 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, with degradation persisting on both longer-horizon benchmarks. Trajectory analysis shows agents may retain conflicting code or replace it without sufficiently re-inspecting the repository or validating revised code with targeted tests, indicating limited awareness of the evolving workspace.

Conclusion: Strong autonomous performance does not yet ensure the state awareness and adaptive behavior needed for shared-workspace collaboration. Key capabilities for future optimization include detecting workspace changes, reconciling conflicting edits with the task, and verifying affected behavior.

Abstract: Real-world software development requires coding agents to operate in shared workspaces where users may inspect and modify code during an ongoing task, yet existing repository-level benchmarks typically evaluate agents working alone or restrict user participation to messages. This leads us to ask: how do coding agents understand and respond to code changes in a shared workspace? We introduce SWE-Touch, a framework that stress-tests this setting through validated Counter-Edits: plausible edits to task-relevant code that conflict with task completion. SWE-Touch mines task-critical regions from multiple repair trajectories, uses a separate User Patch Generator to construct the edits, and injects them with contextual user messages when agents reach the relevant code. We evaluate nine coding models on SWE-bench Verified, with additional experiments on longer-horizon tasks from SWE-Bench Pro and DeepSWE. Counter-Edit lowers average resolve rate by 7.7 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, with degradation also persisting on both longer-horizon benchmarks. Trajectory analysis links these failures to limited awareness of the evolving workspace: agents may retain conflicting code or replace it without sufficiently re-inspecting the repository and validating the revised code with targeted tests. These findings show that strong autonomous performance does not yet ensure the state awareness and adaptive behavior needed for shared-workspace collaboration, and point to detecting workspace changes, reconciling conflicting edits with the task, and verifying the affected behavior as key capabilities for future optimization.

</details>


### [331] [Decomposing the Doer Effect in Programming Practice: Code Writing Stands Out Among Active Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02541)
*Arun Balajiee Lekshmi Narayanan,Gillian Gold,Jordan Barria-Pineda,Quinn K Wolter,Peter Brusilovsky,Paulo Carvalho*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether the "doer effect" extends to computer science instruction and whether specific forms of active practice (code writing, tracing, completion, visualizations, explanations) differ in their association with learning outcomes, finding that code writing is uniquely and most strongly associated with improved posttest performance among active practice types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior doer effect research treats all active practice as equivalent, leaving open whether some types of doing are more effective than others. This paper aims to disaggregate active practice types to identify which forms are most beneficial, specifically in the context of computer science education.

Method: The authors analyzed log data from 334 students across 11 semesters of introductory and intermediate Java courses, who used an interactive practice system containing five content types: Code Writing, Code Tracing, Code Completion, Code Visualizations, and Code Explanations.

Result: Active practice activities were associated with 3.2 times better learning outcomes than passive activities, consistent with prior doer effect work. Among active practice types, code writing was the most strongly associated with improved posttest performance, while no other activity type showed a comparable association.

Conclusion: The doer effect extends to computer science instruction, but not all forms of doing are equally effective. Code writing problems, which are challenging and feedback-supported, stand out as the most effective active practice type, highlighting the importance of designing practice activities that require generative, effortful engagement.

Abstract: The "doer effect" suggests that actively doing practice activities is more strongly associated with learning outcomes than passively viewing content. In the doer effect literature, "doing" refers specifically to active practice. However, this categorization treats different forms of active practice as equivalent, leaving open whether some types of active practice are more effective than others. In this paper, we investigate whether the doer effect extends to computer science instruction and whether some forms of doing stand out compared to other forms. We analyze log data from 334 students across 11 semesters of introductory and intermediate Java who used an interactive practice system with five content types: Code Writing, Code Tracing, Code Completion, Code Visualizations, and Code Explanations. Consistent with prior doer effect work, we find that active practice activities were associated with 3.2 times better learning outcomes than passive activities. Interestingly, among the active practice, code writing was the most strongly associated with improved posttest performance, while no other activity type showed a comparable association. These results highlight the importance of challenging, feedback-supported practice activities, such as code writing problems.

</details>


### [332] [ACEM: A Cost Estimation Model for Agentic Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02582)
*Mohammad El-Ramly*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes ACEM (Agentic Cost Estimation Model), a framework that decomposes agentic software development costs into three additive dimensions—LLM token consumption, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) oversight, and infrastructure—and introduces three novel constructs (Revision Factor, Context Factor, HITL Intensity Score) to model nondeterministic cost dynamics, while mapping traditional sizing metrics to token usage for reuse of existing scoping data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional software cost estimation models (COCOMO II, Function Points, Story Points) assume human labor dominates effort. Agentic software engineering, where autonomous AI agents perform substantial implementation, introduces fundamentally different and nondeterministic cost drivers—token consumption, HITL oversight, infrastructure orchestration—that existing models cannot capture. A bridging framework is needed to connect standard sizing metrics to this new cost structure.

Method: ACEM decomposes total agentic development cost into three additive dimensions (LLM, HITL, infrastructure). It introduces three constructs: Revision Factor (RF) for token overhead from output rejection/retries, Context Factor (CF) for rising token consumption with accumulating context, and the four-level HITL Intensity Score (HIS) for oversight classification. The model maps Use Case Points, Story Points, and Function Points to estimated token consumption. Constants are left symbolic pending empirical calibration.

Result: The paper presents a fully specified model structure and calibration methodology, though it remains an early-stage proposal with symbolic constants awaiting empirical grounding. No validated empirical results are yet reported; the contribution is chiefly the modeling framework and invitation for community calibration and testing.

Conclusion: ACEM offers a structured, dimensional approach to estimating agentic software costs, addressing the nondeterminism absent in traditional models. As an initial proposal, it calls for the research community to calibrate, test, and extend the model using real project data.

Abstract: Traditional software cost estimation models, such as COCOMO II, Function Points, and Story Points, assume that development effort is primarily driven by human labor in design, coding, and testing. Agentic software engineering, where autonomous AI agents perform substantial implementation work and humans focus on planning, specification, and validation, challenges this assumption. New cost dimensions arise: large language model (LLM) token consumption across agent actions, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) oversight effort, and infrastructure costs for agent orchestration and tooling. These costs are nondeterministic: identical tasks may consume different tokens, follow divergent reasoning paths, and require varying human correction, phenomena absent in traditional development. A new framework is needed to bridge standard sizing metrics with this cost structure.
  This paper proposes ACEM (Agentic Cost Estimation Model), which decomposes total agentic development cost into three additive dimensions: LLM, HITL, and infrastructure cost. ACEM introduces three constructs for agentic dynamics: the Revision Factor (RF), modeling token overhead from output rejection and retries; the Context Factor (CF), capturing rising token consumption as context accumulates; and the HITL Intensity Score (HIS), a four-level oversight classification scheme. It further maps Use Case Points, Story Points, and Function Points to estimated token consumption, enabling organizations to reuse existing project-scoping data for agentic cost forecasting.
  ACEM is presented as a fully specified model structure and calibration methodology, with constants left symbolic pending empirical grounding. As an early-stage proposal, it invites the research community to calibrate, test, and extend the model through real project data.

</details>


### [333] [Distilling Reasoning Traces into Advisory Prompts for Software Engineering Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00437)
*Faizan Faisal,Prem Devanbu,Toufique Ahmed*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Language models are widely used for generating and otherwise processing code (e.g., identifying code hallucinations, possible inputs, or predicting outputs); however, LLMs can make mistakes, which can be serious. One key issue is that models are trained on (still) largely human-written, and thus imperfect, code; it's not easy to find sufficiently large code corpora that are entirely free of bugs. Thus, other inference-time ways of reducing LLM errors, without additional training, are desirable. "Reasoning" or "thinking" modes, exposed as a togglable feature by hybrid reasoning models, do reduce errors; however, reasoning consumes additional resources. This paper asks if better performance can be achieved without always incurring the cost of reasoning. Human students of programming learn to avoid mistakes by (a) identifying them, (b) reflecting upon the cognitive lapses that led to them (essentially, "thinking through" the errors), (c) inferring general rules or lessons from these reflections, and (d) internalizing these lessons into rules. In tutorial sessions with an instructor, this is a common Socratic interaction. Examples of such internalizable rules might include the nugget "Before coding, restate the requirements to clarify them." Inspired by this process, this paper describes an approach where we first identify examples in which "thinking mode" in a (low-resource) LLM avoids errors. These errors, and their avoidance via "thinking" in the same LLM, are then examined by a bigger LLM to generate summary explanations; these are then summarized by a large LLM into brief advisory prompts. This approach works on many modest-sized models; in some cases, the "advisory prompts" thus learned can also be gainfully transferred to other models. We also present investigations into the nature of coding errors that language models make, and a characterization of when this approach can be helpful.

</details>


### [334] [AiFlow: Token-Native Reactive Orchestration with Bounded Backpressure for Streaming LLM Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00558)
*Qunhui Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly operate as streaming workflows combining retrieval, tool calls, safety filters, and multi-agent coordination. Although contemporary frameworks expose provider deltas, workflow nodes often treat generation as coarse request-response steps, leaving queue management, worker allocation, ordering, and backpressure to ad hoc callback code. This paper presents AiFlow, a token-native reactive orchestration model that normalizes provider deltas into typed Context<T> events propagated through a directed streaming graph. Each node is managed by a Node Guardian that declares and enforces local queue bounds, worker concurrency, ordering, overflow policy, cancellation propagation, and retry discipline. We formalize the bounded-memory property, present the compilation from a compact DSL and JSON graph form, and provide static validation for type safety, state concurrency, and injection compatibility. Controlled microbenchmarks, captured DeepSeek trace replay (30 runs), descriptive online runs, LangGraph baselines, a streaming RAG workload, and an Ollama local-backend check show that AiFlow does not alter provider-side Model TTFT but reduces Application TTFPT by 70.9-94.7\% versus aggregation and keeps runtime-owned queue depth within declared bounds (93.7-96.5\% MaxQ reduction versus unbounded policies). The supplementary artifact contains scripts, raw traces, machine-readable tables, checksums, and an API-free smoke test; the public implementation is available through the FIT Framework repository.

</details>

### [335] [Revisiting Classic Thought Experiments to Measure Consciousness for Artificial Intelligence Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00001)
*Peter David Fagan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This research note applies a Conservation-Congruent Encoding (CCE) framework to classic thought experiments (Leibniz's mill, Turing's imitation game, Searle's Chinese Room), distinguishing task performance (W_causal,T) from operational consciousness (κ_T), showing that behaviourally equivalent systems can diverge in their internal organisational efficiency, with implications for AI safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classic philosophical disputes about machine understanding conflate outward behaviour with the internal organisation that produces it. The authors aim to separate these dimensions formally so that questions about understanding and consciousness can be analysed independently of task performance, which may matter for AI safety.

Method: The paper formalises a toy symbolic setting using the CCE framework. It defines W_causal,T as a measure of successful task behaviour and κ_T as a measure of the efficiency with which preserved internal structure supports that behaviour (operational consciousness). It contrasts two systems: an uncompressed lookup system with an expanding store of unreused mappings, and a compact generative system that reuses internal structure.

Result: Both an uncompressed lookup system and a compact generative system can achieve comparable behavioural success (W_causal,T) but diverge sharply in κ_T, since the former accumulates unreused mappings while the latter reuses compact internal structure.

Conclusion: The paper reframes classic disputes about understanding by decoupling outward performance from the organisational structure that sustains it, and suggests this distinction may be relevant for later AI-safety analysis.

Abstract: This research note revisits Leibniz's mill, Turing's imitation game, and Searle's Chinese Room through the Conservation-Congruent Encoding (CCE) framework. It formalises a toy symbolic setting in which successful behaviour is measured by task performance ($W_{causal,T}$), while the efficiency with which preserved internal structure supports that behaviour is measured by operational consciousness ($κ_T$). Within this setup, an uncompressed lookup system and a compact generative system can in principle achieve comparable behavioural success, yet diverge sharply in $κ_T$: the former relies on an expanding standing store of unreused mappings, whereas the latter reuses compact internal structure. The note therefore reframes classic disputes about understanding by separating outward performance from the organisation that sustains it, and motivates why this distinction may matter for later AI-safety analysis.

</details>


### [336] [AutoFOAM: The Self-Refining Autonomous OpenFOAM Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00003)
*Arun Govind Neelan,A Seshaditya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoFOAM is a self-evolving LLM agent based on Qwen-coder 2.5-14B that automates OpenFOAM CFD simulations from natural-language instructions, using a 7-stage evolution loop with anti-collapse mechanisms (RAG, dictionary-level patching, prompt paraphrasing) to create, evaluate, run, and iterate on simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-source CFD solvers like OpenFOAM require substantial expertise and tedious configuration file setup, creating a high barrier to entry that limits accessibility for engineers without specialized CFD knowledge.

Method: The agent is pre-trained on Qwen-coder 2.5-14B and fine-tuned on 252 text prompts covering 7 OpenFOAM solvers, 13 parametrized mesh templates, and a y+-aware numerical policy. It employs a 7-stage self-evolution loop, protected against degeneration by three anti-collapse strategies: RAG-augmented retry context, surgical dictionary-level patching, and prompt-diversity paraphrasing.

Result: AutoFOAM autonomously generates, evaluates, runs, and evolves CFD simulations from natural-language instructions, demonstrating the feasibility of LLM-driven automated CFD workflows with self-improvement capabilities.

Conclusion: By bridging generative AI with rigorous fluid simulation, AutoFOAM accelerates rapid prototyping and democratizes advanced CFD workflows, making them accessible to non-specialists.

Abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) plays an important role in modern engineering, but using open-source solvers such as OpenFOAM requires considerable knowledge and skills, as well as time-consuming configuration file setup. To reduce this burden, we propose AutoFOAM - a self-evolving large language model (LLM) agent that creates, evaluates, runs, and evolves its own OpenFOAM simulations based solely on natural-language instructions. Our model is pre-trained on the Qwen-coder 2.5-14B, which is then fine-tuned on 252 text prompts targeting 7 OpenFOAM solvers, 13 parametrized mesh templates, and a y plus-aware numerical policy. The crucial element of the algorithm is a sophisticated evolution loop composed of 7 stages. To prevent model degeneration under repeated self-training, the agent employs three complementary anti-collapse streams: RAG-augmented retry context, surgical dictionary-level patching, and prompt-diversity paraphrasing. By bridging generative artificial intelligence with rigorous fluid simulations, AutoFOAM accelerates rapid prototyping and democratizes advanced CFD workflows.

</details>


### [337] [Enhancing LLMs with Context-Specific Knowledge for Mitigating Misinformation in SMEs: A RAG-based Modeling and Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00006)
*Md. Samiul Islam,Iqbal H. Sarker,Chadni Islam,Ahmad Mohsin,Ahmed Ibrahim,Helge Janicke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates how VectorRAG and GraphRAG, two Retrieval-Augmented Generation approaches, mitigate hallucinations and misinformation in LLM outputs used by Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). Evaluated across LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen models, RAG-enhanced LLMs significantly reduce hallucinations and improve response quality, contextual relevance, and trustworthiness for SME decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly adopted by SMEs for question-answering and business decision-making, but hallucinations in generated outputs reduce user confidence and pose misinformation risks. RAG is proposed as a promising solution to address these reliability and trustworthiness concerns in SME environments.

Method: The authors present two RAG-based modeling approaches—VectorRAG and GraphRAG—that incorporate external knowledge sources into LLM generation. They evaluate these approaches on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs including LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen, assessing performance across useful response generation, hallucination risk, contextual relevance, and human-interpretation metrics.

Result: The experimental evaluation shows that RAG-enhanced LLMs significantly improve response quality by reducing hallucinations and misinformation, enabling more reliable, trustworthy, and context-aware decision-making in SME environments across the tested LLM models.

Conclusion: RAG-enhanced approaches (VectorRAG and GraphRAG) effectively mitigate hallucination and misinformation risks in LLM outputs, making them a viable strategy for improving reliability and trustworthiness of AI-assisted decision-making in SME contexts.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), a part of artificial intelligence (AI), are increasingly being adopted by Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to enhance question-answering capabilities and support business decision-making processes. However, hallucinations in LLM-generated outputs can serve as a source of misinformation, reducing user confidence in their reliability and trustworthiness within SMEs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge by incorporating external knowledge sources into the modeling process. In this paper, we present VectorRAG and GraphRAG modeling approaches to mitigate hallucinations and misinformation risks and evaluate their effectiveness in SME environments. Our experimental evaluation is conducted on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, including LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen, to assess performance in terms of useful response generation, risk of hallucination, contextual relevance, as well as human-interpretation. The results demonstrate that RAG-enhanced LLMs can significantly improve response quality by reducing hallucinations and misinformation, thereby supporting more reliable, trustworthy, and context-aware decision-making in SME environments.

</details>


### [338] [Energy Efficiency of Locally Deployed LLMs: A Preliminary Quantitative GPU Power Benchmark on Consumer Hardware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00008)
*Philipp M. Zähl,Anika Hennig*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A reproducible hardware-level energy benchmark of nine open-source LLMs (1B-7B) on a consumer RTX 4060Ti GPU using Ollama, measuring power draw via nvidia-smi at 2Hz. Results show gemma3:1b (0.56 J/token) and llama3.2:1b (0.65 J/token) are most energy-efficient with >170 tok/s throughput, while 7B-Mistral uses up to 4.4x more energy per token. The study reveals architecture and quantization strategy matter more than raw parameter count, and qwen3.5:2b exhibits anomalous per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Local LLM deployment is growing due to privacy concerns, yet energy costs on consumer hardware are poorly characterized since most benchmarks only measure accuracy. This gap motivates a hardware-level energy benchmark to inform practitioners and researchers about the real energy footprint of on-premise LLM inference.

Method: Nine open-source LLMs (1B to 7B parameters) were executed on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4060Ti 16GB) using the Ollama inference engine. GPU power draw was sampled at 2Hz via nvidia-smi across a fixed prompt set. Metrics computed include mean/peak power, total energy per prompt (J/prompt), energy per output token (J/token), and throughput (tok/s).

Result: gemma3:1b and llama3.2:1b achieved the lowest energy cost (0.56 J/token and 0.65 J/token) and highest throughput (>170 tok/s). The 7B-Mistral model consumed up to 4.4x more energy per token than the most efficient model. qwen3.5:2b showed anomalously high per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning.

Conclusion: Energy efficiency in LLM inference is driven by factors beyond parameter count, including model architecture and quantization strategy. The need to distinguish between token generation modes (e.g., reasoning vs. output tokens) in efficiency metrics is highlighted, as different reasoning behaviors can significantly skew energy measurements.

Abstract: The local deployment of large language models (LLMs) is gaining traction due to privacy concerns and the desire for on-premise inference. However, the energy costs on consumer hardware remain poorly characterized, as most benchmarks focus solely on accuracy. This paper presents a reproducible, hardware-level energy benchmark of nine open-source LLMs (1B to 7B parameters) executed on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4060Ti 16GB). Using the Ollama inference engine, GPU power draw was sampled at 2Hz via nvidia-smi across a fixed prompt set. We evaluate mean/peak power, total energy per prompt (J/prompt), energy per output token (J/token), and throughput (tok/s). Our findings suggest that factors beyond raw parameter count, including model architecture and quantization strategy, drive energy efficiency. Specifically, gemma3:1b and llama3.2:1b achieve the lowest energy cost (0.56 J/token and 0.65 J/token) and the highest throughput (>170 tok/s). In contrast, the 7B-Mistral model consumes up to 4.4x more energy per token than the most efficient model. Notably, qwen3.5:2b exhibits anomalously high per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning, highlighting the need to distinguish between token generation modes in efficiency metrics.

</details>


### [339] [CoT-Core: Accelerating LLM Evaluation via CoT-Aware Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00014)
*Qihua Pan,Zhenheng Tang,Peijie Dong,Xiang Liu,Huacan Wang,Bo Li,Xiaowen Chu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoT-Core is a training-free framework that selects core evaluation questions for LLMs by prompting zero-shot Chain-of-Thought reasoning trajectories and clustering them in latent space based on logical equivalence rather than lexical similarity, reducing evaluation costs while maintaining high-fidelity score estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating LLMs during continuous development is computationally prohibitive. Existing coreset selection methods suffer from either a "cold start" bottleneck requiring massive historical logs (e.g., Item Response Theory) or superficial lexical bias that fails to capture the underlying reasoning structure of tasks.

Method: CoT-Core prompts LLMs to generate zero-shot Chain-of-Thought reasoning trajectories for questions, projects these trajectories into a latent space, and clusters questions by intrinsic logical equivalence rather than surface text similarity, enabling training-free core question selection.

Result: Experiments on GSM8K, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA show CoT-Core drastically reduces evaluation costs while maintaining high-fidelity score estimation. The analysis also delineates boundary conditions of reasoning-aware pruning, showing its efficacy is gated by task complexity.

Conclusion: Reasoning-aware coreset selection via CoT trajectory clustering is an effective training-free approach for efficient LLM evaluation, but its benefits are contingent on the inherent complexity of the task domain.

Abstract: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) incurs prohibitive computational overhead during continuous development processes. While coreset selection accelerates evaluation, existing methods either suffer from a severe ``cold start'' bottleneck requiring massive historical logs (e.g., Item Response Theory) or exhibit a surface lexical bias that misses the underlying reasoning manifold of tasks. We propose CoT-Core, a novel training-free core question selection framework. Recognizing that lexically disparate questions can share equivalent underlying logic, CoT-Core prompts LLMs to unroll zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning trajectories. Projecting these paths into a latent space effectively clusters questions by intrinsic logical equivalence rather than superficial text similarity. Extensive experiments on GSM8K, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA demonstrate that CoT-Core drastically reduces evaluation costs while maintaining high-fidelity score estimation, and delineate the boundary conditions of reasoning-aware pruning, revealing that its efficacy is intrinsically gated by task complexity.

</details>


### [340] [Optimization and Constraint Modeling using LLMs with a Retrieval Augmented Generation Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00015)
*Prateek Roy,Akash Singirikonda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline built on a curated synthetic dataset of 500 optimization problems to improve LLM optimization modeling performance. Using Qwen 3 30B Instruct, accuracy improved from 40% to 72% on NL4OPT, 40% to 56% on MAMO Easy, and 32% to 56% on MAMO Complex, demonstrating that synthetic data + retrieval augmentation is an effective alternative to fine-tuning for optimization modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimization and constraint modeling require deep domain expertise and proficiency in modeling formalisms. Current LLMs frequently produce structurally inconsistent or incomplete optimization formulations, particularly in combinatorial settings. The paper seeks a practical, cost-effective way to improve LLM optimization modeling without expensive fine-tuning.

Method: The authors synthesized 500 optimization problems from Text2Zinc seed descriptions combined with LLM-generated professional personas, specified in JSON with validated Python solver scripts. These were indexed in a Chroma vector database. For each inference problem, semantically similar problems were retrieved and fed as contextual guidance into a LangChain LLM agent. Evaluation used three benchmark testbeds (NL4OPT, MAMO Easy, MAMO Complex) with the Qwen 3 30B Instruct model.

Result: Accuracy improved from 40% to 72% on NL4OPT, 40% to 56% on MAMO Easy, and 32% to 56% on MAMO Complex. The use of semantically validated synthetic examples substantially improved both solution accuracy and structural correctness.

Conclusion: Synthetic dataset generation combined with retrieval augmentation provides an effective, low-cost alternative to fine-tuning for improving LLM optimization modeling. This approach can serve as a practical pathway for deploying LLM-based optimization tools in real-world decision-support contexts without costly model retraining.

Abstract: Both optimization modeling and constraint modeling are non-trivial problems requiring deep domain expertise and proficiency in modeling formalism languages. Despite their importance across logistics, healthcare, and supply chain management, current large language models regularly produce structurally inconsistent or incomplete optimization formulations, particularly in combinatorial settings. This paper evaluates whether a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline built on a curated synthetic dataset can meaningfully improve LLM optimization modeling performance. A total of 500 optimization problems were synthesized using seed descriptions from the Text2Zinc dataset and professional personas created using an LLM, specified in JSON and associated with validated Python solver scripts. These problems were encoded in a Chroma vector database. For each inference problem, semantically similar problems were retrieved and used as contextual guidance for a LangChain LLM agent. Three benchmark testbeds were used to evaluate the proposed pipeline under the Qwen 3 30B Instruct model. Accuracy rose from 40% to 72% on NL4OPT, 40% to 56% on MAMO Easy, and 32% to 56% on MAMO Complex. The use of semantically validated synthetic examples greatly improves both solution accuracy and structure. The combination of synthetic dataset generation with retrieval augmentation provides an effective alternative to fine-tuning, suggesting that domain-specific synthetic corpora paired with retrieval augmentation can serve as a practical pathway for deploying LLM-based optimization tools in real-world decision-support contexts without costly model retraining.

</details>


### [341] [Memory Reward Inflation in Self-Improving LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00017)
*Mohammad Asadolahi,Amir Amini,Samira Talebi,Amirfarhad Farhadi,Azadeh Zamanifar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and formalizes the "Echo Gap"—a failure mode in memory-based self-improving LLM agents where LLM-assigned proxy rewards inflate scores of incorrect episodes, causing agents to preferentially reuse their most-confident mistakes. The authors prove the Error-Independence Assumption (EIA) is necessary for correcting this score inflation, show the error compounds under both reward-ranking and similarity retrieval, and introduce LUCID, an answer-free de-inflation algorithm that achieves 56.9% execution accuracy on BIRD text-to-SQL, outperforming both self-graded and memory-less baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-based self-improving LLM agents store, score, and retrieve past episodes to shape future behavior without weight updates. However, in deployment ground-truth labels are unavailable, so stored rewards rely on LLM self-assessment. The authors aim to expose and formalize the reliability problem this substitution creates—specifically why LLM-assigned rewards systemically inflate scores of incorrect episodes and why this inflation cannot be corrected by ordinary verification.

Method: The authors (1) formulate stored scores as proxy rewards for an implicit non-parametric policy, viewing retrieval as a policy-improvement step; (2) formalize the Error-Independence Assumption (EIA) and prove it is a necessary condition for correcting score inflation, deriving a closed-form expression of the recoverable payoff as a function of truth-tracking and error-decorrelation; (3) analyze how inflation compounds under both score-based ranking and plain similarity retrieval; and (4) propose LUCID, an answer-free de-inflation algorithm that counteracts the score inflation without access to ground-truth labels.

Result: The Echo Gap failure mode is empirically confirmed across memory-based self-improving agents and model families. LUCID yields a consistent end-to-end gain on the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark, improving execution accuracy to 56.9%, surpassing a Memento-style self-graded agent (54.0%, +2.9 points mean across seeds) and a memory-less agent of identical architecture (52.4%).

Conclusion: The Echo Gap reveals a fundamental limitation of memory-based self-improvement: when the reward signal is an LLM self-assessment, errors are correlated with the original bias and compound through memory rather than averaging out. Correcting the inflation requires the Error-Independence Assumption as a necessary condition, and the LUCID algorithm demonstrates that answer-free de-inflation can provide consistent downstream gains even under similarity retrieval, the regime deployed agents use.

Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents increasingly learn from experience without updating any weights. Each episode is stored in an external memory, scored, and retrieved for similar future tasks to shape later behavior. Viewed through a reward lens, the stored score is a proxy reward for an implicit, non-parametric policy. Each retrieved episode then becomes a policy-improvement step whose reliability hinges on how that score is produced. In deployment, ground-truth labels are unavailable, so the stored reward is at best an LLM assessment. This substitution creates a failure mode, the *Echo Gap*, across the memory-based self-improving agents and model families studied. Incorrect episodes receive inflated rewards; thus, the agent preferentially reuses the very mistakes it has most confident in. Because the error compounds through memory rather than averaging out and the confirming judge's errors remain correlated with the original self-grading bias, so it cannot identify which memories are overvalued. The missing property is formalized as the *Error-Independence Assumption* (EIA), which we prove is a *necessary* condition for correcting the inflation, not merely a description of a good verifier: a usable signal must track truth *and* decorrelate its error from the memory bias, and the recoverable payoff is a closed-form function of exactly those two quantities. We further show the inflation compounds not only when retrieval ranks by the stored score but also under plain similarity retrieval which is the regime the deployed agent uses. Finally, the answer-free de-inflation algorithm LUCID delivers a consistent end-to-end gain on the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark. It raises execution accuracy to $56.9\%$, above both a Memento-style self-graded agent ($54.0\%$, a $+2.9$-point mean gain across seeds) and a memory-less agent of identical architecture ($52.4\%$).

</details>


### [342] [RL-Lock: Reinforcement Learning for Generating Interlocking Assemblies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01744)
*Xuyang Ma,Chaewoon Kim,Haonan Zhang,Rulin Chen,Ziqi Wang,Peng Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RL-Lock is the first reinforcement learning framework for generating interlocking assemblies, formulating the problem as a sequential decision-making task and combining structured action chunking with MCTS-guided policy-value learning to efficiently navigate the combinatorial search space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generating interlocking assemblies is inherently a sequential decision-making problem, yet existing works rely on handcrafted search heuristics that are slow or fail on challenging cases. The authors observe this decision-making nature and propose to leverage reinforcement learning to avoid manual heuristic design.

Method: RL-Lock formulates the interlocking assembly generation (a voxel grid shape decomposition problem) as a sequential decision-making process where an agent assigns each voxel to a piece. It combines structured action chunking with MCTS-guided policy-value learning to efficiently navigate the large combinatorial search space.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that RL-Lock enables effective generation of interlocking assemblies, particularly excelling in challenging cases where existing approaches take excessively long or fail to find valid solutions.

Conclusion: RL-Lock provides a viable RL-based alternative to handcrafted heuristics for interlocking assembly generation, achieving better efficiency and success on difficult instances.

Abstract: An interlocking assembly is an assembly in which component parts are connected purely through their geometric arrangement, without relying on external connectors such as glue and nails. Such assemblies have been widely used in a variety of real-world applications due to their structural stability. The problem of generating interlocking assemblies is generally formulated as a shape decomposition problem, where a target 3D object represented as a voxel grid is partitioned into a prescribed number of interlocking pieces. We observe that generating interlocking assemblies is inherently a sequential decision-making problem, where an agent repeatedly decides which piece each voxel should be assigned to. Inspired by the observation, we propose the first reinforcement learning framework RL-Lock for generating interlocking assemblies, without relying on handcrafted search heuristics as existing works did. RL-Lock combines structured action chunking with MCTS-guided policy-value learning to efficiently navigate the large combinatorial search space for interlocking assembly generation. We demonstrate through experiments that RL-Lock allows effective generation of interlocking assemblies, especially for challenging cases in which existing approaches take too long or even fail to find a valid solution.

</details>


### [343] [Request-Level Energy Attribution for Batched LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00026)
*Qi Luo,Kunlin Li,Ziwen Wang,Dongsheng Wang,Yun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JouleShare is a request-level energy attribution framework for batched LLM serving. It establishes exact Shapley energy ground truth via offline replay under vLLM and trains a lightweight calibration model (JCalib) to predict fair energy shares online from cheap features. Token-proportional attribution deviates from exact Shapley by ~0.44-0.46 normalized L1 across GPUs, while JCalib reduces this to 0.116 (static) and 0.177 (continuous batching).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Batched LLM serving complicates energy accounting because GPU power telemetry is aggregate, not request-level. Existing benchmarks give model-, phase-, or token-level energy; Shapley fairness is only conceptually motivated by carbon-accounting work. No measured request-level ground truth exists, so the gap between practical accounting rules and fair allocation is unknown.

Method: (1) An offline harness replays request subsets under vLLM with a reproducible protocol, integrates GPU power telemetry, and computes exact Shapley energy per request as ground truth. (2) JCalib, a lightweight calibration model, learns to predict Shapley shares from cheap request features for serving-time use. Sampled Shapley extends the measured reference to larger group sizes.

Result: Across 16 model/workload runs, token-proportional attribution differs from exact Shapley by 0.440 normalized L1 (static batching) and 0.458 (continuous batching), reproducible across three data-center GPUs. JCalib reduces error to 0.116 (static) and 0.177 (continuous), beating a standalone-measurement baseline while preserving exact batch-energy efficiency.

Conclusion: Token attribution is not a reliable proxy for marginal energy under batched execution. Measured Shapley ground truth can calibrate low-cost request features toward fairer, deployable energy attribution.

Abstract: Batched LLM serving improves throughput but complicates energy accounting. GPU power telemetry is aggregate, whereas sustainability reporting, chargeback, and workload analysis often require request-level energy charges. Existing inference-energy benchmarks report model-, phase-, or token-level energy, and recent carbon-accounting work motivates Shapley fairness conceptually. Neither provides measured request-level ground truth, so how far the accounting rules used in practice deviate from a fair allocation has remained unknown. We present JouleShare, an attribution framework with two components. An offline harness establishes this ground truth by replaying request subsets under vLLM with a reproducible protocol, integrating GPU power telemetry, and computing exact Shapley energy for each request. A lightweight calibration model, JCalib, then learns to predict Shapley shares from cheap request features for use at serving time. Across 16 model/workload runs, token-proportional attribution differs from exact Shapley by 0.440 normalized L1 on average under static batching and by 0.458 under continuous batching, a gap that reproduces across three data-center GPUs. JCalib reduces this error to 0.116 under static batching and 0.177 under continuous batching, below even a standalone-measurement baseline that is unavailable online, while preserving exact batch-energy efficiency. Sampled Shapley extends the measured reference to larger group sizes, where the gap persists and a single offline calibration remains the most accurate deployable rule. The results show that token attribution is not a reliable proxy for marginal energy under batched execution, and that measured Shapley ground truth can calibrate low-cost request features toward fairer attribution.

</details>


### [344] [Motif-Mamba: network motif improved mamba for long-range sequence modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00027)
*Chonghe Hao,Yue Sun,Jian Zhang,Yansong Wang,Wangzi Yao,Yunjie Yao,Tielin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Motif-Mamba enhances Mamba's linear-time state space model by adding a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway that projects hidden states into a compact dynamical subspace with three-node motif-inspired interactions, improving cross-dimensional communication while maintaining linear-time complexity. It achieves consistent improvements over Mamba on long-sequence extrapolation, language modeling, and brain-computer interface decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mamba's diagonal state transitions limit explicit interactions among state dimensions, restricting its representational capacity for long-range sequence modeling despite offering linear-time complexity.

Method: Motif-Mamba augments Mamba with a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway. The pathway projects hidden states into a compact dynamical subspace, applies motif-guided interactions inspired by three-node network motifs, and maps the dynamics back to the original state space—preserving Mamba's linear-time recurrent structure.

Result: Consistent improvements over Mamba backbones across long-sequence extrapolation, language modeling benchmarks, and brain-computer interface decoding.

Conclusion: Motif-guided low-rank dynamics serve as an effective structural prior for long-range sequence modeling, enhancing cross-dimensional communication without sacrificing linear-time efficiency.
