Abstract: Efficient long-sequence modeling remains a central challenge for large language models, as self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length. Mamba offers a linear-time alternative through selective state space recurrence, but its predominantly diagonal state transitions restrict explicit interactions among state dimensions. We propose Motif-Mamba, a structured state space model that augments Mamba with a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway. Inspired by the dynamics of three-node network motifs, the proposed pathway projects hidden states into a compact dynamical subspace, imposes motif-guided interactions, and maps the resulting dynamics back to the original state space. This design enhances cross-dimensional communication while preserving the linear-time recurrent structure of Mamba. Experiments on long-sequence extrapolation, language modeling benchmarks, and brain--computer interface decoding show consistent improvements over Mamba backbones, suggesting that motif-guided low-rank dynamics provide an effective structural prior for long-range sequence modeling.

</details>


### [345] [Nova: An End-to-End MLIR Compiler for Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00029)
*Adwaid Suresh,Aparna A,Harshini V M,Jona Delcy C A,Killi Uma Maheswara Rao,Ram Charan Golla,Surendra Vendra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Nova is an automated end-to-end JIT compiler that bridges the gap between high-level tensor frameworks and physical hardware by fusing operations, optimizing memory hierarchies, and tuning execution to the register level. It achieves performance parity or modest gains over cuBLAS/XLA on matmuls, up to 10.6% greater throughput than PyTorch on models, and enables training larger models by reducing memory footprint by up to 29%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models at scale suffer from inefficient hardware utilization because eager execution frameworks lack whole-graph visibility and granular control over hardware and memory mapping, limiting physical hardware performance.

Method: Nova captures eager executions and unifies forward/backward passes into a single value-semantic dialect for aggressive whole-graph optimizations. It employs an Analytic Configurator to deterministically derive optimal execution schedules based on arithmetic intensity (zero search time), and a structural hashing runtime to synthesize fine-grained kernels from computation structure.

Result: On an RTX 3060, Nova matches or modestly exceeds cuBLAS and XLA on TF32 matmuls for most shapes (error < 5e-4). At model level, it achieves up to 10.6% higher throughput than PyTorch and 4.4% higher than XLA on a 42M-parameter model, and reduces memory footprint by up to 29%, enabling training a 144M-parameter model at 17,900 tokens/s where PyTorch OOMs on the same 12 GB GPU.

Conclusion: By providing absolute control over hardware mapping through whole-graph optimization, deterministic analytic scheduling, and structural-hash-based kernel synthesis, Nova demonstrates that JIT compilation can significantly outperform eager frameworks in both performance and memory efficiency without sacrificing numerical fidelity.

Abstract: The performance of deep learning models at scale relies heavily on how effectively high-level mathematical operations are mapped to underlying physical hardware. While high-level tensor frameworks provide flexible abstractions for model design, their eager execution models inherently lack the whole-graph visibility and granular control over hardware and memory required to maximize physical hardware utilization natively. To bridge this gap, we designed Nova, an automated end-to-end JIT compiler whose defining purpose is to achieve absolute control over this hardware mapping: fusing operations across operation boundaries, optimizing complex memory hierarchies, and tuning execution down to the register level. By capturing eager executions and unifying forward and backward passes into a single value-semantic dialect, Nova unlocks aggressive whole-graph optimizations. It then utilizes an Analytic Configurator to deterministically derive optimal execution schedules based on arithmetic intensity, dropping search time to zero. Backed by a structural hashing runtime, Nova synthesizes fine-grained kernels directly from the computation's structure. In our evaluations on an RTX 3060, Nova matches or modestly exceeds cuBLAS and XLA on TF32 matmuls on most shapes, maintaining a stringent < 5e-4 relative error. At the model level, Nova achieves up to 10.6% greater throughput than PyTorch and 4.4% greater than XLA on a 42-million parameter model, without compromising on numerical fidelity. Crucially, by reducing the memory footprint by up to 29% relative to PyTorch, Nova successfully trains a 144-million parameter model at 17,900 tokens/s where PyTorch encounters Out-Of-Memory (OOM) failures on the same 12 GB consumer GPU.

</details>


### [346] [SIRIN: A Unified Toolkit for Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented and Memory-Grounded LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00033)
*Julia Belikova,Rauf Parchiev,Mikhail Filimonov,Konstantin Polev,Andrey Savchenko,Maksim Makarenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SIRIN is a unified toolkit and interactive web UI for detecting contextual hallucinations in retrieval-augmented, agentic, and memory-grounded LLM systems, integrating three detector paradigms (representation probing, uncertainty estimation, judge-style verification) plus pre-generation query answerability under one interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detecting contextual hallucinations requires integrating multiple complementary detection paradigms, but existing tools lack a unified interface, configuration system, and evaluation pipeline that work across white-box and black-box settings.

Method: SIRIN provides a single framework unifying three detector paradigms (representation probing, uncertainty estimation, and judge-style verification) alongside the task of pre-generation query answerability. It supports response- and span-level inspection in white-box and black-box settings, offers a web UI for live analysis of context-query-answer triples with hallucination scores and unsupported-span highlighting, and uses a lightweight plug-in design for adding new detectors.

Result: The toolkit is demonstrated on hallucination detection, query answerability, and as a faithfulness gate within long-term memory systems. Source code is publicly available.

Conclusion: SIRIN offers a unified, extensible platform for contextual hallucination detection and answerability assessment across multiple LLM system architectures, with interactive inspection capabilities and flexibility for augmenting with new detectors.

Abstract: SIRIN (Semantic Inconsistency Recognition and Inspection Nexus) is a unified toolkit and interactive web UI for detecting contextual hallucinations (fluent, plausible responses unsupported by the provided evidence) in retrieval-augmented, agentic, and memory-grounded LLM systems. SIRIN unifies three detector paradigms (representation probing, uncertainty estimation, and judge-style verification) and the complementary task of pre-generation query answerability under one interface, configuration system, and evaluation pipeline, supporting response- and span-level inspection in both white-box and black-box settings. The web UI enables live analysis of user-supplied context-query-answer triples through hallucination scores, unsupported-span highlighting, and side-by-side detector comparison, with a lightweight plug-in design for adding new detectors. We demonstrate SIRIN on hallucination detection, query answerability, and as a faithfulness gate within long-term memory systems.
  The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sb-ai-lab/SIRIN.

</details>


### [347] [Linguistic Context Recodes Visual Representations in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00035)
*Brian Song,Michael A. Lepori,Ellie Pavlick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how vision-language models (VLMs) dynamically recode visual representations in response to goal-directed language, identifying two specific mechanisms: abstract reference representations (steering vectors that denote goal-relevant objects and generalize across objects, tasks, and image types) and language-induced attribute modulation (later layers selectively amplify goal-relevant attributes). Both are shown to be causally implicated in model predictions via interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While VLMs are frequently used for goal-directed tasks like categorization and search, prior work treats visual representations in VLMs as static repositories of information manipulated by language. The authors aim to characterize how visual representations are dynamically recoded when prompted with goal-directed language, challenging the static view.

Method: The authors extract contrastive steering vectors from VLMs that correspond to an abstract reference representation denoting goal-relevant objects under natural language prompts. They then demonstrate causal involvement of these vectors in model predictions, test their generalization across objects, task contexts, and synthetic-to-naturalistic image domains. Additionally, they identify language-induced attribute modulation in later layers that selectively amplifies goal-relevant attributes in visual representations, and perform causal interventions to demonstrate that attribute modulation mediates the VLM's response distribution.

Result: The authors provide evidence for two concrete instances of language-induced recoding: (1) abstract reference representations that generalize across diverse objects, task contexts, and even from synthetic to naturalistic images, and (2) selective amplification of goal-relevant attributes in later layers across a range of prompts. Both mechanisms are causally implicated in model predictions through interventions.

Conclusion: Vision-language models dynamically modulate visual representations to support goal-directed queries in language, rather than treating vision tokens as static information repositories. This supports a more dynamic account of cross-modality processing in VLMs.

Abstract: Goal-directed visual processing is a hallmark of human visual intelligence, resulting in representations that support downstream tasks such as categorization or search. Though vision-language models (VLMs) are often faced with these same tasks, their ability to recode visual representations when presented with goal-directed language remains poorly characterized. Indeed, prior work largely treats visual representations in VLMs as static repositories of visual information that are manipulated by language representations. In the present work, we provide evidence for two concrete instances of language-induced recoding of visual representations. First, we identify an abstract reference representation that denotes which objects are goal-relevant under a natural language prompt. We extract contrastive steering vectors corresponding to this reference representation and demonstrate that they are causally implicated in model predictions. These reference representations are abstract in that they generalize to different objects, different task contexts, and even from synthetic to naturalistic images. Second, we demonstrate language-induced attribute modulation: later layers selectively amplify goal-relevant attributes in visual representations of objects. We demonstrate this phenomenon across a range of different prompts. Finally, we provide a causal intervention that demonstrates that attribute modulation mediates a VLM's response distribution. Together, our results support a more dynamic account of cross-modality processing in VLMs -- rather than vision tokens serving as static repositories of information, they are modulated to support queries articulated in language.

</details>


### [348] [RAG-TESTER: Automated End-to-End Testing of Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00054)
*Ange Maiztegi,Jon Ayerdi,Miren Illarramendi,Aitor Arrieta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RagTester is an automated end-to-end testing framework for RAG systems that generates retrieval documents, test inputs, and expected outputs, then uses an LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate answers. Evaluated across 24 configurations (8 LLMs × 6 embedding models) and 72,000 test executions, it detected 21,633 failures—6.6% more than a baseline generator—and outperformed the baseline in 20 of 24 configurations, exposing issues such as inaccurate retrieval, unsupported answers, incomplete context use, and difficulty with complex passages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems integrate multiple components (generative model, embedding model, retrieval mechanism, prompt strategy) whose interactions determine reliability, yet there is a lack of automated, end-to-end testing approaches to expose failures before deployment.

Method: RagTester generates retrieval documents, test inputs, and expected outputs; executes tests against the RAG system; and evaluates answers using an LLM-as-a-judge. Its test-generation strategy targets complex passages, unsupported queries, and document-coverage criteria to systematically probe the RAG pipeline.

Result: Across 72,000 test executions with 8 LLMs and 6 embedding models (24 configurations), RagTester detected 21,633 failures—6.6% more than the baseline—and outperformed the baseline in 20 of 24 configurations. Detected failures include inaccurate retrieval, unsupported answers, incomplete context usage, and difficulty interpreting complex passages.

Conclusion: Coverage-oriented test generation can effectively expose failures arising from the interaction between retrieval and generation components, and supports the assessment and comparison of RAG configurations prior to deployment.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to use external and domain-specific knowledge, but its reliability depends on the interaction between the generative model, embedding model, retrieval mechanism, and prompt construction strategy. We present RagTester, an automated end-to-end testing approach for RAG systems. RagTester generates retrieval documents, test inputs, and expected outputs; executes the tests; and evaluates the resulting answers using an LLM as a judge. Its test-generation strategy targets complex passages, unsupported queries, and document-coverage criteria. We evaluate RagTester using eight LLMs and six embedding models, yielding 24 compatible configurations, and compare it with a baseline test-input generator. Across 72,000 test executions, RagTester detected 21,633 failures, 6.6% more than the baseline, and outperformed it in 20 of the 24 configurations. The detected failures include inaccurate retrieval, unsupported answers, incomplete use of retrieved context, and difficulties interpreting complex passages. These results show that coverage-oriented test generation can effectively expose failures caused by the interaction between retrieval and generation components and support the assessment of RAG configurations before deployment.

</details>


### [349] [H+ Embedding: Harmonizing Global and Token-Level Retrieval with Context-Dependent Phrases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00065)
*Shusen Zhang,Junyi Hu,Ye Feng,Ziteng Wang,Zhaoyuan Pan,Guosheng Dong,Xiaojun Yuan,Jiangshou Hong,Xiangzhi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: H+ Embedding is a multi-granularity retriever that predicts variable-length phrase partitions as an intermediate representation unit between global vectors and token-level late interaction, achieving strong retrieval quality with reduced indexing costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Terminology-intensive retrieval (especially medical) requires preserving multi-word entities and compositional concepts, but existing representations are polarized: single-vector retrievers over-compress local relevance, while token-level late interaction retains every subword at substantial indexing/storage/scoring cost. This motivates exploring context-dependent phrases as an intermediate retrieval unit.

Method: H+ Embedding is a unified multi-granularity retriever that: (1) predicts variable-length phrase partitions from documents, (2) preserves uncovered tokens as singletons, and (3) applies importance-guided unit selection with weighted MaxSim interaction.

Result: Across 16 scientific, medical, and bilingual tasks: the phrase retrieval branch beats the global retrieval branch by 6.91 macro nDCG@10, nearly matches Token-level interaction while using 13.7% fewer document vectors, and outperforms content-independent grouping rules under moderate vector budgets.

Conclusion: Context-dependent phrase interaction offers an intermediate quality-cost operating point between global compression and token-level interaction, making it practical for real-world retrieval systems.

Abstract: Terminology-intensive retrieval, especially in medical settings, depends on preserving multi-word entities, abbreviations, numerical constraints, and compositional concepts. However, existing representations lie at two extremes: single-vector retrievers often over-compress local relevance signals, while token-level late interaction retains every tokenizer subword at substantial indexing, storage, and scoring cost. This mismatch raises a natural question: can context-dependent phrases provide a useful retrieval unit between global vectors and tokens? We introduce H+ Embedding, a unified multi-granularity retriever that predicts variable-length phrase partitions, preserves uncovered tokens as singletons, and applies importance-guided unit selection with weighted MaxSim interaction. Across 16 scientific, medical, and bilingual tasks, its phrase retrieval branch exceeds the global retrieval branch by 6.91 macro nDCG@10. It also nearly matches Token while using 13.7% fewer document vectors and outperforms content-independent grouping rules under moderate vector budgets. Context-dependent phrase interaction therefore provides an intermediate quality-cost point between global compression and token-level interaction for practical retrieval systems.

</details>


### [350] [Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00101)
*Banruo Liu,Haoran Qiu,Íñigo Goiri,Rodrigo Fonseca,Ricardo Bianchini,Esha Choukse*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: First production-scale characterization of AI coding agent workloads using GitHub Copilot traces (3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, 95T tokens), revealing agentic sessions differ fundamentally from chatbots: sparse user turns unfold into autonomous agent loops with tool execution, yielding ~90% KV cache hit rates within turns but dropping to ~55% across turn boundaries, with long-tailed token/tool consumption patterns and a lightweight idle-time predictor capturing 86-90% of idle time to enable proactive resource orchestration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex) interleave multi-step LLM inference with tool execution, creating a workload fundamentally different from traditional chatbots. However, there is no empirical characterization of this workload at production scale, and existing LLM-serving systems assume chatbot-like patterns. This gap motivates a data-driven analysis to inform agent-native infrastructure design.

Method: The authors analyze sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June 2026, comprising 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens. They characterize workload properties including session structure, KV cache hit rates within and across turns, token consumption patterns, tool call behavior, turnaround times, and user idle periods. They also design and evaluate a lightweight idle-time predictor for resource orchestration.

Result: Key findings include: (1) agentic sessions have sparse user-initiated turns that unfold into autonomous agent loops of LLM calls almost always coupled with tool execution; (2) KV cache hit rates average 90% within a turn but drop to 55% across turn boundaries and are drastically invalidated by model switches or context compaction; (3) diverse workflows exhibit variable and long-tailed token consumption, time spans, and tool calls; (4) a clear distinction between quick agentic turnaround times and minutes-long user idle periods at turn boundaries; (5) the proposed idle-time predictor captures 86-90% of total idle time, enabling proactive resource orchestration.

Conclusion: The findings challenge assumptions underlying current LLM-serving systems designed for chatbot workloads, demonstrating that agentic coding workloads have distinct structural and temporal properties. The work provides an empirical foundation for building agent-native infrastructure, specifically highlighting opportunities for cache-aware scheduling, idle-time-based proactive resource management, and differentiated serving strategies suited to agentic turn structures.

Abstract: AI coding agents like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Codex interleave multi-step LLM inference with tool execution, creating a workload different from chatbots. We present the first production-scale characterization of this workload using sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June 2026, comprising 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens.
  Our analysis reveals distinctive workload properties with important systems implications. For example, agentic coding sessions consist of sparse user-initiated turns, each unfolding into an autonomous agent loop of LLM calls almost always coupled with tool execution. This structure yields KV cache hit rates averaging 90% within a turn, but falling to 55\% across turn boundaries and drastically invalidated after events like model switches or context compaction. Diverse workflows and user behaviors are observed with variable and long-tailed token consumption, time span, and tool calls. We highlight the difference between quick agentic turnaround times and the minutes-long user idle periods at turn boundaries, and design a lightweight idle-time predictor that captures 86-90\% of total idle time, enabling proactive decisions for efficient resource orchestration. These findings challenge assumptions underlying current LLM-serving systems and provide an empirical foundation for agent-native infrastructure.

</details>


### [351] [Can LLM Agents Price Competitively? A Dynamic Multi-Attribute Auction Benchmark for Agentic Commerce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00102)
*Shimaa Ahmed,Yiwei Cai,Mohsen Minaei,Rahul Rachuri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid benchmark for multi-attribute auctions that tests whether LLM-based agents can price competently under realistic market conditions (hidden customer preferences, real-time competitor adaptation, demand shocks). Despite grounding in closed-form customer utilities for exact evaluation, even the best LLM captures less than a third of hindsight-optimal profit, with rankings varying wildly depending on whether customer acquisition, profit, or post-shock recovery is measured.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic commerce is moving toward real deployment with agents transacting on behalf of merchants/consumers, yet no systematic test exists of whether LLMs behind these agents can price competently in real markets where customer preferences are hidden, competitors adapt in real time, and demand shifts unpredictably.

Method: The paper introduces Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid benchmark for multi-attribute auctions. The benchmark incorporates market dynamics (hidden customer preferences, real-time competitor adaptation, demand shocks) while remaining grounded in closed-form customer utilities to enable exact evaluation. It evaluates 11 frontier LLMs from four providers.

Result: Leading agents on customer acquisition (e.g., Gemini 3.1 Pro) differ from leading agents on profit (e.g., Opus 4.6). Rankings shift again under demand shocks: the fastest learners pre-shock are typically slowest to revise beliefs afterward, while Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers fastest despite not leading on profit. The strongest agent captures less than one-third of hindsight-optimal profit.

Conclusion: Current LLMs are making progress in agentic commerce pricing but leave substantial headroom; no single frontier model dominates across all metrics, and even the best performers are far from optimal pricing in dynamic real-world-like auction settings.

Abstract: Agentic commerce is moving from concept to deployed infrastructure: payment networks, retailers, and AI platforms are setting the stage for agents to transact on behalf of merchants and consumers. Yet whether the LLMs behind these agents can price competently in real markets, where customer preferences are hidden, competitors adapt in real time, and demand can shift without warning, has not been systematically tested. We introduce Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid benchmark for multi-attribute auction under these conditions. Despite its dynamics, the benchmark is grounded in closed-form customer utilities, enabling exact evaluation. Across 11 frontier LLMs from four providers, the leading agents on customer acquisition (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro) are often not the leading agents on profit (e.g. Opus 4.6). The ranking shifts again under demand shocks: agents that learned fastest pre-shock are typically the slowest to revise their beliefs afterwards, while Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers fastest despite not leading on profit. However, even the strongest agent captures less than a third of hindsight-optimal profit, suggesting current LLMs are progressing in agentic commerce but leave substantial headroom.

</details>


### [352] [Shared Organizational Memory for Enterprise Coding Agents: System Design and Deployment Snapshot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00122)
*Harsh Rao Dhanyamraju,Leonidas Raghav*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A production deployment of a shared organizational memory system for enterprise coding agents that automatically captures task-adjacent developer experience at the platform level, curates it into reusable Q&A memories with contributor approval, filters security/privacy risks, and retrieves them for future agent sessions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise coding agents struggle because critical knowledge (internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions, tacit workflows) is not in public training data or formal documentation. Existing knowledge interfaces require agents to explicitly recognize and record lessons, disconnecting capture from the coding workflow and causing repeated rediscovery of experience.

Method: A shared organizational memory system deployed at the platform level of coding work. It collects task-adjacent experience with contributor approval, curates the captured content into reusable question-answer memories, applies gates to filter security and privacy risks, and retrieves relevant memories for future coding agents.

Result: The system is in ongoing production deployment. The paper describes its deployed lifecycle and an operational snapshot; effects on retrieval and coding tasks are still under evaluation.

Conclusion: Making knowledge capture a first-class, platform-level part of the coding workflow addresses the disconnect between capture and use, but quantitative impact on agent retrieval and coding effectiveness remains to be validated.

Abstract: Enterprise coding agents rely on tools and retrieval, yet enterprise knowledge often remains outside public training data and formal documentation: internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions, recent fixes, and tacit workflows. Existing knowledge interfaces expose stored resources but still depend on agents recognizing and explicitly recording lessons worth reusing, disconnecting capture from the coding workflow and leaving development experience repeatedly rediscovered. We report an ongoing production deployment of a shared organizational memory system that makes capture a platform-level part of coding work: it collects task-adjacent experience with contributor approval, curates it into reusable question-answer memories, gates obvious security and privacy risks, and retrieves memories for future agents. This short paper describes the deployed lifecycle and an operational snapshot. Effects on retrieval and coding tasks remain under evaluation.

</details>


### [353] [AgentStream: How Well Do Self-Evolving LLM Agents Perform Under Streaming Tasks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00155)
*Dong Yan,Jian Liang,Dapeng Hu,Ran He,Nicholas Jing Yuan,Qi Zhang,Tieniu Tan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces AgentStream, a unified framework for evaluating self-evolving LLM agents in realistic streaming settings (Isolated, Sequential, and Interleaved scenarios). By combinatorially evaluating five self-evolution methods across three frontier foundation models, the authors find that self-evolution reliability varies across streaming scenarios, its benefit is gated by model capability and non-monotonic in model strength, and no single method dominates across all models and scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing studies of self-evolving LLM agents predominantly use independent evaluation, leaving the behavior of these agents in realistic streaming settings—where they adapt to diverse and complex task streams—poorly understood. This gap motivates the need for a framework that evaluates self-evolution under realistic task streams.

Method: AgentStream is a unified framework that organizes agentic benchmarks into a configurable task stream and instantiates three streaming scenarios—Isolated, Sequential, and Interleaved—at test time, progressively varying the scope and domain composition of the stream. Five representative self-evolving methods are combinatorially evaluated across three frontier foundation models.

Result: Results show that self-evolution reliability varies across streaming scenarios, the benefit of self-evolution is gated by model capability and non-monotonic in model strength, and no single method dominates across models and scenarios. These findings provide concrete guidance for selecting self-evolving methods across different models and streaming scenarios.

Conclusion: The paper advocates that self-evolving agents should be evaluated under realistic task streams rather than isolated single-task settings, emphasizing the importance of streaming-aware evaluation for understanding and deploying self-evolving LLM agents.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve by continually improving from their own accumulated experience. However, existing studies predominantly adopt independent evaluation. Consequently, the behavior of self-evolving agents in realistic streaming settings, where agents adapt to diverse and complex task streams, remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce AgentStream, a unified framework that evaluates self-evolving agents spanning diverse evolution components by organizing agentic benchmarks into a configurable task stream and instantiating the \texttt{Isolated}, \texttt{Sequential}, and \texttt{Interleaved} streaming scenarios at test time, which progressively vary the scope and domain composition of the stream. Over these scenarios, we combinatorially evaluate five representative self-evolving methods across three frontier foundation models, disentangling how model capability, method architecture, and streaming scenario jointly shape self-evolution. Our results show that self-evolution reliability varies across streaming scenarios, the benefit of self-evolution is gated by model capability and non-monotonic in model strength, and no single method dominates across models and scenarios. These findings offer concrete guidance for selecting self-evolving methods across models and streaming scenarios. Overall, we advocate that self-evolving agents should be evaluated under realistic task streams rather than isolated single-task settings.

</details>


### [354] [Allocation Before Ranking: Decoupled Token Compression for OmniLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01665)
*Zhenghui Guo,Yilin Yang,Yuanbin Man,Miao Yin,Weidong Shi,Rabimba Karanjai,Omprakash Gnawali,Chengming Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Macer is a training-free token compressor for OmniLLMs that assigns explicit audio and video budgets before per-modality allocation-normalized ranking, significantly reducing token cost (preserving 98.7% and 97.3% performance at 25% retention on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and 3B respectively) while outperforming shared top-K ranking baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper argues that token compression in OmniLLMs is mis-specified as a single saliency-ranking problem. A shared top-K rule simultaneously decides both modality capacity allocation and within-modality token selection, which introduces an audio-favoring bias where audio tokens consume retained capacity before video tokens can compete, degrading multimodal performance.

Method: Macer is a training-free compressor that (1) assigns explicit audio and video token budgets first, then (2) performs allocation-normalized ranking within each modality at modality-specific shallow layers. This decouples capacity allocation from token selection, removing the shared top-K bias.

Result: At 25% retention, Macer preserves 98.7% of full-token performance on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and 97.3% on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B. On Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, 25% retention matches OmniZip at 45% retention with lower FLOPs. On OmniVinci-9B, it improves over shared top-K ranking by up to 12.9 points.

Conclusion: Allocation-before-ranking is a more principled formulation for multimodal token compression than a single global saliency ranking, as it preserves accuracy across diverse benchmarks (audio-grounded, audio-video joint, visual-dominant, and video-centric) at significantly lower token costs.

Abstract: Token compression in OmniLLMs is typically posed as a single saliency-ranking problem: score each multimodal token, keep the top-K. We argue this abstraction is mis-specified. The same attention score simultaneously decides two things: how much retained capacity each modality receives, and which tokens within a modality are kept. A shared top-K rule therefore inherits this audio-favoring allocation prior, spending retained capacity on audio before video tokens have a chance to compete. We propose Macer, a training-free compressor that first assigns explicit audio and video budgets, then performs allocation-normalized ranking within each modality at modality-specific shallow layers. Macer significantly reduces token cost while preserving accuracy across audio-grounded, audio--video joint, visual-dominant, and video-centric benchmarks. At 25 % retention, Macer preserves 98.7 % of full-token performance on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and 97.3 % on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B. On Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, this 25 % setting reaches OmniZip-level performance at 45 % retention while using lower FLOPs. On OmniVinci-9B, the same allocation-before-ranking principle improves over shared top-K ranking by up to 12.9 points.

</details>


### [355] [TRACE-TS: Attribution-Grounded and Traceable Sensor-Language Reasoning for Human Activity Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00200)
*Sparsh Rastogi,Tanmay Kumar,Baiyu Chen,Jatin Bedi,Zechen Li,Flora D. Salim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE-TS is a framework for structured, signal-grounded reasoning over wearable time-series data. It uses expert classifier attribution to identify salient sensor regions, constructs DAG reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance, trains a compact LM to generate these traces via gated cross-attention, and introduces an LLM-as-judge metric (SNM) for diagnosing reasoning fidelity. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven wearable benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LM-based approaches generate natural-language explanations for wearable sensor data that are fluent but weakly grounded in the underlying signal, making them unverifiable. There is a need for structured, traceable reasoning that is explicitly tied to signal evidence.

Method: TRACE-TS comprises three components: (1) attribution from an expert classifier identifies salient spatio-temporal sensor regions; (2) these regions are used to construct DAG reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance; (3) a compact language model is trained to generate these traces via gated cross-attention over sensor memory tokens. At inference, the model jointly outputs activity predictions and reasoning traces without requiring attribution computation or teacher guidance. A novel LLM-as-judge metric, Semantic Node Match (SNM), diagnoses reasoning fidelity at observation, inference, and synthesis levels.

Result: Across seven wearable benchmarks, TRACE-TS achieves the best average accuracy (84.43%) and F1 (81.24%) among all evaluated methods, and outperforms the best LLM-based baseline by 17.96% in F1.

Conclusion: TRACE-TS demonstrates that grounding language-model reasoning in signal attribution produces both more accurate activity predictions and more verifiable, traceable explanations for wearable sensor data. SNM provides a principled way to diagnose reasoning fidelity beyond standard NLG metrics.

Abstract: Wearable sensors capture fine-grained motion patterns that support rich behavioral understanding, yet most existing methods reduce these signals to activity labels. Recent LM-based approaches generate natural-language explanations for sensor data, but their reasoning is weakly grounded in the underlying signal, leading to fluent yet unverifiable explanations. We introduce TRACE-TS (Traceable Reasoning with Attribution-Grounded Evidence), a framework for structured and signal-grounded reasoning over wearable time series. TRACE-TS uses attribution from an expert classifier to identify salient spatio-temporal sensor regions, uses them to construct DAG reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance, and trains a compact language model to generate these traces through gated cross-attention over sensor memory tokens. At inference, the adapted model jointly outputs the activity prediction and its reasoning trace, without requiring attribution computation or teacher guidance. We introduce Semantic Node Match(SNM), an LLM-as-judge metric that diagnoses reasoning fidelity at the observation, inference, and synthesis levels, localizing hallucinated observations and broken evidence chains missed by standard NLG metrics. Across seven wearable benchmarks, TRACE-TS achieves the best average accuracy and F1 among all evaluated methods (84.43%/81.24%), and outperforms the best LLM-based baseline by 17.96% in F1. Our code is available at https://github.com/SparshRastogi/TRACE-TS.

</details>


### [356] [Personalizing Large Language Model Agents with Small Policy Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00215)
*Dian Jin,Zhi Zhang,Huichao Li,Yihe Pan,Rundong Huang,Doudou Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FABLE (Factorized Adaptive Bandit Layer for Execution) is a lightweight policy layer that personalizes frozen LLM agents by learning per-user execution policies from scalar feedback via Bayesian contextual Thompson sampling, without fine-tuning the underlying (possibly black-box) model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents make execution decisions (memory retrieval, tool calls, clarifying questions, response style) but adapting these to individual users is difficult. Fine-tuning separate LLMs is costly or impossible for proprietary systems, and prompts/memory only expose user info rather than adapt execution decisions from feedback.

Method: FABLE is a policy layer external to a frozen host agent. It factorizes memory, information-acquisition, and response decisions so feedback updates related choices; filters candidate actions through an externally specified feasible set before exploration; and learns user-specific residual preferences relative to a fixed default-and-cost score using Bayesian contextual Thompson sampling. A calibrated variant inherits an expected-regret bound against the best feasible action under a linear residual-reward model, with anytime-valid false-promotion control.

Result: Across personalized-reasoning, controlled-feedback, and executable tool-use evaluations, FABLE improves preference-sensitive behaviors relative to rule-only control while remaining competitive on end-to-end task performance.

Conclusion: Personalization of frozen LLM agents can be effectively achieved through an external lightweight bandit layer that learns user-specific execution preferences from sparse scalar feedback, with theoretical guarantees on regret and false-promotion control, and practical gains over rule-based baselines.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can retrieve memory, call tools, ask clarifying questions, and vary response style, yet adapting these execution decisions to an individual user remains difficult. Fine-tuning a separate LLM is costly or impossible for proprietary systems, while prompts and memory primarily expose user information to the agent rather than adapt its execution decisions from feedback. We formulate personalization of a frozen agent as online learning of a per-user execution policy from scalar feedback observed only for the executed action. We propose FABLE (Factorized Adaptive Bandit Layer for Execution), a lightweight policy layer outside a potentially black-box host agent. FABLE factorizes memory, information-acquisition, and response decisions so feedback updates related choices; filters actions through an externally specified feasible set before exploration; and learns user-specific residual preferences relative to a fixed default-and-cost score via Bayesian contextual Thompson sampling. Under a linear residual-reward model, a calibrated variant inherits an expected-regret bound against the best feasible action. We also characterize preferences unidentifiable under persistent feasibility constraints and provide anytime-valid false-promotion control. Across personalized-reasoning, controlled-feedback, and executable tool-use evaluations, FABLE improves several preference-sensitive behaviors relative to rule-only control while remaining competitive on end-to-end task performance.

</details>


### [357] [More Debate, Same Evidence: Structural Limits of Homogeneous Multi-Agent Groundedness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00243)
*Yuelyu Ji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper empirically tests whether multi-agent LLM judge panels with exchanging critiques improve groundedness verification. Evaluating a homogeneous three-agent panel on six benchmarks shows mixed results: system-level accuracy differences range from +8.5 to -4.4 percentage points versus a fixed single-agent reference, with only two datasets showing reliable gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM panels are increasingly used under the assumption that exchanging critiques improves judgment quality. The authors aim to test whether this assumption actually holds for groundedness verification tasks.

Method: The authors evaluate a homogeneous three-agent panel on six public fact-verification and hallucination-detection benchmarks, comparing against a fixed single-agent reference judge. The reference and panel use different model variants, so differences characterize complete systems rather than isolate a causal debate effect.

Result: Relative to the fixed single-agent reference, the panel's accuracy difference ranges from +8.5 to -4.4 percentage points across datasets: two datasets show reliable gains, one shows a reliable loss, and three are statistically inconclusive.

Conclusion: The assumption that multi-agent critique exchange improves judgment quality is not universally supported. The gains are inconsistent and dataset-dependent, and the comparison captures whole-system differences rather than an isolated causal debate effect.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly organized as multi-agent panels under the assumption that exchanging critiques improves judgment quality. We test this assumption for \emph{groundedness verification}, where a judge must determine whether a claim is supported by the supplied evidence. We evaluate a homogeneous three-agent panel on six public fact-verification and hallucination-detection benchmarks. Relative to a fixed single-agent reference, the panel's system-level accuracy difference ranges from $+8.5$ to $-4.4$ percentage points: two datasets show reliable gains, one shows a reliable loss, and three are statistically inconclusive. Because the reference and panel use different model variants, these differences characterize the complete systems rather than isolate a causal debate effect.

</details>


### [358] [Geometric Self-Supervised Pre-training for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00270)
*David Aguado,Daniel Fuertes,Carlos R. del-Blanco,Fernando Jaureguizar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes GSPTSP, a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework for Neural Combinatorial Optimization applied to routing problems like TSP. By applying isometric transformations (rotations and reflections) to learn spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions, the model achieves 7.23% improvement in tour length for zero-shot extrapolation to TSP1,000 and speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over Concorde.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NCO techniques are efficient alternatives to exact algorithms for routing problems, but RL-based models severely struggle with generalization when scaling to high-dimensional instances. While self-supervised pre-training has mitigated this issue in other domains (CV, NLP), its application to routing graphs is challenging because they lack complex topological attributes beyond 2D spatial coordinates.

Method: The paper introduces a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework that captures spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions. The method applies isometric transformations—specifically rotations and axial reflections—to learn robust structural representations of TSP instances before the policy optimization (RL training) phase.

Result: The strategy consistently outperforms models trained from scratch, achieving a 7.23% improvement in tour length for massive zero-shot extrapolation scenarios (TSP1,000). The model also demonstrates remarkable computational efficiency, delivering speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over the exact solver Concorde at massive scales.

Conclusion: Geometric self-supervised pre-training with isometric transformations effectively addresses the generalization gap in NCO for routing problems, enabling superior performance and computational efficiency at massive scales. The source code and pre-trained models are publicly available.

Abstract: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) techniques have emerged as a highly efficient alternative to traditional exact algorithms for solving routing problems such as the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). However, the generalization capabilities of these Reinforcement Learning-based models are severely hindered when scaling to high-dimensional instances. This issue has been mitigated in other domains, like computer vision and natural language processing, by adopting a self-supervised pre-training strategy. Nevertheless, its application to routing graphs, which lack complex topological attributes beyond 2D spatial coordinates, remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework specifically designed to capture spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions. By applying isometric transformations, such as rotations and axial reflections, the model learns robust structural representations prior to the policy optimization phase. Empirical results demonstrate that this strategy consistently outperforms models trained from scratch (baselines), achieving a 7.23\% improvement in tour length for massive zero-shot extrapolation scenarios (TSP1,000). Furthermore, the proposed model exhibits remarkable computational efficiency, delivering speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over the exact solver Concorde at massive scales.
  The source code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/davidaguadocosano/TSP-GeoPretrain.git.

</details>


### [359] [RF-HOI: Recognize Human-Object Interaction with Radio Frequency Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00289)
*Lihao Wang,Linlu Gao,Jiacan Yu,Yanyu Lin,Yifan Yin,Jianxin Wang,Tianmin Shu,Renjie Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RF-HOI is the first framework that uses only radio frequency (RF) signals—combining mmWave radar and RFID via a novel modality fusion—for privacy-preserving Human-Object Interaction (HOI) recognition. It overcomes limited training data using a simulator that synthesizes multimodal RF data at scale, enabling fine-tuning with minimal real-world data. Experiments show it outperforms baselines and approaches vision-model performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-based HOI methods suffer from privacy concerns and poor light conditions, motivating a need for alternative sensing modalities. However, single-modality RF sensing cannot simultaneously recognize both actions and interacted objects, and limited diverse training data impairs generalization.

Method: RF-HOI combines mmWave radar and RFID through a novel modality fusion mechanism for simultaneous action recognition and target identification. To address data scarcity, a simulator synthesizes multimodal RF data for diverse HOIs at scale, allowing the model to be fine-tuned with only a small amount of real-world data.

Result: RF-HOI outperforms all baselines, approaching vision model performance. Synthetic training data significantly boosts real-world performance.

Conclusion: Multimodal RF sensing is a viable, robust, and privacy-preserving alternative for HOI recognition, and RF data synthesis is effective for scaling training data.

Abstract: Recognizing Human-Object Interactions (HOI) is essential for intelligent systems, underpinning applications in virtual and augmented reality, embodied AI, and assistive robotics. However, vision-based HOI methods face challenges in privacy concerns and poor light conditions. In this work, we introduce RF-HOI, the first framework that only uses radio frequency (RF) signals for HOI recognition. A key challenge of RF-HOI is that single-modality RF sensing is insufficient to recognize both actions and the objects being interacted with. RF-HOI addresses this through a novel modality fusion that combines mmWave radar and RFID, enabling simultaneous action recognition and target identification. Another challenge is limited training data across diverse setups, which impairs the generalizability of the recognition model. To overcome this, we develop a simulator that synthesizes multimodal RF data for diverse HOIs at scale, allowing us to fine-tune with only a small amount of real-world data. Experiment results show that RF-HOI outperforms all baselines, approaching vision model performance, and that our diverse synthetic training data can significantly boost our system's performance on real-world scenarios. These results highlight the potential of multimodal RF sensing for robust and privacy-preserving HOI recognition as well as the effectiveness of our RF data synthesis.

</details>


### [360] [WM-Cov: Test Adequacy for Interactive World-Model-Style Autonomous Driving Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00298)
*Jianxun Cui,Ping Wu,Stanisa Peric,Marko Milojkovic,Vladan Devedzic*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces WM-Cov, a provider-agnostic evaluation layer for interactive world-model-style autonomous driving testing. It formulates testing adequacy in terms of valid closed-loop evidence (requested, realized, and valid) rather than raw generated rollouts, reporting on coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism, artifact suppression, duplicate accounting, and valid-evidence precision. Evaluations on TeraSim/SUMO events, mixed trace pools, and a DriveArena matrix show that dangerous-looking events may mix valid ADS failures, duplicates, partial realizations, and artifacts. Results across 360 ego-route requests (304 fully realized, 56 partial) and an 80-request disjoint route-slice check (74 fully realized, 6 partial) support assessing world-model-style testing by convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interactive world models generate counterfactual, rare, and safety-critical rollouts that react to the ego planner, turning fixed replayed scenarios into scenario families whose evolution depends on the planner under test. The open problem is what valid closed-loop evidence suffices to support a specified testing intent and stopping decision, beyond merely generating dangerous rollouts.

Method: The paper formulates interactive world-model-style testing adequacy and proposes WM-Cov, a provider-agnostic evaluation layer that converts raw provider outputs into three evidence categories—requested, realized, and valid. WM-Cov measures adequacy via seven metrics: coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism, artifact suppression, duplicate accounting, and valid-evidence precision.

Result: Experiments on executed TeraSim/SUMO events, WM-like mixed trace pools, and a real DriveArena TrafficManager–WorldDreamer matrix show dangerous-looking events can include valid ADS failures, duplicates, partial realizations, and artifacts. In the DriveArena matrix (two planners, two horizons, six prompt conditions, 360 ego-route requests), 304 attempts became fully realized evidence and 56 remained partial. A disjoint 80-request route-slice check yielded 74 fully realized and 6 partial attempts.

Conclusion: World-model-style testing should be evaluated by the convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget constraints rather than by raw generated failures or prompt coverage alone.

Abstract: World models and generative simulators are emerging as interactive testing infrastructure for autonomous driving because they can react to the ego planner and produce counterfactual, rare, and safety-critical rollouts. This changes a test scenario from a fixed replayed trajectory into an interactive scenario family whose realized evolution depends on the planner under test. The unresolved question is therefore not only whether dangerous rollouts can be generated, but what valid closed-loop evidence is enough to support a specified testing intent and stopping decision. This paper formulates interactive world-model-style testing adequacy and introduces WM-Cov, a provider-agnostic evaluation layer that converts raw provider outputs into requested, realized, and valid evidence. WM-Cov reports adequacy through coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism, artifact suppression, duplicate accounting, and valid-evidence precision. Studies on executed TeraSim/SUMO events, WM-like mixed trace pools, and a real DriveArena TrafficManager--WorldDreamer matrix show that dangerous-looking events can include valid ADS failures, duplicates, partial realizations, and artifacts. The DriveArena matrix evaluates two planners, two horizons, six prompt conditions, and 360 ego-route requests; 304 attempts become fully realized evidence and 56 remain partial. A disjoint 80-request route-slice check yields 74 fully realized and 6 partial attempts. The results support evaluating world-model-style testing by convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget, rather than by raw generated failures or prompt coverage alone.

</details>


### [361] [CrystalMem: Elastic Memory for Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Knowledge Crystallization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00303)
*Beining Wu,Jun Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CrystalMem is an elastic memory sidecar for LLM agents that prevents capability loss (memory hysteresis) after memory budget squeeze-and-recover cycles by demoting entries across four fidelity states under a crystallization-energy schedule and recovering via verified recrystallization, achieving the highest restored capability across all baselines and environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real cloud platforms dynamically adjust memory quotas with load and cost, and the authors observe that LLM agent capability does not recover after a budget squeeze-and-recover cycle—a gap called memory hysteresis. This is structural: deletion and one-way compression discard material needed for later rebuilding, and any keep-or-drop policy carries a residual-deficit floor.

Method: CrystalMem is an elastic memory sidecar that demotes entries across four fidelity states under a crystallization-energy schedule. Demotions are ordered by advantage-weighted influence with dependency coupling. Capability recovery is done through verified recrystallization under explicit compute and byte caps, providing a principled alternative to binary keep/drop policies.

Result: Across seven environments, seventeen methods, and six backbones, including multi-tenant serving and a physical edge-cloud deployment, CrystalMem achieves the highest restored capability in every setting. From a 50% byte budget, it matches the strongest budgeted baseline at full provision on every environment; at equal budgets it leads by +4.6 pp on average.

Conclusion: CrystalMem closes the capability-recovery gap left open by all baselines, demonstrating that elastic multi-fidelity memory management with verified recrystallization avoids the memory hysteresis floor that plagues simple keep-or-drop policies.

Abstract: Memory for self-evolving large language model (LLM) agents is often provisioned as if its byte budget only grows. Cloud platforms, however, adjust quotas with load and cost, and we show that capability does not follow the budget back up: after a squeeze-and-recover cycle, the agent settles below its pre-squeeze level, a gap we call memory hysteresis. The cause is structural. Deletion and one-way compression discard the material needed for later rebuilding, and we prove that any policy that only keeps or drops entries carries a residual-deficit floor. We propose CrystalMem (Crystallized Memory), an elastic memory sidecar that demotes entries across four fidelity states under a crystallization-energy schedule, orders demotions by advantage-weighted influence with dependency coupling, and recovers capability through verified recrystallization under explicit compute and byte caps. Across seven environments, seventeen methods, and six backbones, with multi-tenant serving and a physical edge-cloud deployment, CrystalMem achieves the highest restored capability in every setting and closes the loop left open by every baseline. From a 50% byte budget, CrystalMem matches the strongest budgeted baseline at full provision on every environment; at equal budgets, it leads by +4.6 pp on average.

</details>


### [362] [Trust and Its Betrayal under Three Representational Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00321)
*Mihnea C. Moldoveanu,Joel A. C. Baum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper formalizes trust as a subjunctive epistemic state (A trusts B's competence: were P true, B would know it; B's integrity: were B to know P, he would disclose it). It develops three representations—lexicographic assumption, ordinal closeness in a Lewis-Stalnaker sphere system, and strong belief in a conditional probability system—and examines whether the Brandenburger-Keisler impossibility on common belief survives when rationality is replaced by trustworthiness. All three agree that finite depths of common trust are realizable while the completed fixed point creates difficulty, but differ in how betrayal manifests: it refutes level ordering (lexicographic), contaminates closeness ordering proportionally to deliberateness (ordinal), and merely shifts the operative conditioning hypothesis while keeping belief structure coherent (strong-belief).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trust differs qualitatively from prediction since betrayal, not mere disappointment, follows from trust broken. The paper seeks a rigorous epistemic-logical treatment of trust and asks whether the Brandenburger-Keisler paradox about common belief in rationality recurs when trustworthiness replaces rationality as the assumed attitude.

Method: Trust is modeled as a subjunctive epistemic state with three formal representations: (1) lexicographic assumption, (2) ordinal closeness via Lewis-Stalnaker sphere systems, and (3) strong belief in conditional probability systems. Each representation is analyzed for how common trust of finite and completed depth behaves, and how betrayal interacts with the underlying ordering structures.

Result: All three representations agree that finite depths of common trust are realizable while the completed common-trust fixed point is where difficulty arises. However, they diverge sharply in how betrayal manifests: the lexicographic representation's level ordering is refuted, the ordinal representation's closeness ordering is contaminated in proportion to the betrayer's deliberateness, and the strong-belief representation remains coherent, only shifting the operative conditioning hypothesis.

Conclusion: The choice of representation for subjunctive trust determines how betrayal is interpreted and how robust the epistemic framework is. The strong-belief representation appears most resilient to betrayal, suggesting that conditional-probability-based formalizations may be best suited for modeling trust under potential violation.

Abstract: Trust is a propositional attitude of a distinctive kind: to trust is to rely on another under conditions where reliance could be disappointed, and the disappointment of trust---betrayal---differs qualitatively from the disappointment of a prediction. We treat trust as a \emph{subjunctive} epistemic state: $A$ trusts $B$'s competence when $A$ believes that \emph{were $P$ true, $B$ would know it}, and $B$'s integrity when $A$ believes that \emph{were $B$ to know $P$, he would disclose it to $A$}. We develop three representations of this state---as lexicographic \emph{assumption} as \emph{ordinal closeness} in a Lewis--Stalnaker sphere system , and as \emph{strong belief} in a conditional probability system and for each we ask whether the Brandenburger--Keisler impossibility on common belief survives when the assumption of rationality is replaced by an assumption of trustworthiness. The three representations agree that every \emph{finite} depth of common trust is realizable while the \emph{completed} common-trust fixed point is the locus of difficulty, but they differ sharply in \emph{how} the difficulty manifests, and---our organizing finding---in how each survives a concrete betrayal. W show that the same betrayal refutes an agent's \emph{level ordering} under the lexicographic representation, contaminates her \emph{closeness ordering} in proportion to the betrayer's deliberateness under the ordinal representation, and merely \emph{shifts her operative conditioning hypothesis} while leaving her belief structure coherent under the strong-belief representation.

</details>


### [363] [Learning to Coordinate Symbolic Tools: LLM Agents for Verified Sum-of-Squares Certificates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00326)
*Bohan Chen,Shivam N. Patel,Richard Hoffmann,Sam Looi,Tony Yue Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops an LLM agent for weighted sum-of-squares (SOS) polynomial decomposition—a machine-checkable route to proving polynomial nonnegativity—by combining algebraic task training on 1.35M synthetic examples, native SymPy tool calling, and GRPO with verifier-grounded rewards. The full SFT+GRPO+tools pipeline achieves 78.96% verified success on weighted SOS (vs. 44.73% for the base model with tools) and 91.75% macro accuracy across nine polynomial tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool calling enables LLMs to invoke external computation, which is valuable for AI-for-mathematics. However, finding a valid weighted SOS decomposition is hard because candidate decompositions are non-unique and require coordinating multiple symbolic transformations (expansion, collection, reordering, factorization). The authors aim to build an agent that can reliably perform this exactly checkable mathematical task by combining domain skill training, symbolic tools, and verifier-grounded optimization.

Method: The approach has three pillars: (1) a 1.35M-example synthetic corpus covering eight supporting polynomial tasks plus weighted-SOS decomposition; (2) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on direct algebra problems and simulated symbolic traces (notably, the SFT corpus contains no native tool-calling messages—tools are introduced only at evaluation time via native SymPy calls); (3) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-specific symbolic rewards. Every final SOS answer is verified by exact expansion and coefficient comparison.

Result: On held-out same-generator synthetic problems, the full SFT+GRPO+tools system is the strongest of four evaluated configurations, achieving 78.96% verified success on weighted SOS compared to 44.73% for the base model with the same tools, and 91.75% macro accuracy across nine polynomial tasks.

Conclusion: Within this controlled setting, the work provides a case study of combining domain-specific skill training, executable symbolic tools, and verifier feedback. The findings may inform the design of tool-calling agents in other domains that have exactly checkable outputs, suggesting that strong base capabilities plus targeted skill training and verifier-grounded RL can substantially boost tool-augmented mathematical problem solving.

Abstract: Tool calling allows large language models (LLMs) to invoke external computation during problem solving, a useful capability in various fields including AI for mathematics. We study this setting through weighted sum-of-squares (SOS) decomposition, a machine-checkable route to proving polynomial nonnegativity and hence polynomial inequalities. A candidate decomposition can be checked exactly, but finding one requires choosing among non-unique regroupings and coordinating multiple symbolic transformations. We develop an agent that combines algebraic task training, symbolic tools, and verifier-grounded optimization for this task. Rather than training only on the composite SOS task, we construct 1.35 million synthetic examples covering eight supporting polynomial tasks together with weighted-SOS decomposition. We first apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to direct algebra problems and simulated symbolic traces, and then use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-specific symbolic rewards. The SFT corpus contains no native tool-calling messages; at evaluation, the agent uses native SymPy calls for expansion, collection, reordering, and factorization. Every final SOS answer is checked by exact expansion and coefficient comparison. On held-out, same-generator synthetic problems, the full SFT+GRPO+tools system is the strongest of four evaluated configurations, reaching 78.96% verified success on weighted SOS, compared with 44.73% for the base model with the same tools, and 91.75% macro accuracy across nine polynomial tasks. Within this controlled setting, our work provides a case study of combining domain-specific skill training, executable tools, and verifier feedback, and may inform the design of tool-calling agents in other domains with exactly checkable outputs.

</details>


### [364] [RMSWeb: Reflection, Failure-Mode Mining, and Salvage-DS for Web Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00335)
*Chengbo Liu,Lifang Zhou,Ruijie Yan,Pei Tan,Ao Sun,Haojun Huang,Guichun Hua,Sining Wei,Yining Chen,Yingying He,Yutao Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RMSWeb is a three-part recipe for training compact web agents (Qwen3-VL-Instruct at 8B and 32B) that addresses data collection inefficiency and weak RL signal issues via reflection-conditioned retries, failure-mode mining, and the Salvage-DS reward/sampling scheme, achieving up to 19.7% fewer action steps and 2.4-7.7 points improvement over SFT across three benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compact web agents reduce deployment cost but are hard to train: successful trajectories are expensive to collect and inefficient, full trajectory corpora are dominated by routine states post-SFT, and inadequately designed action-level rewards in group-relative RL yield weak/misleading updates while rejected groups receive no fallback learning signal.

Method: RMSWeb consists of three components: (1) reflection-conditioned retries that increase collection yield and shorten successful trajectories; (2) failure-mode mining that focuses offline RL on critical states exposed by the SFT policy; (3) Salvage-DS which combines an action-semantic polarized reward, contrast-and-competence-gated dynamic sampling, and an action-only anchor for rejected groups.

Result: Reflection-collected data policies use up to 19.7% fewer action steps on solved tasks. RMSWeb improves over SFT by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B on WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench. The 8B model achieves the strongest reported Online-Mind2Web result among similarly sized open-weight models and a leading accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench.

Conclusion: RMSWeb effectively addresses the data collection and RL training challenges for compact web agents, achieving better efficiency (fewer action steps) and accuracy across multiple benchmarks, with the caveat that external evaluation protocols differ.

Abstract: Compact web agents can reduce deployment cost, but training them poses challenges in both data collection and post-SFT reinforcement learning (RL). Successful trajectories are expensive to collect and often contain inefficient detours. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), full trajectory corpora are dominated by routine states; moreover, when group-relative RL is applied to web actions, inadequately designed action-level rewards can yield weak or misleading relative updates, while groups rejected as unsuitable for such updates receive no fallback learning signal. We present RMSWeb, a three-part recipe for Qwen3-VL-Instruct at 8B and 32B. Reflection-conditioned retries increase collection yield and shorten successful trajectories; failure-mode mining concentrates offline RL on critical states exposed by the SFT policy; and Salvage-DS combines an action-semantic polarized reward, contrast-and-competence-gated dynamic sampling, and an action-only anchor for rejected groups. Policies trained with reflection-collected data use up to 19.7% fewer action steps on solved tasks. On WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench, RMSWeb improves over SFT by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B. Our 8B model also achieves the strongest reported Online-Mind2Web result among similarly sized open-weight models in our comparison and a leading reported accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench, with the caveat that external evaluation protocols differ.

</details>


### [365] [Bayesian and Motivated Reasoning in AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00339)
*Eddie Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI agents draw different conclusions from identical numerical data when the substantive framing changes, influenced by their prior beliefs across high-stakes domains like medicine, election forensics, and geopolitical forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents are increasingly delegated open-ended tasks that can guide consequential decisions, there is a risk that their decisions depend on unstated prior beliefs. This paper aims to demonstrate that framing changes alter agent conclusions even when evidence is held fixed.

Method: Held numerical evidence fixed while changing the scenario/framing context in which the evidence appears across twelve agent-domain comparisons spanning medicine, election forensics, and geopolitical forecasting. Analyzed how agents' conclusions, search behavior, analytical specifications, and evidence evaluation changed with framing.

Result: Agents' conclusions are strongly influenced by their prior beliefs. They reach affirmative conclusions more often when framing aligns with a proposition they already regard as likely, and less often when framing conflicts. Framing also alters agent behavior—more extensive search, different analytical specifications, and different evaluation of the same evidence.

Conclusion: Delegating decision-making to AI agents carries a particular risk: decisions may depend on prior beliefs neither specified in the task nor visible in the decision record, making agent outputs potentially unreliable in high-stakes contexts.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly perform open-ended tasks in settings where their conclusions can guide consequential decisions. We provide evidence that AI agents draw different conclusions from identical numerical data when the substantive framing changes. We demonstrate this behavior in high-stakes domains in medicine, election forensics, and geopolitical forecasting by holding the evidence fixed while changing the scenario in which the evidence appears. Across twelve agent-domain comparisons, agents' conclusions are strongly influenced by their prior beliefs. They are more likely to reach an affirmative conclusion when it is framed around a proposition they already regard as likely, while the reverse holds when the framing conflicts with their prior. The framing also changes how some agents work: they search more extensively, choose different analytical specifications, and evaluate the same evidence differently. These results identify a particular risk of delegating decision-making to AI agents, as their decisions may depend on prior beliefs that are neither specified in the task nor visible in the decision record.

</details>


### [366] [Gene Ontology-Guided Hierarchical Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathology Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00405)
*Zhiwen Xu,Xiaoming Yan,Chengkun Wu,Juan Chen,Haoang Chi,Liyang Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSGR is a plug-in decoder for spatial gene expression prediction from histopathology images that uses Gene Ontology as a structural prior. It organizes genes into a four-level GO tree and refines predictions from coarse functional domains to fine genes via residual corrections under scale-weighted supervision, consistently outperforming flat decoders across the HEST-1k benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods decode target genes as flat, unstructured vectors, ignoring inter-gene dependencies from shared biological pathways and regulatory programs. This forces models to infer these dependencies entirely from limited paired data, constraining prediction quality.

Method: MSGR incorporates Gene Ontology (GO) as an explicit structural prior. It organizes target genes into a four-level GO tree and uses a GO-guided decoder that progressively refines predictions from coarse functional domains to fine individual genes via residual corrections under scale-weighted supervision. The decoder operates solely on the gene side as a plug-in replacement, requiring no image-side modifications.

Result: Experiments on nine datasets from the HEST-1k benchmark show GO-structured decoding consistently outperforms flat decoding, even against a state-of-the-art generative baseline. The gain is attributable to biological ontology structure rather than hierarchical decomposition per se, confirmed by a +0.027 margin over a structurally equivalent random hierarchy.

Conclusion: Incorporating biological ontology structure as a prior improves spatial gene expression prediction from histopathology images, and the improvement stems from the biological relevance of the hierarchy rather than hierarchical structure alone. MSGR serves as a seamless plug-in that can enhance existing architectures.

Abstract: Predicting spatial gene expression from histopathology images enables large-scale transcriptomic profiling without the cost of direct measurement. Existing methods decode the target gene set as a flat, unstructured vector, ignoring the inter-gene dependencies arising from shared biological pathways and regulatory programs. Without explicit structural guidance, models must infer these dependencies entirely from limited paired data, constraining prediction quality. We propose MSGR (Multi-Scale Gene Refiner), which bridges this gap by incorporating the Gene Ontology (GO), a curated functional hierarchy of genes, as an explicit structural prior. MSGR organizes target genes into a four-level GO tree. Its GO-guided decoder then progressively refines predictions from coarse functional domains to fine individual genes via residual corrections under scale-weighted supervision. Operating solely on the gene side, the GO-guided decoder serves as a seamless plug-in replacement that consistently improves existing architectures without requiring any image-side modifications. Extensive experiments on nine datasets from the HEST-1k benchmark provide empirical evidence for two central claims: GO-structured decoding consistently outperforms flat decoding, even against a state-of-the-art generative baseline, and the gain is attributable to biological ontology structure rather than hierarchical decomposition per se, as confirmed by a +0.027 margin over a structurally equivalent random hierarchy.

</details>


### [367] [Where did the ambiguity go? Examining how multimodal models interpret polysemous words](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00410)
*Jasin Cekinmez,Addison J. Wu,Raja Marjieh,Thomas L. Griffiths*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies how polysemy (multiple word meanings) surfaces across text-to-image and text generation models. Testing 17 image models and 15 text models with ambiguous words and no disambiguating context, they find a "multimodal gap": image models produce far fewer distinct senses than text models (normalized entropy 0.10 vs 0.25), and both are much less diverse than human imagination (0.47). Interestingly, when models are asked to self-report their output distributions, they predict more diversity than they actually exhibit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs are known to handle polysemy well in text, little is known about whether the multiplicity of meaning transfers to image generation. The authors aim to quantify whether foundation models express meaning faithfully and equally across modalities.

Method: The authors present 17 text-to-image models and 15 text-generation models with polysemous words lacking disambiguating context, sample many outputs per model, and measure the entropy of the distribution of senses produced. They compare cross-modal entropy, benchmark against human imagination diversity, and also elicit models' self-predicted output distributions.
