Result: Generated images concentrate on far fewer senses than generated sentences (normalized entropy 0.10 vs 0.25), and both fall well short of human imagination diversity (0.47). Models' self-reported distributions are more diverse than their actual sampled outputs, indicating a mismatch between model introspection and behavior.

Conclusion: There is a systematic multimodal gap in how foundation models express polysemous meaning: their understanding of word ambiguity does not transfer faithfully or equally across text and image modalities, and models overestimate their own output diversity.

Abstract: Human language is highly polysemous. Many common words (e.g., 'bank' or 'palm') carry several distinct meanings that shape what humans communicate and imagine. Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to understand this multiplicity of meaning, but much less is known about how polysemy surfaces in other modalities such as images. We study this across 17 text-to-image and 15 text-generation models by giving each a polysemous word with no context to fix its meaning and measuring which senses are produced over many samples. We find a clear multimodal gap, where within every model family, generated images settle on far fewer senses than generated sentences (normalized entropy 0.10 vs. 0.25), and both are far less varied than what people imagine for the same words (normalized entropy 0.47). However, when we instead ask a model to list how often it would generate outputs corresponding to each possible meaning of a word, it predicts distributions that are more diverse than the actual space of outputs. These results reveal a multimodal gap in how foundation models express meaning, and how their understanding may not transfer faithfully nor equally across modalities.

</details>


### [368] [SymboUQ: Symbolic Uncertainty Quantification for Spatial Reasoning in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00417)
*Dahai Yu,Lin Jiang,Rongchao Xu,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SymboUQ is a symbolic uncertainty quantification framework that estimates final-answer reliability from LLM reasoning traces by separating symbolizability (whether a claim can be formalized in a verifier's language) from semantic determinacy (whether execution yields a definite verdict), achieving ~8% relative AUROC improvement and ~7% relative reduction in class-balanced Brier loss across five spatial reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can generate fluent spatial reasoning traces, but intermediate relations often fail to support final conclusions, making token-level confidence unreliable for final-answer confidence estimation. Existing formal verifiers provide stronger semantic evidence but have limited applicability since parsed claims may not yield definite semantic verdicts.

Method: SymboUQ consists of three components: (i) a Layout Auditor that executes ordered spatial claims and extracts feasibility, conflict, and repair evidence; (ii) a label-free Determinacy Profile characterizing effective executable coverage; and (iii) a Determinacy-Aware Reliability Composer that integrates constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based scores according to verifier applicability.

Result: On five spatial reasoning benchmarks with four frozen LLM backbones, SymboUQ achieves approximately 8% relative improvement in AUROC and 7% relative reduction in class-balanced Brier loss over the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: By explicitly distinguishing between symbolizability and semantic determinacy, SymboUQ provides more reliable final-answer uncertainty quantification for LLM spatial reasoning than token-level confidence or existing formal verifiers alone.

Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent spatial reasoning traces, their intermediate relations may fail to support the final conclusion, making token-level confidence insufficient for final-answer reliability estimation. Existing formal verifiers provide stronger semantic evidence, but their applicability is partial: a parsed claim need not yield a definite semantic verdict. To address this issue, we introduce SymboUQ, a symbolic uncertainty quantification framework that estimates final-answer reliability from reasoning traces by distinguishing symbolizability, whether a claim can be represented in the verifier's formal language, from semantic determinacy, whether its execution yields an entailed or contradicted verdict rather than an unknown or not-evaluable outcome. SymboUQ comprises (i) a Layout Auditor that executes ordered spatial claims and extracts feasibility, conflict, and repair evidence; (ii) a label-free Determinacy Profile that characterizes effective executable coverage; and (iii) a Determinacy-Aware Reliability Composer that integrates constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based scores according to verifier applicability. Extensive experiments on five spatial reasoning benchmarks with four frozen LLM backbones show that SymboUQ achieves approximately an 8% relative improvement in AUROC and a 7% relative reduction in class-balanced Brier loss over the strongest baseline.

</details>


### [369] [Mask-Based Priors Are More Persistent than Query-Key Initializations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00418)
*Mingze Ma,Hemanth Saratchandran,Cameron Gordon,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Transformers fail to extrapolate on Boolean tasks due to a minimum-degree inductive bias. The authors propose initializing the additive attention mask directly (learnable attention-logit bias) from task-level interaction structure, which persists through training and achieves near-perfect extrapolation where vanilla and QK-initialized Transformers fail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers generalize in a systematically wrong way on Boolean extrapolation tasks, defaulting to a simpler minimum-degree interpolator rather than the true target function. Existing structured-initialization methods (QK-based priors) can be rapidly overwritten during training and fail to change the learned extrapolation rule. The authors ask whether this failure mode can be corrected by injecting explicit structural priors into attention.

Method: The authors propose initializing the additive attention mask directly rather than via QK projections. The mask is a finite, learnable attention-logit bias initialized from task-level interaction structure. This separates the structural prior from content-dependent attention scores, allowing it to persist throughout optimization instead of being overwritten. It differs from standard hard masks used for causality or locality attention by being learnable.

Result: Mask-based initialization achieves near-perfect extrapolation on Boolean reasoning tasks where vanilla and QK-initialized Transformers remain trapped by default inductive bias. The method also improves low-data arithmetic performance and remains competitive on vision and language benchmarks.

Conclusion: Attention masks can serve not only as architectural constraints but as a simple substrate for encoding persistent inductive bias in Transformers, offering a more robust alternative to QK-projection-based structured initialization for injecting structural priors.

Abstract: Transformers do not merely lack data on some Boolean extrapolation tasks; they generalize in a systematically wrong way. Recent work on generalization on the unseen has shown that, despite fitting the observed domain, Transformers often extrapolate according to a simpler minimum-degree interpolator rather than the true target function. These Boolean tasks are not practical applications, but controlled stress tests for understanding Transformer inductive bias. We ask whether this failure mode can be corrected by injecting explicit structural priors into attention. Existing structured-initialization methods alter Transformer inductive bias indirectly, by choosing query and key projections whose similarity scores approximate a desired attention pattern. However, we find that when applied to Boolean extrapolation, these QK-based priors can be rapidly overwritten during training and fail to change the learned extrapolation rule. We propose a simpler alternative: initialize the additive attention mask directly. Unlike standard hard masks used for causality or locality attention, our mask is a finite, learnable attention-logit bias initialized from task-level interaction structure. This separates the structural prior from content-dependent attention scores, allowing it to persist throughout optimization. On Boolean reasoning tasks, mask-based initialization achieves near-perfect extrapolation where vanilla and QK-initialized Transformers remain trapped by the default inductive bias. The same mechanism also improves low-data arithmetic performance and remains competitive on vision and language benchmarks. These results show that attention masks can serve not only as architectural constraints, but as a simple substrate for encoding persistent inductive bias in Transformers.

</details>


### [370] [TrAC: Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency for Efficient Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00422)
*Dahai Yu,Lin Jiang,Rongchao Xu,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrAC is a correctness-supervised uncertainty quantification framework for LLM reasoning that combines active re-elicitation of a short answer conditioned on a completed reasoning trace (PCE) with passive token-level uncertainty profiling of the original trace (TUP), integrated by a lightweight head. It improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4% over eight-sample self-consistency while using only one complete trace, and improves AUROC by 4.3% when augmenting existing multi-sample consensus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can produce fluent but incorrect reasoning traces, making uncertainty estimation critical for abstention and adaptive compute. Existing methods are passive (token-level signals), sampling-based (multiple full traces, high cost), or active prefix-based (probing partial traces), yet none actively re-elicits an answer from a completed reasoning trace to measure consistency between the trace and its original answer. This gap motivates TrAC.

Method: TrAC has two components: (1) an active component, Prefix-Conditioned Elicitation (PCE), which re-elicits a short answer conditioned on the completed reasoning trace and captures both its consistency with the original answer and token-level probabilistic support; and (2) a passive component, Trace Uncertainty Profile (TUP), which summarizes token-level uncertainty evolution across the original generation without extra decoding. A lightweight head integrates both representations to score response correctness.

Result: Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three LLM families, TrAC improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4% relative to eight-sample self-consistency, while using only one complete reasoning trace and a short cached answer probe. When eight samples are already available, augmenting sample consensus with re-elicitation improves macro AUROC by 4.3% and reduces AURC by 8.3% without additional full-trace generation.

Conclusion: TrAC effectively bridges the gap between passive and active uncertainty estimation by re-eliciting answers from completed traces, demonstrating that a single trace can rival or surpass multi-sample self-consistency. It is also complementary to existing sampling-based methods, providing further gains when combined with multi-sample consensus at no additional full-trace cost.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent reasoning traces that nevertheless lead to incorrect answers, making response-level uncertainty estimation important for abstention, human review, and adaptive compute allocation. Existing approaches generally fall into three categories: passive single-trace methods use token-level confidence signals, sampling-based methods compare multiple complete traces at higher generation cost, and active prefix-based methods probe partial traces to study answer stabilization or preference transitions. However, none actively re-elicits an answer from a completed reasoning trace to measure its consistency with and support for the original answer. To address this gap, we introduce Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency (TrAC), a correctness-supervised uncertainty quantification framework that combines active and passive signals anchored to one completed reasoning trace. Its active component, Prefix-Conditioned Elicitation (PCE), re-elicits a short answer conditioned on the completed trace and represents both its consistency with the original answer and its token-level probabilistic support. Its passive component, Trace Uncertainty Profile (TUP), summarizes how token-level uncertainty evolves throughout the original generation without additional decoding. A lightweight head then integrates the two representations into a response-correctness score. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three LLM families, TrAC improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4% relative to eight-sample self-consistency, while using one complete reasoning trace and a short cached answer probe. When eight samples are already available, augmenting sample consensus with re-elicitation further improves macro AUROC by 4.3% and reduces AURC by 8.3%, without additional full-trace generation.

</details>


### [371] [Diagnose Before You Compress: Prediction-Independent Bottleneck Witness Refinement for LLM Serving Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00423)
*Liming Liu,Chao Hu,Mingfei Lu,Cong Tan,Yiwei Ge,Chijin Zhou,Yongjun Xie,Runzhe Wang,Xiaohai Shi,Heyuan Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BPW is a quality-constrained framework that constructs compact and diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites by preserving evidence for every bottleneck component (scheduler, prefill, decode, KV-cache), using a three-stage pipeline: workload candidate nomination, coverage-priority sequence construction, and bottleneck truth verification. It outperforms 16 baselines on BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake with 2.3% and 16.3% relative improvements in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and WBRC-AUC respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing trace reduction methods preserve workload distributions or representative requests, but bottleneck-revealing workloads may be rare and non-representative. Also, evidence for one component cannot compensate for missing evidence in another, and using predicted bottlenecks as ground truth creates circular evaluation. This necessitates preserving evidence for every bottleneck component rather than relying solely on workload representativeness.

Method: BPW pipeline consists of three stages: (1) Workload Candidate Nomination using response-blind workload features and closed source-side measurements to identify workloads exposing scheduler, prefill, decode, or KV-cache bottlenecks; (2) Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction that organizes multi-component proposals as reusable hyperedges and prioritizes weak/uncovered dimensions; (3) Bottleneck Truth Verification that derives prediction-independent labels solely from direct target-system measurements, determining the earliest prefix satisfying the direct two-witness requirement for every component.

Result: Experiments on BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake show BPW reaches the verified gate with a compact workload set, outperforming 16 policies with relative improvements of 2.3% in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and 16.3% in WBRC-AUC. Stage-resolved and sensitivity analyses confirm distinct contributions and local stability of its three stages.

Conclusion: Preserving diagnostic evidence for every bottleneck component (rather than workload representativeness alone) is necessary and effective for constructing compact, diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites. BPW's three-stage design achieves superior diagnostic reliability with a compact workload set, as validated across multiple real-world workload datasets.

Abstract: Production LLM serving generates millions of diverse requests, making full-trace replay across serving configurations increasingly expensive. Existing trace reduction methods mainly preserve workload distributions or representative requests, but bottleneck-revealing workloads may be rare and non-representative. Moreover, evidence for one component cannot compensate for missing evidence in another, while using predicted bottlenecks as target truth creates circular evaluation. These limitations make it necessary to preserve evidence for every bottleneck component rather than rely on workload representativeness alone. We propose Bottleneck-Preserving Witnessing (BPW), a quality-constrained framework for compact and diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites. BPW first performs Workload Candidate Nomination using response-blind workload features and closed source-side measurements. This stage identifies workloads that may expose scheduler, prefill, decode, or KV-cache bottlenecks. Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction then organizes multi-component proposals as reusable hyperedges and prioritizes weak and uncovered dimensions. Finally, Bottleneck Truth Verification derives prediction-independent labels solely from direct target-system measurements. The verified results determine the earliest prefix satisfying the direct two-witness requirement for every component. Experiments on BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake show that BPW reaches the verified gate with a compact workload set and outperforms 16 policies, achieving relative improvements of 2.3% and 16.3% in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and WBRC-AUC, respectively. Stage-resolved and sensitivity analyses confirm the distinct contributions and local stability of its three stages. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/llmllmllm/BPW

</details>


### [372] [Ekova: A Personality-Support Agent for Self-Discovery Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00478)
*Yuyan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Personality Support (PS), a new paradigm distinct from Emotional Support (ES) focused on helping users achieve cognitive clarity and self-articulation rather than symptom relief. The authors present DSD, a Chinese self-discovery dataset of 8,590 samples; DeepSupport, a multi-persona PS system trained with OrthoTune (style-specific adapters and style-consistency regularizer); and Ekova, a unified persistent personality-support agent with cross-session memory and adaptive routing. OrthoTune-trained models achieve a 16.3% average relative gain over the strongest prompt-based baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Emotional Support systems only optimize for alleviating momentary emotional distress. The authors argue this misses a complementary need—helping users see themselves more clearly—which defines a distinct paradigm (Personality Support) that is neither counseling nor clinical intervention but targets cognitive clarity and self-articulation.

Method: The paradigm is instantiated in three layers: (1) DSD, a Chinese self-discovery PS dataset of 8,590 samples from real longitudinal interaction across five minimal persona units (Coach, Warm, Tsukkomi, Real, Gonzo); (2) DeepSupport, a multi-persona PS system trained with OrthoTune, a PS-tailored framework using style-specific adapters and a style-consistency regularizer; (3) Ekova, a persistent agent unifying the five personas with a shared cross-session memory layer supporting both adaptive routing and user-customized persona selection.

Result: Experiments show OrthoTune-trained models outperform all baselines with an average relative gain of 16.3% across all metrics over the strongest prompt-based baseline.

Conclusion: Personality Support is a viable and distinct paradigm from Emotional Support, and the proposed DSD dataset, DeepSupport/OrthoTune training framework, and Ekova agent together provide a complete instantiation that substantially outperforms existing baselines. Code is publicly released at https://github.com/Yukyin/Ekova.

Abstract: Emotional Support (ES) systems have long optimized a single objective: alleviating the user's emotional distress in the moment. We argue that a complementary need, helping users see themselves more clearly, defines a distinct paradigm we call Personality Support (PS). PS is not counseling or clinical intervention: it targets cognitive clarity and self-articulation, not symptom relief or diagnosis. We instantiate this paradigm in three layers. First, we present DSD, a Chinese self-discovery PS Dataset of 8,590 samples collected through real longitudinal interaction across five minimal units, Coach, Warm, Tsukkomi, Real, and Gonzo. Second, we build DeepSupport, a multi-persona PS system trained with OrthoTune, a PS-tailored framework with style-specific adapters and a style-consistency regularizer. Third, we unify the five DeepSupport personas into Ekova, a persistent personality-support agent with a unified cross-session memory layer, supporting both adaptive routing and user-customized persona selection. Experiments show that OrthoTune-trained models outperform all baselines with an average relative gain of 16.3% across all metrics over the strongest prompt-based baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Yukyin/Ekova.

</details>


### [373] [F-WANDA: Fisher-Reweighted Post-Training Pruning for Sustainable Deployment of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00481)
*Himanshu Mishra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: F-WANDA is a drop-in modification of WANDA that improves one-shot post-training pruning by reallocating the per-row keep budget across output neurons based on empirical Fisher information of the pre-activation, collected via a single additional backward pass. It matches WANDA's fluency, beats both WANDA and SPARSEGPT on MMLU, and incurs only one-third of SPARSEGPT's pruning cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing one-shot post-training pruning methods for LLMs face a fundamental trade-off: WANDA is fast and cheap but sacrifices quality, while SPARSEGPT achieves better quality but at high computational and energy cost. The authors seek a method that sits on the Pareto frontier of quality versus pruning cost without extra calibration data or fine-tuning.

Method: F-WANDA modifies WANDA by reallocating the per-row retention budget across output neurons in proportion to the empirical Fisher information of the pre-activation. The Fisher signal is obtained from a single additional backward pass over the same calibration corpus already used by WANDA, and no weights are updated during pruning.

Result: On LLAMA-2-7B at 50% unstructured sparsity, F-WANDA achieves WikiText-2 perplexity of 6.85, matches WANDA's fluency, improves 5-shot MMLU by +1.6 pp over WANDA and +1.1 pp over SPARSEGPT, while using only one-third of SPARSEGPT's pruning wall-clock time and energy.

Conclusion: F-WANDA achieves the headline quality-versus-cost trade-off without additional calibration data or fine-tuning, placing it on the Pareto frontier of quality versus pruning cost for sustainable LLM compression.

Abstract: One-shot post-training pruning is the most energy-frugal compression strategy for largelanguage models (LLMs), yet existing approaches trade either quality (WANDA) or compute cost (SPARSEGPT). We introduce F-WANDA, a drop-in modification of WANDA that reallocates the per-row keep budget across output neurons in proportion to the empirical Fisher information of the pre-activation. The Fisher signal is collected in a single additional backward pass over the same calibration corpus WANDA already uses; no weights are updated. On LLAMA-2-7B at 50 % unstructured sparsity, F-WANDA attains WikiText-2 perplexity of 6.85, matches WANDA fluency, and improves 5-shot MMLU by +1.6 pp over WANDA and +1.1 pp over SPARSEGPT, while incurring only one-third of SPARSEGPT pruning wall-clock and energy. The headline trade-off is achieved without extra calibration data or fine-tuning, placing F-WANDA on the Pareto frontier of quality versus pruning cost for sustainable LLM compression.

</details>


### [374] [The Bayesian Reflex: A Predictive Coding Engine for Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00492)
*Sourabh Bhattacharya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Bayesian reflex, a computational framework that instantiates predictive coding theory through three pillars: hierarchical generative models for belief maintenance, sequential Bayesian updating via prediction-error minimization, and uncertainty-driven action via active inference. It leverages recent algorithmic breakthroughs—ellipsoidal decomposition, recursive Gaussian processes, and derivative-aware Bayesian optimization—to enable scalable, brain-inspired continual learning, perception, and decision-making, demonstrated across applications from climate modeling to prime number discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predictive coding is a powerful theory of cortical computation, but scalable algorithmic implementations for artificial intelligence have remained elusive. The paper aims to bridge this gap by providing concrete, mathematically principled algorithmic ingredients that make predictive coding computationally viable for scalable AI systems.

Method: The framework, called the Bayesian reflex, is built on three pillars: (1) belief maintenance via hierarchical generative models, (2) sequential Bayesian updating via prediction-error minimization, and (3) uncertainty-driven action via active inference. The method integrates three recent algorithmic breakthroughs as enabling components: ellipsoidal decomposition for exact i.i.d. sampling, recursive Gaussian processes for deep hierarchical inference, and derivative-aware Bayesian optimization.

Result: The resulting framework enables mathematically principled, scalable, and brain-inspired continual learning, perception, and decision-making. Its versatility is illustrated through diverse applications including climate model evaluation and prime number discovery, demonstrating adaptive behavior across heterogeneous domains.

Conclusion: The Bayesian reflex provides a concrete blueprint for truly adaptive artificial intelligence grounded in predictive coding principles, showing that the missing algorithmic ingredients for scalable implementation now exist and can be unified within a single computational framework.

Abstract: Predictive coding offers a powerful theory of cortical computation, but corresponding scalable algorithmic implementations for artificial intelligence have remained elusive. This paper introduces the Bayesian reflex, a computational framework that directly instantiates predictive coding through three pillars: belief maintenance via hierarchical generative models, sequential Bayesian updating via prediction-error minimization, and uncertainty-driven action via active inference. We show that recent breakthroughs---ellipsoidal decomposition for exact $i.i.d.$ sampling, recursive Gaussian processes for deep hierarchical inference, and derivative-aware Bayesian optimization---provide the missing algorithmic ingredients. The resulting framework enables mathematically principled, scalable, and brain-inspired continual learning, perception, and decision-making. We illustrate its versatility through applications ranging from climate model evaluation to prime number discovery, offering a blueprint for truly adaptive artificial intelligence.

</details>


### [375] [TaPR: Test-Aware Policy Refinement for Feedback-Conditioned Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00494)
*Aofan Liu,Jingxiang Meng,Fangxin Liu,Yongbiao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TaPR transforms execution feedback into a dense per-turn test-pass-ratio reward for multi-turn code agents, improving three-turn success rate (Pass@3) by 2.44 pp across six models on 219 LiveCodeBench problems, with gains up to +3.31 pp on 7B/8B models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL paradigms for code agents use single-shot outcome rewards, which conflates initial generation with feedback-driven refinement, discards granular execution signals across turns, and fails to assess whether policies truly acquire self-repair capabilities.

Method: TaPR transforms execution feedback into a dense per-turn test-pass-ratio reward under a consistent multi-turn interaction protocol, enabling reward decomposition that separates first-shot generation quality from multi-turn repair competence.

Result: Across six models on 219 LiveCodeBench problems, TaPR improves pooled Pass@3 by 2.44 pp. On 7B/8B models, accuracy rises from 30.25% to 33.56% (+3.31 pp) with 42 improvements and 13 regressions. Dense reward supplies nonzero feedback in all first ten steps and reaches higher Hard-subset peak than outcome-only GRPO, though GRPO nearly matches pooled Pass@3 by step 300.

Conclusion: The primary contribution is a reward-decomposition framework and a turn-aware evaluation protocol that decouple first-shot generation quality from multi-turn repair competence, better aligning RL optimization with the sequential nature of code agent self-repair.

Abstract: Multi-turn code agents rely on execution feedback to repair incorrect programs, yet standard reinforcement learning paradigms optimize and evaluate policy performance primarily using single-shot outcome rewards. This misalignment conflates initial code generation with feedback-driven refinement, discards granular execution signals across intermediate turns, and fails to evaluate whether the policy actually acquires self-repair capabilities. We propose Test-aware Policy Refinement (TaPR), a framework that transforms execution feedback into a dense per-turn test-pass-ratio reward under a consistent multi-turn interaction protocol. Across six models on 219 code-generation problems from LiveCodeBench, TaPR improves the pooled three-turn success rate (Pass@3) by 2.44 percentage points. In the predefined 7B/8B high-headroom slice, pooled accuracy increases from 30.25% to 33.56% (+3.31 pp), with 42 improvements and 13 regressions in paired trials. On a matched Qwen3-8B ablation, the dense reward supplies nonzero feedback in all of the first ten steps and reaches a higher Hard-subset peak than outcome-only GRPO within the tested budget, although GRPO nearly matches pooled Pass@3 by step 300. Our primary contribution is a reward-decomposition framework and a turn-aware evaluation protocol that decouple first-shot generation quality from multi-turn repair competence.

</details>


### [376] [BayesSeg: A Bayesian Optimization Framework for State Segmentation of Electricity Consumption Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00513)
*Zhenya Zhang,Wendi Zhu,Ping Wang,Hongmei Cheng,Shuguang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BayesSeg is a unified framework for adaptive segmentation in Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM), integrating segmentation, multidimensional evaluation, and Bayesian optimization. It achieves a weighted composite score of 0.7149 and event_F1 of 0.9340 on SustDataED2, while reducing optimization time from ~5300 seconds to under 1 second (5700x speedup).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prevailing NILM segmentation methods suffer from heuristic parameter tuning, boundary sensitivity, and metric saturation, limiting their effectiveness for appliance recognition.

Method: The framework has three layers: (1) a segmentation layer using a dual steady-state criterion (tail value and mean of preceding subsequences) with sequential extraction and complement-set parsing for unsupervised partitioning; (2) an evaluation layer mapping results to binary state sequences and computing a composite metric of event-level F1 (with tolerance matching) and Normalized Mutual Information; (3) an optimization layer using Bayesian optimization with a TPE surrogate model to maximize the composite score.

Result: Bayesian optimization requires only ~100 objective evaluations to reach within 0.35% of the exhaustive grid-search optimum. The framework achieves a weighted composite score of 0.7149 and event_F1 of 0.9340, with optimization latency reduced from ~5300 seconds to under 1 second—a speedup exceeding 5700x.

Conclusion: BayesSeg automates segmentation configuration and provides a scalable, efficient solution for time-series analysis in NILM and related domains.

Abstract: In Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM), adaptive segmentation of electricity consumption time series is critical for appliance recognition. However, prevailing methods face challenges including heuristic parameter tuning, boundary sensitivity, and metric saturation. This paper proposes BayesSeg, a unified framework integrating time-series segmentation, multidimensional evaluation, and automatic parameter optimization. The segmentation layer employs a dual steady-state criterion based on the tail value and mean of preceding subsequences, combined with a sequential extraction and complement-set parsing strategy, to achieve precise unsupervised partitioning of steady-state and transition-state segments. The evaluation layer maps segmentation results to binary state sequences and formulates a composite metric integrating an event-level F1 score (event_F1) with Normalized Mutual Information (NMI). The event_F1 quantifies switching-event precision and recall via tolerance matching, while NMI captures global structural consistency, jointly overcoming the boundary sensitivity and limited discriminability of point-wise metrics. In the optimization layer, the composite score serves as the objective function for Bayesian optimization, which constructs a TPE surrogate model for efficient global parameter-space exploration. Experiments on the SustDataED2 dataset demonstrate that Bayesian optimization requires only ~100 objective evaluations to locate a parameter region within 0.35% deviation of the exhaustive grid-search optimum. The framework achieves a weighted composite score of 0.7149 and an event_F1 of 0.9340 while reducing optimization latency from ~5300 seconds to under 1 second, a speedup exceeding 5700x. BayesSeg automates segmentation configuration and provides a scalable, efficient solution for time-series analysis in NILM and related domains.

</details>


### [377] [CURE: Local Uncertainty Repair for Block-Parallel Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00531)
*Aofan Liu,Jingxiang Meng,Fangxin Liu,Yongbiao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CURE is a budget-aware dynamic repair tree mechanism for speculative decoding that identifies and repairs high-uncertainty token errors in parallel draft generation, improving average accepted length by 4.2-7.5% over parallel baselines and achieving 2.66-3.49x end-to-end speedup over target-only decoding across code and math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parallel drafting backends in speculative decoding suffer from rapid accuracy degradation over long horizons, leading to high rejection rates and suboptimal speedups. The paper observes that drafting errors are not uniformly distributed but stem from localized high-uncertainty tokens that destabilize downstream generation trajectories.

Method: CURE introduces a budget-aware dynamic repair tree that: (1) uses predictive confidence margins to dynamically locate candidate error tokens within a block-parallel draft, (2) expands bounded repair paths only at fragile high-uncertainty nodes, and (3) employs a novel repair resynchronization mechanism to realign draft states post-verification. It is designed as a plug-and-play module compatible with standard parallel drafting frameworks.

Result: Evaluations on HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench-lite, and GSM8K show CURE increases average accepted length by 4.2-7.5% over parallel baselines without repair, translating to 2.66-3.49x end-to-end speedup over target-only decoding.

Conclusion: CURE effectively addresses the error propagation problem in parallel speculative decoding by targeting repair to localized uncertainty focal points, and characterizes the trade-off between draft compute and verification efficiency, offering a practical plug-and-play solution for existing parallel drafting frameworks.

Abstract: Speculative decoding mitigates the latency of sequential generation in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) by interleaving draft generation with target verification. However, existing parallel drafting backends often suffer from rapid accuracy degradation over long horizons, leading to high rejection rates during verification and suboptimal wall-clock speedups. We observe that drafting errors are not uniformly distributed but typically stem from localized high-uncertainty tokens that destabilize downstream generation trajectories. Motivated by this token error pattern, we propose CURE, a budget-aware dynamic repair tree designed to repair errors at uncertainty focal points without incurring prohibitive tree-verification overheads. Specifically, our method uses predictive confidence margins to dynamically locate candidate error tokens within a block-parallel draft, expands bounded repair paths only at these fragile nodes, and employs a novel repair resynchronization mechanism to realign draft states post-verification. Evaluations on code-generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench-lite) and mathematical reasoning benchmark (GSM8K) demonstrate that CURE increases the average accepted length by 4.2-7.5% over parallel baselines without repair, translating to an end-to-end speedup of $2.66-3.49\times$ over target-only decoding. Furthermore, we provide a plug-and-play repair module compatible with standard parallel drafting frameworks. We also characterize the trade-off between draft compute and verification efficiency.

</details>


### [378] [Through the LENS: Local Geometric Decomposition of Vision-Language Model Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00561)
*Shalom Kachko,Raz Lapid,Margarita Vald,Almog Dubin,Moshe Sipper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LENS (Local Explanation of Neighborhood Subspaces) is a method that decomposes VLM activations into local low-rank Gaussian neighborhoods using Mixture of Factor Analyzers, revealing depth-dependent cross-modal fusion trajectories in LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B, and enabling causal steering and improved retrieval through local geometric representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most interpretability methods for vision-language models identify global linear directions in the shared residual stream, but these may miss representations that are globally high-dimensional yet locally low-dimensional. Understanding how image patches and text tokens interact locally in the geometry of VLM activations remains an open problem.

Method: The authors introduce LENS, which uses a Mixture of Factor Analyzers (MFA) to decompose VLM activations into local low-rank Gaussian neighborhoods. They apply this to LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B, use an automated multimodal labeling pipeline for semantic annotation, and perform causal steering by interpolating activations toward neighborhood centroids. They also use the MFA coefficient space for retrieval tasks and run ablations on component counts, local ranks, and modality-purity thresholds.

Result: LENS reveals distinct fusion trajectories: LLaVA progressively mixes modalities at later layers while Qwen3-VL mixes early, partially re-segregates, and recombines near output. Steering via MFA outperforms difference-in-means and VL-SAE in most conditions, achieving 5.7x VL-SAE score in one vision-to-vision setting. MFA steering is competitive with prompting and stronger than other baselines. Image-to-rendered-text retrieval improves from 14.9% to 48.6% R@1 at the deepest evaluated layer. Ablations confirm trajectory stability.

Conclusion: Local geometric neighborhoods serve as useful interpretable and causal units for analyzing cross-modal representations in VLMs, offering advantages over global linear methods for understanding and steering multimodal models.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) process image patches and text tokens in a shared residual stream, but the local geometry through which the two modalities interact remains poorly understood. Most interpretability methods identify global linear directions, which may miss representations that are globally high-dimensional but locally low-dimensional. We introduce LENS (Local Explanation of Neighborhood Subspaces), a method that decomposes VLM activations into local low-rank Gaussian neighborhoods using a Mixture of Factor Analyzers. Applied to LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B, LENS reveals distinct depth-dependent fusion trajectories consistent with each model's fusion mechanism: LLaVA progressively mixes modalities at later layers, whereas Qwen3-VL mixes them early, partially re-segregates them, and recombines them near the output. An automated multimodal labeling pipeline assigns concise semantic descriptions to these neighborhoods. Interpolating activations toward neighborhood centroids causally redirects generation within and across modalities and outperforms difference-in-means and VL-SAE in most evaluated conditions; in one LLaVA vision-to-vision setting, MFA achieves 5.7 times the VL-SAE score. Human evaluation finds MFA steering competitive with prompting and substantially stronger than the other intervention baselines. Finally, the MFA coefficient space improves Qwen3-VL image-to-rendered-text retrieval at the deepest evaluated layer from 14.9% to 48.6% R@1. Ablations show that the reported fusion trajectories are stable across component counts, local ranks, and modality-purity thresholds. These results support local geometric neighborhoods as useful interpretable and causal units for analyzing cross-modal representations in the evaluated VLMs.

</details>


### [379] [Why Does the Future Branch? Identifiable Closure Tests for Stochastic Physical World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00591)
*Yibin Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Stochastic world model evaluation based on forecast accuracy/calibration is decision-relevant ambiguous: the same predictive distribution can arise from state aliasing (observation maps to multiple physical states) or genuine process noise (inherent randomness given full state). This attribution is unidentifiable from ordinary transition data. The paper introduces ClosurePairs, an interventional evaluation protocol crossing compatible microstates with repeated exogenous disturbances, using a two-way variance decomposition to identify state aliasing, process noise, and their interaction. Experiments show large reductions in attribution error and sensing regret across Gaussian systems, 18 nonlinear Langevin conditions, pixel-conditioned recurrent models, and a REFINE/BRANCH router test, all without degrading NLL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard evaluation metrics for stochastic world models (accuracy and calibration of predicted futures) leave a decision-relevant ambiguity: they cannot distinguish whether a conditional future distribution branches because observations alias different physical states or because dynamics are genuinely stochastic given the full state. This attribution matters for downstream decisions (e.g., sensing, control) but is provably unidentifiable from ordinary transition data, even with an optimal probabilistic predictor.

Method: Introduces ClosurePairs, an interventional evaluation protocol that crosses compatible microstates with repeated exogenous disturbances. A two-way variance decomposition separates state aliasing, process noise, and their nonlinear interaction. An independent-repeat variant handles settings where disturbances cannot be reused. The protocol is applied across likelihood-equivalent Gaussian systems, nonlinear Langevin systems, and a pixel-conditioned recurrent model with a frozen shared-state probe.

Result: Paired supervision reduces alias-fraction error 15.96-fold at identical test NLL on Gaussian systems. Across 18 nonlinear Langevin conditions, attribution MAE drops from 0.372 to 0.051 and sensing regret from 0.0138 to 0.0003 without changing NLL. On a pixel-conditioned recurrent model, alias-fraction MAE against a deep ensemble drops from 0.584 to 0.130 (in-distribution) and 0.630 to 0.170 (out-of-distribution) over ten seeds. In a matched-total-variance REFINE/BRANCH test, ClosurePairs reaches 99.99%±0.02% accuracy vs. 66.48%±1.06% for a total-variance router, improving selected NLL from -2.087 to -2.717 over five seeds.

Conclusion: ClosurePairs measures why futures branch—information that proper forecast scores cannot identify. By using paired interventions with variance decomposition, it provides a way to attribute stochasticity to state aliasing vs. process noise, improving downstream sensing and model selection decisions without sacrificing predictive likelihood.

Abstract: Stochastic world models are usually evaluated by the accuracy and calibration of their predicted futures. These criteria leave a decision-relevant ambiguity: the same conditional future distribution can arise because an observation aliases different physical states, or because the dynamics remain random after the declared full state is fixed. We prove that this attribution is not identifiable from ordinary transition data, even with an optimal probabilistic predictor. We introduce ClosurePairs, an interventional evaluation protocol that crosses compatible microstates with repeated exogenous disturbances. A two-way variance decomposition identifies state aliasing, process noise, and their nonlinear interaction; an independent-repeat variant applies when disturbances cannot be reused. On likelihood-equivalent Gaussian systems, paired supervision reduces alias-fraction error 15.96-fold at identical test NLL. Across 18 nonlinear Langevin conditions, it reduces attribution MAE from 0.372 to 0.051 and sensing regret from 0.0138 to 0.0003 without changing NLL. On a pixel-conditioned recurrent model, a frozen shared-state probe reduces alias-fraction MAE against a deep ensemble from 0.584 to 0.130 in distribution and from 0.630 to 0.170 out of distribution over ten seeds. Finally, in a matched-total-variance REFINE/BRANCH test, a total-variance router reaches 66.48 percent plus or minus 1.06 percent accuracy, whereas ClosurePairs reaches 99.99 percent plus or minus 0.02 percent and improves selected NLL from -2.087 to -2.717 over five seeds. ClosurePairs therefore measures why futures branch, information that proper forecast scores cannot identify.

</details>


### [380] [Escaping Confidence Trap: Evolutionary Decoding for Mathematical Reasoning in Diffusion LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00605)
*Zhenhong Sun,Hanqing Zhao,Yatao Bian,Rongcheng Tu,Liuyue Xie,Xu Zhang,Jue Wang,Davide Modolo,Daoyi Dong,Dacheng Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper identifies a "diffusion confidence trap" in diffusion large language models (dLLMs) where local token confidence misaligns with global reasoning correctness during math reasoning, and proposes Evolutionary Decoding—a training-free test-time scaling framework combining step-wise selection and block-wise mutation—to improve LLaDA 2.0's mathematical reasoning reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While diffusion LLMs like LLaDA 2.0 achieve strong general-purpose performance via block-wise progressive unmasking, they fail to reliably handle mathematical reasoning because correctness depends on maintaining coherent numerical-symbolic reasoning trajectories. The misalignment between local token confidence and global reasoning correctness during decoding undermines their reliability.

Method: The authors first analyze LLaDA 2.0's decoding trajectories and identify two failure regimes: sampling-sensitive failures (correct paths exist but unstable) and sampling-consistent failures (repeated sampling converges to repetitive high-confidence but incorrect continuations). They then propose Evolutionary Decoding, a training-free test-time scaling framework that treats diffusion decoding as an evolutionary process over candidate reasoning states, combining step-wise selection (preserving useful numerical-symbolic signals, suppressing repetition) with block-wise mutation (introducing structured alternatives to escape incorrect high-confidence basins).

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show Evolutionary Decoding improves LLaDA 2.0 over confidence-based decoding, leading to more reliable mathematical reasoning.

Conclusion: The evolutionary decoding framework effectively addresses the confidence-reasoning misalignment in dLLMs, offering a training-free approach to enhance mathematical reasoning reliability without requiring model modifications.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, offering efficient generation through block-wise progressive unmasking. However, their strong general-purpose performance does not necessarily translate into reliable mathematical reasoning, where correctness depends on preserving coherent numerical-symbolic reasoning trajectories. In this work, we analyze the decoding trajectories of LLaDA 2.0 and identify a recurring diffusion confidence trap: local token confidence can become misaligned with global reasoning correctness during progressive block decoding. Our analysis reveals two representative failure regimes: sampling-sensitive failures, where correct paths exist but are unstable, and sampling-consistent failures, where repeated sampling converges to repetitive high-confidence but incorrect continuations. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evolutionary Decoding, a training-free test-time scaling framework that views diffusion decoding as an evolutionary process over candidate reasoning states. The framework combines step-wise selection, which preserves useful numerical-symbolic signals and suppresses repetitive patterns, with block-wise mutation, which introduces structured alternatives to escape incorrect high-confidence basins. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that Evolutionary Decoding improves LLaDA 2.0 over confidence-based decoding, leading to more reliable mathematical reasoning.

</details>


### [381] [Slides2MindMap: Reconstructing Cognitively Efficient Knowledge Hierarchies from Lecture Slides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00610)
*Yuzhi Wang,Rongjun Ye,Shengyuan Chen,Huachi Zhou,Jiaqi Bai,Chuang Zhou,Zhicong Hong,Xiao Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Slides2MindMap task: automatically generating cognitively efficient mind maps from lecture slide collections. It presents S2M-Bench, a benchmark with 12,774 slides and expert-annotated mind maps across 24 university courses, and proposes AutoMindMap, an agentic framework inspired by the Structure Building Framework that uses Skeleton Laying, Iterative Knowledge Integration, and Dual-Stage Refinement to balance local faithfulness with global coherence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mind map generation from lecture slides can aid learners in assimilating fragmented knowledge for intelligent education, but dedicated automatic generation and evaluation frameworks are underexplored. Challenges include balancing global-local knowledge focus and handling large-scale heterogeneous slide decks.

Method: The paper formulates the Slides2MindMap task and introduces: (1) S2M-Bench, a benchmark of 12,774 slides from 24 university courses with expert-annotated mind maps and a cognitive-science-grounded evaluation framework (ground-truth comparison, structure conformity analysis, VLM-as-a-Judge); (2) AutoMindMap, an agentic framework with three components: Skeleton Laying for global scaffold anchoring, Iterative Knowledge Integration with context-aware summarization, and Dual-Stage Refinement using a local-global decoupling mechanism.

Result: Experiments on S2M-Bench show AutoMindMap outperforms baselines and achieves superior robustness across different models and scenarios, demonstrating its pedagogical application value.

Conclusion: AutoMindMap effectively reconciles local knowledge faithfulness with global coherence in automatic mind map generation from lecture slides, and the S2M-Bench benchmark enables systematic evaluation for this new task.

Abstract: Generating mind maps from lecture slides can help learners efficiently assimilate fragmented knowledge, promising substantial benefits for intelligent education. However, dedicated automatic generation and evaluation frameworks remain underexplored and challenging, requiring a global-local knowledge focus balance and handling large-scale, heterogeneous slides. We formulate the Slides2MindMap task, which aims to reconstruct cognitively efficient knowledge hierarchies from a course's slide deck collection. For systematic evaluation, we introduce S2M-Bench, a benchmark comprising 12,774 slide pages with expert-annotated mind maps spanning 24 university courses. S2M-Bench includes a cognitive-science-grounded evaluation framework that integrates ground-truth-based comparison, structure conformity analysis, and VLM-as-a-Judge. To address this task, we propose AutoMindMap, an agentic framework inspired by the Structure Building Framework. AutoMindMap comprises Skeleton Laying for global scaffold anchoring, Iterative Knowledge Integration augmented by context-aware summarization, and Dual-Stage Refinement with a local-global decoupling mechanism. The framework reconciles local knowledge faithfulness with global coherence, and adapts to slide-specific features. Experiments on S2M-Bench demonstrate that AutoMindMap outperforms baselines and achieves superior robustness across different models and scenarios, underscoring its pedagogical application value.

</details>


### [382] [DASH: Decoupled Adaptive Surrogate - Acquisition Harness for Automated Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00641)
*Changquan Zhao,Yuxiang Sun,Ruihao Zhu,Cheng Hua,Yulian He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DASH is a decoupled adaptive surrogate-acquisition harness for LLM-enhanced automated Bayesian optimization that separately adapts surrogate selection (based on predictive reliability, calibration, and ranking consistency) and acquisition strategies (via a two-stage controller with LLM-based final selection), outperforming the best AutoBO baseline by 12.51% in trajectory-level Acceleration Factor and 5.00% in endpoint Enhancement Factor across four chemical optimization tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AutoBO methods either adapt only one BO component (leaving the other mismatched and creating a bottleneck) or jointly select surrogate-acquisition pairs under a shared criterion, failing to account for their distinct roles: surrogate selection depends on predictive reliability, whereas acquisition adaptation should respond to campaign context.

Method: DASH selects surrogates based on predictive reliability, uncertainty calibration, and ranking consistency. It employs a two-stage acquisition controller that periodically reallocates quotas across acquisition functions, builds a BO shortlist, and delegates final selection to an LLM. An integrated harness with knowledge-guided warm start and structured memory grounds optimization in domain knowledge and accumulated feedback.

Result: Across four chemical optimization tasks, DASH outperforms the best AutoBO baseline by 12.51% in trajectory-level Acceleration Factor and 5.00% in endpoint Enhancement Factor. Results remain strong across LLM backbones, and ablations confirm complementary contributions of all components. Contamination checks find no evidence of benchmark memorization or source-cell leakage.

Conclusion: Decoupled adaptation of surrogate and acquisition components, each guided by its appropriate criterion, is superior to joint or single-component adaptation in AutoBO, and LLM-enhanced selection combined with domain-knowledge grounding delivers robust gains across tasks.

Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) relies on a surrogate model and an acquisition function, yet the most suitable choices vary across tasks and optimization stages. Automated Bayesian optimization (AutoBO) addresses this variability by adapting BO components online. However, existing AutoBO methods either adapt one component, leaving the other mismatched and creating a bottleneck, or jointly select surrogate--acquisition pairs under a shared criterion, overlooking their distinct roles: surrogate selection depends on predictive reliability, whereas acquisition adaptation should respond to campaign context.In this paper, we propose DASH, a Decoupled Adaptive Surrogate--Acquisition Harness for large-language- model (LLM)-enhanced AutoBO. DASH selects surrogates by predictive reliability, uncertainty calibration, and ranking consistency; its two-stage acquisition controller periodically reallocates quotas across acquisition functions, builds a BO shortlist accordingly, and delegates final selection to an LLM. DASH also incorporates an integrated harness, consisting of knowledge-guided warm start and structured memory, to ground optimization in domain knowledge and accumulated feedback. Across four chemical optimization tasks, DASH outperforms the best AutoBO baseline by 12.51% in trajectory-level Acceleration Factor and 5.00% in endpoint Enhancement Factor. Results remain strong across LLM backbones, and ablations verify the complementary contributions of all components. Full-table and behavioral contamination checks find no detectable evidence that direct benchmark memorization or source-cell leakage explains these gains.

</details>


### [383] [HetGPS: Scalable Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Physics-Anchored Adaptive Safety for EV Charging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00679)
*Xiangwei Wang,Nanduni Nimalsiri,Yu Xia,Peng Wang,Saman Halgamuge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HetGPS is a hybrid graph-control framework that combines learned graph risk for scheduling intervention authority with physics-anchored correction direction, applied to EV charging in distribution networks. It reduces bus-step voltage violations from 3.93–7.74% to 0.52–3.44% while maintaining 99.06–100% departure success, with a model size independent of fleet size (383,702 parameters, ~170× smaller than a centralized SAC at 3,218 EVs), and demonstrates zero-shot transfer across network scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety interventions for large populations of network-coupled agents must protect shared constraints (e.g., voltage limits) without unnecessarily overriding task-oriented policy decisions. Existing approaches face a trade-off between safety and preserving agent autonomy, and scale poorly with fleet size.

Method: HetGPS separates intervention magnitude from corrective direction: an action-conditioned graph residual model (learned graph risk) schedules state-dependent intervention authority, while a physics model determines the corrective direction. This filter is coupled with a parameter-shared heterogeneous graph soft actor-critic (SAC) policy for topology-aware coordination, with model size independent of fleet size. The learned policy-and-risk model contains 383,702 parameters across all scales.

Result: Across five nested distribution networks with 200–3,218 EVs and 100 evaluation days, Adaptive Authority reduces bus-step voltage violations from 3.93–7.74% (unfiltered) to 0.52–3.44%, while maintaining 99.06–100% departure success. Compared to fixed-authority physics projection, it improves mean reward on all five networks and lowers mean safety score on four. At 3,218 EVs, a matched centralized SAC actor is ~170× larger. A policy trained on the 8-transformer system transfers zero-shot to 16- and 32-transformer systems with 0.57–0.75% violation rates and ≥99.99% departure success.

Conclusion: Learned graph risk can effectively allocate intervention authority at scale while physics anchoring determines corrective action, achieving a strong balance between safety compliance and preserving task-oriented policy behavior, with excellent scalability and zero-shot transfer capability.

Abstract: Safety interventions for large populations of network-coupled agents must protect shared constraints without unnecessarily overriding task-oriented policy decisions. We present HetGPS, a hybrid graph-control framework synergizing learned graph risk with physics-anchored correction by separating intervention magnitude from corrective direction. An action-conditioned graph residual model schedules state-dependent intervention authority, while a physics model determines its direction. For electric vehicle (EV) charging, we couple this filter with a parameter-shared heterogeneous graph soft actor-critic policy, enabling topology-aware coordination with a learned model size independent of fleet size. Across five nested distribution networks with 200--3,218 EVs and 100 evaluation days, Adaptive Authority reduces bus--step voltage violations from 3.93--7.74\% without filtering to 0.52--3.44\%, while maintaining 99.06--100\% departure success. Relative to the same physics-directed projection with fixed authority, it improves mean reward on all five networks and lowers the mean safety score on four. The deployed policy-and-risk model contains 383,702 learned parameters at every scale; at 3,218 EVs, a matched centralized SAC actor is about $170\times$ larger. A policy trained on the eight-transformer system transfers zero-shot to the 16- and 32-transformer systems, attaining 0.57--0.75\% violation rates and at least 99.99\% departure success. These results show that learned graph risk can allocate intervention authority at scale while feeder physics anchors corrective action.

</details>


### [384] [From AI Technical Debt to Agentic Technical Debt: A Systematic Mapping of Root Causes and Manifestations in Agentic AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01001)
*Muhammad Tukur,Hayatullahi B. Adeyemo,Tao Chen,Nour Ali,Anis Zarrad,Marco Agus,Rick Kazman,Rami Bahsoon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Agentic Technical Debt (AgTD), a new construct that captures how technical debt emerges, accumulates, propagates, and amplifies in Agentic AI systems. Building on a prior systematic review of 31 AITDs, the authors use a theory-informed transformation methodology to map established AI technical debts to their agentic manifestations, creating the first systematic mapping and a taxonomy of AgTD, along with implications for AI TRiSM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI Technical Debt (AITD) models assume static, component-level architectures and cannot capture the dynamic, emergent, and autonomous behaviors of Agentic AI systems. This gap necessitates a new conceptual framework to understand technical debt in agentic environments.

Method: Building on a prior systematic scoping review of 31 AITDs across seven root-cause categories, the authors employ a theory-informed transformation methodology with three lenses: direct transformation, contextual transformation, and manifestation expansion, to reinterpret technical debts in the Agentic AI context.

Result: The paper provides the first systematic mapping of established AITDs to agentic manifestations, revealing system-level liabilities such as memory inconsistencies, orchestration fragility, cascading failures, and unsafe autonomous decision-making. It demonstrates that technical debt extends beyond software artifacts to encompass agent behaviors, coordination mechanisms, and inter-agent/tool/environment interactions.

Conclusion: AgTD is established as a foundational software engineering construct for autonomous multi-agent AI systems. The work contributes a transformation framework, taxonomy, and research agenda for managing technical debt, with significant implications for AI Trust, Risk, and Security Management (AI TRiSM), trustworthiness, governance, security, operational resilience, and sustainability.

Abstract: The emergence of Agentic AI systems, characterized by autonomous reasoning, multi-agent collaboration, tool orchestration, adaptive decision-making, and persistent memory, represents a fundamental shift from traditional AI pipelines to dynamic software ecosystems. While AI Technical Debt (AITD) has been widely studied in machine learning and software engineering, existing models assume static, component-level architectures and fail to capture the dynamic and emergent behaviors of agentic environments. To address this gap, this paper introduces Agentic Technical Debt (AgTD), defined as technical debt that emerges, accumulates, propagates, and amplifies due to the autonomous and collaborative nature of Agentic AI systems. Building on our prior systematic scoping review of 31 AITDs across seven root-cause categories, we employ a theory-informed transformation methodology to reinterpret these debts in Agentic AI through direct transformation, contextual transformation, and manifestation expansion. We present the first systematic mapping of established AITDs to their agentic manifestations, showing how conventional debts evolve into system-level liabilities, including memory inconsistencies, orchestration fragility, cascading failures, and unsafe autonomous decision-making. Our findings show that technical debt extends beyond software artifacts to encompass agent behaviors, coordination mechanisms, and interactions among agents, tools, and execution environments. We further examine its implications for AI Trust, Risk, and Security Management (AI TRiSM), highlighting impacts on trustworthiness, governance, security, operational resilience, and Sustainability Technical Debt. Overall, this work establishes AgTD as a foundational software engineering construct and provides a transformation framework, taxonomy, and research agenda for managing technical debt in autonomous multi-agent AI systems.

</details>


### [385] [Multi-Dimensional Assessment for AI Cognition (MAAC): A Theoretical Framework for Process-Oriented Cognitive Evaluation of Text-Based AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00680)
*Abdalla Doleh,Ratna Babu Chinnam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAAC is a theoretically grounded framework for evaluating text-based AI systems by analyzing cognitive processes across nine dimensions (Cognitive Load, Tool Execution, Content Quality, Memory Integration, Complexity Handling, Hallucination Control, Knowledge Transfer, Processing Efficiency, Process-Outcome Alignment), grounded in established cognitive science theories and supported by five theoretical analyses, shifting AI evaluation from outcome-based metrics to process-level cognitive assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing outcome-based benchmarks (accuracy, robustness, fairness) fail to provide diagnostic insight into the underlying cognitive processes of AI systems—leaving critical questions unanswered about reasoning, memory integration, complexity management, and hallucination avoidance. A new evaluation paradigm is needed that examines how AI systems think, not just what they produce.

Method: MAAC defines nine cognitively inspired dimensions grounded in cognitive science theories including Marr's tri-level hypothesis, Baddeley's working memory model, Sweller's cognitive load theory, and unified theories of cognition. The framework is supported by five theoretical analyses: dimension-to-theory mapping, a coverage matrix for breadth and non-redundancy, a formal gap analysis versus current evaluation practice, a worked diagnostic illustration, and a priori interdependency predictions for empirical validation.

Result: The authors provide initial theoretical support for MAAC's coherence and empirical testability through the five analyses, establishing the framework as a viable complement to outcome-based benchmarks for principled process-level cognitive assessment of text-based AI systems.

Conclusion: MAAC offers a theoretical and operational framework for shifting AI evaluation from outcome-focused benchmarking toward cognitively grounded, multi-dimensional process assessment—providing a foundation for future empirical testing and more diagnostically meaningful evaluation of AI cognition.

Abstract: Evaluating artificial intelligence systems has historically relied on outcome-based benchmarks that measure task accuracy, robustness, or fairness. While indispensable, these benchmarks provide limited diagnostic insight into the underlying cognitive processes that generate performance-leaving critical questions unanswered about how AI systems reason, integrate memory, manage complexity, or avoid generating false information. This paper introduces the Multi-Dimensional Assessment for AI Cognition (MAAC), a theoretically grounded framework for shifting evaluation from what text-based AI systems produce to how they think. MAAC defines nine cognitively motivated dimensions: Cognitive Load, Tool Execution, Content Quality, Memory Integration, Complexity Handling, Hallucination Control, Knowledge Transfer, Processing Efficiency, and Process-Outcome Alignment. Each dimension is grounded in established cognitive science theory-drawing on Marr's tri-level hypothesis, Baddeley's working memory model, Sweller's cognitive load theory, and unified theories of cognition. Five theoretical analyses provide initial support for the framework's coherence and empirical testability: dimension-to-theory mapping; a coverage matrix assessing breadth and non-redundancy; a formal gap analysis relative to current evaluation practice; a worked diagnostic illustration; and a set of a priori interdependency predictions for future empirical testing. MAAC provides a theoretical and operational framework for principled process-level cognitive assessment of text-based AI systems, complementing existing outcome-based benchmarks with cognitively grounded, multi-dimensional evaluation.

</details>


### [386] [When Does LLM Orchestration Pay Off? A Controlled Evaluation of Accuracy, Cost, and Task Difficulty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00685)
*Nicolas Leins,Nico Pelleriti,Jana Gonnermann-Müller,Sebastian Pokutta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper performs a controlled evaluation of LLM orchestration methods (Self-Refine, Best-of-N, Debate) against single-call baselines across five LLM backbones and three domains, finding that orchestration yields only moderate gains (up to ~4.6 percentage points) at 2-4x token cost, with effectiveness strongly dependent on the backbone model rather than task difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM orchestration is often assumed to improve reasoning by adding inference-time computation, but its gains may not justify costs, and existing comparisons often overlook differences in optimization effort, making it hard to isolate the value of orchestration itself.

Method: Controlled evaluation of Self-Refine, Best-of-N, and Debate against task-only and chain-of-thought (CoT) single-call baselines across five LLM backbones and three domains (competitive programming, chess puzzles, mathematics). All methods are optimized with GEPA under the same optimization budget, and evaluated on the same difficulty-stratified benchmark items. Mixed-effects analyses explore interactions between orchestration method, backbone model, and task difficulty.

Result: Orchestration yields moderate but benchmark-dependent gains: averaged across backbones, the largest improvement is 4.6 points over optimized CoT and 4.5 points over task-only inference, at 2-4x token cost. Human-derived difficulty correlates with lower absolute accuracy, but within-benchmark analyses show orchestration effects do not increase with difficulty. Strong interactions between orchestration method and backbone model are found across all three benchmarks.

Conclusion: Orchestration decisions should be model-specific, accounting for whether moderate accuracy gains justify additional inference cost. Evaluations of LLM orchestrations should control optimization effort and report model-specific accuracy-cost trade-offs rather than treating additional inference-time structure as uniformly beneficial.

Abstract: LLM orchestration is often assumed to improve reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation, yet its gains may not justify its cost. Existing comparisons also frequently overlook differences in optimization effort, making it difficult to isolate the value of orchestration itself. We conduct a controlled evaluation of Self-Refine, Best-of-$N$, and Debate against task-only and chain-of-thought (CoT) single-call baselines across five LLM backbones and three domains: competitive programming, chess puzzles, and mathematics. For comparability, we optimize each method with GEPA under the same optimization budget and evaluate all methods on the same difficulty-stratified benchmark items. Orchestration yields moderate but benchmark-dependent gains: averaged across backbones within each benchmark, the largest improvement is 4.6 percentage points over optimized CoT inference and 4.5 points over task-only inference, while requiring approximately 2 to 4 times the mean total tokens of task-only inference. Human-derived difficulty is associated with lower absolute accuracy in all three benchmarks, but within-benchmark analyses do not indicate that orchestration effects increase with task difficulty. By contrast, exploratory mixed-effects analyses reveal strong interactions between orchestration method and backbone model across all three benchmarks, showing that orchestration effectiveness depends substantially on the underlying model. Our results suggest that orchestration decisions should be model-specific and account for whether moderate accuracy gains justify the additional inference cost. More broadly, evaluations of LLM orchestrations should control optimization effort and report model-specific accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than treating additional inference-time structure as uniformly beneficial.

</details>


### [387] [Don't Offer What Can't Be Done: Deterministic Executability Gating for LLM Skill Selection at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01050)
*Ortal Ashkenazi,Vitalii Kloz,Mykhailo Ulianchenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a deployed three-stage selection pipeline for Wix's Helpmate customer-care assistant that filters large skill libraries by combining semantic relevance matching with a deterministic executability gate before LLM invocation. Production analysis of 756.6K user messages shows the gate removes 59.4% of matched skill-message pairs (1,039,462 pairs), reducing skill-description context by 90.5% overall, and a counterfactual replay of 1,000 conversations shows the model would have selected blocked skills in 7.8% of cases if all skills were exposed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production LLM agents with large skill libraries face a limitation where semantic relevance alone is insufficient: a skill may match the user's topic but be impossible to execute in the current account state. This necessitates an executability-aware selection mechanism beyond pure semantic matching.

Method: A three-stage retrieval pipeline for skill selection: (1) a recall-oriented semantic matcher identifies messages related to a ten-skill domain family without consulting account state; (2) a deterministic executability gate removes candidates whose internal hard-stop conditions hold, using the same exit predicates as the skill itself with a guarantee of predicate parity and fresh authoritative state observation; (3) an LLM decides whether to invoke one of the remaining candidates.

Result: From 756.6K user messages across 267.6K conversations, semantic matching retained 174,927 messages (23.1%). The gate removed 1,039,462 of 1,749,270 skill-message pairs (59.4%), saving 228.8 million skill-description tokens (59.1% of post-semantic footprint). Combined semantic matching and executability gating reduced skill-description context by 90.5%. A counterfactual replay of 1,000 risk-enriched conversations showed the model selected a production-blocked skill in 7.8% of conversations, demonstrating that gating prevents non-executable candidates from influencing model selection.

Conclusion: Deterministic executability gating provides a principled complement to semantic matching, preventing non-executable skills from being selected by the LLM. The authors caution that this work demonstrates pruning effects on model behavior rather than claiming downstream tool-execution success or customer-outcome improvements.

Abstract: Production LLM agents that select from large skill libraries face a limitation that semantic relevance alone cannot resolve: a skill may match a user's topic yet be impossible to execute in the current account state. We present a deployed three-stage selection pipeline for Helpmate, Wix's customer-care assistant. First, a recall-oriented semantic matcher identifies messages related to a ten-skill domain family without consulting account state. Second, a deterministic executability gate removes candidates whose internal hard-stop conditions hold. Because the gate and the skill evaluate the same exit predicates, every blocked candidate would be unable to complete under the same account state, provided predicate parity is preserved and both checks observe fresh authoritative state. Finally, the LLM decides whether to invoke one of the remaining candidates.
  In a post-launch production analysis of 756.6K user messages across 267.6K conversations, semantic matching retained 174,927 messages (23.1%). Within this matched stream, the gate removed 1,039,462 of 1,749,270 skill-message pairs (59.4%), saving 228.8 million skill-description tokens -- 59.1% of the post-semantic skill-description footprint. Together, semantic matching and executability gating reduced skill-description context by 90.5% relative to exposing all ten skills to every message.
  To test whether this pruning affects model behavior rather than context size alone, we replayed a risk-enriched cohort of 1,000 conversations with all ten skills exposed. The model selected a production-blocked skill in 78 conversations (7.8%). This counterfactual result shows that deterministic gating prevents non-executable candidates from influencing model selection, while not claiming downstream tool execution or customer-outcome effects.

</details>


### [388] [Evolutionary Curriculum Learning Improves Biological Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00697)
*Richard Zhu,Kento Nishi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL), a training strategy for variational autoencoders on biological sequences that progressively exposes the model to sequences of increasing evolutionary distance from anchors following a power-law schedule, improving downstream performance on protein variant effect prediction (EVE) and RNA family sequence generation (RfamGen) compared to standard exchangeable training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard biological VAE training treats all sequences as exchangeable, ignoring the rich evolutionary structure that organizes homologous sequences from evolutionarily close to highly divergent.
