We study black-box, sampling-based training-data leakage through a probabilistic lens, treating N samples from p(.|x) as an estimate of the output distribution and casting leakage signals as functionals of it. We extend the blind-baseline critique into the sampling regime: on WikiMIA a blind bag-of-words classifier reaches AUC 0.97 (TPR 0.90 at 5% FPR) and sampling adds nothing, while on an IID Pile split (MIMIR) neither self-concentration nor gold-continuation recovery significantly beats a blind baseline (incremental AUC 95% CI includes zero). Aggregate metrics hide the real harm. The same sampling verbatim-extracts training data for a tail of documents no blind attack can reach. On Pythia-6.9B, 83 of 500 Pile documents bearing a real identifier (16.6%; 21.3% of those bearing an email address) have that exact identifier reproduced AND not reproduced under a mismatched-prefix control, so each leak is attributable to that document, not to a globally common string. This per-document disclosure is invisible to aggregate AUC and grows with capacity (5.6% to 16.6% from 410M to 6.9B). The risk is uneven: identifier leakage is ~3x stronger in code than prose, though prose stays clearly positive and also grows with capacity (4.0% to 12.1%), while recovery of arbitrary held-out continuations is confined to code (+0.44 member gap on GitHub vs at most +0.014 on prose). Temperature and nucleus sampling matter little, a 16-token prefix suffices, and we detect no reduction from corpus deduplication. Privacy audits should report per-document extraction, decomposed by domain, not a single AUC. We release leakit, a black-box extraction-audit tool.

</details>


### [540] [Response Magnitude as a Dominant Signal for Held-Out CRISPRi Perturbation Effect Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00152)
*Mehrdad Shoeibi,Niloofar Yousefi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes why simple baselines outperform deep perturbation predictors on the Virtual Cell Challenge under held-out target-gene splits, showing that the log Anderson-Darling distance from non-targeting controls is predictable from four deterministic scalar functions of the input, and that magnitude-only predictors transfer positively across cell types while expression-only predictors do not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting CRISPRi perturbation transcriptomic effects on held-out target genes is an open problem in single-cell biology. Recent work shows simple baselines often match or exceed deep predictors, but the underlying reasons for this gap are not well understood.

Method: The authors study the Virtual Cell Challenge (VCC) benchmark under a strict held-out target-gene split, analyze the log Anderson-Darling distance from non-targeting controls, compare a deep MLP encoder against classical models (linear regression, Random Forest), and evaluate zero-shot transfer to two external CRISPRi screens with target-gene endpoints rebuilt from single-cell data.

Result: A linear regression on four magnitude scalars exceeds the strongest x-only classical model; a Random Forest on input plus scalars substantially outperforms the deep encoder. Per-row alignment (not added dimensionality) drives the magnitude gain. Magnitude-only predictors transfer positively while expression-only predictors are negative or unresolved. The Anderson-Darling column measures transcriptome-wide response breadth rather than target-gene effect strength.

Conclusion: The performance gap favoring simple baselines on this benchmark is driven by a low-dimensional magnitude signal that is well-captured by scalar features, and deep encoders fail to leverage this signal effectively. Evaluating transfer with the Anderson-Darling endpoint scores response breadth rather than target-gene specificity, which has implications for how CRISPRi perturbation prediction should be benchmarked.

Abstract: Predicting the magnitude of a CRISPRi perturbation's transcriptomic effect on held-out target genes is an important open problem in single-cell biology. Recent work has documented that simple baselines often match or exceed deep perturbation predictors on related protocols. We study this phenomenon on the Virtual Cell Challenge (VCC) benchmark under a strict held-out target-gene split, identify the specific low-dimensional signal that drives the gap, and characterize how it transfers across cell types. The target is the log Anderson-Darling distance from non-targeting controls, which is strongly predictable from four deterministic scalar functions of the 2,000-dimensional input. A deep MLP encoder with direct access to the full input collapses toward the marginal training mean, and standard remedies do not close the gap. A linear regression on the four magnitude scalars alone exceeds the strongest x-only classical model, while a Random Forest on the input plus the four scalars substantially outperforms our deep proof-of-concept encoder. Two pre-specified controls attribute the magnitude gain to per-row alignment rather than added dimensionality. Under zero-shot transfer to two external CRISPRi screens evaluated against a target-gene endpoint rebuilt from single-cell data, magnitude-only predictors transfer positively whereas expression-only predictors are negative or unresolved. Exposing magnitude to the deep encoder improves transfer over its expression-only counterpart, yet the encoder does not outperform a four-scalar linear regression on the same features. We also find that the Anderson-Darling column distributed with these screens measures transcriptome-wide response breadth rather than target-gene effect strength, so evaluating transfer against it scores a different outcome.

</details>


### [541] [Inference-Time Policy Alignment for Fair Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00175)
*Umer Siddique,Peilang Li,Conor Wallace,Yongcan Cao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an inference-time policy shaping framework that steers pretrained deep RL policies toward welfare-based fairness objectives without updating the base policy's parameters. The method multiplicatively adjusts action probabilities using action-dependent welfare scores, improving fairness while preserving core task performance across multiple domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep RL agents optimize scalar rewards but their policies are rigid and costly to adapt to new criteria such as fairness. Existing fairness-in-RL approaches assume preferences are known a priori and require complete retraining, which is inefficient and impractical.

Method: The paper formalizes inference-time fairness alignment as a policy shaping problem and proposes a multiplicative policy shaping framework that adjusts action probabilities using action-dependent welfare scores, without modifying the base policy's parameters. The framework is general and compatible with any deep RL agent.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple domains show that inference-time policy shaping substantially improves welfare-based fairness objectives while preserving core task performance.

Conclusion: Inference-time policy shaping is an effective and parameter-free approach to aligning pretrained RL policies with welfare-based fairness objectives, inspired by inference-time alignment techniques in large language models.

Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents achieve strong performance by optimizing scalar reward functions. However, once deployed, the policies of these RL agents are often rigid and costly to adapt to new performance criteria. For instance, an agent trained to maximize expected cumulative reward may not accommodate previously unknown stakeholder preferences. Existing approaches to achieve fairness, a type of preference, in RL typically assume that such preferences are known a priori and require complete retraining of the policy under a fairness-oriented metric. Inspired by inference-time alignment in large language models, we investigate the problem of steering a pretrained RL policy toward welfare-based fairness objectives at inference time without updating the base policy's parameters. We formalize inference-time fairness alignment as a policy shaping problem and propose a multiplicative policy shaping framework that adjusts action probabilities using action-dependent welfare scores, thus requiring no modification to the base policy. Our framework is general and compatible with any deep RL agent. Through extensive experiments across multiple domains, we demonstrate that inference-time policy shaping substantially improves welfare-based fairness objectives while preserving core task performance.

</details>


### [542] [AutoCause: A Python framework that automates expert decisions in environmental time-series causal discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00198)
*Marco Ruiz,Miguel Arana-Catania,David R. Ardila,Rodrigo Ventura*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoCause is an open-source Python workflow that standardizes environmental time-series causal discovery by recording every analysis decision, deriving defaults from a causal-audit module, and supporting domain-informed overrides. It wraps four established causal-discovery methods from three families, adds non-causal reference models, and grades links by cross-method support. Evaluated on 145 datasets, majority-supported links are more precise than single-method links on synthetic benchmarks but not against river topology references.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Applied inconsistently across datasets, expert decisions about causal-discovery choices (method, conditional-independence tests, lag horizons, sample size, multiple-testing control, evidence interpretation) yield graphs that cannot be compared, reproduced, or audited. AutoCause addresses this by converting inconsistent expert practice into an auditable, repeatable analysis pipeline.

Method: AutoCause records each decision in an open-source Python workflow, derives defaults from an extended causal-audit module, and admits domain-informed overrides. It wraps four established causal-discovery methods from three families, adds non-causal reference models, and grades links by method-count support. Evaluation uses 145 datasets from DGP-Atlas, TimeGraph, and a topology-derived CausalRivers reference.

Result: The four methods recover complementary parts of reference graphs across the 145 datasets. Majority-supported links are more precise than single-method links on synthetic benchmarks but not against river topology references. The workflow produces auditable, repeatable analyses.

Conclusion: AutoCause converts inconsistent expert practice into an auditable, repeatable causal-discovery analysis for environmental time series, while leaving causal interpretation with the analyst.

Abstract: Environmental time-series causal discovery requires expert decisions about method choice, conditional-independence tests, lag horizons, sample-size adequacy, multiple-testing control, and evidence interpretation. Applied inconsistently across datasets, these choices yield graphs that cannot be compared, reproduced, or audited. We present AutoCause, an open-source Python workflow that records each decision, derives defaults from an extended causal-audit module, and admits domain-informed overrides. The workflow wraps four established causal-discovery methods from three families, adds non-causal reference models, and grades links by method-count support. On 145 datasets from DGP-Atlas, TimeGraph, and a topology-derived CausalRivers reference, the methods recover complementary parts of the reference graphs. Majority-supported links are more precise than single-method links on the synthetic benchmarks but not against river topology. AutoCause converts inconsistent expert practice into an auditable, repeatable analysis; causal interpretation remains with the analyst. Available at https://github.com/marcoruizrueda/autocause.

</details>


### [543] [A Physics-Chemistry-Informed Neural Network (PCINN) for Real-Time Spatial-ALD Coverage Prediction and Reliable Kinetics Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00212)
*Ning Hu,Chang Liu,Yunlei Jiang,Yuan Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a physics-chemistry-informed neural network (PCINN) as a hybrid surrogate for spatial atomic layer deposition (SALD), achieving CFD-level accuracy (~7 ms query time, ~5×10^4× faster than CFD, R²_log = 0.998) from only 30 training cases. The architecture hard-codes known surface kinetics into a trainable chemistry layer, with a single-scalar bottleneck capturing the operating-condition-to-near-wall concentration closure. A full identifiability analysis (Fisher information, profile likelihood) reveals E_ads and k_des are robustly identifiable, while k_ads is only identifiable as k_ads·c_wall at a single temperature; across four temperatures, ν and E_ads lie along a degeneracy valley of slope 0.065 eV/decade (derived as k_B·T_eff·ln(10)), which serves as a reliability diagnostic for unmodelled site heterogeneity. The study uses simulation-based data with known ground truth, verifying pipeline self-consistency rather than real parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Design and control of spatial ALD are limited by the cost of predicting surface coverage: high-fidelity CFD is too slow for operating-window scans, while analytic models miss transport modulation such as the gas curtain.

Method: A hybrid physics-chemistry-informed neural network where a small network learns only the operating-condition-to-near-wall concentration closure, while known surface kinetics is a hard-coded, trainable chemistry layer integrated along the substrate trajectory. Identifiability is assessed via Fisher information and profile likelihood, and a mismatch matrix over seven chemistries is constructed to derive a degeneracy-slope diagnostic.

Result: Queries return coverage in ~7 ms (~5×10^4 times faster than CFD) with test R²_log = 0.998 (leave-one-out R²_raw = 0.974) from only 30 training cases spanning four orders of magnitude in coverage. E_ads and k_des are robustly identifiable; k_ads is not separately identifiable at a single temperature. The ν–E_ads degeneracy slope of 0.065 eV/decade is invariant to any single-Arrhenius mismatch and shifts only when a second thermally activated process appears.

Conclusion: The PCINN provides accurate, interpretable, and invertible real-time surrogates for SALD, and the degeneracy-slope diagnostic flags unmodelled site heterogeneity. Since data come from simulation with known ground truth, the study verifies pipeline self-consistency and identifiability boundaries rather than extracting real physical parameters.

Abstract: Spatial atomic layer deposition (SALD) is a leading atmospheric-pressure, high-throughput route to industrial ALD, but design and control are limited by the cost of predicting surface coverage: high-fidelity CFD is far too slow for operating-window scans, while analytic models miss transport modulation such as the gas curtain. We present a physics-chemistry-informed neural network (PCINN), a hybrid surrogate with CFD-level accuracy at real-time speed: a query returns coverage in about 7 ms, roughly 5x10^4 times faster than a CFD solve, reaching a test R^2_log = 0.998 (leave-one-out R^2_raw = 0.974) from only 30 training cases spanning four orders of magnitude in coverage.
  The architecture is not a black box: a small network learns only the operating-condition to near-wall concentration closure, while the known surface kinetics is a hard-coded, trainable chemistry layer integrated along the substrate trajectory. This single-scalar bottleneck keeps it accurate under sparse data, interpretable and invertible.
  We add a full identifiability analysis (Fisher information, profile likelihood). The adsorption energy E_ads and desorption rate k_des are robustly identifiable; k_ads is not separately identifiable at a single temperature (only k_ads*c_wall is). Across four temperatures the prefactor nu and E_ads bind along a weakly identifiable degeneracy valley of slope 0.065 eV/decade, derived analytically as k_B T_eff ln(10) and turned into a reliability diagnostic: a seven-chemistry mismatch matrix shows it is invariant under any single-Arrhenius mismatch and shifts only when a second thermally activated process appears, so a slope departure flags unmodelled site heterogeneity.
  Data come from simulation with known ground truth inverted by the same kinetic form, so the study verifies pipeline self-consistency and the identifiability boundary, not real parameters.

</details>


### [544] [Verifier-Induced Support Reshaping in On-Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00220)
*Shaohang Wei,Zikun Su,Feifan Song,Wen Luo,Wei Li,Guangyue Peng,Houfeng Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies and analyzes "verifier-induced support reshaping" in on-policy RLVR: optimizing for one verifier can make successful trajectories for other objectives too rare to sample and reinforce, degrading joint capabilities. Across math reasoning and instruction following, RLVR improves the target metric (e.g., pass@1) while reducing best@k under sampling and shifting output distributions (e.g., from step-by-step to direct answers). These effects concentrate in the first few response tokens, and proposed mitigations only partially preserve cross-task support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy RLVR is increasingly used to improve model capabilities, but it is unclear whether optimizing for one verifiable objective preserves or degrades success on other tasks that may be trained later. The authors aim to understand whether endpoint improvements in one objective come at the cost of future trainability or joint capability.

Method: The authors conduct repeated verifier-scored sampling and bidirectional training (Math-RLVR and IF-RLVR) on mathematical reasoning and constrained instruction following across two model families. They measure pass@1, best@k, token-distribution shifts, and causal effects via controlled opening interventions. They also test mitigations including reference-policy constraints, routing priors, and on-policy distillation, plus joint training (MathIF, ReasonIF).

Result: Math-RLVR improves instruction-following success on average but reduces the number of prompts with any successful response under repeated sampling. On IFEval with Qwen3-8B-Base, pass@1 rises by 6.5 percentage points while best@32 falls by 9.8 percentage points; the divergence appears across both models and both IF benchmarks. IF-RLVR shifts math responses toward direct answers, lowers best@k, and reduces reward variation for later Math-RLVR. Changes concentrate in the first few response tokens; RLVR mainly reranks openings from the base policy, and the chosen opening causally affects math searchability. Proposed mitigation strategies preserve cross-task support only partially.

Conclusion: Endpoint improvements under on-policy RLVR do not guarantee future trainability or joint capability. Verifier-induced support reshaping is a systematic risk: optimizing one objective can shrink the effective rewardable support for others, and current constraints/distillation approaches only partially mitigate this effect.

Abstract: We show that on-policy reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve the current objective while making successful behaviors for later objectives too rare to sample and reinforce. We call this verifier-induced support reshaping and define effective rewardable support as successful trajectories reachable within a fixed rollout budget. Across two model families, we study this effect through repeated verifier-scored sampling and bidirectional training on mathematical reasoning and constrained instruction following, including sequential training with the opposite verifier. Math-RLVR raises average instruction-following success but reduces the number of prompts with any successful response under repeated sampling. On IFEval with Qwen3-8B-Base, pass@1 rises by 6.5 percentage points while best@32 falls by 9.8 percentage points, and the same divergence appears across both models and IF benchmarks. Conversely, IF-RLVR shifts math responses from step-by-step openings toward direct answers, lowers best@k across sampling budgets, and reduces reward variation for later Math-RLVR. Token-distribution analyses and controlled opening interventions show that these changes concentrate in the first few response tokens. RLVR mainly reranks openings already available in the base policy, and the selected opening causally affects math searchability. The tested reference-policy constraints, routing priors, and on-policy distillation preserve cross-task support only partially; MathIF and ReasonIF show that marginal gains translate only partly into responses that are both correct and constraint-following. Therefore, endpoint improvements do not guarantee future trainability or joint capability under on-policy optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/sylvain-wei/verifier-induced-support-reshaping

</details>


### [545] [Similarity-Aware Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00246)
*Madhavan Citalamangalam Kumaran,Midhun Parakkal Unni,Vicky Kouni,Haripriya Harikumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a retain-aware localization method for machine unlearning that selects influential parameters based on importance to both forgotten and retained data, reducing collateral damage to semantically similar retained examples. The method is evaluated across eleven settings on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18, using a novel retain-similar evaluation set built via cosine similarity in embedding space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing localization-based unlearning methods select parameters based solely on forget-set importance, neglecting parameter roles in the retained dataset. This causes collateral damage to semantically similar retained examples during unlearning.

Method: A retain-aware localization approach that considers parameter importance to both forgotten and retained data when selecting influential parameters for unlearning. Additionally, a retain-similar evaluation set is constructed using cosine similarity in the model embedding space to directly measure collateral damage.

Result: Across eleven experimental settings on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18, the method consistently reduces collateral damage while improving standard unlearning metrics.

Conclusion: Retain-aware localization is effective for similarity-aware machine unlearning, demonstrating that considering both forgotten and retained data during parameter selection reduces collateral damage while improving overall unlearning performance.

Abstract: Machine unlearning removes the influence of user-specified training examples from a trained model, avoiding the need to retrain it from scratch. Localization-based methods improve unlearning efficiency by identifying a subset of influential model parameters. However, existing approaches select parameters based solely on forget-set importance, neglecting their role in retained dataset and often causing collateral damage to semantically similar retained examples. We address this limitation with a retain-aware localization method that considers parameter importance to both forgotten and retained data. We also introduce a retain-similar evaluation set, constructed using cosine similarity in the model embedding space, to directly measure collateral damage. Across eleven experimental settings on CIFAR-10 dataset and ResNet18 model, our method consistently reduces collateral damage while improving standard unlearning metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of retain-aware localization for similarity-aware machine unlearning.

</details>


### [546] [Stabilized Best-of-$K$ Training for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00296)
*Melveena Jolly,Midhun Xavier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper tests whether replacing Leader Reward's binary leader/non-leader distinction with a stabilized rank signal indexed by sampling budget K improves POMO training for TSP-100. Under Best-of-8 independent sampling, the stabilized K=8 recipe lowers cost in all three paired training seeds (7.7944 vs 7.8136), but Leader Reward remains better at K=1 and under the original augmented-greedy protocol. The authors make limited claims due to only three seeds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether a narrow modification to Leader Reward training—using a stabilized rank signal instead of binary leader classification—can improve performance in neural combinatorial optimization (TSP).

Method: Replace Leader Reward's binary leader/non-leader reward distinction with a stabilized rank signal indexed by a sampling budget K. The authors reimplement Leader Reward on the POMO architecture with a 3,050-epoch schedule and TSP-100 test set, comparing under (a) 100-start, 8-augmentation greedy decoding, and (b) independent sampling with Best-of-K evaluation. Paired training seeds are used to compare stabilized K=8 versus Leader Reward.

Result: The Leader Reward reimplementation achieves 7.7662 under 100-start, 8-augmentation greedy decoding, matching the reported 7.766. Under independent sampling, stabilized K=8 lowers realized Best-of-8 cost in all three paired seeds: 7.7944 versus 7.8136. However, Leader Reward is better at sampled K=1 and remains slightly better under its original augmented-greedy protocol.

Conclusion: The stabilized rank signal shows a consistent improvement over Leader Reward specifically under Best-of-8 independent sampling across three seeds, but the finding is estimation-only and decoder-specific. No claims of universal superiority, unbiased estimation, or state-of-the-art performance are made, and more seeds are needed to solidify the observation.

Abstract: Leader Reward modifies POMO training to emphasize the best trajectory produced by repeated inference. We test a narrow extension: replace its binary leader/non-leader distinction with a stabilized rank signal indexed by a sampling budget $K$. With the POMO architecture, 3,050-epoch schedule, and TSP-100 test set held fixed, the Leader Reward reimplementation obtains $7.7662$ under 100-start, 8-augmentation greedy decoding, matching the reported $7.766$ at its displayed precision. Under independent sampling, the stabilized $K=8$ recipe lowers realized Best-of-8 cost in all three paired training seeds: $7.7944$ versus $7.8136$. This observation is estimation-only and decoder-specific: three seeds are below the six-seed testing floor, Leader Reward is better at sampled $K=1$, and it remains slightly better under its original augmented-greedy protocol. We make no unbiased-estimator, universal superiority, or state-of-the-art claim.

</details>


### [547] [Abstention as an Action Can Kill Both the Reward Gradient and the KL Anchor: Collapse Law and Repair for Error-Penalized Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00301)
*Xujun Che,Yuchen Yuan,Weida Zhao,Chenyang Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proves that error-penalized scoring rules (e.g., +1 correct, -λ wrong, 0 abstain) can drive KL-anchored gradient learners to catastrophic abstention—refusing everything—despite appearing to improve in training reward. The failure stems from gate-saturation sharing that kills both reward gradient and anchor restoring force; the advantage estimator compounds it by silently replacing designed penalties with effective penalty 1 (shifting the threshold to 1/2). The proposed structural repair is to train a mandatory confidence report with a strictly proper score plus correctness reward, abstaining only at deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Error-penalized scoring rules are increasingly prescribed to combat hallucination, but their theoretical behavior under gradient-based learning with discrete abstention actions is poorly understood. The paper seeks to uncover whether such rules actually work as intended for rational agents trained via gradient methods.

Method: The authors provide theoretical analysis proving that KL-anchored gradient learners drift toward blanket abstention under explicit conditions (blanket answering loses score in expectation, bounded prompt readout). They analyze the gate-saturation factor throttling both the reward gradient and anchor restoring force, examine the advantage estimator's effect of normalizing penalties to effective penalty 1, and propose a structural repair: mandatory confidence report training with strictly proper scoring plus correctness reward, with abstention only at deployment. They validate with simulations and LLM experiments at two scales.

Result: Simulations confirm all theoretical predictions. LLM experiments at two scales confirm the mechanism live: the rule silences questions models demonstrably still solve within ten optimizer steps, an ablation isolates the cause, and report-level training simultaneously raises coverage, accuracy, and calibration.

Conclusion: Error-penalized scoring rules with discrete abstention are fundamentally broken for gradient learners due to gate saturation and penalty distortion by advantage estimation. The structural fix is to decouple confidence reporting from abstention: always emit a confidence report trained with proper scoring plus correctness reward, and threshold at deployment. This eliminates the shared gate-saturation factor and achieves a calibrated optimum that is attracting.

Abstract: Error-penalized scoring rules ($+1$ for a correct answer, $-λ$ for a wrong one, $0$ for abstaining) are increasingly prescribed against hallucination: a rational agent facing such a rule answers exactly when its correctness probability exceeds Chow's threshold $t^\ast=λ/(1+λ)$. We prove that a KL-anchored gradient learner can do the opposite. When abstention is a discrete action, the reward gradient and the anchor's restoring force are throttled by the same gate-saturation factor and die together: under explicit conditions (among them, blanket answering loses score in expectation and prompts share a bounded readout) the model drifts toward refusing everything, its mean training reward rising to zero like $1/t$ in training time $t$, so the curve reads as improvement while coverage collapses. The advantage estimator compounds the failure: in its sparse-answer regime, group normalization silently replaces every designed penalty with an effective penalty of one, moving the learned threshold from $t^\ast$ to $1/2$. The repair is structural: train a mandatory confidence report with a strictly proper score plus a correctness reward, and abstain only at deployment by thresholding the report. The always-emitted report has no gate to saturate, so no shared factor can kill its reward gradient and its anchor together, and its calibrated optimum is attracting. Simulations confirm every prediction, and experiments on language models at two scales confirm the mechanism live: the rule silences questions the models demonstrably still solve within ten optimizer steps, an ablation isolates the cause, and report-level training raises coverage, accuracy, and calibration together.

</details>


### [548] [Agentic Bayesian Optimization through Surrogate-Augmented Autoresearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00316)
*Paul Brunzema,Louis Tiao,Nhat Le,Kevin De Angeli,Yao Xuan,Djordje Gligorijevic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces agentic Bayesian optimization, a paradigm where an LLM agent serves as the central decision maker in the BO loop while a Bayesian backend provides uncertainty-aware optimization. The authors instantiate this in Sara (a surrogate-augmented autoresearch agent) and lenz (a modular BoTorch-based backend), demonstrating that Sara preserves state-of-the-art BO reliability, outperforms LLM-based baselines, leverages natural-language priors to improve beyond standard BO, and can dynamically reconfigure the optimization problem on the fly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard BO relies on generic statistical priors and encoding richer domain priors through tailored kernels or problem structures is difficult. LLMs can make informal priors from natural language, code, and documentation directly available to the optimizer, but existing LLM-based BO methods either fix the LLM into a specific role or give it broad control, sacrificing the systematic exploration that makes BO reliable.

Method: The paper proposes agentic Bayesian optimization, where an LLM agent acts as the central decision maker in the BO loop while a Bayesian backend provides uncertainty-aware optimization. The agent configures the problem, queries the backend, selects and commits evaluations, and can revise the optimization strategy during the run (e.g., tightening bounds, switching acquisition functions, proposing targeted evaluations, or reframing the problem). This is instantiated in Sara, a surrogate-augmented autoresearch agent, and lenz, a modular BoTorch-based backend with a structured interface the agent can inspect and modify.

Result: Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, Sara preserves the reliability of state-of-the-art BO without prior knowledge, outperforms LLM-based baselines, and uses natural-language priors to improve beyond standard BO. In dynamic settings, Sara demonstrates the practical value of agentic BO by reconfiguring the full optimization problem on the fly as requirements change.

Conclusion: Agentic Bayesian optimization enables LLM agents to leverage informal domain priors and dynamically adapt optimization strategies, providing a new capability (on-the-fly problem reconfiguration) not previously available in standard BO while maintaining reliability and improving performance.

Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has become the standard tool for sample-efficient optimization and owes its efficiency to uncertainty-aware search driven by generic statistical priors. Richer domain priors can improve BO in principle, but encoding them through tailored kernels or problem structure is difficult and rarely done in practice. LLMs can help sidestep this difficulty by making informal priors from natural language, code, and documentation directly available to the optimizer. However, existing LLM-based BO methods either insert the LLM into a fixed role (surrogate, acquisition proxy, or configuration interface) or hand it broad control, sacrificing the systematic exploration that makes BO reliable. We introduce agentic Bayesian optimization: a paradigm in which an LLM agent is the central decision maker in the BO loop while a Bayesian backend provides the uncertainty-aware optimization substrate. The agent configures the problem, queries the backend, selects and commits evaluations, and can revise the optimization strategy during the run by tightening bounds, switching acquisition functions, proposing targeted evaluations, or even reframing the problem following new instructions or observed evidence. We instantiate this idea in Sara, a surrogate-augmented autoresearch agent, and lenz, a modular BoTorch-based backend that the agent can inspect and modify through a structured interface. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, Sara preserves the reliability of state-of-the-art BO without prior knowledge, outperforms LLM-based baselines, and uses natural-language priors to improve beyond standard BO. We further demonstrate the practical value of agentic BO in dynamic settings, where Sara reconfigures the full optimization problem on the fly as requirements change, a capability not previously available in standard BO.

</details>


### [549] [Neural operator learning for collision-aware trajectory planning of spacecraft swarms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00320)
*Sidhdharth D. Sikka,Suyi Gao,Zehui Lu,Rongjie Lai,Shaoshuai Mou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a permutation-equivariant neural operator that maps distributions of spacecraft, targets, and debris to collision-aware trajectories for an entire swarm in a single forward pass, paired with a batched Gauss-Newton finish for exact orbital dynamics. Trained self-supervised without optimal-trajectory labels on 10 spacecraft, it zero-shot generalizes to swarms of 1,000 amid over 11,000 catalogued objects, matching per-agent optimal-control accuracy, evading worst-case threats that debris-blind baselines cannot, and reducing intra-swarm proximity several-fold.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical trajectory optimization scales poorly for spacecraft swarms because pairwise safety constraints multiply with swarm size, while learning-based planners fail to generalize across swarm sizes or debris densities. A scalable, transferable planning method for crowded orbits is needed.

Method: A permutation-equivariant neural operator is used to map distributions of spacecraft, targets, and debris to collision-aware trajectories for the entire swarm in one forward pass. This is paired with a batched Gauss-Newton refinement step enforcing exact orbital dynamics. Training is self-supervised via physics objectives, with adversarial threats generated against the operator's own rollouts, and requires no optimal-trajectory labels.

Result: Trained on 10 spacecraft, the model zero-shot generalizes to swarms of 1,000 with over 11,000 debris objects, matching a per-agent optimal-control solver's accuracy, evading worst-case adversarial threats that a debris-blind baseline cannot, and reducing proximity within the swarm several-fold.

Conclusion: Physics-grounded operator learning provides a fast, scalable alternative to optimal control for collision-aware trajectory planning in crowded orbital environments.

Abstract: Autonomous spacecraft swarms must plan fuel-efficient, collision-free maneuvers in increasingly congested orbits, yet classical trajectory optimization scales poorly as pairwise safety constraints multiply with swarm size, and learning-based planners rarely transfer across swarm sizes or debris densities. Here we introduce a permutation-equivariant neural operator that maps distributions of spacecraft, targets and debris to collision-aware trajectories for an entire swarm in a single forward pass, paired with a batched Gauss-Newton finish that enforces exact orbital dynamics. The operator is trained without optimal-trajectory labels, combining self-supervised physics objectives with adversarial threats generated against its own rollouts. Trained on ten spacecraft, it generalizes zero-shot to swarms of 1,000 amid more than 11,000 catalogued objects, matching a per-agent optimal-control solver's accuracy, evading worst-case threats that a debris-blind baseline cannot, and reducing proximity within the swarm several-fold. Physics-grounded operator learning thus offers a fast, scalable alternative to optimal control for crowded orbits.

</details>


### [550] [Ensemble of Unsupervised Deep Learning for Clustering Imbalanced Tabular Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00346)
*Pulock Das,Yina Hou,Md. Kamrozzaman Bhuiyan,Manar D. Samad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the performance of deep clustering methods on imbalanced tabular data, proposing two novel cluster ensemble approaches—one aggregating assignments across embedding dimensions and another using majority voting—that outperform individual clustering methods on 16 binary datasets under varying imbalance levels, suggesting deep clustering is a robust alternative to supervised classification when labels are absent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data imbalance causes majority-class bias in supervised classification, leading to false negatives and inflated accuracy. Since unsupervised deep clustering learns representations without class labels, it may be naturally immune to class imbalance. However, the robustness of deep clustering methods on imbalanced tabular data has not been systematically examined.

Method: The authors propose two cluster ensemble approaches: (1) aggregating deep clustering assignments across different embedding dimensions, and (2) applying majority voting to the best-performing clustering algorithms. Experiments are conducted on 16 binary tabular datasets with varying and artificially induced imbalance levels, comparing ensemble methods against individual deep clustering baselines using ACC, NMI, and ARI metrics.

Result: The ensemble methods outperform individual deep clustering methods on average across ACC, NMI, and ARI scores, demonstrating greater resilience to data imbalance when identifying ground-truth classes without supervision. Distinct strengths of different deep clustering methods were observed across imbalance conditions.

Conclusion: Deep clustering serves as a strong alternative to supervised classification in imbalanced data scenarios, and the proposed ensemble strategies further improve robustness and performance for unsupervised learning on imbalanced tabular data.

Abstract: Data imbalance poses a major challenge in supervised classification, where the majority-class bias contributes to false negatives and overestimates classification accuracy. Unsupervised deep clustering can be immune to class imbalance because representation learning for clustering is performed without class labels. Deep clustering has been proposed for images, languages, and graphs, while its application to tabular data has only emerged recently. This paper is among the first to examine the performance of state-of-the-art deep clustering methods under varying levels of data imbalance. We introduce two novel cluster ensemble approaches: one aggregates deep clustering assignments across different embedding dimensions, and the other applies majority voting to the best-performing clustering algorithms. Experiments on 16 binary tabular datasets with varying and artificially induced levels of imbalance reveal distinct strengths of different deep clustering methods. On average, our ensemble methods outperform individual clustering methods in ACC, NMI, and ARI scores, offering greater resilience to data imbalance when identifying ground-truth classes without supervision. Therefore, in an imbalanced data scenario, deep clustering can serve as a strong alternative to supervised classification.

</details>


### [551] [Interpretable MEG Decoding of Perceived Speech: Cortical Sources and the Stimulus Features That Drive Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01481)
*Ilia Semenkov,Daria Kleeva,Ivan Dakhtin,Zarina Maksudova,Alex Ossadtchi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper improves a MEG-to-audio retrieval architecture by redesigning its front end (spherical harmonics on 3D helmet geometry, 25 subject-specific branches down from 270, temporal filters, shallower decoder) and decoder, achieving 39.75% Top-1 accuracy on MEG-MASC with ~20x fewer decoder parameters. The model's weights map to source space revealing speech-perception network generators with left-lateralized high-frequency components. Occlusion and word-list experiments show that silence, sound intensity, vowels, and acoustic onsets drive retrieval, and that narrative structure carries recoverable information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MEG-to-audio retrieval models using CLIP-style objectives against wav2vec2 embeddings achieve high performance but their weights do not map onto electrophysiological quantities, leaving unclear which speech properties drive retrieval and whether the architecture is interpretable at the neural level.

Method: The authors redesign a high-performing MEG-to-audio retrieval architecture: (1) replace flattened-sensor spatial attention with spherical harmonics on the 3D MEG helmet geometry; (2) reduce subject-specific branches from 270 to 25; (3) add temporal filtering per branch to align with neuronal sources in space and time; (4) make the convolutional decoder shallower; (5) remove ocular and cardiac components before training. They then perform source mapping, occlusion analysis on 19 stimulus features, and random word-list experiments to assess what drives retrieval.

Result: The model achieves 39.75 +/- 0.34% Top-1 accuracy among 1005 candidates on MEG-MASC with ~20x fewer decoder parameters. Weights map to source space recovering speech-perception network generators; left-lateralized branches carry higher-frequency rhythmic components. Occlusion shows 15 of 19 stimulus features contribute (largest: silence, intensity, vowels, acoustic onsets). Random word lists behave oppositely, confirming narrative structure matters. The wav2vec target can be compressed to ~12 feature dimensions without loss, but strong temporal compression degrades accuracy.

Conclusion: Through source mapping and input interventions, the paper reveals the specific neural generators and stimulus features that drive successful MEG-to-audio retrieval, showing the model captures genuine speech-perception activity rather than artifacts, and that both spatial (source mapping) and temporal (rhythmic components) aspects of neural processing contribute to retrieval.

Abstract: Short segments of perceived speech can be retrieved from non-invasive magnetoencephalographic (MEG) recordings by deep networks trained with a CLIP-style objective against wav2vec 2.0 audio embeddings. Yet their weights do not map onto electrophysiological quantities, and it remains unclear which speech properties drive retrieval.
  We build on a high-performing MEG-to-audio retrieval architecture but redesign both its front end and decoder. Its spatial attention operates on a flattened sensor layout; we replace it with spherical harmonics defined on the three-dimensional MEG helmet geometry. We reduce the subject-specific representation from 270 to 25 branches, add a temporal filter to each branch to match it to a neuronal source in space and time, and make the convolutional decoder shallower. Ocular and cardiac components are removed before training to reduce the risk of stimulus-locked shortcuts.
  On MEG-MASC, the model reaches 39.75 +/- 0.34% Top-1 accuracy among 1005 candidates across six trained solutions, with about 20 times fewer decoder parameters. Its weights map to source space, recovering generators consistent with the speech-perception network, while left-lateralized branches carry higher-frequency rhythmic components not evident on the right. Paired MEG occlusion shows that 15 of 19 stimulus features contribute, with the largest effects for silence, sound intensity, vowels, and acoustic onsets. Random word lists behave oppositely: substituting narrative MEG into them improves retrieval, indicating that activity without narrative structure carries less recoverable information than activity during coherent speech. The wav2vec target can be reduced to about twelve learned feature dimensions without loss of accuracy, whereas strong temporal compression causes a clear loss.
  Together, source mapping and input interventions reveal what drives retrieval.

</details>


### [552] [Modeling Unknown Nonlocal PDE Systems via Flow Map Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00400)
*Zhongshu Xu,Ying Li,Yanzhi Zhang,Dongbin Xiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a flow-map learning (FML) framework for modeling unknown nonlocal PDEs directly from solution data, bypassing explicit evaluation of nonlocal operators by learning finite-time evolution operators in modal or nodal space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Nonlocal PDEs arise in many applications but are difficult to model and learn due to the presence of nonlocal operators, motivating a data-driven approach that avoids approximating these operators directly.

Method: The FML framework learns the finite-time evolution operator from solution data rather than the underlying nonlocal operators. Two complementary formulations are developed for spectral (modal) and grid-based (nodal) solution representations.

Result: Numerical experiments on 1D and 2D fractional diffusion and wave equations demonstrate accurate and stable long-time prediction using only short observation windows.

Conclusion: The proposed approach provides an effective data-driven framework for learning unknown nonlocal dynamics without explicit evaluation of nonlocal operators.

Abstract: Nonlocal partial differential equations arise in many applications but are often difficult to model and learn because of the presence of nonlocal operators. We present a flow-map learning (FML) framework for modeling unknown nonlocal PDEs directly from solution data. Rather than learning or approximating the underlying nonlocal operators, the proposed approach learns the finite-time evolution operator in either modal or nodal space. Two complementary formulations are developed for spectral and grid-based solution representations. Numerical experiments on one- and two-dimensional fractional diffusion and wave equations demonstrate accurate and stable long-time prediction using only short observation windows. The proposed approach provides an effective data-driven framework for learning unknown nonlocal dynamics without explicit evaluation of nonlocal operators.

</details>


### [553] [DSETA: A Dual-Stage Continual Learning Framework for Travel Time Prediction in Dynamic Traffic Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00402)
*Yanming Lyu,Yue Cheng,Lingkun Li,Ruipeng Gao,Xinyue Liu,Hui Gao,Qiang Ni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSETA is an incrementally updated Dual-Stage ETA prediction framework that separates continual learning into intra-day (real-time data for short-term traffic adaptation) and inter-day (aggregated historical data for long-term distribution shifts) stages, with a Historical Traffic Knowledge Consolidation module to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Deployed in DiDi's production environment, it achieved MAE reductions of 6.62%, 0.73%, and 2.40% in Beijing, Wuhan, and Xi'an respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ETA prediction methods fail to adapt to irregular traffic patterns and sudden congestion, or suffer from new distributions without disentangling long-term trends from short-term fluctuations, degrading model performance in real-world dynamic traffic scenarios.

Method: DSETA divides continual learning into two stages: (1) intra-day learning using entirely real-time data to adapt to short-term traffic patterns from events like holidays or accidents, and (2) inter-day learning using aggregated historical data from a short time window to capture long-term distribution shifts such as seasonal trends and network evolution. A Historical Traffic Knowledge Consolidation module prevents catastrophic forgetting and preserves regular pattern knowledge.

Result: Extensive offline and online experiments on DiDi's real-world datasets showed consistent performance gains. Online A/B tests across Beijing, Wuhan, and Xi'an achieved MAE reductions of 6.62%, 0.73%, and 2.40% respectively. The framework is deployed in DiDi's production environment, processing hundreds of millions of daily requests.

Conclusion: DSETA effectively addresses dynamic traffic adaptation in ETA prediction by disentangling short-term and long-term temporal patterns through dual-stage continual learning, demonstrating strong industrial applicability and robustness in production.

Abstract: Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA) prediction is a core component of intelligent transportation systems. As traffic congestion patterns become increasingly dynamic in large cities, maintaining high prediction accuracy poses a major challenge for ride-hailing platforms. Existing methods either fail to adapt to irregular traffic patterns and sudden congestion, or suffer from new distributions without disentangling long-term trends from short-term fluctuations, thereby degrading model performance in real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, we propose DSETA, an incrementally updated Dual-Stage ETA prediction framework. Specifically, the continual learning process is divided into \textit{inter-day} and \textit{intra-day} stages. We first design the \textit{intra-day} learning stage, which relies entirely on real-time data to enable dynamic adaptation to short-term traffic patterns caused by events like holidays or accidents. Next, we develop the \textit{inter-day} learning stage, which leverages aggregated historical data from a short time window to capture knowledge of long-term distribution shifts, such as seasonal trends and traffic network evolution. Subsequently, to prevent catastrophic forgetting and preserve knowledge of regular patterns, we explore a \textit{Historical Traffic Knowledge Consolidation} module. Finally, we validate DSETA's effectiveness and robustness through extensive offline and online experiments conducted on real-world datasets from DiDi's platform. Online A/B tests across three major cities including Beijing, Wuhan, and Xi'an consistently demonstrated performance gains, achieving MAE reductions of 6.62\%, 0.73\%, and 2.40\% respectively. This framework has been successfully deployed in DiDi's production environment, processing hundreds of millions of daily requests and validating its strong performance in industrial applications.

</details>


### [554] [Unleashing the Potential of Large Language Models: A Blueprint for Real-Time, Enterprise-Ready Deployments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00419)
*Muhammad Faizan Raza,Shuo,Yang,Satish Mahadevan Srinivasan,Joanna F. DeFranco*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a unified LLMOps architecture that integrates real-time data ingestion, continual learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and human-in-the-loop feedback into a single operational pipeline. It introduces four pattern-driven contributions: an adaptive ingestion orchestrator (AIPO), STAR+FAR continual learning with sparse temporal adapter routing, SAGE (SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy), and an automated feedback-driven convergence stage with RLHF triggers, aimed at reducing latency-cost-accuracy trade-offs while supporting auditability and rollback in regulated sectors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models deployed in real-time, regulated settings suffer from knowledge staleness, catastrophic forgetting, hallucination, and weak feedback loops, necessitating a robust operational architecture to address these challenges.

Method: The paper proposes a unified, pattern-driven LLMOps architecture with four key components: (1) an adaptive ingestion pattern orchestrator (AIPO) evaluated on FreshStreamBench, (2) STAR+FAR continual learning using sparse temporal adapter routing and freshness-aware replay, (3) SAGE, an SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy that predicts per-query passage budgets to meet tail-latency targets, and (4) an automated feedback-driven convergence stage with RLHF triggers.

Result: The architecture reduces latency-cost-accuracy trade-offs in LLM deployment pipelines while maintaining auditability and supporting rollback, making it suitable for high-risk sectors such as health care and finance.

Conclusion: The proposed LLMOps architecture integrates multiple operational concerns across the LLM lifecycle, offering a unified solution to deployment challenges in regulated, real-time settings through pattern-driven design principles.

Abstract: Large language models deployed in real-time, regulated settings face knowledge staleness, catastrophic forgetting, hallucination, and weak feedback loops. We present a unified, pattern-driven LLMOps architecture integrating real-time data ingestion, continual learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and human-in-the-loop feedback into a single operational pipeline. Four contributions map to established software design patterns: an adaptive ingestion pattern orchestrator (AIPO) evaluated with FreshStreamBench; STAR+FAR continual learning with sparse temporal adapter routing and freshness-aware replay; SAGE, an SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy predicting a per-query passage budget to meet tail-latency targets; and an automated feedback-driven convergence stage with RLHF triggers. The result reduces latency-cost-accuracy trade-offs while supporting auditability and rollback for high-risk sectors such as health care and finance.

</details>


### [555] [HP-JEPA: Hierarchical Partitioning for Multi-Resolution Graph Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00491)
*Ruichen Xu,Jingxiang Qu,Wenhan Gao,Jiaxing Zhang,Linsey Pang,Ravid Shwartz-Ziv,Yann LeCun,Yuefan Deng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HP-JEPA is a hierarchical partitioning framework for graph joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) that performs context-target latent prediction across multiple coarse-to-fine graph partition resolutions, integrating resolution-specific representations via concatenation or task-specific weighting. It outperforms the fixed-resolution Graph-JEPA baseline on 6 of 8 benchmarks and shows improved accuracy across most graph-size quartiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph JEPAs rely on a single predefined graph partition, which biases learned representations toward one structural granularity and limits their ability to capture complementary patterns across different graph scales. Multi-resolution information is needed for richer, more transferable representations.

Method: HP-JEPA organizes each graph into an ordered bank of coarse-to-fine partition resolutions. It performs context-target latent prediction separately at each resolution using an online encoder, an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder, and a latent predictor. Resolution-specific representations are then integrated via concatenation or task-specific resolution weighting to combine local, regional, and global structural information.

Result: On seven graph classification benchmarks and one graph regression benchmark, HP-JEPA outperforms the fixed-resolution Graph-JEPA baseline on 6 of 8 tasks. Size-stratified analyses show HP-JEPA achieves higher accuracy than Graph-JEPA in most graph-size quartiles on three representative datasets.

Conclusion: Hierarchical multi-resolution partitioning is effective for transferable graph representation learning, enabling models to combine complementary structural information from different graph scales and improving downstream performance.

Abstract: Graph self-supervised learning aims to learn transferable representations from large-scale unlabeled graph data. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) avoid explicit negative-pair construction and raw-input reconstruction by predicting masked targets directly in latent space. However, existing graph JEPAs typically rely on a single predefined graph partition, biasing the learned representations toward one structural granularity and limiting their ability to capture complementary patterns at different graph scales. To address this limitation, we propose HP-JEPA, a hierarchical partitioning framework for multi-resolution graph joint-embedding prediction. HP-JEPA organizes each graph into an ordered bank of coarse-to-fine partition resolutions and performs context-target latent prediction separately at each resolution using an online encoder, an exponential-moving-average target encoder, and a latent predictor. The resulting resolution-specific graph representations are subsequently integrated through concatenation or task-specific resolution weighting, allowing downstream models to combine complementary local, regional, and global structural information. Experiments on seven graph classification benchmarks and one graph regression benchmark show that HP-JEPA outperforms the fixed-resolution Graph-JEPA baseline on 6 of 8 tasks, improving upon Graph-JEPA on most evaluated benchmarks. Size-stratified analyses further show that HP-JEPA achieves higher accuracy than Graph-JEPA in most evaluated graph-size quartiles on three representative datasets. These results highlight the effectiveness of hierarchical multi-resolution partitioning for transferable graph representation learning.

</details>


### [556] [Agentic Graph Token Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00542)
*Zhuoyi Peng,Yi Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces agentic graph token reasoning, a method that integrates graph tokenization into the LLM's step-by-step reasoning process. Instead of statically encoding a predefined graph view, the model dynamically chooses which graph view to encode at each reasoning step, invokes a graph encoder on demand, and splices the resulting tokens into its context. A three-stage training pipeline (self-supervised token reading, token-robust trajectory learning, and preference optimization) enables this, yielding large improvements over baselines across seven graph domains and zero-shot transfer to unseen domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-token methods for LLM-based graph analysis encode a fixed, predefined graph view in a single-shot manner before the model sees the target and never revise it. This leaves the model's step-by-step reasoning ability unused and forces it to work with static graph representations that may be suboptimal for the task at hand.

Method: The paper proposes agentic graph token reasoning, where graph tokenization is recast as part of the reasoning process. At each step, the model selects which graph view (node, k-hop neighbourhood, cluster) to encode and at what granularity; a graph encoder is invoked on demand to produce the corresponding graph tokens, which are spliced into the running context. Training uses a three-stage pipeline: (i) self-supervised tasks to teach reading heterogeneous graph tokens, (ii) a token-robust trajectory stage with a graph-token consistency regulariser, and (iii) preference optimisation rewarding trajectories where graph-token evidence agrees with node-text evidence.

Result: Across seven graph domains, the method outperforms a broad set of baselines by a large margin and transfers zero-shot to unseen domains without per-target fine-tuning.

Conclusion: This work shifts LLM-based graph analysis from static graph-token encoders toward a graph-native agent paradigm, where the model actively and iteratively shapes its own graph-level observations during reasoning.

Abstract: Graphs model relational data throughout science and industry, from citation networks to product co-purchase graphs. Because the nodes of many such graphs carry rich text, a growing line of work applies large language models (LLMs) to graph analysis. The most graph-native of these methods use graph tokens: a graph encoder compresses a graph view, such as a node, its k-hop neighbourhood, or a cluster, into a short block of continuous tokens that jointly encodes node attributes and topology and is read directly by the model. Existing methods, however, use graph tokens in a static single-shot manner: they encode one predefined graph view before the model has even seen the target and never revise it, leaving the model's step-by-step reasoning ability unused. We introduce agentic graph token reasoning, which recasts graph tokenization as part of the reasoning process itself. At each step, the model chooses which graph view to encode and at what granularity; a graph encoder is invoked on demand to materialise the corresponding graph tokens; and the resulting block is spliced into the running context. The model thus reasons step by step in the graph token space, and the tokens it reads are trajectory-dependent. We realise this with a three-stage training pipeline: (i) self-supervised tasks that teach the model to read heterogeneous graph tokens, (ii) a token-robust trajectory stage with a graph-token consistency regulariser, and (iii) preference optimisation that rewards trajectories in which the graph-token evidence and the node-text evidence agree. Across evaluations spanning seven graph domains, our models outperform a broad set of baselines by a large margin and transfer zero-shot to unseen domains without any per-target fine-tuning. More broadly, this work pushes LLM-based graph analysis from static graph-token encoders towards a graph-native agent paradigm.

</details>


### [557] [Crushing the Evidence: A Dual-Penalty Evasion Framework for Fooling White-Box Explainable AI Auditors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00566)
*Niraj Kumar,Harsh Kasyap*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a white-box gradient-regularized evasion attack framework that embeds adversarial evasion logic directly into model parameters via a continuous-embedding dual-penalty approach, allowing attackers to hide algorithmic biases from post-hoc explainers (LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients) without leaving anomaly footprints detectable by Conditional Anomaly Detection defenses. The method achieves near-zero target feature attribution (<0.02) and >90% Attack Success Rates across four benchmark tabular datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior adversarial explanation attacks relied on out-of-distribution (OOD) scaffolding wrappers to toggle predictions when queried by explainers, these attacks leave anomalous perturbation footprints that existing defenses can detect. The authors aim to demonstrate a more critical vulnerability by creating evasion attacks that produce smooth, in-distribution predictions with no anomaly footprint, bypassing current defenses entirely.

Method: The proposed method is a white-box, gradient-regularized evasion attack framework. It employs a continuous-embedding dual-penalty framework that directly penalizes trigger feature gradients during training on in-distribution data. This embeds the evasion logic natively into the model parameters (rather than relying on OOD scaffolding wrappers), producing predictions that remain in-distribution and leave no anomaly signature.

Result: Empirical evaluations across four benchmark tabular datasets (COMPAS, German Credit, IEEE-CIS, and Communities & Crime) show that the method: (1) systematically reduces target feature attribution to near-zero (<0.02), (2) maintains >90% Attack Success Rates, and (3) fundamentally bypasses Conditional Anomaly Detection defenses.

Conclusion: The paper reveals a critical vulnerability in the explainability pipeline that existing defense mechanisms cannot neutralize, highlighting that even state-of-the-art anomaly-based defenses are insufficient against white-box attackers who can embed evasion logic directly into model parameters. This underscores the need for fundamentally different defense strategies beyond anomaly footprint detection.

Abstract: Post-hoc model explainers such as LIME, SHAP, and Integrated Gradients are widely deployed to audit models in high-stakes sensitive domains, including finance, healthcare, and social welfare. This ensures the model's transparency and acceptability. However, a few studies have examined potential attacks in the explainability pipeline. Adversaries can attempt to conceal algorithmic biases or backdoors using adversarial explanation attacks. These attacks have relied on scaffolding out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors that toggle predictions when queried by an explainer. Consequently, defenses have been developed to successfully neutralize these black-box attacks by identifying their anomalous perturbation footprints. In this paper, we demonstrate a critical vulnerability by introducing a more potent white-box, gradient-regularized evasion attack framework. By employing a continuous-embedding dual-penalty framework, we directly penalize trigger feature gradients during training on in-distribution data. Since our approach embeds the evasion logic natively into the model parameters, without relying on OOD scaffolding wrappers, it generates smooth, in-distribution predictions that leave no anomaly footprint. Empirical evaluations across four benchmark tabular datasets (COMPAS, German Credit, IEEE-CIS, and Communities & Crime) confirm that our method systematically crushes target feature attribution to near-zero (<0.02), maintains >90% Attack Success Rates, and fundamentally bypasses Conditional Anomaly Detection.

</details>


### [558] [Fairness Auditing: Lower Bounds on Company Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00568)
*Rachit Verma,Padala Manisha,Sujit Gujar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper quantifies the unavoidable post-audit manipulation that persists even when fairness audits are conducted, by modeling fairness auditing as a min-max game between an unbounded company and a budget-constrained auditor. The authors derive explicit lower bounds on worst-case demographic parity deviation for both fixed-size audit sets and α-tolerant auditors, and empirically confirm these limits with linear and neural classifiers, showing that increasing audit budgets reduces but never eliminates manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has established impossibility results for black-box fairness auditing under expressive models, this paper aims to quantify the extent of unavoidable post-audit manipulation when audit resources are finite, providing concrete bounds that characterize how much manipulation persists as a function of budget and fairness tolerance.

Method: The paper formulates fairness auditing as a min-max optimization between a computationally unbounded company and a budget-constrained auditor. Two auditing regimes are studied: (i) a budgeted auditor certifying fairness using a fixed-size audit set, and (ii) a budgeted α-tolerant auditor that requires the audit set to estimate fairness within an α approximation. Explicit lower bounds on worst-case post-audit demographic parity deviation are derived as functions of audit budget, group imbalance, and fairness tolerance. Empirical validation uses simple audit-set construction heuristics with linear and neural network classifiers.

Result: The paper derives explicit lower bounds on post-audit demographic parity deviation for both auditing regimes. Empirical results with linear and neural network classifiers illustrate these theoretical limits, demonstrating that increasing audit resources reduces but does not eliminate the scope for post-audit manipulation.

Conclusion: Finite-budget fairness certification has fundamental limitations: manipulation can be reduced with larger audit budgets but cannot be fully eliminated, highlighting inherent constraints on the reliability of budget-constrained fairness audits.

Abstract: Fairness audits are increasingly mandated in high-stakes applications such as hiring, lending, and automated decision-making. Recent work has established fundamental impossibility results for black-box fairness auditing, showing that sufficiently expressive models can evade any auditing strategy. We complement these results by quantifying the extent of unavoidable post-audit manipulation under finite audit resources. We formulate fairness auditing as a min-max optimization between a computationally unbounded company and a budget-constrained auditor. We study two auditing regimes: (i) a budgeted auditor that certifies fairness using a fixed-size audit set, and (ii) a budgeted α-tolerant auditor that additionally requires the audit set to estimate the fairness of the certified model within an α approximation. For both settings, we derive explicit lower bounds on the worst-case post-audit demographic parity deviation as functions of the audit budget, group imbalance, and fairness tolerance. Finally, we empirically illustrate these theoretical limits using simple audit-set construction heuristics with linear and neural network classifiers. Our results demonstrate that increasing audit resources reduces, but does not eliminate, the scope for post-audit manipulation, highlighting fundamental limitations of finite-budget fairness certification.

</details>


### [559] [CoSynFlow: Conformal Symplectic Neural Flows for Cross-System Prediction of Dissipative Hamiltonian Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00571)
*Baige Xu,Takaharu Yaguchi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoSynFlow is a conformal symplectic neural flow that learns continuous-time solution operators for dissipative Hamiltonian systems by composing symplectic shear maps with explicit conformal scaling, preserving the conformal symplectic structure and enabling generalization to unseen systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural operator methods for differential equations often optimize prediction accuracy without enforcing geometric structure. While SympNets and Symplectic Neural Flows preserve symplectic structure for conservative Hamiltonian systems, the symplectic form in dissipative Hamiltonian systems evolves according to a conformal factor determined by dissipation, which these methods do not address.

Method: CoSynFlow composes symplectic shear maps with explicit conformal scaling to preserve the conformal symplectic structure by construction. It is conditioned on a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian descriptor and the dissipation parameter, enabling a single trained model to predict solution maps for unseen systems without retraining. The model supports physics-informed training.

Result: CoSynFlow maintains structure error at machine precision, achieves the lowest long-horizon error compared to baselines, and supports physics-informed training.

Conclusion: CoSynFlow demonstrates that explicitly enforcing conformal symplectic structure in neural operators yields both geometric fidelity (machine-precision structure preservation) and superior long-horizon predictive accuracy for dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics, while generalizing across systems via finite-dimensional conditioning.

Abstract: Learning solution operators for differential equations is a central problem in scientific machine learning. However, many neural operator methods optimize prediction accuracy without explicitly enforcing the geometric structure of the dynamics. Structure-preserving models such as SympNets and Symplectic Neural Flows address this issue for conservative Hamiltonian systems by preserving the symplectic form. In dissipative Hamiltonian systems with conformal symplectic structure, however, the symplectic form evolves according to a conformal factor determined by the dissipation. We propose CoSynFlow, a conformal symplectic neural flow for learning continuous-time solution maps of dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics. CoSynFlow composes symplectic shear maps with explicit conformal scaling, preserving the conformal symplectic structure by construction. By conditioning it on a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian descriptor and the dissipation parameter, a single trained model predicts solution maps for unseen systems without retraining. CoSynFlow keeps the structure error at machine precision, attains the lowest long-horizon error, and admits physics-informed training.

</details>


### [560] [From field-scale to large-scale spectral libraries: Tabular foundation models in soil spectroscopy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00608)
*Viacheslav Barkov,Jonas Schmidinger,Robin Gebbers,Martin Atzmueller*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper systematically compares regression models (TabPFN, CNN, Cubist, Random Forest, PLSR) and dimensionality reduction strategies (PCA, PLS) across 85 regression tasks from pedometrics benchmark datasets. TabPFN on full spectra outperforms classical baselines, and combining PLS latent variables with TabPFN yields the best overall predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Translating high-dimensional, highly collinear vis-NIR and MIR spectra into accurate soil property predictions remains challenging, especially with machine learning. The paper aims to provide systematic, evidence-based guidance for spectroscopic calibration model selection across operational scales.

Method: The authors compared an in-context learning tabular foundation model (TabPFN), a convolutional neural network (CNN), rule-based regression (Cubist), Random Forest, and partial least squares regression (PLSR), using full spectra as well as features derived from PCA and PLS latent variables, across 85 regression tasks from open benchmark datasets spanning field-scale digital soil mapping and a global soil spectral library.

Result: TabPFN consistently delivered the best overall performance across scales, including large spectral library tasks with tens of thousands of samples. TabPFN on full spectra already surpassed all classical baselines, showing explicit dimensionality reduction is not strictly required. PLS proved effective as a dimensionality reduction strategy for all models, and combining PLS latent variables with TabPFN yielded the best predictions overall.

Conclusion: The long-standing advantages of PLSR and modern tabular foundation models complement each other in chemometrics. The findings provide evidence-based guidance for spectroscopic calibration model selection across operational scales.

Abstract: Visible and near-infrared (vis-NIR) and mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy enable rapid, cost-effective prediction of soil properties. Yet, translating high-dimensional, highly collinear spectra into accurate soil property predictions remains challenging, particularly when employing machine learning. We systematically investigated regression models and dimensionality reduction approaches for spectroscopic modeling across 85 regression tasks from open benchmark datasets in pedometrics spanning field-scale digital soil mapping and a global soil spectral library. We compared an in-context learning tabular foundation model (TabPFN), a convolutional neural network (CNN), rule-based regression (Cubist), Random Forest, and partial least squares regression (PLSR) using full spectra as well as features derived from principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares (PLS) latent variables. TabPFN consistently delivered the best overall performance across scales, including large spectral library tasks with tens of thousands of soil samples. Notably, TabPFN applied directly to full spectra already surpassed all classical baselines, showing that explicit dimensionality reduction is not strictly required for strong performance. Further improvements were achieved through PLS, which proved to be an effective dimensionality reduction strategy for all models. Combining PLS latent variables with TabPFN yielded the best predictions overall. Our findings provide evidence-based guidance for spectroscopic calibration model selection across operational scales, demonstrating that the long-standing advantages of PLSR and modern tabular foundation models complement each other in chemometrics.

</details>


### [561] [RHEA: Reliability-Harmonized Reconstruction and Assignment for Robust Multimodal-Attributed Graph Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00621)
*Yinlin Zhu,Di Wu,Ziyu Han,Zekai Chenm,Wang Luo,Miao Hu,Guocong Quan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RHEA is a reliability-aware framework for clustering multimodal-attributed graphs that estimates node-specific modality reliability from neighborhood consensus, reconstructs unreliable modalities, adaptively weights modality fusion, and performs topology-aware optimal transport clustering, outperforming baselines across four benchmarks under five attribute-quality conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
