Motivation: Existing MAG clustering methods assume equal modality reliability across all nodes, degrading substantially when attributes are noisy or missing, whereas in practice modality reliability is inherently node-specific.

Method: RHEA estimates node-specific modality reliability from neighborhood consensus, reconstructs unreliable or missing modalities from graph neighborhoods, adaptively weights modalities during reliability-aware fusion, and performs topology-aware optimal transport clustering with reliability-aware transport assignment and neighbor-consensus assignment distillation. Reconstructed representation confidence is incorporated into the clustering objective.

Result: On four MAG benchmarks under five attribute conditions, RHEA consistently outperforms the strongest baseline, with NMI gains increasing as attribute quality deteriorates.

Conclusion: Under attribute homophily, graph neighborhoods provide supervision-free evidence for node-specific modality reliability, enabling robust MAG clustering even with degraded, noisy, or missing attributes.

Abstract: Multimodal-attributed graphs (MAGs), whose nodes carry heterogeneous attributes such as text and images over a relational structure, have become a fundamental substrate for label-free entity grouping tasks, including community discovery and product segmentation. Existing MAG clustering methods effectively integrate complementary modalities when attributes are clean and complete, but degrade substantially under noisy or missing attributes because they implicitly assume equal modality reliability across all nodes. In practice, modality reliability is inherently node-specific: images may be corrupted or absent, while textual descriptions are incomplete or noisy. We argue that, under attribute homophily, graph neighborhoods naturally provide supervision-free evidence for estimating node-specific modality reliability. Based on this insight, we propose RHEA, a reliability-aware framework for MAG clustering that estimates node-specific modality reliability from neighborhood consensus and propagates this signal throughout the clustering pipeline. RHEA reconstructs unreliable or missing modalities from graph neighborhoods, adaptively weights modalities during reliability-aware fusion, and performs topology-aware optimal transport clustering with reliability-aware transport assignment and neighbor-consensus assignment distillation. Furthermore, the confidence of reconstructed representations is incorporated into the clustering objective, allowing uncertain reconstructions to contribute proportionally during optimization. Experiments on four MAG benchmarks under five attribute conditions show that RHEA consistently outperforms the strongest baseline, with NMI gains increasing as attribute quality deteriorates.

</details>


### [562] [Towards Effective Federated Multimodal Graph Learning via Navigating Multifaceted Heterogeneity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00623)
*Yinlin Zhu,Di Wu,Yi Zhang,Xunkai Li,Wang Luo,Wei-Jin Huang,Miao Hu,Guocong Quan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedTCR is the first systematic federated learning algorithm for multimodal-attributed graphs, addressing task, modality, and topology heterogeneity through a two-stage paradigm (federated task-agnostic pre-training followed by isolated task-oriented fine-tuning) and a topology-aware cross-modal routing mechanism with tri-level cross-modal contrastive learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated graph learning methods are insufficient for federated multimodal graph learning because they fail to handle the multifaceted heterogeneity inherent in decentralized multimodal-attributed graphs: task heterogeneity from diverse client objectives, modality heterogeneity from discrepant modality quality and semantic domains, and topology heterogeneity from divergent topological patterns with low cross-modality correlation.

Method: FedTCR employs a two-stage paradigm (federated task-agnostic pre-training followed by isolated task-oriented fine-tuning) to handle task heterogeneity. For modality and topology heterogeneity, it introduces a topology-aware cross-modal routing mechanism: clients distill modality-specific knowledge into compact prototypes using topology-aware importance-weighted aggregation informed by graph structure; the server evaluates cross-client cross-modal relationships among these structure-informed prototypes and routes informative ones as contrastive references, driving a tri-level cross-modal contrastive learning scheme that jointly aligns cross-client modalities while preserving discrimination.

Result: Experiments across 7 domains demonstrate that FedTCR outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on both graph-centric and modality-centric tasks.

Conclusion: FedTCR provides a systematic and effective solution for federated multimodal graph learning by explicitly addressing task, modality, and topology heterogeneity, achieving superior performance over existing baselines across multiple domains and task types.

Abstract: Multimodal-attributed graphs (MAGs), where nodes carry heterogeneous semantic content across multiple modalities while edges encode relational dependencies, have been widely adopted across diverse domains. Federated multimodal graph learning (FMGL) extends federated graph learning (FGL) to MAGs, enabling collaborative optimization across decentralized MAGs without exposing raw data. However, naively applying existing FGL methods to FMGL is insufficient, as they fail to navigate the multifaceted heterogeneity inherent in decentralized MAGs, including task heterogeneity across diverse client objectives, modality heterogeneity from discrepant modality quality and semantic domains, and topology heterogeneity arising from divergent topological patterns with low cross-modality correlation. To address these challenges, we propose Federated multimodal graph learning with Topology-aware Cross-modal Routing (FedTCR), the first systematic algorithm designed for FMGL. To handle task heterogeneity, FedTCR employs a two-stage paradigm that comprises federated task-agnostic pre-training followed by isolated task-oriented fine-tuning. To jointly address modality and topology heterogeneity, FedTCR introduces a topology-aware cross-modal routing mechanism. Concretely, each client distills modality-specific knowledge into compact prototypes via topology-aware importance-weighted aggregation informed by graph structure; the server then evaluates cross-client cross-modal relationships among these structure-informed prototypes and routes informative ones as contrastive references, driving a tri-level cross-modal contrastive learning scheme that jointly aligns cross-client modalities while preserving discrimination. Experiments across 7 domains demonstrate that FedTCR outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on both graph-centric and modality-centric tasks.

</details>


### [563] [Relative Parameter Importance in Task-Agnostic Replay-Free Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00630)
*Malavika Suresh,Ikechukwu Nkisi-Orji,Nirmalie Wiratunga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a continual learning method for deep neural networks that uses a novel "relative parameter-importance" measure to balance stability and plasticity, enabling both backward knowledge transfer and effective regularization, with demonstrated improvements on class-incremental and domain-incremental text classification tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to address two key challenges in continual learning: (1) the stability-plasticity trade-off, where networks must retain past knowledge while learning new tasks, and (2) enabling backward knowledge transfer, where learning new tasks improves performance on old ones. They target realistic constraints of no access to prior task data and no task-id at inference time.

Method: The proposed method introduces a relative parameter-importance measure that evaluates each parameter's importance with respect to both current and past tasks simultaneously. Parameters with high relative importance are heavily regularized to maintain past-task stability, while those with low relative importance are free to be updated. Crucially, this approach permits updating parameters that are important for past tasks when they have low relative importance relative to the current task, enabling backward knowledge transfer.

Result: The method demonstrates improvements over state-of-the-art continual learning approaches on both class-incremental and domain-incremental learning benchmarks for text classification problems. The paper also provides insights for extending the approach to text generation tasks.

Conclusion: The relative parameter-importance based approach effectively balances stability and plasticity while simultaneously enabling backward knowledge transfer, outperforming existing CL methods under realistic constraints (no prior task data and no task-id at inference).

Abstract: Achieving continual learning (CL) with deep neural networks requires balancing stability and plasticity while enabling knowledge transfer. In this work, we focus on offline learning algorithms under the constraints: (I) no access to training data from prior tasks (II) no access to task-id at inference time. We introduce a novel measure, the relative parameter-importance, which measures the relative importance of each parameter with respect to both the current and past tasks. Parameters with high relative importance are interpreted as more important for maintaining past-task stability and thus heavily regularised, whereas parameters with low relative-importance are allowed to be more freely updated. Unlike existing methods, our approach allows the update of parameters with high past-task importance when they have low relative-importance, thus enabling backward knowledge transfer in addition to tackling the stability-plasticity trade-off. We demonstrate improvements against state-of-the-art CL methods on both class-incremental and domain-incremental learning text classification problems and provide insights for extending our method to text generation problems. Code available at: https://github.com/itsmemala/LACL

</details>


### [564] [Learning the Pareto Frontier of Predictive Models under Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00632)
*Yiming Dong,Jiwei Zhao,Yang Young Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Frontier Learning is a framework that treats a library of pretrained models with different access regimes (black-box vs. white-box) as complementary sources, concatenating their representations and predictions to train a lightweight supervised learner on target data. The resulting hypothesis class subsumes zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, and direct training as special cases, guaranteeing performance no worse than any individual baseline on the training sample. Evaluated on simulations, DomainNet/VisDA, and MIMIC-IV-Notes, it matches or outperforms the strongest individual strategy, with largest gains when no single baseline is reliable under distribution shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Under distribution shift, no single model reuse strategy—zero-shot application, fine-tuning, or target-specific training—is uniformly best across settings. Pretrained models differ not only in performance but in accessibility (black-box vs. white-box), and current approaches treat these models as mutually exclusive alternatives rather than complementary sources of information.

Method: Frontier Learning constructs a unified target-domain feature by concatenating internal representations from white-box candidates with prediction outputs from black-box candidates, then fits a lightweight, regularized supervised learner on this concatenated representation using labeled target data. The hypothesis class contains zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, and direct training as special cases, so empirical risk minimization guarantees the frontier learner is no worse than any individual baseline on the training sample.

Result: Evaluated across simulations with varying source-target compatibility and two real-world distribution-shift settings (visual domain adaptation on DomainNet/VisDA and clinical mortality prediction on MIMIC-IV-Notes), Frontier Learning matches or outperforms the strongest individual reuse strategy in all settings, with the largest gains occurring precisely when no single baseline is reliable across the range of shift considered.

Conclusion: Treating a library of mixed-access pretrained models as complementary rather than competitive sources yields a robust learning framework that is guaranteed to be at least as good as any individual baseline on the training sample, and delivers the greatest practical advantage in settings where no single strategy is consistently reliable under distribution shift.

Abstract: Modern machine learning pipelines increasingly rely on reusing pretrained and foundation models across downstream tasks. These pretrained models can differ not only in performance but also in how they can be used: some only provide black-box predictions, while others may permit white-box access to internal representations that can be probed or fine-tuned. When deployed to the target domain in the presence of distribution shift, no single strategy, including zero-shot application, fine-tuning, or directly training a target-specific model, is uniformly the best.
  In this work, we propose Frontier Learning, a framework that treats a library of candidate models spanning different training histories and access regimes as complementary sources of information rather than mutually exclusive alternatives. Frontier Learning constructs a unified target-domain feature by concatenating internal representations from white-box candidates as well as prediction outputs from black-box candidates, then fits a lightweight, regularized supervised learner on this concatenated representation using labeled target data. Because the resulting hypothesis class contains predictors obtained by zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, and direct training as special cases, empirical risk minimization over the frontier learner is guaranteed to be no worse, on the training sample, than any individual baseline.
  We evaluate the framework in simulations spanning varying degrees of source-target compatibility and in two real-world distribution-shift settings: visual domain adaptation on DomainNet/VisDA and clinical mortality prediction across intensive care unit domains using MIMIC-IV-Notes. Across all settings, Frontier Learning matches or outperforms the strongest individual reuse strategy, with the largest gains arising precisely when no single baseline is reliable across the range of shift considered.

</details>


### [565] [Mitigating Backdoors via Decoy Shortcuts and Knowledge Decoupling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00732)
*Zixuan Zhu,Rui Wang,Lihua Jing,Jinwen Zhong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes TR (Trapping and Removing), a training-time defense against backdoor attacks that introduces a lightweight shortcut branch (honeypot) to absorb backdoor knowledge during training, then removes backdoors by discarding the shortcut without extra data. It uses knowledge decoupling with entropy-based weight assignment to isolate poisoned samples into the honeypot while preserving benign performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Backdoor attacks threaten deep neural networks when training relies on third-party data, as adversaries can inject malicious behaviors through data poisoning. The authors identify that backdoor behaviors are naturally absorbed by simpler parallel branches during joint training, motivating a defense that leverages this phenomenon.

Method: TR introduces a lightweight shortcut branch as a honeypot to trap backdoor knowledge during training. It employs a knowledge decoupling strategy with entropy-based weight assignment to encourage poisoned samples to flow through the honeypot while guiding the main network toward benign learning. An automatic shortcut generation strategy improves generalization across different model architectures. After training, backdoors are removed by discarding the shortcut branch without requiring additional data.

Result: Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets and five model architectures show that the approach effectively mitigates a wide range of backdoor attacks while preserving performance on benign data.

Conclusion: TR provides a simple yet effective training-time defense against backdoor attacks by trapping malicious knowledge in a disposable shortcut branch, achieving strong defense capability without requiring extra data and generalizing across diverse model architectures.

Abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a serious threat to deep neural networks, especially when training relies on third-party data, allowing adversaries to inject malicious behaviors through data poisoning. In this work, we reveal that backdoor behaviors tend to be absorbed by a simpler parallel branch when jointly trained with the main network. Motivated by this insight, we propose Trapping and Removing (TR), a simple yet effective training-time defense that introduces a lightweight shortcut branch as a "honeypot" to trap backdoor knowledge. After training, backdoors can be removed by discarding the shortcut, without requiring any additional data. To further enhance backdoor isolation while maintaining benign performance, we design a knowledge decoupling strategy with entropy-based weight assignment, encouraging poisoned samples to flow through the honeypot while guiding the main network to focus on benign learning. In addition, we introduce an automatic shortcut generation strategy to improve generalization across model architectures. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets and five model architectures demonstrate that our approach effectively mitigates a wide range of backdoor attacks while preserving performance on benign data. Code: https://github.com/Zixuan-Zhu/TR}{github.com/Zixuan-Zhu/TR.

</details>


### [566] [An Embedded RISC-V Evaluation of Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks in Hard-Constrained Recurrent Physics-Informed Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00737)
*Enzo Nicolas Spotorno,Josafat Leal Filho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether KAN-based residual branches in HRPINNs, which are parameter-efficient compared to MLPs in terms of discovery accuracy, maintain that advantage during actual deployment on embedded scalar RISC-V hardware. Using identical trained weights, the authors measured latency, energy per integration step, and robustness under INT8 quantization on a StarFive VisionFive 2 (SiFive U74, RV64GC no vector extensions). KANs were 4.7–14.5x slower, consumed 4.7–18.7x more energy, and diverged up to 43x earlier under INT8 quantization compared to matched MLPs. The study concludes that KAN parameter efficiency does not transfer to deployment on scalar embedded cores, making the MLP residual branch a more dependable default for embedded HRPINN deployment unless quantization co-design is employed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work characterized when a vanilla B-spline KAN matches or underperforms an MLP as an HRPINN residual branch in discovery accuracy, but it remained an open question whether KAN's parameter efficiency survives actual deployment on embedded platforms, given that KAN's learnable B-spline activations follow a markedly different execution profile than MLPs.

Method: Using identical trained weights, the authors benchmarked execution latency, energy per integration step, and dependability under post-training quantization in the closed recurrent loop on a RISC-V RV64GC platform without vector extensions (StarFive VisionFive 2 / SiFive U74). They compared KAN and MLP residual branches across four parameter-matched size tiers and two accuracy-comparable pairs.

Result: KAN residual branches executed 13.5x and 8.0x slower and consumed 11.3x and 5.6x more energy per integration step for the two accuracy-comparable pairs (3.7 µJ vs 0.33 µJ for the smallest pair). Across all four size tiers, the ranges were 4.7x–14.5x (latency) and 4.7x–18.7x (energy). Under INT8 quantization, KAN trajectories diverged up to 43x earlier than matched MLPs, with damage traced to weight quantization rather than input-side knot-interval misassignment.

Conclusion: The parameter efficiency reported for KANs does not transfer to deployment cost on scalar embedded cores. The MLP residual branch is a more dependable default for embedded HRPINN deployment unless specific quantization co-design is used.

Abstract: Hard-constrained recurrent physics-informed networks (HRPINNs) embed known dynamics inside a recurrent numerical integrator and restrict a neural branch to learning only the residual dynamics that the first-principles model does not capture. Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (KANs) have been proposed as parameter-efficient replacements for multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in such residual branches, but their learnable B-spline activations follow a markedly different execution profile. Building on prior work that characterized when a vanilla B-spline KAN matches or underperforms an MLP as an HRPINN residual branch in discovery accuracy, this paper asks whether that parameter efficiency survives deployment. Using identical trained weights, we measured execution latency, energy per integration step, and dependability under post-training quantization in the closed recurrent loop on a RISC-V RV64GC platform without vector extensions (StarFive VisionFive~2, SiFive U74). For the two accuracy-comparable pairs, the KAN residual branch executed $13.5\times$ and $8.0\times$ slower and consumed $11.3\times$ and $5.6\times$ more energy per integration step (3.7\,$μ$J against 0.33\,$μ$J for the smallest pair); across all four parameter-matched size tiers the ranges are $4.7\times$--$14.5\times$ and $4.7\times$--$18.7\times$. Under INT8 quantization, KAN trajectories diverged up to $43\times$ earlier than matched MLPs; the damage traces to weight quantization, not to input-side knot-interval misassignment. These results indicate that the parameter efficiency reported for KANs does not transfer to deployment cost on scalar embedded cores, and that an MLP residual branch is the more dependable default for embedded HRPINN deployment unless specific quantization co-design is used.

</details>


### [567] [Generic Vision and Cross-Attention for Reaction Yield Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00776)
*Qiwei Han,Chi Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A dual-modal Vision Cross-Attention architecture fuses tabular physical-organic data with 2D molecular topology images for reaction yield prediction, achieving superior accuracy (Test RMSE = 5.27%) over quantum-descriptor baselines and providing mechanistic interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional reaction yield prediction relies on 1D quantum descriptors that lack explicit spatial information, limiting predictive accuracy.

Method: A dual-modal Vision Cross-Attention architecture that fuses tabular physical-organic data with 2D molecular topology representations, using a generic computer vision backbone to process skeletal structures alongside quantum descriptors.

Result: The generic CV backbone processing 2D skeletal structures alone outperforms purely quantum-based baselines; the cross-attention fusion achieves Test RMSE = 5.27%, surpassing traditional methodologies. Mechanistic probing reveals active descriptor-guided spatial querying and learned prioritization of steric bottlenecks (e.g., aryl halide), while residual skip connections protect non-spatial electronic parameters.

Conclusion: Provides a scalable, interpretable blueprint for augmenting physical chemistry with deep visual learning by synergizing spatial and non-spatial modalities.

Abstract: Traditional reaction yield prediction is constrained by 1D quantum descriptors that lack explicit spatial information. To address this gap, a dual-modal Vision Cross-Attention architecture is proposed, fusing tabular physical-organic data with 2D molecular topologies. Notably, it is demonstrated that a generic computer vision backbone processing simple 2D skeletal structures independently outperforms purely quantum-based baselines. By synergizing both modalities, superior predictive accuracy compared to traditional methodologies is achieved by the optimal cross-attention framework (Test RMSE = 5.27%). Through mechanistic probing, active, descriptor-guided spatial querying is observed, effectively offloading macroscopic steric identification to the visual pathway. Furthermore, a dynamic chemical hierarchy is learned by the network to heavily prioritize critical steric bottlenecks, such as the aryl halide. Concurrently, residual skip connections are utilized to protect non-spatial electronic parameters from destructive attenuation during fusion. Collectively, a scalable and highly interpretable blueprint is provided for augmenting physical chemistry with deep visual learning.

</details>


### [568] [Paris as a 15-Minute City: An Explainable AI Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00815)
*András J. Molnáar,Csaba I. Sidló,Rita Rónai,Domonkos Rózsay*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study examines the relationship between the 15-minute city concept and actual mobility behavior in the Paris metropolitan area using ~70,000 trip segments from NetMob 2025 data, enriched with INSEE sociodemographic data and OpenStreetMap POIs. Using walking/cycling accessibility indicators and explainable gradient-boosted tree models, the authors find that higher local service availability is associated with less private motorized travel and more active mobility, though this effect weakens in outer suburbs. The results support 15-minute city assumptions while revealing spatial and demographic heterogeneity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The 15-minute city concept is widely promoted but its relationship with observed mobility behavior remains difficult to quantify empirically. This paper aims to bridge that gap by linking local service availability indicators to actual trip characteristics derived from real mobility trajectories.

Method: The study uses mobility trajectories from the NetMob 2025 Data Challenge for the Paris metropolitan area, enriched with INSEE sociodemographic data and OpenStreetMap points of interest (POIs). After stop-based segmentation and data cleaning, approximately 70,000 trip segments are analyzed. Walking- and cycling-based indicators of local service availability are constructed, and gradient-boosted tree models with explainable machine-learning methods (XAI) are used to examine associations with trip duration, transport mode, and short-trip car use, including robustness checks under alternative variable orderings.

Result: Higher POI availability is associated with less private motorized travel and more active mobility, though this association is substantially weaker in the outer agglomeration. Key predictors include trip purpose, home-work distance, local service availability, vehicle ownership, public-transport subscription, and sociodemographic context. For short trips, high POI density correlates with lower car use while car ownership and driving-licence availability correlate with higher car use; in service-sparse areas, public-transport subscription reduces predicted car dependence.

Conclusion: The results are consistent with central assumptions of the 15-minute city while revealing substantial spatial and demographic heterogeneity. The study demonstrates that explainable machine-learning methods can complement traditional accessibility indicators and identify locally relevant hypotheses for urban-mobility policy formulation.

Abstract: The 15-minute city promotes access to everyday services within a short walk or bicycle ride, but its relationship with observed mobility remains difficult to quantify. We investigate this relationship in the Paris metropolitan area using mobility trajectories from the NetMob 2025 Data Challenge, enriched with INSEE sociodemographic data and OpenStreetMap points of interest (POIs), yielding approximately 70,000 trip segments after stop-based segmentation and data cleaning.
  We construct walking- and cycling-based indicators of local service availability and examine their associations with trip duration, transport mode, and short-trip car use. Higher POI availability is associated with less private motorized travel and more active mobility, although this relationship is substantially weaker in the outer agglomeration. Gradient-boosted tree models interpreted with explainable machine-learning methods consistently identify trip purpose, home--work distance, local service availability, vehicle ownership, public-transport subscription, and sociodemographic context as important predictors. For short trips, high POI density is associated with lower car use, while car ownership and driving-licence availability are associated with higher predicted car use; where services are sparse, public-transport subscription is associated with lower predicted car dependence. Finally, explainable AI (XAI) methods are used to examine how feature attributions change under alternative assumed variable orderings.
  The results are consistent with central assumptions of the 15-minute city while revealing substantial spatial and demographic heterogeneity. They also demonstrate how explainable machine-learning methods can complement accessibility indicators and identify locally relevant hypotheses for urban-mobility policy.

</details>


### [569] [AdvPlan-Bench: Adversarial Evaluation of Structured Plan-Generation Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00832)
*Alina Kapanova,Arun Kanhai,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AdvPlan-Bench is an offline benchmark for adversarially evaluating structured plan-generation agents. It introduces a general evaluation object (typed plans, adversarial response sets, selector diagnostics, candidate-frontier metrics) and uses BLUE-vs-RED advantage and Nash-gap diagnostics across 150 synthetic scenarios spanning five planning templates. Empirical results show that increasing response candidates reduces BLUE advantage, and the benchmark provides reproducibility for studying adversarial plan evaluation, response-budget sensitivity, and multi-agent critique.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most plan-generation agents are evaluated as if plan quality exists in isolation, but real planning tasks require understanding how a candidate plan behaves when another agent can actively search for responses (adversarial settings). The paper addresses the lack of a general, reproducible evaluation framework for such adversarial plan evaluation.

Method: AdvPlan-Bench represents plans as typed action chains with optional branches, assigns synthetic quality scores, and compares opposing plans using BLUE-vs-RED advantage and Nash-gap diagnostics, plus a heuristic rubric for qualitative constraint coherence. It evaluates across 150 synthetic scenarios in five planning templates, testing policies including a sampled best-response policy (drawing eight candidates), an offline LLM-policy contract baseline, and a two-stage multi-agent council, alongside a three-rater rubric-sensitivity study over 600 rating records.

Result: The sampled best-response policy reduces BLUE advantage from .518 to .486 and BLUE win rate from .900 to .820 versus a single-sample response. The offline LLM-policy contract baseline reaches .496 BLUE advantage and .700 BLUE win rate, while the two-stage multi-agent council obtains .509 BLUE advantage and .813 win rate. The three-rater rubric-sensitivity study yields .978 inter-rater agreement.

Conclusion: AdvPlan-Bench is a reproducible benchmark artifact for studying adversarial plan evaluation, response-budget sensitivity, candidate frontiers, and multi-agent critique-and-revision traces. It is explicitly not an operational planner and provides no evidence about real-world decision quality.

Abstract: Structured plan-generation agents are often evaluated as if a plan has quality in isolation, yet many realistic planning tasks require asking how a candidate behaves when another agent can search for responses. We introduce AdvPlan-Bench, an offline benchmark for adversarial evaluation of structured plan-generation agents. The contribution is a general evaluation object: a typed plan, an adversarial response set, selector diagnostics, and traceable candidate-frontier metrics. AdvPlan-Bench represents plans as typed action chains with optional branches, assigns synthetic quality scores, compares opposing plans with BLUE-vs-RED advantage and Nash-gap diagnostics, and evaluates qualitative constraint coherence with a transparent heuristic rubric. In 150 synthetic scenarios spanning five planning templates, a sampled best-response policy that draws eight response candidates reduces BLUE advantage from .518 to .486 and BLUE win rate from .900 to .820 relative to a single-sample response. An offline LLM-policy contract baseline reaches .496 BLUE advantage and .700 BLUE win rate, while a two-stage multi-agent council obtains .509 BLUE advantage and .813 BLUE win rate. A three-rater rubric-sensitivity study over 600 rating records yields .978 inter-rater agreement. AdvPlan-Bench is not an operational planner and provides no evidence about real-world decision quality; it is a reproducible benchmark artifact for studying adversarial plan evaluation, response-budget sensitivity, candidate frontiers, and multi-agent critique-and-revision traces.

</details>


### [570] [Deep Learning CNN and Recurrence Analysis for Alpha Gamma EEG Biomarkers in Fragile X Syndrome](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00835)
*Zag ElSayed,Payton Siekierski,Jack Yanchen Liu,Ernest Pedapati*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a multi-representation deep learning framework combining CNNs, LSTMs, and recurrence plot analysis to automatically characterize EEG phenotypes in Fragile X Syndrome (FXS). The framework decomposes band-limited EEG into alpha and gamma oscillations, transforms them into complementary representations (temporal sequences, time-frequency maps, and recurrence plots), and uses a hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture to jointly capture spatial, temporal, and nonlinear dependencies, outperforming single-modality baselines in subject-independent evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fragile X Syndrome is characterized by disrupted synaptic plasticity, cortical hyperexcitability, and impaired network synchronization linked to FMRP deficiency. EEG reveals reproducible abnormalities in alpha and gamma oscillations that relate to inhibitory control, sensory processing, and cognition, yet automated characterization of these phenotypes remains challenging, motivating a deep learning framework that integrates multiple complementary signal representations.

Method: The framework (1) decomposes band-limited EEG into alpha (8-12 Hz) and gamma (30-100 Hz) components; (2) transforms signals into complementary representations including temporal feature sequences, time-frequency maps, and recurrence plot (RP) images encoding nonlinear recurrence structure; (3) uses CNN modules to learn discriminative spatial-spectral and dynamical textures from image-based representations; (4) uses LSTM modules to model temporal modulation of oscillatory activity; and (5) integrates these in a hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture that jointly captures spatial, temporal, and nonlinear dependencies. Subject-independent evaluation is performed against single-modality baselines.

Result: The hybrid model outperforms single-modality baselines in subject-independent evaluation. Gamma features provide strong discriminative power on their own, while integration of alpha and gamma features yields the best overall performance across classification tasks.

Conclusion: Deep learning with nonlinear representations provides a scalable approach for EEG biomarker development in FXS, with potential utility for diagnosis, patient stratification, and treatment monitoring in translational settings.

Abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by reduced expression of fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP), leading to disrupted synaptic plasticity, cortical hyperexcitability, and impaired network synchronization. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a noninvasive window into these mechanisms and consistently reveals abnormalities in alpha (8 to 12 Hz) and gamma (30 to 100 Hz) oscillations that relate to inhibitory control, sensory processing, and cognition. This paper proposes a multi representation deep learning framework for automated characterization of FXS EEG phenotypes by integrating convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, and recurrence plot (RP) analysis. Band limited EEG signals are decomposed into alpha and gamma components and transformed into complementary representations, including temporal feature sequences, time frequency maps, and RP images encoding the nonlinear recurrence structure. CNN modules learn discriminative spatial-spectral and dynamical textures from image based representations, while LSTM modules model temporal modulation of oscillatory activity; a hybrid CNN LSTM architecture jointly captures spatial, temporal, and nonlinear dependencies. Subject-independent evaluation demonstrates that the hybrid model outperforms single modality baselines, with gamma features providing strong discriminative power and alpha gamma integration yielding the best overall performance. These findings support deep learning with nonlinear representations as a scalable approach for EEG biomarker development in FXS, with potential utility for diagnosis, stratification, and treatment monitoring in translational settings.

</details>


### [571] [Nonlinear Laplacians Improve Signed-Directed Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00836)
*Ali Parviz,Yuichi Yoshida*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a non-linear Laplacian operator for signed and directed networks (NLSD) and proposes a spectral GNN framework (NLSD-GNN) built on top of it. The operator selectively propagates messages only along edges where potential discrepancies align with edge direction, and the framework achieves superior performance on node classification and link prediction across diverse datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While linear Laplacians have been applied to signed-directed graphs for GNN design, there is little research on non-linear Laplacian operators for such networks. This paper aims to fill this gap by developing a non-linear operator that simultaneously handles both sign and direction information in graphs.

Method: The authors define a non-linear Laplacian operator (NLSD) that extends both the signed Laplacian (for signed graphs) and the directed Laplacian (for directed graphs). The operator computes node-specific potentials based on features and applies selective message passing, only propagating information across edges where the potential discrepancy aligns with the edge's direction, ignoring mismatched edges. This operator is used to build an efficient spectral GNN framework called NLSD-GNN.

Result: Comprehensive evaluations on node classification and link prediction across scenarios involving signed, directed, or both types of information show that NLSD-GNN effectively integrates signed and directional data and achieves superior performance across diverse datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed nonlinear Laplacian framework successfully unifies signed and directed graph information and outperforms existing approaches, demonstrating the value of non-linear operators in spectral GNN design for such complex network structures.

Abstract: While signed-directed graphs have been studied using linear Laplacians in the design of graph neural networks, relatively little research has focused on developing non-linear Laplacian operators for such networks. We introduce a non-linear Laplacian operator specific to signed and directed networks (NLSD). This non-linear operator extends the concepts of the signed Laplacian for signed graphs and the Laplacian for directed graphs. The NLSD calculates node-specific potentials based on features More precisely, if the potential discrepancy is not aligned with the edge direction, we ignore it (and vice versa) leveraging message-passing techniques only across edges where potential discrepancies align with the edge's direction. Utilizing this novel operator, we propose an efficient spectral GNN framework (NLSD-GNN). We conducted comprehensive evaluations focusing on node classification and link prediction, examining scenarios involving signed, directional, or both types of information. Our findings reveal that this spectral GNN framework not only integrates signed and directional data effectively but also achieves superior performance across diverse datasets.

</details>


### [572] [Adaptive Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differential Equations with Applications to Fluid Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00850)
*Fabio Pereira dos Santos,Renato Portugal,Júlio de Castro Vargas Fernandes,Lucas Timotheo Sanches*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical framework that enhances Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks (QPINNs) through adaptive collocation point sampling, loss-aware attention mechanisms, and trainable loss-weighting. The method improves solution accuracy by at least 60% for benchmark fluid flows and reaction-diffusion systems, and the authors argue that optimization—not just expressivity—is a critical bottleneck in QPINNs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs struggle with high-dimensional or multiscale PDEs, and QPINNs are commonly assumed to be limited by quantum circuit expressivity. The authors aim to address accuracy and efficiency challenges in QPINNs for complex PDEs.

Method: The framework employs (1) adaptive collocation point sampling that dynamically prioritizes regions with large PDE residuals or steep solution gradients to mitigate spectral bias, (2) loss-aware attention mechanisms, and (3) a trainable loss-weighting scheme balancing physics residuals, boundary conditions, and data fidelity. These are integrated with variational quantum circuits and quantum gradient estimation.

Result: Across diverse differential equations, optimization (not just expressivity) was identified as a key bottleneck. The proposed hybrid framework achieves at least a 60% improvement in solution accuracy under specific regimes for benchmark fluid flows and reaction-diffusion systems.

Conclusion: Merely increasing model expressivity is insufficient for resolving complex PDEs via QPINNs, as structural optimization limitations persist. The framework offers a scalable pathway for quantum-enhanced scientific machine learning.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a versatile approach for solving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), yet achieving high accuracy efficiently using these techniques remains challenging for high-dimensional or multiscale systems. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical framework that enhances Quantum PINNs (QPINNs) through adaptive collocation point sampling and loss-aware attention mechanisms. By dynamically prioritizing points in regions with large PDE residuals or steep solution gradients, our method mitigates the spectral bias inherent in conventional PINNs. Current Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks are commonly assumed to be limited by the expressive power of quantum circuits. In our work, we observed that, across diverse differential equations, optimization - not only expressivity - can be an important bottleneck. Furthermore, a trainable loss-weighting scheme balances contributions from physics residuals, boundary conditions, and data fidelity during training. Integrating these strategies with quantum computing techniques (including variational quantum circuits and quantum gradient estimation) can yield at least a 60% improvement in solution accuracy under specific regimes for benchmark fluid flows and reaction-diffusion systems. Finally, we argue that merely increasing model expressivity is insufficient for resolving complex PDEs via QPINNs, as they remain constrained by the structural optimization limitations of classical PINNs. This framework provides a scalable pathway for quantum-enhanced scientific machine learning, bridging physics-based modeling with emerging quantum computational capabilities.

</details>


### [573] [HyperODE: Zero-Shot Surrogate for Simulation and Inference of Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00852)
*Ajitesh Srivastava*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HyperODE is a unified machine learning surrogate that operates across an entire class of compartmental ODE models without retraining by mapping ODE structure into directed hypergraphs, enabling zero-shot forward trajectory prediction (with quantile uncertainty) and single-pass inverse parameter calibration from noisy trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional ML surrogates must be retrained from scratch whenever the underlying dynamical system (ODE) is modified—even slight changes like adding a state or altering a contact network invalidate trained models. Since thousands of simulations are often needed across vast parametric landscapes, this retraining cost is prohibitive.

Method: HyperODE decouples the functional form of system interactions from the neural architecture by mapping ODE structures into directed hypergraphs. It takes a compartmental ODE with arbitrary parameter distributions defined via quantiles, converts it to a hypergraph, and outputs trajectory distributions as quantiles. A shared encoder is additionally built to map noisy trajectories to parameter distributions for calibration in a single pass.

Result: On unseen families and system sizes, HyperODE produces calibrated quantile bands in a single forward pass with weighted-interval score and coverage on par with structure-specialized surrogates. Its inverse inference produces calibration from noisy trajectories in milliseconds with a single shared encoder, competitive with existing methods. It also extends zero-shot to non-mass-conserving ODEs and external forcing.

Conclusion: HyperODE demonstrates that a single surrogate can generalize zero-shot across an entire class of compartmental models, eliminating the need for per-model retraining while maintaining accuracy comparable to specialized surrogates for both forward simulation and inverse parameter calibration.

Abstract: Understanding and controlling complex dynamical systems often requires executing thousands of numerical simulations across vast parametric landscapes, which is time-consuming. Machine learning surrogates significantly accelerate simulation by predicting state trajectories across different initializations and parameter values. However, surrogate models are specialized to one simulation model. Modifying the underlying differential equations - e.g., adding a physiological state or altering an epidemiological contact network - renders trained models obsolete and forces computationally expensive retraining from scratch. We introduce HyperODE, a surrogate capable of operating across an entire class of approximately mass-conserving compartmental models without retraining. By mapping the structure of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) into directed hypergraphs, HyperODE decouples the functional form of system interactions from the neural network architecture. HyperODE takes a compartmental model in the form of an ODE with an arbitrary parameter distribution defined through quantiles and transforms it into a hypergraph. It outputs the distribution of the trajectories for all the states in the original ODE in the form of quantiles. We then use this surrogate to build an encoder that takes a noisy trajectory and outputs a distribution over the parameters of the original ODE, thus calibrating the model in a single pass. On families and system sizes never seen in training, HyperODE produces calibrated quantile bands in a single forward pass, with weighted-interval score and coverage on par with specialized surrogates for each structure. For inverse inference, HyperODE produces calibration from noisy state trajectories in a few milliseconds with a single shared encoder, competitive with existing methods. HyperODE extends zero-shot to ODEs that break mass conservation and to external forcing.

</details>


### [574] [SparseKAN: Compressing Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks Across Basis Functions, Neurons, and Bits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00859)
*Kazi Ahmed Asif Fuad,Lizhong Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SparseKAN is a unified compression framework for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks that introduces hierarchical learnable gates to prune basis functions, neurons/channels, and numerical precision simultaneously, then physically compacts the pruned structure into dense tensors. It achieves up to 73% parameter reduction without accuracy loss on MNIST, 0.51x CUDA latency, and 23.63x inference speedup on FPGA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KANs replace scalar weights with learnable univariate functions parameterized by multiple basis coefficients, creating a redundancy structure that conventional neural-network compression methods do not directly address. Existing approaches cannot effectively expose or exploit this new source of redundancy across the multiple structural axes unique to KANs.

Method: SparseKAN compresses KANs along three complementary axes: basis functions, neurons/channels, and numerical precision. It equips the base branch, nonlinear basis branch, and individual basis terms with hierarchical learnable gates trained under a differentiable active-cost objective. The learned importance structure is then hardened under explicit basis and width budgets, recovered in full or low precision, and physically compacted into smaller dense tensors rather than retained as sparse masks.

Result: Experiments across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with spline, polynomial, RBF, wavelet, and convolutional KAN variants show structural axes compose predictably in cost. Coefficient-based selection outperforms low-order truncation by up to 15.25 accuracy points in Gram-polynomial settings. Eight-bit quantization is robust, while 4-bit convolutional KANs require quantization-aware adaptation. Physical compaction removes up to 73% of parameters without accuracy loss on MNIST, reduces CUDA latency to 0.51x dense, and achieves 23.63x lower inference latency on ZCU104 FPGA.

Conclusion: SparseKAN effectively converts functional redundancy in KANs into measurable software and hardware efficiency through a unified, axis-composable compression framework with hierarchical gating, demonstrating robustness across diverse KAN variants and deployment targets.

Abstract: Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (KANs) replace scalar edge weights with learnable univariate functions parameterized by multiple basis coefficients. This introduces a source of redundancy that conventional neural-network compression does not directly expose. We present \textbf{SparseKAN}, a unified approach that compresses KANs along three complementary axes: basis functions, neurons/channels, and numerical precision. SparseKAN equips the base branch, nonlinear basis branch, and individual basis terms with hierarchical learnable gates trained under a differentiable active-cost objective. The learned importance structure is subsequently hardened under explicit basis and width budgets, recovered in full or low precision, and physically compacted into smaller dense tensors rather than retained as sparse masks. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 across spline, polynomial, RBF, wavelet, and convolutional KAN variants show that the structural axes compose predictably in cost. We also find strong basis-dependent differences in term importance: coefficient-based selection outperforms matched low-order truncation by up to 15.25 accuracy points in the evaluated Gram-polynomial settings. Eight-bit quantization is broadly robust, whereas 4-bit convolutional KANs require quantization-aware adaptation. Physical compaction removes up to 73.0\% of parameters without accuracy loss on MNIST and reduces large-batch CUDA latency to as little as $0.51\times$ dense execution. On a ZCU104 FPGA, the resulting sparse low-bit models achieve up to $23.63\times$ lower inference latency, demonstrating that SparseKAN converts functional redundancy into measurable software and hardware efficiency. The SparseKAN implementation is available at https://github.com/OSU-STARLAB/SparseKAN.

</details>


### [575] [Kilobyte Models: Neural Networks as a Seed and a Quantized Latent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00860)
*Sahil Rajesh Dhayalkar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an extreme model compression approach where instead of storing network weights, only a compact latent vector and a random seed are stored, from which the full network can be regenerated via a Mapping Network architecture. The method achieves accuracy comparable to aggressive weight quantization while using far fewer bytes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The storage and transmission cost of neural networks scales with parameter count, creating bottlenecks for over-the-air updates, on-device libraries, and bandwidth-bound deployments. The authors aim to dramatically reduce this cost by moving beyond weight storage to storing a short recipe for regenerating weights.

Method: Building on Mapping Networks, the approach expresses network weights as a nonlinear function of a compact trainable latent and a fixed random basis. Only the latent needs to be stored since the basis and initialization center are reproducible from an integer seed. The artifact is a seed plus a quantized latent, with size determined by latent dimension and bit width. A seeded block-wise basis is introduced to scale to networks whose projection cannot fit in memory, and quantization-aware fine-tuning of the latent is used for aggressive bit widths.

Result: A mapped model achieves accuracy comparable to aggressive few-bits-per-weight quantization while taking significantly fewer bytes to store. Results are independent of the specific random basis, and a structured basis enables nearly free weight regeneration even for large networks.

Conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates that neural networks can be compressed to a seed-plus-latent representation that is far smaller than quantized weights while maintaining comparable accuracy, offering an extreme form of compression suitable for bandwidth-constrained deployment scenarios.

Abstract: The cost of storing and transmitting a trained neural network scales with its parameter count, a bottleneck for over-the-air updates, on-device libraries, and other bandwidth-bound deployments. We study an extreme form of model compression in which the deployable artifact is not the weights but a short recipe for regenerating them. Building on Mapping Networks, which express a network's weights as a nonlinear function of a compact trainable latent and a fixed random basis, we observe that only the latent need be stored, because the basis and initialization center are reproducible from an integer seed. A model becomes a seed together with a quantized latent, whose size is set by the latent dimension and bit width rather than the parameter count. We formalize this artifact and introduce a seeded block-wise basis that scales to networks whose projection cannot be held in memory. In our experiments, a mapped model is as accurate as the same network quantized aggressively to a few bits per weight, while taking far fewer bytes to store. Reaching the most aggressive bit widths depends on fine-tuning the latent with quantization in the loop. The results do not depend on the particular random basis, and a structured basis lets the weights be regenerated almost for free even for large networks.

</details>


### [576] [GeoArbiter: Verifiability-Guided Grounding for Remote-Sensing Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00877)
*Xuechen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GeoArbiter is a training-free pipeline that filters geographic retrieval records by cross-modal verifiability, injecting only image-unverifiable facts into remote-sensing MLLMs. This preserves most of the accuracy gains from full retrieval while reducing hallucination and improving robustness to conflicting records.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Remote-sensing MLLMs often make claims about attributes like facility identity or function that cannot be established from imagery alone. Geographic retrieval can supply this missing knowledge, but retrieved records can also contradict visible evidence, and models tend to follow records even when the image is decisive.

Method: GeoArbiter operationalizes cross-modal verifiability: it measures whether each attribute is verifiable from imagery, injects only geographic facts that the image cannot verify, and filters out conflicting records via content-level filtering rather than prompt-based arbitration. The pipeline is training-free.

Result: GeoArbiter preserves 84.69-87.15% of the full-retrieval accuracy gain, reduces claim-level hallucination by 9.58-26.34% under a source-blinded judge, and improves robustness to conflicting records across all three open MLLMs. Coordinate-keyed retrieval alone improves fMoW land-use accuracy by 12.06-17.19 points.

Conclusion: Verifiability-guided content selection is a simple, effective mechanism for grounding remote-sensing MLLMs in fallible geographic knowledge, offering a better accuracy-hallucination trade-off than arbitration prompts.

Abstract: Remote-sensing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often assert facts that imagery cannot establish, such as a facility's identity or function. Coordinate-keyed geographic retrieval can supply this missing knowledge, improving fMoW land-use accuracy by 12.06--17.19 points across three open MLLMs. However, retrieved records can also contradict visible evidence, and we find that models frequently follow the records even when the image is decisive. We argue that source trust should therefore depend on \emph{cross-modal verifiability}: geographic records are most useful for attributes the image cannot verify and most dangerous when they dispute visually verifiable attributes. We introduce GeoArbiter, a training-free pipeline that operationalizes this principle by injecting only image-unverifiable geographic facts. Unlike arbitration prompts, which leak across attribute types and bias yes/no responses, content-level filtering preserves 84.69--87.15\% of the full-retrieval accuracy gain, reduces claim-level hallucination by 9.58--26.34\% under a source-blinded judge, and improves robustness to conflicting records across all three models. These results identify verifiability-guided content selection as a simple, effective mechanism for grounding remote-sensing MLLMs in fallible geographic knowledge.

</details>


### [577] [AOSpec: Action and Observation Co-Speculation for Low-Latency Agent Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00881)
*Hao Mark Chen,Jinnan Guo,Wayne Luk,Hongxiang Fan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AOSpec is a lossless framework that co-speculates both actions and observations across the full agent-environment loop, using Expected Value Decoding (EVD) to prioritize observation speculation with the greatest latency benefit, isolated forks for latency-critical actions, and Joint Action-State Verification (JASV) to break the lookahead-accuracy tradeoff. It reduces mean end-to-end latency by 11.8-32.5% and p99 latency by up to 42.8% across four harnesses, five actor models, and five serving speeds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As decoding accelerates, tool execution becomes a growing bottleneck in LLM agents with stateful tools. Existing action-only or observation-only speculation leaves latency exposed because value is concentrated in few slow calls, some outcomes are only revealed via execution, and longer lookahead requires increasingly unlikely chains of action predictions.

Method: AOSpec introduces three components: (1) Expected Value Decoding (EVD) that directs observation speculation toward outcomes with the greatest expected latency benefit, optimizing expected hidden time rather than hit rate; (2) isolated forks that launch latency-critical target actions to contain their effects for outcomes only execution can reveal; (3) Joint Action-State Verification (JASV) that verifies both the action and its origin state against committed execution, recasting long-horizon action dependency from full-chain prediction into target action-state verification to enable long-range overlap without sacrificing serial semantics.

Result: Across Terminal-Bench serving settings with four harnesses, five actor models, and five serving speeds, AOSpec outperforms all practical baselines, reducing mean end-to-end latency by 11.8-32.5% and p99 latency by up to 42.8%. Gains increase as decoding accelerates, and the observation model transfers from Terminal-Bench to SWE-bench Verified without retraining.

Conclusion: Co-speculating both actions and observations across the full agent-environment loop is a more effective approach than action-only or observation-only speculation. JASV successfully breaks the lookahead-accuracy tradeoff, and the approach yields growing benefits as decoding speed improves, with observation model transferability across benchmarks.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly act through stateful tools, yet model generation and environment execution remain serialized at every step. As decoding accelerates, tool execution becomes a growing bottleneck. Existing action- or observation-only speculation leaves much of this latency exposed: value is concentrated in a few slow calls, some outcomes emerge only through execution, and longer lookahead typically requires an increasingly unlikely chain of action predictions. We present AOSpec, a lossless framework that co-speculates actions and observations across the full agent-environment loop. Expected Value Decoding (EVD) directs observation speculation toward outcomes with the greatest expected latency benefit, optimizing expected time hidden rather than hit rate. For outcomes only execution can reveal, AOSpec launches latency-critical target actions in isolated forks that contain their effects, while Joint Action-State Verification (JASV) verifies both the action and its origin state against committed execution before reuse. JASV recasts long-horizon action dependency from full-chain prediction into target action-state verification, breaking the lookahead--accuracy tradeoff and unlocking long-range overlap without sacrificing serial semantics. Across Terminal-Bench serving settings spanning four harnesses, five actor models, and five serving speeds, AOSpec outperforms every practical baseline, reducing mean end-to-end latency by 11.8-32.5% and p99 latency by up to 42.8%. Its gains increase as decoding accelerates, and its observation model transfers from Terminal-Bench to SWE-bench Verified without retraining.

</details>


### [578] [UpliftBench: Revealing Outcome-Regime and Objective Mismatch in Uplift Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00915)
*Binshuang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UpliftBench shows that disagreements among uplift-modeling benchmark results are largely due to evaluation metrics rather than underlying models. It evaluates 12 estimators across 7 dataset families under a multi-objective, outer-test-isolated protocol, finding that (F1) Qini's rank correlation with effect accuracy is near-zero (+0.07, CI [-0.03, +0.16]) on IHDP while AUUC aligns substantially better (+0.49 to +0.73), and (F2) ranking metrics (Qini, AUUC, uplift-at-k) are structurally insufficient for sign-threshold policies on Jobs (14-15% regret) but calibrating the decision threshold removes 81% of Qini-selection regret. Both findings are bounded and not universal, with F1 absent on ACIC/Revenue-Synthetic and F2 vanishing under a budgeted-value objective. The benchmark releases versioned loaders, fixed protocols, artifacts, and a reproducible leaderboard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Published uplift-modeling benchmarks frequently disagree on which estimator performs best, and the authors aim to show that this disagreement is substantially about evaluation metrics rather than the models themselves.

Method: UpliftBench evaluates 12 uplift estimators under an outer-test-isolated, multi-objective protocol across seven dataset families. Two key findings are identified where a reference objective exists: F1 on the standard continuous benchmark (IHDP) comparing Qini vs. AUUC alignment with effect accuracy, and F2 in a within-sample case study on Jobs comparing ranking metrics vs. direct policy-risk selection for a sign-threshold policy.

Result: (F1) On IHDP, Qini shows no detectable alignment with effect accuracy (+0.07 mean rank correlation, CI [-0.03, +0.16] across 100 realizations), while AUUC is consistently more aligned (gap +0.49 [+0.40, +0.59]; cumulative-gain AUUC +0.73). (F2) On Jobs, ranking metrics are structurally insufficient for sign-threshold policies yielding 14-15% regret, while calibrating the decision threshold removes 81% of Qini-selection regret. Both findings are bounded: F1 not detected on ACIC/Revenue-Synthetic, F2 vanishes under a budgeted-value objective.

Conclusion: Benchmark conclusions depend fundamentally on the evaluation metric chosen; ranking-based metrics can misalign with true effect accuracy and policy relevance in specific settings. The authors release UpliftBench as a reproducible, versioned benchmark with a living leaderboard to enable continued, rigorous comparison.

Abstract: Uplift modeling (conditional-average-treatment-effect estimation) drives personalized targeting, yet published uplift benchmarks frequently disagree on which estimator performs best; we show the disagreement is substantially about metrics, not models. UpliftBench evaluates 12 uplift estimators under an outer-test-isolated, multi-objective protocol across seven dataset families; its two findings are identified where a reference objective exists -- F1 on the standard continuous benchmark (IHDP), F2 in a within-sample case study on Jobs. On that benchmark, Qini shows no detectable alignment with effect accuracy -- across all 100 IHDP realizations its mean rank correlation with effect accuracy is +0.07, 95% CI [-0.03, +0.16] -- while AUUC is consistently more aligned (paired prefix-mean-AUUC-over-Qini gap +0.49 [+0.40, +0.59]; the shipped cumulative-gain AUUC aligns better still, +0.73). On Jobs, ranking metrics are structurally insufficient for a sign-threshold policy because they discard the score level; empirically, within the released split-rotation analysis direct policy-risk selection yields lower benchmark regret than random model selection while Qini, AUUC, and uplift-at-$k$ do not (14-15% regret). Calibrating the decision threshold removes 81% of the Qini-selection regret. Both findings are bounded, not universal: F1 is not detected on either validation family (the ACIC and Revenue-Synthetic gaps are both indistinguishable from zero), and F2 vanishes under a budgeted-value objective where rank suffices. UpliftBench releases versioned loaders, fixed protocols, result artifacts, and a reproducible living leaderboard; the public repository accompanies the paper.

</details>


### [579] [Subtype Robustness Is Not Just Accuracy: Calibration Under Unseen Subtype Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00928)
*Hanyu Su,Carlota Julbe i Juanola,Yibo Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents the first systematic study of calibration under subtype robustness—where test examples come from fine-grained subtypes unseen in training but within a known coarse category. Across ImageNet, BREEDS, iNaturalist, and CIFAR-100 with five architectures, the authors find that calibration breaks down on unseen subtypes: models become systematically overconfident exactly where accuracy drops, with confidence barely following the accuracy loss. This is not a general consequence of accuracy loss, since generic corruption causes a larger confidence drop at matched accuracy loss. Recalibration on seen subtypes narrows but does not close the gap, and OOD scores only weakly flag affected inputs. The authors conclude subtype robustness should be evaluated through calibration, not accuracy alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on subtype robustness has studied the problem almost entirely through accuracy, asking whether a model keeps the correct coarse prediction when facing fine-grained subtypes unseen in training. The authors argue this misses a critical dimension: whether the model remains calibrated (i.e., whether confidence aligns with true correctness) on such unseen subtypes.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical study across four datasets (ImageNet, BREEDS, iNaturalist, CIFAR-100) and five architectures. They measure both accuracy and calibration (confidence) on fine-grained subtypes absent from training. They compare the calibration breakdown to that caused by generic image corruption at matched accuracy loss, study the effects of recalibration tuned on seen subtypes, and assess whether out-of-distribution scores can flag the affected inputs.

Result: On unseen subtypes, accuracy drops while confidence barely follows, leaving models systematically overconfident exactly where they have become less accurate. At matched accuracy loss, generic image corruption causes a much larger drop in confidence, showing the effect is specific to in-taxonomy novelty rather than a general consequence of losing accuracy. Recalibration tuned on seen subtypes narrows but does not close the gap, and OOD scores flag affected inputs only weakly.

Conclusion: Subtype robustness should be evaluated through calibration in addition to accuracy. The model reacts to visible degradation (like corruption) but not to in-taxonomy novelty (unseen subtypes), so novel-but-coarse-consistent inputs require dedicated calibration-aware evaluation.

Abstract: Subtype robustness asks whether a model keeps the correct coarse prediction when test examples come from fine-grained subtypes absent from training but still inside a known coarse category. Prior work studies this almost entirely through accuracy. We ask whether the model also stays calibrated. We present the first systematic study of the question across ImageNet, BREEDS, iNaturalist and CIFAR-100 with five architectures. Calibration breaks down on unseen subtypes, where accuracy drops while confidence barely follows, leaving the model systematically overconfident exactly where it has become less accurate. At matched accuracy loss, generic image corruption causes a much larger drop in confidence, so the effect is not a general consequence of losing accuracy. The model reacts to visible degradation but not to in-taxonomy novelty. Recalibration tuned on seen subtypes narrows the gap but does not close it, and out-of-distribution scores flag the affected inputs only weakly. Subtype robustness should therefore be evaluated through calibration, not accuracy alone.

</details>


### [580] [xMICD: Explainable Representation of Multiple ICD Codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00935)
*Pat Vatiwutipong,Kumkup Keeratisiwakul,Albert Phuoc Kien Van Truong,Nutcha Yodrabum,Wasin Pansiritanachot,Marvin N. Wright,Thanapon Noraset*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: xMICD is a method that constructs low-dimensional, interpretable patient representations from sets of ICD codes by combining clinically meaningful diagnostic groupings with embeddings, achieving predictive performance comparable to embedding-based methods like ICD2Vec while maintaining clinical interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for representing ICD codes in EHR-based clinical risk prediction face a trade-off: grouping-based representations are interpretable but lose information, while embedding-based representations perform well but are difficult to interpret. A method is needed that achieves both strong predictive performance and clinical interpretability.

Method: xMICD assigns ICD codes to clinically meaningful diagnostic groups via similarity-based relative assignments in a pre-trained ICD embedding space, rather than using binary group membership. This yields features that reflect how closely a patient's diagnoses align with each clinical group, producing low-dimensional patient representations.

Result: Experiments on large-scale EHR datasets demonstrate that xMICD achieves predictive performance comparable to embedding-based representations such as ICD2Vec across multiple clinical prediction tasks, while maintaining clinical interpretability since each feature dimension corresponds to a recognizable diagnostic group.

Conclusion: xMICD provides a practical way to integrate embedding-based semantic relationships into interpretable clinical feature spaces for machine learning models, effectively resolving the performance-interpretability trade-off in ICD code representation.

Abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are widely used for clinical risk prediction using machine learning. International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes provide structured information about patient diagnoses, but representing them effectively remains challenging. Existing approaches often face a trade-off between predictive performance and interpretability: grouping-based representations are interpretable but may lose information, while embedding-based representations achieve strong predictive performance but are difficult to interpret. We propose Explainable Representation of Multiple ICD Codes (xMICD), a method for constructing low-dimensional patient representations from sets of ICD codes. xMICD combines clinically meaningful diagnostic groupings with similarity in a pre-trained ICD embedding space. Instead of using binary group membership, the method assigns codes to groups via similarity-based relative assignments, yielding features that reflect how closely a patient's diagnoses align with each clinical group. Experiments on large-scale EHR datasets demonstrate that xMICD achieves predictive performance comparable to embedding-based representations such as ICD2Vec across multiple clinical prediction tasks. At the same time, the resulting features remain clinically interpretable because each dimension corresponds to a recognizable diagnostic group. xMICD therefore provides a practical way to integrate embedding-based semantic relationships into interpretable clinical feature spaces for machine learning models.

</details>


### [581] [Data-Driven Pinball-Loss Selection for Vertically Distributed Elastic-Net SVMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00949)
*Xiaofei Wu,Kai Qi,Rongmei Liang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a data-driven elastic-net support vector machine that learns simplex-constrained weights over candidate pinball losses, producing a weighted loss equivalent to a pinball loss with a data-dependent effective parameter. Theoretical guarantees include an empirical oracle inequality bounding excess risk, and a column-partitioned variable-splitting solver with O(1/T) convergence and partition-invariant iterates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The pinball-loss SVM is robust to noise, but its asymmetry parameter is typically fixed a priori, limiting adaptability to data. The authors aim to make this parameter data-driven while retaining a single classifier, rather than relying on manual tuning.

Method: They construct an elastic-net SVM that learns simplex-constrained weights over a set of candidate pinball losses, with the weighted combination equivalent to a single pinball loss whose effective parameter depends on the data. They provide an empirical oracle inequality bounding the objective at a global minimizer relative to the best fixed candidate, with explicit excess bounds when regularization/truncation are nonzero. For high-dimensional scaling, they design a column-partitioned variable-splitting solver and prove best-iterate O(1/T) convergence in squared-step residual; under common initialization and global parameters, any column partition yields identical iterates and solution to centralized training in exact arithmetic.

Result: Theoretical results establish equivalence between the learned weighted loss and a data-dependent pinball loss, along with oracle inequalities. The solver achieves O(1/T) best-iterate convergence and partition-invariance (identical results to centralized training). Experiments evaluate predictive behavior, numerical equivalence, and multi-process scalability.

Conclusion: The proposed method enables automatic, data-adaptive selection of the pinball asymmetry parameter within an elastic-net SVM framework, with strong theoretical guarantees (oracle inequality and fast convergence) and scalable distributed training that exactly reproduces centralized solutions.

Abstract: The pinball-loss support vector machine is robust, but its asymmetry parameter is usually fixed in advance. We propose a data-driven elastic-net support vector machine that learns simplex-constrained weights over candidate pinball losses while retaining one classifier. The weighted loss is equivalent to a pinball loss with a data-dependent effective parameter. An empirical oracle inequality shows that, when weight regularization and simplex truncation vanish, the classifier objective at a global minimizer does not exceed that of the best fixed candidate; otherwise, the excess is explicitly bounded. For high-dimensional data, we develop a column-partitioned variable-splitting solver. It converges with a best-iterate $O(1/T)$ squared-step residual rate. Under common initialization and global parameters, any column partition produces, in exact arithmetic, the same iterates and solution as centralized training. Experiments assess predictive behavior, numerical equivalence, and multi-process scalability.

</details>


### [582] [Interpretable machine learning for predicting splitting strength of asphalt concrete: insights from SHAP analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00956)
*Jianglei Xing,Xiao Tan,Dongzhao Jin,Pengwei Guo,Yuhuan Wang,Huiya Niu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An interpretable machine-learning framework using six models (TabPFN, ANN, SVR, RF, XGBoost, LightGBM) predicts the splitting strength of asphalt concrete from 296 samples and 14 input variables. TabPFN performed best (R²=0.88, RMSE=0.28), SHAP identified nine dominant variables, favorable parameter ranges were quantified, and a GUI platform was developed for practical application.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide an interpretable machine-learning approach for predicting asphalt concrete splitting strength and supporting data-driven mixture design, addressing the need for both accurate prediction and interpretability in construction material engineering.
