### [702] [Hidden-Domain Routing for All-Type Audio Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00493)
*Yifan Gao,Yao Tian,Hongbin Suo,Haonan Lu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a closed-condition routed system for all-type audio deepfake detection that first recovers the hidden audio domain using an AudioType-BEATs-6s Router, then applies domain-specific experts (Speech-XLSR for speech; EAT-based experts for sound, singing, and music). The system achieves 96.10% Track2 Macro-F1, ranking first on the official AT-ADD Track2 final leaderboard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: All-type audio deepfake detection requires authenticity decisions across multiple audio types (speech, environmental sound, singing voice, and music), yet the audio type is unavailable at inference time. This creates a hidden audio-domain condition where binary real/fake labels are shared across domains but representation structure and detector-score behavior vary by audio type, motivating the need to recover the hidden domain before interpreting detector scores.

Method: The system employs a closed-condition routed architecture: (1) an AudioType-BEATs-6s Router estimates the audio type from a 6-second window; (2) speech inputs are directed to a Speech-XLSR Expert; (3) sound, singing, and music inputs rely on EAT-based general-audio experts with branch-local score interpretation.

Result: On the official AT-ADD Track2 final evaluation, the system achieves 96.10% Track2 Macro-F1 and ranks first on the final leaderboard, with type-wise Macro-F1 scores of 88.07%, 98.18%, 99.07%, and 99.08% for speech, sound, singing, and music, respectively.

Conclusion: The results support recovering the hidden audio domain before interpreting detector scores in all-type audio deepfake detection, demonstrating that audio-domain separation and complementary detector strengths across audio types improve overall detection performance.

Abstract: All-type audio deepfake detection requires authenticity decisions across speech, environmental sound, singing voice, and music, while the audio type is unavailable at inference time. In AT-ADD Track2, this setting creates a hidden audio-domain condition: the binary real/fake label is shared across domains, but representation structure and detector-score behavior vary with audio type. We present a closed-condition routed system that first recovers the hidden audio domain and then interprets detector scores within the selected branch. The AudioType-BEATs-6s Router estimates audio type from a 6-second window; speech inputs are handled by the Speech-XLSR Expert, while sound, singing, and music rely on EAT-based general-audio experts with branch-local score interpretation. Development-set representation analysis, router-family comparisons, and component results show audio-domain separation and complementary detector strengths across audio types. On the official AT-ADD Track2 final evaluation, the system achieves 96.10% Track2 Macro-F1 and ranks first on the final leaderboard, with type-wise Macro-F1 scores of 88.07%, 98.18%, 99.07%, and 99.08% for speech, sound, singing, and music, respectively. These results support recovering the hidden audio domain before interpreting detector scores in all-type audio deepfake detection.

</details>


### [703] [Beyond Prompt Adherence: Auditing Attribute-Level Voice Control in Speech Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00545)
*Xianhao Zhou,Jianghao Wu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper audits three speech-generation systems (CosyVoice3, VoxCPM2, Fish-Speech-S2) using 5,940 controlled paired outputs, finding that prompt-matching responses frequently introduce unintended off-target changes across acoustic, prosodic, content, and speaker dimensions. The authors introduce VoDER-Cal, a training-free candidate selector that preserves target responses while minimizing off-target deviations, raising joint success rates from 4.8% to ~14% and improving listener-rated preservation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of natural-language-controlled speech generation focus primarily on whether an output matches the prompt, but fail to assess whether characteristics outside the intended change remain stable (i.e., preservation). This gap motivates the need for a preservation-sensitive evaluation framework and inference-time remedies.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled paired audit of three TTS systems with 5,940 outputs varying over six speakers, ten texts, three seeds, and eleven conditions. They measure acoustic, prosodic, content, and speaker characteristics to detect off-target changes beyond baseline seed variation. They also propose VoDER-Cal, a training-free candidate reranker that selects from a three-candidate pool to retain strong target responses while favoring smaller off-target deviations.

Result: Off-target changes frequently accompany expected target-direction responses across all systems, and these changes differ substantially across systems. VoDER-Cal increases joint success rate from 4.8% (single-sample) to ~14% with a three-candidate pool, reduces held-out off-target deviation from 0.344 to 0.276, and improves listener-rated preservation relative to target-only selection.

Conclusion: Prompt adherence alone is insufficient for evaluating natural-language-controlled speech generation; preservation-sensitive evaluation is a necessary complement. Candidate reranking at inference time offers a practical, training-free improvement for reducing unintended changes.

Abstract: Natural-language descriptions have become a flexible interface for controlling generated speech. Existing evaluations largely assess whether an output matches a prompt, but prompt matching alone does not reveal whether characteristics outside the intended change remain stable. We examine this distinction through a controlled paired audit of three speech-generation systems: CosyVoice3, VoxCPM2, and Fish-Speech-S2. The evaluation contains 5,940 outputs spanning six reference speakers, ten texts, three random seeds, and eleven conditions. Using acoustic, prosodic, content, and speaker measurements, we find that responses in the expected target direction are frequently accompanied by changes outside descriptor-specific signal-level target sets. This pattern remains among outputs whose target response exceeds baseline seed variation, and the accompanying changes differ substantially across systems. We further introduce VoDER-Cal, a training-free candidate selector that retains sufficiently strong target responses while favoring smaller off-target deviations. A three-candidate pool raises the joint success rate from 4.8% under single-sample direct generation to approximately 14% for all candidate-selection policies. Within the matched three-candidate budget, VoDER-Cal reduces held-out off-target deviation from 0.344 under target-only selection to 0.276 and improves listener-rated preservation. Preservation-sensitive evaluation therefore complements prompt-adherence evaluation, while candidate reranking offers a practical inference-time improvement. Code, configuration files, and analysis scripts are available at https://github.com/intelland/VoDER

</details>


### [704] [AnyBand: Unified Multi-Bandwidth Speech Extension via Frequency-Aware In-Context Spectral Infilling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00572)
*Junchuan Zhao,Minh Duc Vu,Bowen Zhang,Ye Wang*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: AnyBand is a unified bandwidth extension framework that recasts BWE as in-context spectral infilling, using the observed low-frequency spectrum as a frequency-domain prompt. It enables a single model to handle continuous ranges of input bandwidths via missing-band conditional flow matching, an Easy-to-Balanced curriculum, a frequency-aware Diffusion Transformer, and multi-view adversarial refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing BWE methods assume fixed or predefined bandwidth conversion, requiring cutoff-specific models or retraining when input bandwidth changes. This limits real-world applicability where speech arrives with diverse cutoff frequencies.

Method: AnyBand formulates BWE as in-context spectral infilling, conditioning high-frequency generation on the observed low-frequency spectrum as a frequency-domain prompt. It uses missing-band conditional flow matching with an Easy-to-Balanced cutoff curriculum over continuously sampled cutoff frequencies, a frequency-aware Diffusion Transformer for cross-frequency and long-range temporal modeling, and a multi-view adversarial refinement stage for spectral realism.

Result: Experiments on multiple datasets and bandwidth settings show AnyBand consistently improves spectral reconstruction over existing baselines while achieving competitive perceptual quality across both standard and irregular input cutoffs.

Conclusion: AnyBand demonstrates that a single unified model can effectively handle continuous-range bandwidth extension without cutoff-specific retraining, improving spectral reconstruction while maintaining competitive perceptual quality.

Abstract: Bandwidth extension (BWE) aims to recover missing high-frequency content from band-limited speech. Existing methods often formulate BWE as a fixed or predefined bandwidth conversion problem, potentially requiring cutoff-specific models or retraining when the input bandwidth changes. This assumption limits their applicability to practical scenarios where speech may arrive with diverse cutoff frequencies. We propose AnyBand, a unified BWE framework that recasts bandwidth extension as in-context spectral infilling. Motivated by prompt-based zero-shot speech generation, AnyBand conditions high-frequency generation on the observed low-frequency spectrum, using the available band as a frequency-domain prompt that conveys content, speaker, prosodic, and spectral-envelope cues. This formulation enables a single model to perform cutoff-conditioned generation over a continuous range of input bandwidths. AnyBand is trained with missing-band conditional flow matching and an Easy-to-Balanced cutoff curriculum over continuously sampled cutoff frequencies. To better exploit the spectral prompt, we introduce a frequency-aware Diffusion Transformer that models cross-frequency interactions and long-range temporal dependencies, followed by a physically motivated multi-view adversarial refinement stage to enhance spectral realism, envelope coherence, and harmonic consistency. Experiments on multiple datasets and bandwidth settings show that AnyBand consistently improves spectral reconstruction over existing baselines while achieving competitive perceptual quality across both standard and irregular input cutoffs. Audio samples are available.

</details>


### [705] [UOT-IR: Structured Routing of High-Polyphony Symbolic Music into Fixed-Budget Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00576)
*Ziyue Kang,Nan Nan,Chenhao Lin,Xiaohong Guan*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper proposes UOT-IR, a training-free framework based on constrained unbalanced optimal transport, to compress high-polyphony symbolic music into fixed-budget bounded representations while preserving structural roles, orchestration compatibility, and playability. It addresses two settings under the same slot budget—template standardization and adaptive preservation—and demonstrates strong performance on the SymphonyNet corpus, achieving the best Note-F1 (0.9120) in adaptive preservation and lowest structural cost (14.7165) in template standardization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-polyphony symbolic music is widely used in generation, analysis, and arrangement, but many downstream tasks require bounded, fixed-track/slot representations. Existing compression approaches based on heuristic simplification or generic representation-space reduction fail to preserve structural roles, orchestration compatibility, and playability under strict budgets.

Method: The compression problem is reformulated as a fixed-budget structured routing problem and solved via constrained unbalanced optimal transport. UOT-IR combines four components: an orchestration prior, adaptive marginal relaxation, temporal decoding, and playability-aware projection, enabling training-free compression into compact and musically coherent bounded representations.

Result: On the SymphonyNet corpus, UOT-IR achieves strong performance in both settings: the best Note-F1 of 0.9120 in adaptive preservation, and the lowest structural cost of 14.7165 with a bad structural confusion rate of 0.3406 in template standardization.

Conclusion: The work establishes a principled paradigm for fixed-budget symbolic music compression, offering a practical path toward compact, structured, and musically coherent symbolic representations that preserve orchestration and playability constraints.

Abstract: High-polyphony symbolic music is increasingly used in generation, analysis, and arrangement, yet many downstream tasks require bounded representations with fixed tracks or slots. Converting richly orchestrated scores into compact forms is therefore necessary, but existing approaches relying on heuristic simplification or generic representation-space reduction often fail to preserve structural roles, orchestration compatibility, and playability under strict budgets. To address the issue, this study reformulates the compression problem as a fixed-budget structured routing problem and proposes Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Information Routing (UOT-IR), a training-free framework based on constrained unbalanced optimal transport. UOT-IR combines an orchestration prior, adaptive marginal relaxation, temporal decoding, and playability-aware projection to produce compact and musically coherent bounded representations. This work further studies two practical settings under the same slot budget: template standardization, which maps each input to a predefined bounded template, and adaptive preservation, which retains representative content without assuming an external template. Experiments on the SymphonyNet corpus show that UOT-IR delivers strong overall performance across both settings, including the best Note-F1 in adaptive preservation (0.9120), together with the lowest structural cost (14.7165) and bad structural confusion rate (0.3406) in template standardization. This work establishes a principled paradigm for fixed-budget symbolic music compression, offering a practical path toward compact, structured, and musically coherent symbolic representations.

</details>


### [706] [SoniSpeech: A Large-Scale Open-Vocabulary Tri-Modal Dataset for Wearable Silent Speech Interfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00803)
*Ruidong Zhang,Jiacheng Liu,François Guimbretière,Cheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces SoniSpeech, the first large-scale (34 hours, 18,000 utterances), open-vocabulary, trimodal dataset for wearable silent speech interfaces using acoustic-sensing eyewear, with a CTC-based ResNet-34 baseline achieving 26.3% WER on open-vocabulary silent speech recognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wearable silent speech interfaces (SSIs) are currently limited to small, closed vocabularies. While approaches achieving larger vocabularies exist, they require obtrusive hardware like facial electrodes. This motivates the need for an open-vocabulary SSI solution using less obtrusive wearable hardware.

Method: SoniSpeech is a trimodal dataset collected via acoustic-sensing eyewear with three synchronized modalities (ultrasound echo profiles, voiced audio, frontal video) in both voiced and silent modes. It is derived from the SODA dialogue dataset, containing contemporary conversational English with 5,356 unique words and full phoneme coverage. A CTC-based ResNet-34 serves as the baseline model.

Result: The CTC-based ResNet-34 baseline achieves 26.3% word error rate (WER) on open-vocabulary silent speech recognition, establishing the first benchmark for this task.

Conclusion: This work provides the first large-scale open-vocabulary dataset for wearable SSI, enabling future research in silent speech recognition with unobtrusive acoustic-sensing eyewear, and sets a benchmark for the task.

Abstract: Wearable silent speech interfaces (SSIs) are limited to small, closed vocabularies. Approaches achieving larger vocabularies require obtrusive hardware such as facial electrodes. We present SoniSpeech, the first large-scale, open-vocabulary, trimodal dataset for wearable SSI using acoustic-sensing eyewear. It contains 34 hours across 18,000 utterances with three synchronized modalities: ultrasound echo profiles, voiced audio, and frontal video, in both voiced and silent modes. The corpus draws from the SODA dialogue dataset, providing contemporary conversational English with 5,356 unique words and full phoneme coverage. A CTC-based ResNet-34 baseline achieves 26.3% word error rate (WER) on open-vocabulary silent speech recognition, the first benchmark for this task. Dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.7298/xjjr-9m85

</details>


### [707] [DRONEAUDIONET: Noise Suppression for Drone Audition-based Search and Rescue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00875)
*Chitralekha Gupta,Soundarya Ramesh,Yifei Luo,Suranga Nanayakkara*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: DRONEAUDIONET is a drone noise suppression method that reframes a source separation model as a drone noise estimator, using a learnable mask-scaling mechanism and additive residual correction to handle drone-dominant mixtures at SNRs below -10 dB. It improves downstream sound classification on drone audition datasets and generalizes to unseen drone hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Drone rotor noise dominates UAV-mounted microphone recordings at SNRs well below -10 dB, making source recovery extremely challenging. Existing enhancement and source separation methods are designed for near-balanced mixtures and degrade substantially in drone audition settings, yet aerial acoustic scene analysis is critical for applications like search-and-rescue.

Method: The paper proposes DRONEAUDIONET, which reframes a source separation model as a drone noise estimator. It introduces a learnable mask-scaling mechanism allowing mask magnitudes beyond unity, combined with an additive residual correction term to improve drone noise estimation and source recovery in drone-dominant mixtures.

Result: DRONEAUDIONET consistently improves downstream sound classification performance on a publicly available drone audition dataset, with the largest gains for human vocal sounds. It also demonstrates generalization on an out-of-domain dataset with unseen drone hardware and flight modes.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate the importance of drone-specific modeling for robust aerial acoustic perception and highlight the potential of source separation methods for real-world drone-assisted search-and-rescue.

Abstract: Microphones mounted on UAVs enable aerial acoustic scene analysis applications such as search-and-rescue, wildlife monitoring, and industrial inspection. However, drone rotor noise often dominates the mixture signal at SNRs well below -10 dB, making source recovery extremely challenging. Existing enhancement and source separation methods are typically designed for near-balanced mixtures and degrade substantially in drone audition settings. In this work, we propose DRONEAUDIONET, a drone noise suppression method that reframes a source separation model as a drone noise estimator. To better model drone-dominant mixtures, we introduce a learnable mask-scaling mechanism that allows mask magnitudes beyond unity, together with an additive residual correction term for improved drone estimation and source recovery. We train and evaluate our model on a publicly available drone audition dataset and test generalizability on an out-of-domain dataset with unseen drone hardware and flight modes. Results show that DRONEAUDIONET consistently improves downstream sound classification performance, with the largest gains observed for human vocal sounds. Our findings demonstrate the importance of drone-specific modeling for robust aerial acoustic perception and highlight the potential of source separation methods for real-world drone-assisted search-and-rescue.

</details>


### [708] [Separate-and-Detect: Unified Drum Transcription and Stem Generation via Latent Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01093)
*Wei-Han Hsu,Chih-Cheng Chang,Bo-Yu Chen,Li Su,Yi-Hsuan Yang*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper proposes a separate-and-detect formulation for Automatic Drum Transcription (ADT) using a five-stem latent diffusion model for drum source separation, followed by a fixed onset detector. The pipeline outperforms both a strong separation baseline and an end-to-end ADT system, while additionally providing editable audio stems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard ADT formulates transcription as a direct mapping from music mixture to symbolic drum events, discarding the acoustic stems that are valuable for editing, remixing, and production. The authors revisit an alternative separate-and-detect formulation to retain these benefits.

Method: The approach uses a separator built on a five-stem latent diffusion model that jointly generates kick, snare, toms, hi-hats, and cymbals in a compact VAE latent space. Two training-only auxiliary branches (an onset branch and a timbre branch) shape the separator during learning but are discarded at inference. A fixed onset detector then converts each separated stem into symbolic events.

Result: Evaluated on MDB Drums and ENST-Drums, the pipeline consistently improves overall transcription F1 over a strong U-Net-based separation baseline, and outperforms a representative end-to-end ADT system on kick and snare F1, while additionally providing separated audio stems. Ablations show the onset branch provides the most stable transcription gains, whereas the timbre branch modulates trade-offs between reconstruction, stem quality, and onset detection.

Conclusion: Generative drum demixing can serve not only as a source separation model but also as a practical, interpretable front end for automatic drum transcription.

Abstract: Automatic Drum Transcription (ADT) is commonly formulated as a direct mapping from a music mixture to symbolic drum events. While effective for transcription, this formulation discards the acoustic stems that are useful for editing, remixing, and production. We revisit an alternative separate-and-detect formulation, where a drum source separation front end first produces five editable drum stems, and a fixed onset detector then converts each stem into symbolic events. The separator is built on a five-stem latent diffusion model that jointly generates kick, snare, toms, hi-hats, and cymbals in a compact VAE latent space. We further study two training-only auxiliary branches--an onset branch (OB) and a timbre branch (TB)--which shape the separator during learning but are discarded at inference. Trained on synthetic drum multitracks and evaluated on MDB Drums and ENST-Drums, the proposed pipeline consistently improves over a strong U-Net-based drum separation baseline in overall transcription F1. It also outperforms a representative end-to-end ADT system on kick and snare F1 under our evaluation protocol, while additionally providing separated audio stems. The ablation results show that OB gives the most stable transcription gains, whereas TB changes the trade-off between reconstruction, acoustic stem quality, and onset detection. These results suggest that generative drum demixing can serve not only as a source separation model, but also as a practical front end for interpretable drum transcription.

</details>


### [709] [JoyAI-Talker: Full-Duplex Speech Interactive Large Model Built for Empathetic Voice Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01119)
*Yinhao Bai,Jinming Chen,Yafeng Chen,Wei Deng,Boya Dong,Nan Duan,Yu Gu,Weisheng Han,Yankun Huang,Ming Ke,Hao Li,Jingdong Li,Xiangyu Liang,Ning Liu,Yuan Liu,Ji Miao,Jiaqi Wang,Qi Wang,Wenchao Wang,Yuxuan Wang,Zhenfang Wang,Zhangyu Xiao,Chao Xue,Hongfei Xue,Fan Yu,Tianyi Zhang,Yuan Zhang,Yuqi Zhang,Lin Zhu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: JoyAI-Talker is a full-duplex speech dialogue system with a modular Thinker-Talker architecture, unified speech-text joint training to preserve cognitive capabilities, text-controllable expressive speech synthesis, a Persona-Adaptive Empathetic Response (PAER) framework for empathetic interaction, and Joy-Duplex for real-time turn control, achieving competitive results on T2T/S2T benchmarks and 0.88 response rate under interruptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech dialogue systems often suffer from "cognitive degradation," where extending core textual reasoning to speech interaction weakens the model's fundamental capabilities. Additionally, existing systems lack empathy, expressiveness, and natural full-duplex conversational abilities such as handling user interruptions fluidly.

Method: The system employs: (1) a modular Thinker-Talker architecture with unified speech-text joint training to preserve reasoning capabilities; (2) a text-controllable Talker for expressive synthesis with fine-grained control over vocal attributes and paralinguistic events (laughter, sighs); (3) the PAER framework with a hierarchical cognitive pipeline that extracts non-verbal speaker cues (gender, age, emotion) from raw audio and integrates them into CoT reasoning for empathetic, context-adaptive responses; and (4) Joy-Duplex, a state-driven plug-and-play full-duplex gating engine for real-time turn control.

Result: JoyAI-Talker achieves highly competitive performance on foundational T2T and S2T benchmarks. In full-duplex evaluation, it reaches a 0.88 response rate under user interruptions while maintaining an extremely low false-trigger rate under background speech.

Conclusion: JoyAI-Talker demonstrates that a full-duplex speech dialogue system can simultaneously preserve foundational cognitive abilities, deliver expressive and empathetic speech responses, and handle fluid real-time conversational turn-taking, indicating readiness for natural speech dialogue applications.

Abstract: We present JoyAI-Talker, a full-duplex speech dialogue system that delivers robust foundation model capabilities while empowering empathetic interaction and voice agent intelligence. JoyAI-Talker adopts a modular Thinker-Talker architecture and further implements a unified speech-text joint training pipeline to mitigate the common "cognitive degradation" bottleneck, thereby largely preserving the model's core textual reasoning, STEM, and logical capabilities while extending them to speech-based interaction. For expressive speech synthesis, the Talker module employs a text-controllable generation paradigm that enables natural-language instructions to flexibly control vocal attributes and localized paralinguistic events, such as laughter and sighs, supporting more expressive and fine-grained speech responses. To enhance conversational empathy, we introduce the Persona-Adaptive Empathetic Response (PAER) framework. PAER employs a hierarchical cognitive pipeline to extract non-verbal speaker cues, such as gender, age, and emotional state, from raw input audio, incorporate them into the Thinker's CoT reasoning, and generate context-adaptive responses that align semantically appropriate text with fine-grained control over utterance-level expressiveness and localized paralinguistic events, including sighs, speaking rate, and volume. We further integrate Joy-Duplex, a state-driven, plug-and-play full-duplex framework that functions as an efficient gating engine for real-time turn control. Extensive evaluations show that JoyAI-Talker achieves highly competitive performance on foundational T2T and S2T benchmarks. In full-duplex evaluation, the system reaches a high response rate of 0.88 under user interruptions while maintaining an extremely low false-trigger rate under background speech, demonstrating its readiness for fluid and natural speech dialogue.

</details>


### [710] [Comparative Validation of GPT-4o-mini and Teacher Mean Scores for Automated Scoring of Music Analysis Responses: Single-Pass Deployment, Repeatability, and Strategy-Specific Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01783)
*Baicheng Lin,Lingxi Jin,Kyung-Seok Min*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This study evaluates GPT-4o-mini's validity and repeatability for rubric-based scoring of 300 university-level music analysis essays across four dimensions (Harmony, Form, Reasoning, Terminology), comparing three prompting strategies (Fs+CoT, RAG, SC) against teacher mean scores. Fs+CoT showed the strongest agreement with teachers; RAG systematically over-scored; SC was highly repeatable but weaker at individual-level agreement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scoring open-ended music analysis responses is time-consuming and requires nuanced judgments of harmonic knowledge and formal understanding. The study aims to validate whether large language models can reliably perform this complex assessment task.

Method: 300 university-level student responses were scored by teachers on four dimensions (Harmony, Form, Reasoning, Terminology) and by GPT-4o-mini using three prompting strategies: few-shot with chain-of-thought (Fs+CoT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and self-consistency (SC) based on five internal generations. Each strategy was run three times with constant model/prompt/rubric/response. Single-pass scores simulated operational scoring; median aggregation across three runs assessed robustness. Agreement was measured using correlation, ICC, Krippendorff's alpha, quadratic weighted kappa, and scoring error indices.

Result: Fs+CoT demonstrated the strongest agreement with teacher mean scores in both single-pass and median aggregation conditions. RAG exhibited systematic over-scoring. SC produced highly repeatable scores but weaker individual-level agreement. Terminology dimension showed weaker agreement than Reasoning across strategies.

Conclusion: GPT-4o-mini can generate stable scores for complex music analysis responses, but different prompting strategies yield distinct scoring profiles. Operational deployment requires strategy-specific calibration, dimension-level validation, and continued human oversight.

Abstract: Scoring open-ended music analysis responses is time-consuming and requires nuanced judgments of harmonic knowledge and formal understanding. This study evaluates the validity and repeatability of GPT-4o-mini for rubric-based scoring of music analysis essays, using teacher mean scores as the benchmark. A dataset of 300 university-level student responses was scored by teachers on four dimensions: Harmony, Form, Reasoning, and Terminology. GPT-4o-mini scored the same responses using three prompting strategies: few-shot prompting with chain-of-thought reasoning (Fs+CoT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and self-consistency based on five internal generations per administration (SC). Each strategy was administered three times with the model, prompt, rubric, and response held constant. Single-pass scores represented an operational scoring condition, whereas median aggregation across three runs was used to examine robustness. Agreement with teacher mean scores was evaluated using correlation, intraclass correlation, Krippendorff's alpha, quadratic weighted kappa, and scoring error indices. Fs+CoT showed the strongest agreement with teacher mean scores in both single-pass scoring and median aggregation. RAG showed systematic over-scoring, whereas SC produced highly repeatable scores but weaker individual-level agreement. Dimension-level analyses showed that scoring performance varied across rubric components, with Terminology generally showing weaker agreement than Reasoning. These findings indicate that GPT-4o-mini can generate stable scores for complex music analysis responses, but prompting strategies produce distinct scoring profiles. Operational use therefore requires strategy-specific calibration, dimension-level validation, and continued human oversight.

</details>


### [711] [Multi-Backbone Self-Supervised Ensembles for Audio Deepfake Detection and a Cross-Track Analysis of Generation-Detection Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01796)
*Seunghyun Kim,Junghyun Kim,Jiyoung Woo*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper describes the "Go-To-Germany" team's participation in ImageCLEF 2026 Audio Deepfake Detection and Generation tasks, achieving a detection score of 0.9522 using a four-backbone SSL ensemble and winning the generation sub-task with an F5-TTS v1 baseline as an anti-forensic probe, while revealing a pronounced asymmetry between detection and generation performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To participate in the ImageCLEF 2026 competition and investigate the relationship between audio deepfake detection and generation capabilities, particularly exploring how multi-backbone self-supervised learning ensembles can improve detection robustness and how generated audio can evade detection systems.

Method: A four-backbone SSL ensemble combining WavLM-Large, Wav2Vec2-XLS-R-300M, ECAPA-TDNN, and x-vector representations for detection; and a four-model generation program (GLM-TTS, F5-TTS, XTTS v2, CosyVoice3) with the official entry being an F5-TTS v1 baseline processed with uniform reverberation as a deliberate anti-forensic probe. Falsification-based ablation experiments include LOSO 56-speaker cross-validation, three-region backbone geometry, bootstrap confidence intervals, and PCA analysis.

Result: Detection achieved a final score of 0.9522 on the official evaluation, with perfect accuracy (1.0000) on participant-generated deepfakes and 0.8875 on held-out organizer real data. The generation entry ranked first with a final score of 0.4304 (WER 4.99%, CER 2.07%), evading 61.4% and 56.2% of participant and organizer detectors respectively. An 11.25% false-positive gap on organizer real recordings remains the principal open challenge.

Conclusion: The paper proposes an architectural-insurance hypothesis for multi-backbone SSL ensembling, supported by falsification experiments, and reveals a pronounced asymmetry between detection (0.9522) and generation (0.4304) side performance, suggesting that generation-side evasion and detection-side design decisions are interconnected and require cross-track insights for future improvements.

Abstract: This paper describes the participation of team "Go-To-Germany" in the ImageCLEF 2026 Audio Deepfake Detection and Generation task. Our detection system, built on a four-backbone self-supervised learning (SSL) ensemble combining WavLM-Large, Wav2Vec2-XLS-R-300M, ECAPA-TDNN, and x-vector representations, achieved a final score of 0.9522 on the official ImageCLEF 2026 evaluation, with perfect accuracy (1.0000) on participant-generated deepfakes and 0.8875 on the held-out organizer ground-truth real data. For the Generation sub-task, our official team submission, an F5-TTS v1 baseline processed with a uniform reverberation pass and submitted as a deliberate anti-forensic probe, ranked first with a final score of 0.4304 (word error rate (WER) 4.99%, character error rate (CER) 2.07%); details of our four-model program (GLM-TTS, F5-TTS, XTTS v2, CosyVoice3), from which the official entry was drawn, appear in the paper. We present a cross-track analysis revealing a pronounced asymmetry: our detection system identifies 100% of participant-generated deepfakes, while our official generation entry, despite ranking first in the Audio Generation sub-task and evading 61.4% and 56.2% of participant and organizer detectors, attains a Final Score of 0.4304 against 0.9522 on the Detection side. We further report falsification-based ablation experiments (LOSO 56-speaker cross-validation, three-region backbone geometry, bootstrap confidence intervals, and PCA analysis) that motivate our architectural-insurance hypothesis for multi-backbone SSL ensembling. We complement these results with five cross-track insights and five pre-registered falsification experiments connecting generation-side evasion to detection-side design decisions, and we openly report an 11.25% false-positive gap on held-out organizer real recordings as the principal open challenge for deployment.

</details>


### [712] [P-MUSE: Prompt-MIDI-Optional Model for Unified Instrumental Music Synthesis and Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01920)
*Chong Jing,Junan Zhang,Jing Yang,Yulun Wu,Fan Fan,Zhizheng Wu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: P-MUSE is an instrumental MIDI-to-Music framework that unifies two existing paradigms (prompt-audio-only conditional generation and In-Context Learning with paired audio+MIDI) via multi-stage Curriculum-Learning, supporting optional prompt MIDI inputs. It also unifies generation and local editing through a fill-in-the-middle formulation, and introduces phase-aware classifier-free guidance scheduling with a Tail-Drop strategy, plus a comprehensive benchmark covering four instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MIDI-to-Music systems adopt two separate paradigms with complementary strengths: conditional generation using prompt audio alone remains applicable when aligned prompt MIDI is unavailable, while In-Context Learning with paired prompt audio and MIDI provides stronger control on MIDI following and timbre similarity. There is a need to unify these paradigms into a single framework.

Method: P-MUSE unifies both paradigms via a multi-stage Curriculum-Learning approach supporting prompt-MIDI-optional inputs. It uses a shared fill-in-the-middle formulation to unify music generation and local editing. The method also proposes a phase-aware classifier-free guidance scheduling principle for Transcription-to-Audio systems, along with a Tail-Drop strategy, grounded in theoretical analysis and empirical study.

Result: The paper establishes the first comprehensive benchmark for instrumental MIDI-to-Music covering various prompt modes, generation/editing tasks, and four representative instruments: piano, guitar, bass, and drums. Demos are publicly available.

Conclusion: P-MUSE provides a unified framework for instrumental MIDI-to-Music that bridges conditional generation and In-Context Learning paradigms, extends to local editing, and introduces principled training/inference strategies, supported by a new comprehensive benchmark to advance research in the field.

Abstract: MIDI-to-Music system renders the melody and rhythm of a target MIDI sequence into musical segment while cloning instrument timbre from a prompt recording. Existing systems typically adopt one of two distinct paradigms: conditional generation with prompt audio alone, which remains applicable when aligned prompt MIDI is unavailable, and In-Context Learning with paired prompt audio and MIDI, which exploits cross-modal alignment for stronger control on MIDI following and timbre similarity. We introduce P-MUSE, an instrumental MIDI-to-Music framework that unifies both paradigms via a multi-stage Curriculum-Learning supporting prompt-MIDI-optional inputs. P-MUSE further unifies music generation and local editing through a shared fill-in-the-middle formulation. Grounded in theoretical analysis and empirical study, we propose a phase-aware classifier-free guidance scheduling principle for Transcription-to-Audio systems, alongside a Tail-Drop strategy. Finally, to advance research in this field, we establish the first comprehensive benchmark, covering various prompt modes, generation/editing tasks, and four representative instruments: piano, guitar, bass, and drums. Demos are available at https://p-muse.github.io/.

</details>


### [713] [An End-to-End Workflow for Fin Whale Song Detection, Note Characterization, and Localization with Distributed Acoustic Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02387)
*Dídac Diego-Tortosa,Miriam Romagosa,Arantza Ugalde,Hugo Latorre,Sergi Ventosa,Jose Enrique García,Antonio Villaseñor*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents an end-to-end workflow for detecting, characterizing, and localizing fin whale notes using submarine fiber-optic cables instrumented with distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). Tested on two telecom cables in the Strait of Gibraltar and western Alboran Sea, the method achieves median pick-level precision of 0.990 and recall of 0.744, and median cluster-level precision of 0.880 and recall of 0.806, enabling separation of overlapping vocalizations, note-type discrimination, and apparent source movement inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide an effective, large-scale approach for monitoring fin whales by leveraging submarine fiber-optic cables instrumented with distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), enabling broad spatial coverage for bioacoustic monitoring.

Method: The workflow comprises: (1) a kurtosis-value picker adapted to narrow-band fin whale notes for channel-wise detection; (2) density-based spatio-temporal clustering, cluster agglomeration, and hyperbolic fitting to group detections into individual notes and reject incoherent picks; (3) characterization of retained clusters via temporal, spectral, and energy-related descriptors for note-type discrimination and inter-note interval estimation; and (4) a grid-search procedure using relative arrival times across DAS channels to estimate candidate source locations.

Result: Evaluation against manually annotated detections from six fin whale songs yielded median pick-level precision of 0.990 and recall of 0.744, and median cluster-level precision of 0.880 and recall of 0.806. Applications demonstrate separation of overlapping vocalizations, characterization of type-A and type-B notes, and inference of apparent source movement.

Conclusion: The workflow transforms dense DAS recordings into compact note-level bioacoustic information, providing an integrated framework for fin whale monitoring and a basis for adaptation to other synchronized acoustic receiver arrays.

Abstract: Submarine fiber-optic cables instrumented with distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) provide an effective approach for large-scale monitoring of fin whales. We present an end-to-end workflow for detecting, characterizing, and localizing fin whale notes, tested on two submarine telecom cables in the Strait of Gibraltar and western Alboran Sea. The workflow applies a kurtosis-value picker adapted to narrow-band fin whale notes. Channel-wise detections are grouped into individual notes using density-based spatio-temporal clustering, cluster agglomeration, and hyperbolic fitting to reject incoherent picks. The retained clusters are characterized through temporal, spectral, and energy-related descriptors that support note-type discrimination and estimation of inter-note intervals. Relative arrival times across DAS channels are then used in a grid-search procedure to estimate candidate source locations. Evaluation against manually annotated detections from six fin whale songs yielded median pick-level precision of 0.990 and recall of 0.744, and median cluster-level precision of 0.880 and recall of 0.806. Representative applications demonstrate separation of overlapping vocalizations, characterization of type-A and type-B notes, and the inference of apparent source movement. By transforming dense DAS recordings into compact note-level bioacoustic information, the workflow provides an integrated framework for fin whale monitoring and a basis for adaptation to other synchronized acoustic receiver arrays.

</details>


### [714] [Can Foundation Models Hear What Made That Sound? A Tiered Benchmark of Audio-Language Models and Traditional Classifiers for Closed-Set Sound Source Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02397)
*Sajjad Abdoli,Ghassan Al-Sumaidaee,Ahmad ElShiekh,Ahmed Rashad*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks eleven audio classification methods (closed-set LLMs, fixed-vocabulary taggers, a zero-shot audio-text model, and an audio-grounded LLM) on closed-set sound-source identification over 2,242 clips across 23 fine-grained classes and 11 categories. Methods are grouped into four evaluation tiers with per-tier macro Precision, Recall, F1, and false-negative rate. Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview leads (85.6% category F1, 56.7% fine-grained F1). Analysis of Gemini chain-of-thought (8,968 responses) reveals response length doesn't predict accuracy, an apparent "holistic judgment beats detailed analysis" effect is a difficulty confound, and wrong answers are stated confidently 92-100% of the time. Full per-class confusion matrices and practical guidance are provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio classification methods have diverged into fundamentally different families (closed-set LLMs, fixed-vocabulary taggers, zero-shot audio-text models, and audio-grounded LLMs) that differ in task formulation, output scoring, and granularity. A fair, structured comparison across these heterogeneous approaches is needed to understand which method families are best suited for sound-source identification at different granularities, and to expose structural strengths and failure modes.

Method: Eleven methods are benchmarked: five task-aware closed-set LLMs (four Gemini models and Kimi-Audio-7B-Instruct), four fixed-vocabulary taggers (YAMNet, PANNs, Whisper-AT, SSLAM), CLAP (zero-shot audio-text), and BAT (audio-grounded LLM). All are evaluated on a closed-set task with 2,242 clips covering 23 fine-grained classes and 11 categories. Because task input and output scoring differ fundamentally across families, models are grouped into four evaluation tiers with separate scoring. Metrics include macro Precision, Recall, F1, and false-negative rate. Additional analysis includes Gemini chain-of-thought (8,968 responses) examining response length vs. accuracy, confidence calibration, and error structure via per-class confusion matrices.

Result: Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview achieves the best overall performance: 85.6% category-level F1 and 56.7% fine-grained F1. Kimi-Audio-7B-Instruct is competitive for its size (67.5% category F1, 32.9% fine-grained F1) but fails to answer 1.6% of samples. SSLAM and CLAP match or exceed the best closed-set model at category level without candidate lists but lag at fine-grained level. Chain-of-thought analysis shows response length does not predict accuracy; the apparent "holistic judgment over detailed analysis" effect is a difficulty confound; and wrong answers are confidently stated 92-100% of the time.

Conclusion: No single method family dominates across all granularities: closed-set LLMs excel overall, while simpler fixed-vocabulary and zero-shot models are competitive at coarse (category) levels but degrade at fine-grained discrimination. Confidence scores from LLMs are unreliable indicators of correctness. Structural error modes explain most accuracy loss between granularities, and the paper provides practical guidance for choosing among method families based on task granularity and resource constraints.

Abstract: We benchmark eleven audio classification methods: five task-aware closed-set LLMs (four Gemini models plus open-weight Kimi-Audio-7B-Instruct), four fixed-vocabulary taggers (YAMNet, PANNs, Whisper-AT, and SSLAM), a zero-shot audio-text model (CLAP), and an audio-grounded LLM (BAT). We evaluate them on a closed-set sound-source identification task over 2,242 clips spanning 23 fine-grained classes and 11 categories. Since these methods differ fundamentally in how they receive the task and how outputs are scored, we group them into four evaluation tiers rather than one leaderboard, reporting macro Precision, Recall, F1, and false-negative rate per tier. The best model, Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview, reaches 85.6 percent category-level F1 and 56.7 percent fine-grained F1. Kimi-Audio is competitive for its size, reaching 67.5 percent category-level F1 and 32.9 percent fine-grained F1, but fails to answer 1.6 percent of samples. SSLAM and CLAP match or exceed the best closed-set model at the category level without seeing the candidate list, but fall behind at the fine-grained level. Analyzing the Gemini models' chain-of-thought across 8,968 responses, we find that response length does not predict accuracy, an apparent "holistic judgment beats detailed analysis" effect is better explained as a difficulty confound, and wrong answers are stated confidently 92 to 100 percent of the time. We report full per-class confusion matrices and metrics for all eleven methods, identify the structural error modes behind most of the accuracy loss between granularities, and give practical guidance for choosing among these method families.

</details>


### [715] [Uncertainty-Aware Crossmodal Fusion for Classification of Animal Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02104)
*Ehsan Yaghoubi,Florian Haselbeck*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Artificial intelligence offers substantial potential for acoustic monitoring of animals, from welfare assessment in precision livestock farming to wildlife conservation and ecological research, where vocalizations can indicate health, stress, and social states earlier and at lower cost than manual observation. However, recordings in these settings are obtained under uncontrolled conditions, including environmental noise, reverberation, overlapping calls, and sensors that degrade without notice. As a consequence, automated classification of animal vocalizations remains challenging, and the two dominant acoustic representations show complementary limitations: raw waveforms preserve temporal microstructure but degrade under clipping and reverberation, while log-Mel spectrograms capture harmonic organization but lose phase information and are sensitive to broadband noise. To address these challenges, we propose Uncertainty-Aware Fusion (UAF), a dual-stream framework that estimates Gaussian uncertainty for each representation and fuses them via uncertainty weighting. This mechanism assigns greater weight to the more confident representation with no reliability labels required. In a cross-species, identity-based evaluation excluding all individuals seen during training, UAF (mean pooling) achieves 59.4\% accuracy / 39.7\% macro F1 on the 17-class SoundWel pig vocalization benchmark and 73.1\% accuracy / 71.5\% macro F1 on the 3-class DogBark dataset, outperforming static-concatenation fusion by 15.7\% and 20.4\% relative macro F1, respectively. Ablations over four temporal aggregation strategies show that uncertainty fusion, rather than the temporal characteristics of animal calls, is the primary driver of the performance gain.

</details>
